Counters need and have, and formed — how many letters are covered; it changes only when crossing need[c]
Run ADOBECODEBANC / ABC and show where the window loses coverage
State the complexity: O(|s| + |t|) time, O(σ) memory
Edge cases: |t| > |s|, a letter of t missing from s, repeats in t such as "AA"
cards.explain: First agree on repeats and case — they change the solution. Then the baseline, the window idea, the key trick — formed instead of comparing dictionaries — a run, the complexity and edge cases. Repeats in t are the main source of bugs, so check them out loud.

lessons.title: Monotonic deque
lessons.sub: The maximum of every window in O(n): who can be forgotten for good, and what to use instead of the Deque<T> .NET lacks

cards.title: The problem: the maximum of every window
cards.body:
Sliding Window Maximum (LeetCode #239, hard). Given an array nums and a number k, a window of length k slides from left to right one element at a time; return the maximum at every window position — n − k + 1 numbers in total. Constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁵, −10⁴ ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10⁴, 1 ≤ k ≤ n.

Example: [1, 3, −1, −3, 5, 3, 6, 7], k = 3 → [3, 3, 5, 5, 6, 7].

It is a fixed-size window, but the “add the incoming, subtract the leaving” trick fails: you cannot “subtract” a maximum. Window [3, −1, −3], the 3 leaves — who is the maximum now? You need to remember the next candidates, and not all of them, only those that still stand a chance.

Signals: the maximum or minimum at every window position — fixed or variable (for example, “the longest subarray where max − min ≤ limit”). In a game: the worst frame over the last N frames, the highest terrain cell within a radius, the peak threat over the last k AI ticks.

cards.q: Where do you need the maximum or minimum over a sliding window? Select all.
options: The worst frame time over the last 120 frames, updated every frame
The longest subarray where max − min ≤ limit
The average frame time over the last 120 frames
The largest number in the whole array
The lowest price over every k consecutive days
cards.explain: The worst frame is a maximum over a fixed-size window, the lowest price over k days is a minimum over a window. max − min ≤ limit is a variable-size window that needs both the maximum and the minimum. The average is a sum with subtraction, no deque needed. The maximum of the whole array is a single pass with no window at all.

cards.title: Brute force and O(n log k) solutions
cards.body:
Brute force: scan k elements for every window — O(n·k). With k ≈ n/2 and n = 10⁵ that is ≈ 2.5·10⁹ comparisons — too slow.

An ordered set. Keep the window’s elements in a SortedSet — a red-black tree: insertion and removal are O(log k), the maximum is the rightmost node. The trap: SortedSet is a set, so equal values collapse into one. Window [3, 1, 3]: the first 3 leaves, you remove 3 — and the second 3, still in the window, is gone too. So store the pair (value, index): the pairs are distinct, and tuples compare by the first field, then the second. The result is O(n log k), memory O(k).

A heap. A max-heap with lazy deletion: push (index, value), and before answering discard everything at the top that has left the window. No removal from the middle of the heap is needed, but stale elements can pile up — O(n log n) and O(n) memory. PriorityQueue<TElement, TPriority> exists since .NET 6; Unity does not have it, but it does have SortedSet.

Either is a fine first answer in an interview. But the interviewer will ask: can you do it in O(n)?

cards.q: Why put the pair (value, index) into the SortedSet rather than just the value?
options: A set collapses equal values: removing the 3 that left would also lose the other 3 still in the window
Without the index, SortedSet cannot compare the elements
The index is needed for Max to run in O(1)
cards.explain: SortedSet stores each value once: Add of the second 3 returns false and adds nothing. When the first 3 leaves, Remove(3) deletes the only entry, and the window [1, 3] is left without its 3. A pair with the index makes every window element unique.

wrong.1: ints are comparable as they are. The problem is not comparison but that equal values are one entry of the set.
wrong.2: SortedSet.Max walks to the rightmost node of the tree, O(log k) with or without the pair.

cards.title: The key idea: who can be forgotten for good
cards.body:
Let j < i and nums[j] ≤ nums[i]. Then j will never be the maximum again: every future window that contains j also contains i — it is further right and leaves later — and its value is no smaller. Such a j can be thrown away immediately.

Who remains? Candidates with nobody greater or equal to their right. Keep their indices in a deque — a queue you can push to and pop from at both ends:

— the indices in the deque increase, and the values strictly decrease;
— nums[i] arrives — pop from the back everyone ≤ it, then push i to the back;
— the index at the front has left the window (≤ i − k) — pop it;
— the window maximum is at the front.

Why O(n): every index enters the deque once and leaves at most once — at most 2n operations in total, just like the left edge of the window in the previous lessons. The deque holds at most k indices — memory O(k).

At most one index leaves from the front per step: only i − k drops out of the window. That is why it is an if there, not a while.

cards.q: Assemble the deque solution. The deque is an array plus two indices: the live part is dq[head..tail−1].
cards.explain: The window is [i − k + 1..i], so index i − k is already outside it: the condition is <=. Pop from the back everyone not greater than the new value: that keeps the deque values strictly decreasing. The maximum is at the front, nums[dq[head]]. At most one index leaves from the front per step, so an if is enough; a while would also be correct. No ring is needed: every index is pushed once, an array of length n suffices, and head only grows.

cards.task: Step through the trace on [2, 7, 4, 1, 3, 6, 5, 8], k = 3. The rig stops twice before a new number arrives and asks what the deque does first.

options.label: Pops index 1 (value 7) from the front
Pops index 3 (value 1) from the back
Pushes index 4 (value 3) to the back

asks.q: The deque is [1, 2, 3] — values 7, 4, 1. i = 4, x = 3 arrives. What does the code do first?
asks.explain: The front comes first: index 1 ≤ i − k = 1, the 7 has dropped out of the window [2..4] and leaves. Only then the back: the 1 ≤ 3 is popped, the 4 is greater than 3 and stays. The deque becomes [2, 4], and the window maximum is 4.

options.label: Pushes index 6 (value 5) to the back: deque [5, 6]
Pops index 5 (value 6) from the back
Pops index 5 from the front and pushes 6

asks.q: The deque is [5] — value 6. i = 6, x = 5 arrives. What does the code do?
asks.explain: Only those ≤ the new value are popped from the back: 6 > 5, so the 6 stays. Index 5 has not dropped out of the window [4..6]. The 5 goes to the back: it is smaller than the 6 for now, but the 6 drops out of the window earlier (index 5 would leave from the front at i = 8), and then the 5 may become the maximum. The deque values still decrease: 6, 5. This array never gets to i = 8: at i = 7 the 8 pops both from the back.

cards.q: On nums = [5, 1, 1, 1], k = 2 this code returns [5, 5, 1] instead of [5, 1, 1]. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: At i = 2 the window is [1..2], and index 0 with the 5 must leave: 0 ≤ 2 − 2. The < condition does not pop it, so the 5 stays the maximum of a window of length k + 1. Index i − k is the first one already outside the window, hence <=.

cards.title: .NET has no deque: what to use instead
cards.body:
The .NET standard library has no Deque<T>. What it has, and why it does not fit:

— Queue<T> is a circular array, but you can only remove from the front: popping the back is impossible;
— Stack<T> — only the top;
— List<T>.RemoveAt(0) shifts the whole array — O(n) per operation;
— LinkedList<T> does everything in O(1): AddLast, RemoveLast, RemoveFirst, First, Last. But every AddLast is a new node object on the heap (about 48 bytes for an int on 64-bit), the nodes are scattered in memory, and they are garbage for the collector. In Unity with the Boehm GC, such code running every frame shows up.

Your own deque on a circular array: an array, a head index and a count. With a power-of-two capacity, “wrapping around” is & (Length − 1) instead of %. Every operation is O(1), growth by doubling is amortised O(1), as with List<T>. After warm-up there are no allocations.

#239 itself does not even need that: every index is pushed once, so an array of length n and two indices are enough — head only grows, no ring required. The price is O(n) memory instead of O(k); a ring of k slots brings it back to O(k), since the deque never holds more than k indices. Your own deque is needed when the number of elements in the stream is not bounded in advance — say, in a game that runs for hours.

cards.q: Deques in .NET and Unity. Which statements are true? Select all.
options: LinkedList<T> gives O(1) at both ends but allocates a node object on every add
Queue<T> works as a deque: it can remove from the back
In a deque on a circular array with capacity 2ᵏ the wrapped index is computed with & (Length − 1)
List<T>.RemoveAt(0) is O(1) because there is an array inside
For #239 an array of length n with two indices is enough, no ring needed
cards.explain: LinkedList is a doubly linked list: operations at the ends are O(1), but every node is a heap object. Queue<T> can only remove from the front. The mask only works for a power-of-two capacity: x & (2ᵏ − 1) is x mod 2ᵏ, and for −1 it also gives the last index. RemoveAt(0) shifts every element — O(n). In #239 every index is pushed once, so an array of length n suffices, and head only grows.

cards.title: Where else a deque works, and when it is not needed
cards.body:
A variable-size window + two deques (LeetCode #1438): the longest subarray where max − min ≤ limit. One deque keeps the maximum candidates (values decrease), the other the minimum candidates (values increase). When the window is bad, move l and pop from the fronts any indices that fell below l.

Negative numbers (LeetCode #862): the shortest subarray with sum ≥ k. The window from lesson 2 breaks here; what works is prefix sums (in a long: with n and |nums[i]| up to 10⁵ they reach 10¹⁰) plus a deque of indices with increasing prefixes, O(n) — the same principle of “throw away whoever will never be useful again”.

Unity: inflating obstacles on a grid by the agent radius with a square kernel. A cell becomes blocked if the (2r + 1)×(2r + 1) square around it contains an obstacle — that is a maximum over a window: first along rows, then along columns. The deque gives O(W·H) for any radius instead of O(W·H·r²).

When a deque is overkill. The worst frame over the last 120 frames is 120 comparisons per frame — a fraction of a microsecond. A plain scan of the ring buffer is simpler and harder to get wrong. A deque pays off when the window is large and there are many steps: n and k around 10⁵, large grids, server metrics.
cards.deep:
The exact count. In #239 every index is pushed to the back once and popped at most once — from the back or the front. So there are at most 2n deque operations in total, even though a single step may pop k − 1 elements. It is the same amortised argument as for the left edge of the window and for the monotonic stack (the stacks unit): a deque is a monotonic stack whose “bottom” also leaves the window.

Heap versus deque in memory. With lazy deletion the heap keeps elements that have left the window until they surface at the top. On a decreasing array the top is always the oldest element, and it leaves on time. On an increasing array the new element is always on top while the old ones pile up below — up to n elements, though the window holds k. The deque holds at most k.

Cache and Burst. A deque on an array is sequential memory, with no pointers and no GC. In a Burst job the same solution is written on a NativeArray<int> with two indices — managed collections are not available there. Inflating obstacles row by row parallelises naturally: every row is an independent task (IJobParallelFor over rows, then over columns).

Why a tuple works in SortedSet. ValueTuple<int, int> implements IComparable: compare by the first field, then by the second on a tie. The default comparer uses it, with no boxing.

cards.q: Match each approach to the window maximum with its cost.
pairs: O(n log n) and up to O(n) memory
O(n), but a node object per element

cards.q: You are solving Sliding Window Maximum out loud. Put the steps in order.
items: Clarify: k ≤ n, how many numbers to return, whether there are repeats
Name the O(n·k) brute force and why a sum with subtraction does not work here
Offer O(n log k): a SortedSet of (value, index) pairs — and the trap with repeats
The O(n) idea: a left element no greater than a right one is never the maximum again — a deque of decreasing values
Write the code: front left the window — pop; back ≤ x — keep popping; push i; answer from the front
Run [1, 3, −1, −3, 5, 3, 6, 7], k = 3, showing the deque at every step
Complexity O(n): every index enters and leaves once; .NET has no Deque<T> — an array with two indices
cards.explain: The O(n log k) solution is an honest stepping stone: the interviewer sees you know the cost of collections and will ask for better. Then the domination idea, the code, a run and the complexity with the “enters and leaves once” argument. Mention the missing Deque<T> in .NET yourself — it is a platform-knowledge question.

lessons.title: Unit finale: window and deque
lessons.sub: New problems, a Minimum Window Substring trace with repeats in t, a trap and explaining out loud

cards.q: New problems. Match each statement with its technique.
pairs: The longest run of ones if you may flip at most k zeros
Variable-size window: zeros in the window ≤ k
Every position in s where a permutation of p starts
A window of length |p| and letter counters
How many subarrays sum to exactly k, numbers of any sign
The minimum of every window of k elements
The largest sum of k consecutive numbers
Fixed-size window: + the incoming, − the leaving

cards.q: Max Consecutive Ones III (LeetCode #1004): an array of 0s and 1s, you may flip at most k zeros; find the longest run of ones. What do you keep in the window and when do you shrink?
options: A count of zeros in the window; shrink from the left while there are more than k zeros
A count of ones in the window; shrink while there are fewer than k ones
A window does not fit: you need prefix sums
cards.explain: A window is valid if its zeros can be flipped: zeros ≤ k. The condition is monotonic — a valid window’s sub-windows have no more zeros — so the “longest” template works: grow on the right, shrink while the window is bad, take the answer after the while. It is #424 with budget k, except the “extra” letters are always zeros. O(n), O(1) memory.

wrong.1: Ones cost nothing — the budget is spent on zeros. The window is bad when there are more than k zeros.
wrong.2: There are no negative numbers here, and “zeros ≤ k” is monotonic. Prefixes are needed when monotonicity breaks.

cards.q: The shortest subarray with sum ≥ k, numbers from −10⁵ to 10⁵, n ≤ 10⁵. What do you choose?
options: Prefix sums and a monotonic deque of indices
A variable-size window: shrink while the sum is ≥ k
A fixed-size window for every length from 1 to n
cards.explain: Negative numbers break monotonicity: shrinking can increase the sum, and the window misses the answer — as on [1, −1, 5] with target 5. This is LeetCode #862: prefixes plus a deque of indices with increasing prefixes, O(n). Trying every length is O(n²): about n²/2 = 5·10⁹ operations for n = 10⁵.

wrong.1: On [1, −1, 5], target 5, the window returns 3, but the answer is 1: reaching [5] requires dropping the −1, which would increase the sum.
wrong.2: It works, but it is O(n²): n lengths, a pass over the array for each. For n = 10⁵ that is about 5·10⁹ operations.

cards.task: Step through the Minimum Window Substring trace on s = "BAXAYBAA", t = "AAB" — t has two As. The rig asks twice what happens to the formed counter.

options: formed = 1
formed = 2
asks.q: need = {A: 2, B: 1}, need.Count = 2. The window is “B”, formed = 1. The first “A” arrives. What does formed become?
asks.explain: have[A] = 1, but 2 are needed: the letter A is not covered yet, so formed stays 1. formed grows only at the moment have[c] becomes exactly need[c] — for A that happens on the second “A”.

options.label: Drops the “A” — coverage is lost, formed = 1
Drops the “A”, coverage holds: there is another A in the window
Records “AYBA” as the new best window

asks.q: The window “AYBA” covers t, and an “A” is on the left. The best so far is “BAXA”. What does the code do?
asks.explain: “AYBA” has length 4 — no shorter than “BAXA”, so the record stays (it must be strictly less). The “A” leaves: have[A] drops from 2 to 1 < 2, the letter A becomes uncovered, formed = 1. One A is still in the window, but two are needed. Then another “A” arrives, and the window shrinks to the answer “BAA”.

cards.q: On the string "abcbd" this code returns 4, but the right answer is 3. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: At r = 3 a “b” arrives at the window “abc”. The if removes only the “a”, l = 1, while the first “b” stays; Add of the second “b” returns false. The window “bcb”, which has a repeat, counts as valid, and at r = 4 “bcbd” gives 4. Shrink while the duplicate is inside: a while, not an if.

cards.q: Window maximum, k = 3, nums = [6, 2, 5, 3, 4]. After i = 3 the deque holds indices [2, 3] — values 5, 3. i = 4, x = 4 arrives. What is in the deque after the step, and what is the window maximum?
options: [2, 4] — values 5, 4; maximum 5
[4] — value 4; maximum 4
[2, 3, 4] — values 5, 3, 4; maximum 5
[3, 4] — values 3, 4; maximum 4
cards.explain: The front: index 2 ≤ 4 − 3 = 1? No — the 5 is still in the window [2..4]. The back: 3 ≤ 4 — pop it; 5 ≤ 4 — no, stop. Push 4. The deque is [2, 4], the values decrease, and the maximum is the front, 5.

wrong.1: The 5 at index 2 is still in the window [2..4]: only an index ≤ i − k = 1 leaves from the front. And only those ≤ x leave from the back.
wrong.2: The 3 is ≤ 4 and to its left — it will never be the maximum again, so it is popped. Otherwise the deque values would stop decreasing.
wrong.3: The 5 is greater than the 4 — it is not popped from the back, and it has not left the window.

cards.q: The complexity of this unit’s solutions. Which statements are true? Select all.
options: A variable-size window with a while inside a for is O(n) because l only grows
Minimum Window Substring is O(|s|·|t|)
A monotonic deque for the window maximum is O(n): every index enters and leaves once
The honest #424 that recomputes the maximum over 26 counters is O(26·n)
A SortedSet for the window maximum is O(n) because Max takes O(1)
cards.explain: A nested while does not make the window quadratic: l moves at most n times per pass. Minimum Window is O(|s| + |t|): t is counted once and formed is checked in O(1). The deque is ≤ 2n operations. The honest #424 is 26 operations per step. A SortedSet is O(n log k): insertion and removal in the tree are O(log k), and Max also walks to the rightmost node.

cards.q: Unity: the HUD needs the worst frame over the last 120 frames. What is the sensible choice?
options: Scan the ring buffer of 120 values every frame: 120 comparisons take a fraction of a microsecond
A monotonic deque only: otherwise it is O(n·k) and the game will stutter
A SortedSet of frame times with removal of the leaving one
cards.explain: k = 120 and one window per frame: a plain scan costs a fraction of a microsecond, with no allocations and no chance of a bug. “O(n·k)” here means 120 operations per frame, not per game. A deque pays off when the window and the stream are large. A SortedSet allocates a tree node on every insertion — garbage every frame.

wrong.1: There is one window per frame, and scanning it is 120 comparisons. Asymptotics matter when k and n are large; here the constant is tiny.
wrong.2: It works, but every insertion into a SortedSet is a new heap node, which is GC garbage every frame. And it is more complex than a plain scan.

cards.q: You are solving Max Consecutive Ones III out loud. Put the steps in order.
items: Clarify: the array holds only 0s and 1s, k can be 0, n up to 10⁵
Name the brute force: every subarray with a count of zeros — O(n²)
Recognise the pattern: the longest subarray with the monotonic condition “zeros ≤ k” — a variable-size window
Write the code, saying the invariant out loud: after the while there are at most k zeros in the window
Run [1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0, 1], k = 2 and show where the window shrinks
State the complexity: O(n) time, O(1) memory — l only grows
Edge cases: k = 0, all zeros, all ones, k ≥ the number of zeros
cards.explain: The same script as in every lesson of the unit: the statement, the baseline, the pattern from its signals (a contiguous piece, “the longest”, a monotonic condition), code with the invariant, a run, the complexity, edge cases. With k ≥ the number of zeros the answer is n, and the code should produce it on its own, with no special case.

units.title: Bit manipulation
units.blurb: Masks and bit counting, XOR, bits as a table, arithmetic without operators and maximum XOR. In games: layer masks, flags, bitboards and autotiles; BitOperations in .NET and math in Unity.

lessons.title: Masks and counting bits
lessons.sub: Number of 1 Bits, Power of Two and Hamming distance: Kernighan’s trick, Unity layer masks and the built-in popcount

cards.title: A number is 32 bits
cards.body:
An int in C# is 32 bits, and bit k is worth 2ᵏ: 52 = 110100₂ = 32 + 16 + 4. In hexadecimal one digit is exactly 4 bits: 0x34 = 0011 0100 = 52, and 0xFF is eight ones.

Six operators: & (AND: 1 where both are 1), | (OR), ^ (exclusive OR: 1 where the bits differ), ~ (flips all 32 bits), << k (shift left: multiply by 2ᵏ, bits pushed past bit 31 are lost) and >> k (shift right).

A mask is a number with 1s in the positions you care about. With bit k you do four things: test (x >> k) & 1, set x | (1 << k), clear x & ~(1 << k), toggle x ^ (1 << k). A mask is also a set of up to 32 elements: union is |, intersection is &, “nothing in common” is (a & b) == 0. The k lowest 1s are (1 << k) − 1. The letters of a word are a 26-bit mask m |= 1 << (c - 'a'); all subsets of n elements are the numbers 0 to 2ⁿ − 1.

Sign. Negative numbers are stored in two’s complement: bit 31 is worth −2³¹. So −1 is all 32 ones, int.MinValue has a 1 only in bit 31, and ~x == −x − 1. The >> shift on an int copies the sign bit (−8 >> 1 = −4); on a uint it shifts in zeros. When you want “just 32 bits” with no sign, use uint.
cards.code:
int x = 52;                       // 0b_0011_0100 = 0x34
bool has2 = ((x >> 2) & 1) != 0;  // true: bit 2 is set
x |= 1 << 0;                      // 53: set bit 0
x &= ~(1 << 4);                   // 37: cleared bit 4
x ^= 1 << 5;                      // 5: toggled bit 5
int all = -1;                     // 0xFFFFFFFF: all 32 ones
uint top = 0x80000000;            // bit 31 only; as an int this is int.MinValue

for (int mask = 0; mask < 1 << 3; mask++) { }   // 8 subsets of 3 elements: 000 … 111

cards.title: Unity: LayerMask and [Flags]
cards.body:
The most common place for bits in Unity is layers. gameObject.layer is the layer index, 0 to 31, while a LayerMask is a 32-bit mask: bit k is set if layer k is included. Physics takes the mask: Physics.Raycast(ray, out hit, dist, mask) only hits the included layers.

The classic mistake is passing an index instead of a mask. Raycast(…, 8) is the mask 0b1000, which is layer 3, not layer 8. The mask for layer 8 is 1 << 8. By name: LayerMask.GetMask("Enemy", "Ground") returns a mask, while LayerMask.NameToLayer("Enemy") returns an index that you still have to shift into a mask. “Every layer except” is ~mask. Whether an object is in a mask: (mask & (1 << go.layer)) != 0.

Flags. A [Flags] enum is the same mask with names: values are powers of two, you combine them with | and test with &. On .NET Core 2.1+ the JIT turns HasFlag into that same test with no allocation. In Unity it depends on the version and the backend (Mono, IL2CPP): older versions boxed the enum and allocated on every call. In hot code write (s & X) != 0 — it is cheap everywhere.

cards.q: In the project the Enemy layer has index 8. The raycast must hit enemies only. Which call is right?
options: Physics.Raycast(ray, out hit, 100f, 8)
Physics.Raycast(ray, out hit, 100f, 1 << 8)
Physics.Raycast(ray, out hit, 100f, ~8)
Physics.Raycast(ray, out hit, 100f, LayerMask.NameToLayer("Enemy"))
cards.explain: The last parameter is a mask, not an index. The mask for layer 8 is a 1 in bit 8, that is 1 << 8 = 256. LayerMask.GetMask("Enemy") gives the same value.

wrong.0: 8 = 0b1000 is the mask for layer 3. The raycast hits layer 3 and never sees the enemies.
wrong.2: ~8 is every bit except bit 3: almost every layer except layer 3.
wrong.3: NameToLayer returns the index 8 — the same mistake as the first option. You need 1 << LayerMask.NameToLayer("Enemy").

cards.title: Number of 1 Bits: the problem and the brute-force loop
cards.body:
Number of 1 Bits (LeetCode #191): how many 1s are in the binary form of a 32-bit number. This is the Hamming weight, or popcount. Example: 52 = 110100₂ → 3. LeetCode currently uses the signature HammingWeight(int n) with 1 ≤ n ≤ 2³¹ − 1, but in an interview ask whether negatives can occur. If the number comes in as an int, convert it to uint right away: you care about the bits, not the sign.

Brute force checks all 32 bits: add the lowest bit and shift right. That is O(32) = O(1), and the interviewer will immediately ask: can you take as many steps as there are 1s? For sparse masks — flags, layers, 1–3 ones out of 32 — that is several times less work.

Why uint and not int: with while (x != 0) the loop never ends on a negative int — >> copies the sign bit, and −1 >> 1 is −1 again.

cards.title: Kernighan’s trick: n & (n − 1)
cards.body:
Subtracting 1 borrows from the lowest 1: it becomes 0, every 0 below it becomes 1, and the bits above do not change. 52 = 110100, 51 = 110011. In n & (n − 1) the bits above that position agree and survive, while from it downwards they are opposite and cancel. The result: exactly the lowest 1 is cleared, 52 → 48.

Invariant: each turn of the loop removes one 1, so there are exactly popcount(n) turns. Time O(k), where k is the number of 1s; memory O(1).

Power of Two (#231) is a number with a single 1: one Kernighan step gives 0. The test is n > 0 && (n & (n − 1)) == 0. The n > 0 part is required: zero has no 1s at all, and int.MinValue also has a single 1 — the sign bit 31 — so the bit test alone would call it a power of two.

cards.q: Build a popcount that runs once per 1 bit, and the power-of-two test.
cards.explain: The (uint)n cast keeps the bits and drops the sign; without it, uint x = n does not compile. x &= x − 1 clears the lowest 1 — one turn per 1 bit. For the power of two, n > 0 rules out zero and every negative number, int.MinValue included.

cards.task: Step through the trace on n = 52 = 110100₂: each step is n − 1 first, then n & (n − 1). The rig stops twice and asks what the next step gives.

asks.q: count = 1, n = 48 = 110000₂. What is n − 1?
asks.explain: The subtraction borrows from the lowest 1, bit 4: it goes out, the four 0s below it turn into 1s, and bit 5 stays. 110000 − 1 = 101111 = 47. The 32 = 100000 is n & (n − 1) — that comes on the next step.

options.label: n = 0, count = 3 — the loop ends
n = 16, count = 3
n = 31, count = 3

asks.q: count = 2, n = 32 = 100000₂, n − 1 = 011111₂. What does n &= n − 1 do?
asks.explain: 32 has a single 1, and all six bits of 32 and 31 are opposite, so the AND gives 0. count = 3: exactly as many steps as 52 has 1s, not 32.

cards.q: This IsPowerOfTwo returns true for n = int.MinValue. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: int.MinValue has a 1 only in bit 31. n − 1 wraps around to int.MaxValue = 0x7FFFFFFF — no 1s in common, the AND gives 0, and the bit test passes. A negative number is not a power of two, so rule out every n <= 0: if (n <= 0) return false.

cards.title: Hamming distance: XOR, then popcount
cards.body:
Hamming Distance (#461): in how many positions the bits of x and y differ. Minimum Bit Flips to Convert Number (#2220): how many bits of start to flip to get goal. It is one problem: the differing bits are exactly the 1s of x ^ y, and each of them is flipped once. The answer is popcount(x ^ y).

Built-in popcount. .NET Core 3.0+ has BitOperations.PopCount in System.Numerics: when the CPU supports it, this is a single POPCNT instruction on x86 or a short vector sequence on ARM64. .NET 7+ also has int.PopCount. Unity has no BitOperations: neither its .NET Standard 2.1 profile nor its .NET Framework profile includes it. There, use math.countbits from Unity.Mathematics (under Burst it also becomes an instruction) or the Kernighan loop. For powers of two Unity has Mathf.IsPowerOfTwo, and .NET 6+ has BitOperations.IsPow2.

In an interview, write and explain the loop first, then say that in production you would use the built-in popcount — that is the senior answer.

cards.q: Which statements are true? Select all.
options: The Hamming distance between 1 (0001₂) and 4 (0100₂) is 2
If x & (x − 1) == 0, then x is a power of two
The Kernighan loop takes 32 steps on uint.MaxValue
BitOperations.PopCount can be called from a Unity script
(mask & (1 << go.layer)) != 0 means the object is on one of the mask’s layers
cards.explain: 1 ^ 4 = 0101₂ — two 1s. x & (x − 1) == 0 holds for zero and for int.MinValue too, so you also need x > 0. uint.MaxValue has 32 ones — one step each. BitOperations arrived in .NET Core 3.0, and Unity’s API profiles (.NET Standard 2.1 and .NET Framework) do not have it: there you use math.countbits. The last option tests bit number go.layer of the mask.

cards.q: You are solving Number of 1 Bits out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
items: Clarify: is the number 32-bit, signed or not, how often is it called
Brute force: check all 32 bits with a shift — O(32)
Idea: n & (n − 1) clears the lowest 1 — one step per 1 bit
Code on a uint so that the sign-copying shift does not get in the way
Run it on 52 = 110100₂: 48, 32, 0 — three steps
Complexity: O(k) in the number of 1s, O(1) memory
Edge cases: 0, uint.MaxValue, a negative int; in production, the built-in popcount
cards.explain: The problem, the baseline, the idea, the code, a check on an example, complexity and edge cases. Mentioning BitOperations.PopCount and math.countbits at the end shows you know how real code does it.

cards.title: Counting 1s faster than a loop
cards.body:
The Kernighan loop is good when there are few 1s. Without a loop or branches, SWAR — “SIMD within a register” — counts them: add neighbouring bits in pairs, pairs into nibbles, nibbles into bytes, and a single multiplication collects the bytes. 12 operations for any number, independent of the data.

This is exactly how the built-in popcount falls back when there is no POPCNT instruction. Nobody expects the code by heart in an interview, but explaining the idea of “parallel sums in bit fields” is a plus.
cards.deep:
Why the multiplication adds the bytes. 0x01010101 = 2⁰ + 2⁸ + 2¹⁶ + 2²⁴, so x * 0x01010101 is the sum of x shifted by 0, 8, 16 and 24 bits. The top byte ends up holding the sum of all four bytes of x. Each byte is ≤ 8 and the sum is ≤ 32, so nothing carries between bytes.

A table. Another way is an array of 256 precomputed answers and four lookups by byte. In a hot loop it loses to SWAR and POPCNT: memory accesses and cache misses.

.NET. BitOperations.PopCount(uint) and PopCount(ulong) are intrinsics: the JIT emits POPCNT (on x86 with POPCNT support) or a vector instruction on ARM64, and falls back to a SWAR-style software version otherwise. On x86 you can check with System.Runtime.Intrinsics.X86.Popcnt.IsSupported.

Unity. math.countbits exists for int, uint, long, ulong and the vector types. In Burst code the compiler emits the instruction when the target supports it; outside Burst it is plain C# — the same SWAR arithmetic. Next to it are math.tzcnt and math.lzcnt (the number of trailing and leading zeros); the first one comes in handy in the bitboards lesson.

cards.q: Match the task to the expression.

lessons.title: XOR: every pair cancels out
lessons.sub: Missing Number and Single Number III: a ^ a = 0, sum versus XOR, and the lowest 1 bit x & −x

cards.title: Three properties of XOR
cards.body:
a ^ b has a 1 wherever the bits differ. Three properties follow: a ^ a = 0, a ^ 0 = a, and order does not matter — XOR is commutative and associative. So the XOR of a collection of numbers is the XOR of those that occur an odd number of times: every pair cancels itself out, wherever its two halves sit.

Single Number (LeetCode #136): every number occurs twice, one occurs once. The XOR of the whole array is the answer: O(n) time, O(1) memory, no dictionary.

One more consequence: a ^ b = c ⇔ a ^ c = b. XOR is its own inverse — to “undo” a number, XOR it in once more. Missing Number, position hashing in games and Maximum XOR from the last lesson of this unit all rely on this.

cards.q: Every number occurs exactly three times, except one that occurs once. What does the XOR of the whole array give?
options: The single number: the triples cancel themselves out
The XOR of the single number and all the tripled numbers: each triple leaves one copy
0: everything cancels
cards.explain: Only pairs cancel: a ^ a ^ a = (a ^ a) ^ a = a. What is left is everything that occurs an odd number of times — the single number and one copy of each tripled number. This problem (Single Number II, #137) needs a different count, bit by bit; it is on the variations card.

wrong.0: A triple is a pair plus one more copy: the pair cancels, the copy stays.
wrong.2: Only a collection where every number occurs an even number of times folds down to zero.

cards.title: Missing Number: sum or XOR
cards.body:
Missing Number (#268): nums holds n distinct numbers from 0..n, one is missing — find it. n ≤ 10⁴; you want O(n) time and O(1) memory. Sorting is O(n log n), a HashSet is O(n) memory, and placing values at their indices, as in the hash table unit, destroys the input.

Sum: 0 + 1 + … + n minus the sum of the array. XOR: put the indices 0..n − 1 next to the values. Every number that is present shows up twice — as an index and as a value — and cancels. The missing one only shows up as an index and stays. Index n has no slot in the array, so the XOR starts at n.

The sum’s trap is overflow. The formula n * (n + 1) / 2 in int breaks at n ≥ 46,341: the product exceeds int.MaxValue, wraps around, and halving it ruins the result. Compute it in long. XOR has no carries, so there is nothing to overflow.

cards.q: n = 50,000. The array sum is computed correctly, and the expected one like this: int expected = n * (n + 1) / 2. What happens?
options: The right answer: the overflow cancels out in the subtraction
A wrong answer: n · (n + 1) = 2,500,050,000 does not fit in an int and wraps before the division
An OverflowException on this line
cards.explain: int.MaxValue = 2,147,483,647, and the product is 2,500,050,000. It wraps to −1,794,917,296, after the division that is −897,458,648 instead of 1,250,025,000, and the answer is garbage. The fix is (long)n * (n + 1) / 2, or XOR.

wrong.0: It would cancel if only additions and subtractions followed: in int they work modulo 2³², and a final result that fits in an int would come out right. But halving does not play well with the modulus: −1,794,917,296 / 2 is not half of the real product.
wrong.2: By default C# does not check: the exception only comes inside checked.

cards.q: Build Missing Number with XOR.
cards.explain: x starts at n = nums.Length: index n has no slot in the array, so it goes in up front. The loop runs over indices 0..n − 1, so the condition is i < nums.Length. Each step brings both the index and the value into x: x ^= i ^ nums[i]. Without the indices (x ^= nums[i]) there is nothing to cancel against.

cards.task: Step through the trace on [9, 6, 4, 2, 3, 5, 7, 0, 1]: x collects the indices and values that have not met their pair yet. The rig asks twice what x becomes.

options.label: x = 7 — unchanged

asks.q: x = 7. Step i = 5, nums[5] = 5. What does x become?
asks.explain: The index and the value are the same: i ^ nums[i] = 5 ^ 5 = 0, and x ^ 0 = x. The 5 arrived twice in one step and cancelled itself at once, so x stays 7.

options.label: x = 8 — that is the answer

asks.q: The last step: x = 1, i = 8, nums[8] = 1. What does x become?
asks.explain: x ^= 8 ^ 1. The 1 was already waiting in x — it came in as an index at i = 1 — and cancels. The 8 arrives for the first time, as an index, and will never arrive as a value: it is not in the array. x = 8. The 9 cancelled on the very first step: x started at n = 9, and nums[0] = 9.

cards.title: Single Number III: split the two singles by one bit
cards.body:
Single Number III (#260): exactly two numbers occur once, all the others occur twice. Return both, in O(n) time and O(1) memory. The XOR of the whole array gives x = a ^ b: the pairs cancelled, and the two singles got mixed together.

a ≠ b, so x ≠ 0, and every 1 in x is a bit where a and b differ. Take such a bit and split all numbers into two groups: those that have it and those that do not. a and b land in different groups, while both copies of any pair land in the same one — equal numbers have equal bits. The XOR of each group is one of the answers.

The lowest 1: x & −x. In two’s complement −x = ~x + 1 (the same as ~x == −x − 1). In ~x the trailing zeros of x became 1s; the +1 runs through them as a carry, clears them, and stops exactly at the position of the lowest 1 of x. Above it, −x equals ~x, the opposite of x. The AND keeps a single 1: 6 = 0110₂, −6 = …1010₂, 6 & −6 = 0010₂ = 2.

cards.task: Step through the trace on [1, 2, 1, 3, 2, 5]. The first pass folds the array into x = a ^ b, the second splits the numbers by one bit. The rig asks about that bit and about one group.

options: low = 2
low = 4
low = 6
low = 0
asks.q: x = 6 = 0110₂, −x = −6 = …1010₂. What is low = x & −x?
asks.explain: Compare 0110 and …1010 bit by bit. Bit 3 and up: x has zeros. Bit 2: x has a 1, −x a 0. Bit 1: both are 1. Bit 0: both are 0. Only one 1 in common, bit 1, so low = 2. x has bit 2 set as well, but −x has it cleared: x & −x keeps only the lowest 1.

options.label: Skips it: 3 occurs only once

asks.q: low = 2. The second pass has reached 3 = 011₂; right now a = 2, b = 0. What does the code do?
asks.explain: 3 & 2 = 2 ≠ 0 — the 3 has bit 1 set, so it goes to group a: 2 ^ 3 = 1. It is fine that a is not 3 yet: group a also holds the second 2, which comes next and cancels the first — then a becomes 3. The 5 (101₂) has bit 1 clear and goes to b.

cards.q: On [1, 2, 1, 3, 2, 5] this code returns [0, 6] instead of [3, 5]. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: v & low is either 0 or low itself. Here low = 2, so v & low is 0 or 2 but never 1: every number goes to else, b = the XOR of the whole array = 6, a = 0. Compare with zero instead: (v & low) != 0. The same bug in a bit-k test: (x & (1 << k)) == 1 only works for k = 0.

cards.title: Variations, and XOR in games
cards.body:
Single Number II (#137): everything occurs three times, one number once. XOR will not do. Count each bit separately: how many numbers have it. The triples contribute a multiple of three, so count % 3 is the answer’s bit. O(32·n) time, O(1) memory; “everything k times” is solved the same way.

Set Mismatch (#645): the numbers 1..n, one is duplicated and another is missing. The XOR of 1..n and the array gives dup ^ miss — from there it is #260: split by the lowest 1, plus one more pass to tell which of the two is the duplicate.

The XOR swap a ^= b; b ^= a; a ^= b; is a party trick, not an optimisation: a plain swap through a temporary (or (a, b) = (b, a)) is no slower, and if a and b are the same slot (arr[i] and arr[j] with i == j), the XOR swap zeroes it.

In games the “undo = do it again” property gives Zobrist hashing: every (piece, square) pair gets a random 64-bit number, and the position hash is the XOR of the numbers of all pieces. A move updates the hash in O(1): XOR with the old square removes the piece, XOR with the new one places it. Turn-based game AIs use it to cache positions they have already evaluated, and networked games use it to compare client states.
cards.deep:
#137 without a loop over bits. Two counter words, ones and twos, keep for each bit the count modulo 3 (0, 1 or 2 — two bits of state): ones = (ones ^ v) & ~twos; twos = (twos ^ v) & ~ones;. After the pass, the answer is ones. It is a three-state machine applied to all 32 bits at once; O(n), but harder to explain in an interview than counting per bit.

x & −x on int.MinValue. If a ^ b = int.MinValue, −x wraps to the same int.MinValue, and x & −x = int.MinValue — the correct lowest 1 (bit 31). Inside checked, though, the negation throws OverflowException; write unchecked(x & -x) there.

Zobrist. Generate the table of random numbers once with a fixed seed — otherwise clients will not agree on hashes. Collisions happen: with 64 bits and a million positions the chance of at least one is about 3·10⁻⁸ by the birthday estimate (n² / 2⁶⁵), which is why transposition tables often store check bits next to the hash. string.GetHashCode will not do here: on .NET Core it is randomised per process, and other runtimes do not promise it stays the same across versions and platforms.

cards.q: Which statements are true? Select all.
options: x & −x for x = 12 (1100₂) is 4
In #260 any 1 bit of x would do instead of the lowest one
The XOR swap is faster than a swap through a temporary
Missing Number with a long sum and with XOR are both O(n) time and O(1) memory
In #137 (everything three times) the XOR of the whole array is enough
cards.explain: 12 = 1100₂, its lowest 1 is bit 2, which is 4. Any 1 of x is a bit where a and b differ, so you can split by any of them; the lowest one is just the easiest to extract. The XOR swap is not faster and breaks on a single slot. Both Missing Number solutions are one pass and one variable. In #137 XOR leaves copies of the triples — you need the per-bit count.

cards.q: You are solving Single Number III out loud. Put the steps in order.
items: Clarify: exactly two singles, every other number exactly twice; does the order of the answer matter
Brute force: a dictionary of counts — O(n) time, but O(n) memory
XOR of the whole array: pairs cancel, leaving x = a ^ b ≠ 0
A bit where a and b differ: low = x & −x
Second pass: XOR into two groups by (v & low) != 0
Complexity: O(n) and O(1) memory; edge case — negative numbers
cards.explain: The problem, the dictionary baseline, then the two steps of the idea (fold with XOR, pick a bit), the second pass, a run and complexity. Negative numbers break nothing: both XOR and x & −x work in two’s complement.

cards.q: Match the condition to the technique.
pairs: Position hash after a move in O(1)

lessons.title: Bits as a table, and reversing them
lessons.sub: Counting Bits as a first taste of dynamic programming, Reverse Bits, the sign-copying shift and the >>> that Unity lacks

cards.title: Counting Bits: the problem and the brute-force loop
cards.body:
Counting Bits (LeetCode #338): for every i from 0 to n, return the number of 1s in i; n ≤ 10⁵. The answer is an array of n + 1 numbers. The extra requirement: O(n) and no built-in popcount.

Brute force counts the 1s of every i with the Kernighan loop from the first lesson. Each number takes as many steps as it has 1s — on average half its length. In total that is O(n log n), about 10⁶ steps for n = 10⁵. That is fast, but the interviewer wants O(n): one operation per number.

The signal: the answer for i can be built from the answer for a smaller number that is already computed. That is dynamic programming: a state (bits[i]), a transition (how bits[i] is expressed through smaller ones), an order (from smaller to larger) and a base (bits[0] = 0). DP is covered in depth in the “Backtracking and dynamic programming” unit; this is its simplest case.

cards.q: How many inner-loop steps in total does this solution take for n = 2¹⁶ − 1 = 65,535?
options: 524,288 = 16 · 2¹⁵: each bit is set in exactly half of the numbers
65,535: one step per number
cards.explain: The numbers 0 to 2¹⁶ − 1 are all the 16-bit numbers, and each of the 16 bits is set in exactly half of them: 16 · 32,768 = 524,288 steps, 8 per number on average — half the length. That is O(n log n): fast, but not O(n).

wrong.1: One step per number would mean a single 1 in every number. Kernighan takes a step per 1 bit.
wrong.2: 16 steps per number is a loop over every bit. Kernighan skips the zeros: 8 on average.

cards.title: The key idea: drop the last bit
cards.body:
i >> 1 is i without its last bit: 13 = 1101₂ → 110₂ = 6. It has the same 1s as i, except for the last bit. So bits[i] = bits[i >> 1] + (i & 1). For i ≥ 1, i >> 1 < i always holds, so going up in order we always take an answer that is already there.

Invariant: before step i, all of bits[0..i−1] in the table are correct. One operation per number — O(n) time, and the only memory is the answer itself.

A second transition uses Kernighan: i & (i − 1) is smaller than i and has one 1 less, so bits[i] = bits[i & (i − 1)] + 1. Also O(n). The shape of the table shows too: a power of two 2ᵏ has a single 1, and the numbers 2ᵏ..2ᵏ⁺¹ − 1 repeat 0..2ᵏ − 1 with one extra 1.

cards.q: Build Counting Bits in O(n).
cards.explain: The answer covers 0 to n inclusive, n + 1 slots; new already gives bits[0] = 0. i >> 1 is smaller than i and already computed, and (i & 1) adds back the dropped last bit. bits[i − 1] + 1 is wrong: 7 → 8 clears three 1s and sets one. i << 1 is larger than i — it is not in the table yet.

cards.task: Step through the trace on n = 12: the table fills from left to right, and each number takes its answer from i >> 1. The rig asks twice what goes into the table.

options.label: bits[8] = bits[4] + 0 = 1
bits[8] = bits[7] + 1 = 4
bits[8] = bits[4] + 1 = 2

asks.q: The table up to 7 is done, bits[7] = 3. What goes into bits[8]?
asks.explain: 8 = 1000₂, 8 >> 1 = 4 = 100₂, and the last bit is 0. bits[8] = bits[4] + 0 = 1 — a power of two has a single 1. “The previous one plus one” is not always right: 7 → 8 clears three 1s with the carry and sets one.

options.label: bits[11] = bits[5] + 1 = 3
bits[11] = bits[5] + 0 = 2

asks.q: What goes into bits[11]? 11 = 1011₂.
asks.explain: 11 >> 1 = 5 = 101₂ has two 1s, and the last bit of 11 that got dropped is a 1. bits[11] = bits[5] + 1 = 3: 1011₂ has three 1s.

cards.title: Reverse Bits: exactly 32 steps
cards.body:
Reverse Bits (#190): reverse the 32 bits of a number — bit 0 becomes bit 31, bit 1 becomes bit 30, and so on. 1 → 0x80000000 = 2,147,483,648. Work with a uint; if the number comes in as an int, cast it. LeetCode currently uses the signature int ReverseBits(int n) with n even and 0 ≤ n ≤ 2³¹ − 2: bit 0 is zero, so the answer fits in an int. Still reverse a uint inside: return (int)ReverseBits((uint)n);, calling the uint overload below.

The loop: take the lowest bit of n (n & 1), shift it into the result from the right (r = (r << 1) | bit), and shift n right. Over the next 31 shifts the first bit taken travels up to bit 31. There are exactly 32 steps, even if n runs out of 1s earlier: the leading zeros of n are the trailing zeros of the result, and without them the answer ends up not shifted far enough.

cards.task: Step through the loop on n = 11 = 1011₂: every round the low bit of n is pushed into r from the right. n runs out of 1s in round 4 — the rig asks what happens to a zero bit and what the loop does once n is 0.

options.label: r = 110₂ = 6: shifted up, a 0 enters at the bottom
r = 3: a zero adds nothing, no need to shift

asks.q: Rounds 1 and 2 pushed in two 1s: r = 11₂ = 3, n = 10₂. Bit 2 of 1011₂ is 0. What is r after round 3?
asks.explain: r = (r << 1) | 0 = 6. A zero is a bit of the answer too: bit 2 of n must end up in bit 29 of the result, so r shifts every round, whatever comes in at the bottom. Without the shift the next 1s would land in the wrong places.

options.label: Keeps going: r shifts for 28 more rounds, up to 3,489,660,928
Stops: n has no 1s left, the answer is 13
Stops: r is already reversed — 1101 is 1011 backwards

asks.q: Round 4 pushed in the last 1: r = 1101₂ = 13, n = 0. What does the loop do?
asks.explain: There are exactly 32 rounds. 1101₂ is the low 4 bits reversed, but all 32 must be reversed: the leading zeros of n are the trailing zeros of the answer. 28 more shifts lift 1101 into bits 31–28: 0xD0000000 = 3,489,660,928. Stopping as soon as n is 0 would return 13 — too small by a factor of 2²⁸.

cards.q: This reversal returns 1 for n = 1, but it should return 2,147,483,648. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: The loop stops as soon as n has no 1s left — for n = 1, right after the first step. But that 1 still has to travel 31 positions left: the leading zeros of n are the trailing zeros of the answer. It must be exactly 32 steps: for (int i = 0; i < 32; i++).

cards.title: Shifts in C#: sign, >>> and width
cards.body:
The sign-copying shift. >> on int and long is arithmetic: a copy of the sign bit comes in from the left, −8 >> 1 = −4, and −1 >> k = −1 for any k. On uint and ulong it is logical: zeros come in. When you want “just bits”, use an unsigned type.

>>>, the unsigned shift for signed types, only arrived in C# 11 (.NET 7). Unity is on C# 9 and does not have it: write (int)((uint)x >> k).

Shift width. For an int only the 5 low bits of the count are used: 1 << 32 == 1, 1 << 40 == 256; for a long, 6 bits. The shift happens in the type of the left operand, so 64 bits need 1L << k or 1UL << k. And long f = 1 << 31 is −2³¹: the int came out negative, and widening it to long copied the sign into bits 32–63.
cards.code:
int x = -8;
int a = x >> 1;                  // -4: the sign was copied
int b = (int)((uint)x >> 1);     // 2147483644: C# 9, same as x >>> 1 in C# 11
int s = 40;
int c = 1 << s;                  // 256: an int takes the count modulo 32
long d = 1 << s;                 // 256: shifted as an int, widened afterwards
long e = 1L << s;                // 1099511627776
long f = 1 << 31;                // -2147483648 = 0xFFFFFFFF80000000

cards.q: You need a mask of the k lowest 1s, k from 0 to 32: int mask = (1 << k) - 1. Where does this code go wrong?
options: At k = 32: the mask is 0 instead of −1 (all ones), because 1 << 32 == 1
At k = 31: overflow and an OverflowException
Nowhere: the mask is right for every k from 0 to 32
cards.explain: An int takes the shift count modulo 32: 1 << 32 is 1 << 0 = 1, and the mask becomes 1 − 1 = 0. You need a special case, k == 32 ? -1 : (1 << k) - 1, or a shift in long: (int)((1L << k) - 1).

wrong.1: 1 << 31 = int.MinValue, and minus 1 wraps to int.MaxValue, which is 31 ones — exactly what you want. No exception: subtraction is unchecked by default.
wrong.2: At k = 32 the shift moves nothing: a count of 32 modulo 32 is 0.

cards.title: Reversal in 5 steps: swapping blocks
cards.body:
The loop takes 32 iterations. Faster is swapping blocks: the 16-bit halves, the bytes within them, then nibbles, pairs and neighbouring bits. 5 steps = log₂ 32, each with two shifts and an OR, plus two ANDs from the second step on; no loop and no branches. The mask picks the lower block of each pair: 0x00FF00FF is the low byte of each half, 0x0F0F0F0F the low nibble of each byte, 0x33333333 = 0011…₂, 0x55555555 = 0101…₂.

If the function is called many times (the problem’s follow-up), use a 256-entry table of reversed bytes: four lookups and a merge. Unity.Mathematics has a ready-made math.reversebits. .NET has no portable bit reversal (only the ARM intrinsic ArmBase.ReverseElementBits), and BinaryPrimitives.ReverseEndianness reverses the bytes, not the bits — do not mix them up.
cards.deep:
Why this is a reversal. A bit’s position is a 5-bit number b₄b₃b₂b₁b₀. Swapping halves flips b₄, swapping bytes flips b₃, and so on. After five steps all five digits of the position are flipped: bit i has moved to 31 − i. The same “spread the bits with masks” trick builds a Morton code — interleaving the bits of x and y (x = (x | (x << 8)) & 0x00FF00FF, then 4, 2, 1 with the masks 0x0F0F0F0F, 0x33333333, 0x55555555). A Morton code orders grid cells along a Z-curve: neighbouring cells tend to sit close together in memory, which is why it is used as a key in spatial hashes and quadtrees, and GPUs use similar layouts for textures.

Where bit reversal shows up in games. The bit-reversed index permutation is the first step of an FFT (an audio spectrum for a visualiser, procedural noise); a bit-reversed counter gives the van der Corput sequence — evenly spread points for sampling without randomness.

Cost. The loop is 32 iterations, each depending on the previous one; swapping blocks is 5 steps, 23 operations; the table is 4 memory accesses. In an interview the loop plus a mention of block swapping is enough. Rotation, a related operation, is BitOperations.RotateLeft in .NET Core 3.0+ and math.rol in Unity.

cards.q: You are solving Counting Bits out loud. Put the steps in order.
items: Clarify: n up to 10⁵, the answer is an array of n + 1 numbers, no built-in popcount
Brute force: Kernighan for every i — O(n log n)
Idea: i >> 1 is smaller than i and already computed — bits[i] = bits[i >> 1] + (i & 1)
Code: an array of n + 1, a loop from 1, base bits[0] = 0
Run it: bits[5] = bits[2] + 1 = 2, bits[6] = bits[3] + 0 = 2
Complexity: O(n) time, the only memory is the answer
Edge cases: n = 0 → [0]; the second transition is bits[i & (i − 1)] + 1
cards.explain: State, transition, order and base are the whole story of a DP: name them explicitly. The second transition at the end shows you understand the idea rather than remember one formula.

cards.q: Match the task to the expression.
pairs: Reverse the bytes, not the bits

lessons.title: Arithmetic without operators
lessons.sub: Sum of Two Integers and Divide Two Integers: column carries, division by shifts, int.MinValue / −1 and checked

cards.title: Sum of Two Integers: column addition
cards.body:
Sum of Two Integers (LeetCode #371): add a and b without the + and − operators; −1000 ≤ a, b ≤ 1000. The problem checks whether you understand how the processor itself adds.

Binary column addition: in each column 0 + 0 = 0, 0 + 1 = 1, and 1 + 1 = 0 with a carry of 1 into the next column. “The sum without carries” is exactly a ^ b. Carries appear where both bits are 1 and move one column left: (a & b) << 1. Hence a + b = (a ^ b) + ((a & b) << 1) — a sum again, but the second term consists of carries only. Repeat until no carries are left.

Why the loop ends. The carry is shifted left, so each round it has at least one more trailing zero than before. In at most 32 rounds all its 1s move past bit 31 and the carry becomes 0.

cards.q: How many rounds of the loop does a = 7, b = 1 take?
options: 4: the carry runs through the three 1s of 7, one column per round
1: b has a single 1
2: the sum 8 = 1000₂ has a single 1
cards.explain: 0111 + 0001. Round 1: a ^ b = 0110, carry 0010. Round 2: 0100 and carry 0100. Round 3: 0000 and carry 1000. Round 4: a = 1000, no carry. A run of 1s is the worst case for this loop: the carry walks through it column by column.

wrong.1: The single 1 in b produces a carry, and that carry produces the next one while it runs over the 1s of a.
wrong.2: The number of rounds depends not on the answer but on the length of the carry chain.

cards.q: Build the sum without a plus.
cards.explain: The loop runs while there are carries: b != 0. The carry is computed first, while a is still the old value: (a & b) << 1 — the columns where both are 1, moved one column left. Then a ^= b is the sum without carries, and the carries become the new b.

cards.title: Negatives: the carry falls off bit 31
cards.body:
The same loop adds negative numbers too, thanks to two’s complement. −5 = …11111011₂, 7 = 00000111₂. Carries appear in bits 1 and 2, then run left through the solid 1s of −5, one column per round. At bit 31 the carry goes past the edge of the register and simply disappears: << drops the bits it pushes out. That is not a bug: in two’s complement the sum is taken modulo 2³², and that is exactly how −5 + 7 = 2 comes out. It takes 31 rounds.

Hence the cost: 32 rounds in the worst case (−1 + 1), which is O(32) = O(1) at a fixed width. checked does not affect this code: ^, & and << never throw — overflow is only checked for arithmetic (+, −, *, /, ++, --, unary minus) and explicit numeric conversions.

cards.task: Step through the trace on a = −5, b = 7: the carry runs over the 1s of −5 all the way to bit 31. The rig asks about the second round and the last one.

asks.q: Round 2: a = −4 = …11111100₂, b = 6 = 110₂. What comes out?
asks.explain: a ^ b = …11111010 = −6. −4 and 6 share a single 1, bit 2, so the carry goes to bit 3: b = 8. The sum has not changed: −6 + 8 = 2. From here the carry keeps running left over the 1s of a, one column per round.

options.label: a = 2, b = 0 — the carry fell off bit 31
OverflowException
a = 2, b = int.MinValue — the loop never ends

asks.q: Round 31: the carry has reached bit 31 — b = int.MinValue, a = −2,147,483,646. What happens?
asks.explain: a ^ b = 2: both have bit 31 set, and it cancels. a & b = int.MinValue — a 1 in bit 31 — and the left shift pushes it past the edge: the carry is 0 and the loop ends. No exception: shifts are not overflow-checked even in checked. −5 + 7 = 2 modulo 2³², the same way the processor adds.

cards.title: Divide Two Integers: long division
cards.body:
Divide Two Integers (#29): divide without *, / and %, dropping the fraction — rounding toward zero: 7 / −3 = −2. The numbers span the whole int range, the divisor is not 0; if the quotient does not fit in an int, return int.MaxValue.

Brute force subtracts the divisor while it can: as many steps as the quotient, up to 2³¹ ≈ 2·10⁹ when dividing by 1 — too slow. The idea is binary long division: go from bit 31 down to 0 and ask whether b · 2ᵏ fits into what is left. If it does, subtract it and set bit k of the quotient. The test (a >> k) >= b is the same as a >= b · 2ᵏ, but cannot overflow. 32 steps — O(1) at a fixed width, O(log) in the value.

The sign goes separately: divide the absolute values; the quotient is negative if the signs differ. Take the absolute values in long: |int.MinValue| = 2³¹ does not fit in an int.

cards.task: Step through 100 / −7: the sign goes separately, then long division from bit 31 — b · 2ᵏ is subtracted whenever it fits into what is left. The rig asks about one quotient bit and about the answer.

options.label: Bit 2 is 0: right after a subtraction the next bit is always 0

asks.q: k = 3: 7 · 8 = 56 was subtracted from 100, leaving a = 44, q = 8. What happens at k = 2?
asks.explain: The test (a >> k) >= b: 44 >> 2 = 11 ≥ 7, so 7 · 4 = 28 fits into 44. Subtract it — a = 16 — and set bit 2 of the quotient: q = 8 | 4 = 12. A quotient bit is worth 2ᵏ, not 1. Neighboring bits do not depend on each other: only what is left decides.

options.label: −14: the fraction is dropped toward zero
−15: a negative quotient is rounded down
14: the absolute values were divided, the sign is already in q

asks.q: All 32 bits are decided: q = 14, remainder 2. The signs differ. What does Divide return?
asks.explain: 100 / 7 = 14.28…, the quotient is negative — −14.28… — and the fraction is dropped toward zero: −14. Rounding down would give −15. q carries no sign — the absolute values were divided — so the code returns −q when the signs differ.

cards.title: int.MinValue traps
cards.body:
The only quotient that does not fit in an int is int.MinValue / −1 = 2³¹. In .NET this division throws OverflowException even without checked, and so does int.MinValue % −1. The C# standard leaves the unchecked behaviour to the implementation, and .NET chose the exception. That is why #29 checks this case first.

Two more places. Math.Abs(int.MinValue) throws OverflowException. And -x with x == int.MinValue silently returns int.MinValue — a negative “absolute value”. The safe way is to widen to long before taking the absolute value: Math.Abs((long)x).

checked helps find such spots in tests: overflow in addition, subtraction, multiplication, negation and conversions becomes an exception. Shifts and bitwise operations are left alone.
cards.code:
int min = int.MinValue, m1 = -1;
int q = min / m1;                 // OverflowException, even without checked
int abs = Math.Abs(min);          // OverflowException
int neg = -min;                   // -2147483648: silently
long ok = Math.Abs((long)min);    // 2147483648

cards.q: This Divide throws OverflowException for dividend = int.MinValue, divisor = 2. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: Math.Abs(dividend) is called on an int and fails on int.MinValue before the result ever reaches the long: the absolute value 2³¹ does not fit in an int. Widen first, then take the absolute value: Math.Abs((long)dividend).

cards.title: Shifts as multiplication and division
cards.body:
x << k = x · 2ᵏ, with the same wrap-around as unchecked multiplication. x >> k divides by 2ᵏ rounding down, while / rounds toward zero: −7 >> 1 = −4, but −7 / 2 = −3. For non-negative numbers they are the same.

There is no need to write x >> 1 instead of x / 2 “for speed”: the JIT (and the C++ compiler behind IL2CPP) turns division by a power-of-two constant into a shift by itself, with a sign fix-up for int. Replacing it by hand, though, changes the meaning for negatives. The same goes for the remainder: −3 % 2 == −1, so the odd test x % 2 == 1 is false for negatives — write (x & 1) != 0 or x % 2 != 0.

The remainder by a power of two is a mask: x & (m − 1) instead of x % m for non-negative x. This is how a ring buffer of size 2ᵏ (frame history, a network packet queue) computes its index — no division and no negative remainders.
cards.code:
int x = -7;
int a = x / 2;                  // -3: toward zero
int b = x >> 1;                 // -4: down
bool odd1 = x % 2 == 1;         // false: -7 % 2 == -1
bool odd2 = (x & 1) != 0;       // true
int head = 1029;
int slot = head & (1024 - 1);   // 5: same as head % 1024, a buffer of 1024 = 2^10

cards.q: Which equalities hold for every int x (unchecked)? Select all.
options: Math.Abs(x) >= 0
cards.explain: Multiplying by 8 and shifting by 3 give the same 32 bits with the same wrap-around. Division and shift disagree on negative odd numbers: −7 / 2 = −3, −7 >> 1 = −4. The remainder disagrees on negatives: −5 % 8 = −5, but −5 & 7 = 3. −x = ~x + 1 is the definition of two’s complement and holds even for int.MinValue. Math.Abs(int.MinValue) returns nothing — it throws OverflowException.

cards.q: You are solving Divide Two Integers out loud. Put the steps in order.
items: Clarify: rounding toward zero, the int range, what to return on overflow
Brute force: subtract the divisor — up to 2³¹ steps when dividing by 1
Idea: long division — from bit 31 down, subtract b · 2ᵏ when it fits
Code: the int.MinValue / −1 case first, absolute values in long, the sign separately
Run it: 7 / −3 → |7| = 111₂, |−3| = 11₂: at k = 1 subtract 6, remainder 1 → 2, negative sign → −2
Complexity: 32 steps, O(1) memory
Edge cases: int.MinValue as dividend and divisor, a divisor of ±1
cards.explain: The special case int.MinValue / −1 comes up while clarifying the problem and goes on the first line of code: it is the only one that does not fit in an int. Running a small signed example checks both the long division and the rounding toward zero.

cards.title: Multiplying with shifts, and how the processor does it
cards.body:
If * is banned too, multiplication is split over the bits of the multiplier: x · y = the sum of x · 2ᵏ over the 1s of y. It is the same long-hand scheme as in division, just the other way round: 32 steps, each a shift and maybe an addition.

The sum loop from this lesson is a software version of a carry running through the digits. A real adder computes the carries for all digits in parallel and adds in a single cycle, while division is one of the slowest integer operations in a processor: from about ten to a few dozen cycles, against one for an addition. That is why compilers replace division by a constant with a multiplication and a shift.
cards.deep:
#29 without long. The strict version of the problem allows 32-bit numbers only. Then you keep both numbers negative: −2³¹ has no positive counterpart, but every positive int has a negative one. Double the divisor while d >= (int.MinValue >> 1) — then d + d cannot overflow — and compare “backwards”: a <= d means |a| ≥ |d|. The quotient is accumulated as a negative too and negated at the end; the only case where that overflows is int.MinValue / −1, which was handled first.

Division by a constant. The JIT turns x / 10 into a multiplication by a “magic” number and a shift of the high half of the product — several times faster than the divide instruction. For uint and division by 2ᵏ it is just a shift; for int it is a shift with a fix-up so that it rounds toward zero.

.NET and Unity. Math.DivRem returns the quotient and the remainder in one call; Math.BigMul(int, int) gives the exact 64-bit product. Division is expensive in Burst code too: hot loops over a grid often use power-of-two sizes so that / and % become a shift and a mask — like the ring buffer index above.

cards.q: Match the task to the expression.
pairs: The quotient that does not fit in an int

lessons.title: Bit prefixes and bitboards
lessons.sub: Maximum XOR greedily from the top bit, queries with a limit (#1707), bitboards, autotiles and fog of war

cards.title: Maximum XOR: the problem and the cost of brute force
cards.body:
Maximum XOR of Two Numbers in an Array (LeetCode #421): find the maximum of nums[i] ^ nums[j]; n ≤ 2·10⁵, 0 ≤ nums[i] < 2³¹. Example: [3, 10, 5, 25, 2, 8] → 28 = 5 ^ 25.

Trying all pairs is n²/2 = 2·10¹⁰ operations at n = 2·10⁵: minutes instead of a second. Sorting does not help: XOR is not monotonic, and large numbers do not give a large XOR — 25 ^ 10 = 19, while 25 ^ 5 = 28.

The signal is “maximise a XOR”. Bit k is worth 2ᵏ, and all the lower bits together are worth 2ᵏ − 1, which is less. So the answer’s bits are decided greedily from the top: if bit k can be a 1, take it — no combination of lower bits can outweigh it.

cards.q: Bit 4 of the answer can be a 1, but only with a partner that leaves zeros in bits 3..0. Another partner gives 0 in bit 4 and 1s in all of bits 3..0. Which do you choose?
options: The 1 in bit 4: 10000₂ = 16 is more than 01111₂ = 15
The 1s in bits 3..0: there are four of them against one
You have to explore both branches to the end and compare
cards.explain: Bit 4 is worth 16, and all the lower bits together 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 = 15. A 1 in the higher bit beats any combination of lower ones, so the greedy choice from the top bit is never wrong and there is no need to explore branches.

wrong.1: You compare values, not the number of 1s: 01111₂ = 15 < 10000₂ = 16.
wrong.2: Exploring branches means 2³¹ options. It is unnecessary: the higher bit is worth more than all lower bits together.

cards.title: A set of prefixes
cards.body:
Build the answer from the top down. Say the higher bits of the answer are already known — that is best. We want a 1 in the next bit k: the candidate is cand = (best << 1) | 1. It is reachable if there are two numbers whose prefixes — the higher bits, v >> k — XOR to cand.

The check in O(n): put all the prefixes into a HashSet and, for each p, ask whether p ^ cand is there. This is Two Sum with the sum replaced by XOR: p ^ q = cand ⇔ q = p ^ cand — XOR is its own inverse. Found it — bit k of the answer is 1, otherwise 0, and on to the next bit.

31 bits × n numbers is O(31·n) ≈ 6·10⁶ operations, with O(n) memory. Instead of 31 sets you can build a binary trie once, bit by bit from the top: each number is a path of 31 steps, and for x you follow the opposite bits wherever possible. Also O(31·n); tries are covered in depth in the data structure design unit.

cards.q: On [3, 10, 5, 25, 2, 8] this code returns 25 instead of 28. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: The code asks whether some number has the prefix cand, but the question is whether a pair of prefixes XORs to cand. So it simply follows the bits of the largest number and finds 25. The fix: foreach (int p in prefixes) — prefixes.Contains(p ^ cand).

cards.title: A limit m: Maximum XOR With an Element (#1707)
cards.body:
Maximum XOR With an Element From Array (#1707, Hard): queries [x, m] ask for the maximum of x ^ nums[j] over nums[j] ≤ m, or −1 if there are no such numbers; n and the number of queries go up to 10⁵. #421 is the same question without the limit m.

Offline means answering the queries in whatever order suits you. Sort nums, sort the queries by m, and before each query add every number ≤ m. The set only grows; nothing ever needs removing. The answers are put back at the queries’ original indices.

Walking down the bits. For x go from the top bit: you want y to have the bit opposite to x’s, which makes a 1 in x ^ y. If one of the added numbers continues the chosen path with that bit, go there and set the answer’s bit. If not, go with the same bit, and the answer’s bit is 0. The prefixes are stored by level: levels[k] holds every v >> k; this is a trie stored level by level.

In the trace y’s path is written in bits from the top: “prefix 00” means the number has zeros in the two highest bits of the trace. The trace starts at the highest bit present in the input; everything above is zero.

cards.task: Step through the trace on nums = [5, 2, 4, 6, 6, 3] with the queries x:m = 12:4, 8:1, 6:3. The queries go in order of growing m, and the set of numbers grows. The rig asks twice what the code does next.

options.label: y goes on with 1: no prefix 000, bit 1 of the answer is 0
y goes on with 0: bit 1 of the answer is 1
Answer −1: no suitable number

asks.q: Query 6:3, the set holds 2 and 3 (0010₂ and 0011₂). Bits 3 and 2 are decided, y’s path is 00. Bit 1: x = 0110₂ has a 1 here. What next?
asks.explain: We want y to have a 0 here — the path 000. But both numbers have bit 1 set (001·), so nobody continues the path 000. We are forced along 001, and bit 1 of x ^ y is 0. The greedy choice does not suffer: bit 2 is already taken, and it is worth more than all the lower bits together.

options.label: y goes on with 0: 2 and 3 have the prefix 00, bit 2 of the answer is 1
y goes on with 1 — towards the 4: it is the largest allowed number
y goes on with 1: there is no prefix 00

asks.q: Query 12:4: the 4 was just added, the set holds 2, 3 and 4 (0010₂, 0011₂, 0100₂). Bit 3 is taken, y’s path is 0. Bit 2: x = 1100₂ has a 1 here. What next?
asks.explain: We want y to have a 0 in bit 2 — then x ^ y gets a 1 here. The 2 and the 3 have the prefix 00, so we take it. The 4 (01··) drops out, even though it was just added and is the largest: with it bit 2 of x ^ y is 0, and 12 ^ 4 = 8. The walk goes on to y = 3 and the answer 12 ^ 3 = 15.

cards.title: Unity: bitboards
cards.body:
An 8×8 board — 64 cells — fits in one ulong: cell (x, y) is bit y * 8 + x. Such a bitboard answers a question about the whole board with one operation: occupied is white | black, empty is ~occupied, the number of pieces is a popcount, moving every piece one row up is << 8.

Moving right in x is << 1, but a piece on the right edge jumps to the left edge of the next row. That is why horizontal shifts are masked: (b << 1) & ~FileA, where FileA is the bits of column x = 0. Iterating over pieces is Kernighan’s trick from the first lesson: the cell of the lowest piece is the number of trailing zeros (BitOperations.TrailingZeroCount, in Unity math.tzcnt), and b &= b − 1 removes it. A ulong has no unary minus, so the lowest piece as a mask is written b & (~b + 1).

Chess engines are built this way, and in games so are tic-tac-toe (9 bits and 8 winning masks: (board & line) == line), connect four, and the Game of Life on a small board in a few shifts.

cards.q: An 8×8 bitboard: cell (x, y) is bit y * 8 + x. The only piece is on (7, 2). Where does it end up after b << 1 without a mask?
options: On (0, 3): bit 23 → bit 24, the start of the next row
It disappears: it went off the edge of the board
On (7, 3): a shift one row up
cards.explain: (7, 2) is bit 2 · 8 + 7 = 23. Shifting by 1 gives bit 24 = 3 · 8 + 0, that is (0, 3): the piece jumped from the right edge to the left edge of the next row. That is why the right shift is masked: (b << 1) & ~FileA.

wrong.1: Only bits pushed past bit 63 of the whole ulong are lost. Bit 24 is inside — the piece is simply in the wrong place.
wrong.2: Moving one row up is << 8, not << 1.

cards.title: Autotiles and fog of war
cards.body:
Autotiling. A wall tile picks its sprite from its neighbours. Each neighbour gets a bit: north 1, east 2, south 4, west 8. The mask 0..15 is directly the index into a 16-sprite tileset: no branches, no table of conditions. With diagonals there are 8 bits and 256 masks, but a corner neighbour only affects the sprite if both edges next to it are filled — otherwise the corner is hidden anyway. After this rule there are 47 distinct masks left, hence the classic 47-tile tileset. In Unity the RuleTile from the 2D Tilemap Extras package does this, but in an interview you are asked to write the mask by hand.

Fog of war. A 64×64 map is 64 rows of one ulong each. What is visible right now is the mask visible: it is built by ORing the units’ vision circles — precomputed masks shifted to each unit’s position. What has been explored is explored[y] |= visible[y], and it never goes dark. 4,096 cells are 512 bytes per layer, an update is 64 operations instead of 4,096 checks, and the same masks feed the fog texture for the shader.
cards.deep:
Where 47 comes from. Four edges give 16 options. A corner counts only when both its edges are filled: with k pairs of adjacent filled edges you get 2ᵏ corner options. Among the 16 edge masks, 7 have no such pair, 4 have one, 4 have two (three edges), and 1 has four (all edges). 7 + 4·2 + 4·4 + 1·16 = 47. The indices 0..255 are squeezed into 0..46 by a 256-entry table computed once.

Fog wider than 64 cells. A row becomes an array of ulong, and shifting a vision mask to a unit’s position crosses word boundaries: some bits move into the neighbouring word (w[i] << s | w[i − 1] >> (64 − s), with s = 0 as a special case: a shift by 64 on a ulong shifts nothing). Rows are independent, so they are convenient to compute in an IJobParallelFor under Burst, where math.countbits and math.tzcnt on ulong become instructions.

Ready-made structures. .NET has BitArray (bits in an int[], with And, Or, Xor over the whole array). The com.unity.collections package has NativeBitArray and UnsafeBitArray for Jobs. But in an interview you are expected to lay the cells out in ulongs yourself and name the cost: 64 cells per operation.

cards.q: Autotile mask: north 1, east 2, south 4, west 8. A wall cell has wall neighbours above and to the left. What is the tile index?
cards.explain: Above is north, bit 1; left is west, bit 8. 1 | 8 = 9 = 1001₂. The index is the mask itself: no ifs over combinations of neighbours.

wrong.1: 3 = 1 | 2 is north and east, that is above and to the right.
wrong.2: 6 = 2 | 4 is east and south.
wrong.3: 12 = 4 | 8 is south and west, below and to the left.

cards.q: You are solving Maximum XOR of Two Numbers out loud. Put the steps in order.
items: Clarify: n up to 2·10⁵, the numbers are non-negative and below 2³¹
Brute force: all pairs — O(n²), 2·10¹⁰ at n = 2·10⁵
Idea: greedily from the top bit — bit k is worth more than all lower bits together
Code: prefixes v >> k in a HashSet, is p ^ cand there
Complexity: O(31·n) time, O(n) memory
Variations: a bitwise trie; with a limit m — offline by m (#1707)
cards.explain: First the constraints (they rule out brute force), then the greedy principle, and only then the way to test a bit — the set of prefixes. The trie and #1707 come last: in a senior interview a follow-up to the problem often comes right after.

cards.q: Match the condition to the technique.
pairs: Is there a pair with p ^ q = cand
HashSet and a lookup of p ^ cand
Neighbour mask as the tile index

lessons.title: Unit finale: bits
lessons.sub: New problems, a Single Number III trace with negative numbers, a shift trap on a bitboard, and explaining out loud

cards.q: New problems. Match the condition to the technique.
pairs: Product of two word lengths with no common letters (#318)
XOR of 1..n and the array, then x & −x
How many bits to flip to turn a into b

cards.q: Maximum Product of Word Lengths (LeetCode #318): up to 1000 words of lowercase Latin letters, each up to 1000 long. Find the maximum len(a) · len(b) over pairs of words with no letters in common. How do you test a pair?
options: Precompute each word’s letter mask; a pair qualifies if (mask[i] & mask[j]) == 0
For each pair build a HashSet<char> of the first word and scan the second
Sort each word’s letters and merge the two strings as in merge sort
cards.explain: The mask is the set of letters in one int: m |= 1 << (c - 'a'), O(total length) to prepare. “No common letters” is an empty intersection, (a & b) == 0, O(1) per pair. About 5·10⁵ pairs — instant.

wrong.1: Correct, but O(length) per pair: up to 5·10⁵ pairs of 1000 letters is 5·10⁸ operations, plus allocations.
wrong.2: Merging is also O(length) per pair. The mask squeezes a word into 26 bits once.

cards.q: Number Complement (#476): flip every bit of num ≥ 1 except the leading zeros: 5 = 101₂ → 010₂ = 2. What do you return?
options: ~num & mask, where mask has 1s in every bit up to and including the highest 1 of num
~num
num ^ 1
cards.explain: ~num flips all 32 bits, and the leading zeros become 1s — the result is negative. A mask of the k lowest 1s, (1 << k) − 1, where k is the bit length of num, trims the extra: for 5 the mask is 111₂, ~5 & 7 = 2. num ^ mask gives the same answer.

wrong.1: ~5 = −6: the leading zeros became 1s too, the sign bit included.
wrong.2: num ^ 1 only toggles bit 0: 5 → 4.

cards.task: Step through Single Number III on [10, 3, −6, 3, 9, 9]: the singles are 10 and −6. The rig asks which bit splits them and which group −6 goes to.

options: low = 16
low = -16
low = 1
low = 2
asks.explain: The lowest 1 of −16 is bit 4, with four zeros below it. 16 has only bit 4 set, and x has it too, so the AND gives 16. The sign does not get in the way: x & −x works in two’s complement for any x ≠ 0. 10 = 01010₂ and −6 = …11010₂ really do differ first in bit 4.

options.label: Group a: −6 has bit 4 set
Group b: −6 < 16
Group b: bit 4 does not count for negatives

asks.q: Second pass, low = 16. −6 = …11111010₂ arrives. Which group does it go to?
asks.explain: −6 has every bit from 3 to 31 set, bit 4 included: −6 & 16 = 16 ≠ 0, so it is group a. The code compares bits, not values: “less than 16” has nothing to do with it. The 3s and 9s land in b in pairs and cancel, leaving 10 there.

cards.q: An 8×8 board is stored in a long, cells sq from 0 to 63. After Place(40), Has(40) returns false and Has(8) returns true. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: 1 << sq shifts an int, and an int takes the count modulo 32: 1 << 40 = 1 << 8 = 256, so the piece lands on cell 8. At sq = 31 it is worse: 1 << 31 is a negative int, widening to long copies the sign, and 1s appear in every cell from 31 to 63. It needs 1L << sq.
