cards.q: Complexity of this unit’s solutions. Which statements are true? Select all.
options: Counting Bits via bits[i >> 1] is O(n)
Maximum XOR with prefix sets is O(31·n) time and O(n) memory
The Kernighan loop always takes exactly 32 steps
The sum without a plus on an int takes at most 32 rounds
Divide Two Integers by long division is O(quotient)
cards.explain: Counting Bits is one operation per number. Maximum XOR is 31 passes over n prefixes with a HashSet. Kernighan takes a step per 1 bit, not per bit. In the sum the carry moves left every round and leaves bit 31 within 32 rounds. Long division is 32 steps; O(quotient) is the naive subtraction.

cards.q: Unity: 2000 units, each with 5 statuses (burning, frozen, stunned…), and every frame you need to check whether a unit is burning and stunned at the same time. What is the sensible choice?
options: A [Flags] enum field on the unit and the test (s & both) == both, where both = Burning | Stunned
A HashSet<Status> per unit and two Contains calls
s.HasFlag(Status.Burning) && s.HasFlag(Status.Stunned) — the same thing, just more readable
cards.explain: All statuses are bits of one int: testing any combination is one AND and one comparison, with no allocations and the data close together in memory. (s & both) == both requires both bits; (s & both) != 0 requires at least one.

wrong.1: A HashSet per unit is 2000 heap objects, hashing on every Contains and data scattered in memory. For 5 values it costs many times more than a mask.
wrong.2: On .NET Core 2.1+ it really is a single test, but in Unity, depending on the version and the backend, HasFlag may box the enum — that means allocations every frame across 2000 units. A mask is equally cheap everywhere, and it checks both bits in one operation.

cards.q: Interview code tests for odd numbers like this: if (x % 2 == 1). Where does the test go wrong?
options: On negative odd numbers: −3 % 2 == −1
On zero
Nowhere: the remainder of division by 2 is always 0 or 1
cards.explain: In C# the remainder takes the sign of the dividend: −3 % 2 = −1, so the test decides −3 is even. Reliable versions are (x & 1) != 0 or x % 2 != 0: in two’s complement the lowest bit of a negative odd number is 1 as well.

wrong.1: 0 % 2 = 0 — zero is even, so the test is right.
wrong.2: The remainder can be negative: it takes the sign of the dividend.

cards.q: You are solving Single Number II (#137, everything three times, one number once) out loud. Put the steps in order.
items: Clarify: every number three times except one; the range is the whole int, negatives included
Brute force: a dictionary of counts — O(n) time, but O(n) memory
Why not XOR: every triple leaves a copy behind
Idea: for each of the 32 bits count how many numbers have it; the remainder modulo 3 is the answer’s bit
Run it: [2, 2, 3, 2] → bit 0: 1 → 1, bit 1: 4 → 1, the answer is 3
Complexity: O(32·n) time, O(1) memory; bit 31 is collected too, so negatives work
cards.explain: Right after the brute force it is worth saying why the familiar trick fails — that shows you understand what XOR relies on. Running a small array checks both the modulo-3 count and assembling the answer from bits.

units.title: Stacks and linked lists
units.blurb: Matching brackets and a min stack, the monotonic stack, reversing and merging lists, fast and slow pointers, reversing in groups. LinkedList<T> from the inside and an allocation-free list on indices.

lessons.title: Stack: matching and the minimum
lessons.sub: Valid Parentheses and Min Stack: the last one opened closes first, and the minimum lives next to each element

cards.title: The problem and the stack signals
cards.body:
Valid Parentheses (LeetCode #20). Given a string s of the characters ()[]{}, 1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁴. It is valid if every opening bracket is closed by a bracket of the same type and the closings come in the right order: "([]{})" — yes, "([)]" — no, "(()" — no.

The key observation: you can only close the bracket that was opened last. Last in, first out: that is a stack. Stack<T> in .NET is an array whose end is the top; Push, Pop and Peek are O(1).

Stack signals in a problem statement:

1. Nesting and matching: brackets, tags, begin … end blocks.
2. “Undo the last one”, “go back”: undo, a Back button.
3. An element waits until something to its right “closes” it, and the nearest one does: the last open bracket, the next greater element to the right (that is the next lesson).
4. A recursion has to become a loop — an explicit stack instead of the call stack.
cards.code:
IsValid("([]{})"); // true
IsValid("([)]");   // false: ")" arrives while "[" was opened last
IsValid("(()");    // false: one "(" is never closed

cards.q: Which problems have a stack as the natural solution? Select all.
options: Check that markup tags are nested correctly:
Evaluate “3 4 + 2 *”: an operator takes the last two numbers and puts the result back
The Back button in a game menu returns to the previous screen
Hand out jobs to workers in the order they arrived
Find out whether some number appears in the array twice
cards.explain: Tags are the same matching as brackets (signal 1). In the expression an operator takes the last two numbers — the top of the stack — and the result goes back there (Evaluate Reverse Polish Notation, #150). Back returns to the screen opened last (signal 2). Jobs in arrival order are first in, first out: a queue. A repeated number is “have I seen this?”, a hash set from unit 2.

cards.title: Naive solutions and where they break
cards.body:
Cut out pairs. While the string contains "()", "[]" or "{}", remove them; a valid string disappears completely. It is correct, but every Replace is an O(n) pass and a new string, and there can be up to n/2 rounds: on "((((…))))" each round removes one pair. That is O(n²): for n = 10⁴, up to 5000 rounds over 10⁴ characters, on the order of 5·10⁷ operations and thousands of new strings of up to 20 KB thrown to the garbage collector.

A counter. For a single bracket type a number open is enough: +1 on (, −1 on ), never go negative, end at zero. That is O(n) with O(1) memory. But three counters for three types cannot see order: on "([)]" each one honestly returns to zero and never goes negative, yet the string is invalid — ) tries to close [.

We need to remember not how many brackets are open, but which one was opened last.

cards.q: A solution with three counters: one per type, +1 on an opening bracket, −1 on a closing one, never negative, all zero at the end. What does it return on "[(])"?
options: true, while the correct answer is false: counters do not remember which bracket was opened last
false: the square-bracket counter goes negative
true, and that is correct: every bracket is closed by its own type
cards.explain: [ and ( add +1 to their counters, ] and ) bring them back to zero — nothing went negative, the check passes. But ] arrives while ( is the last one opened, so it is too early to close [. Order is lost — you need a stack.

wrong.1: Square brackets: [ gives +1, ] gives −1 — zero, not negative. The counters do not see that ( is open between them.
wrong.2: The types match, the order does not: ] closes [ while ( is still open inside it.

cards.title: The idea: a stack of open brackets
cards.body:
Walk the string. Push every opening bracket. A closing bracket must match the top: pop the top and compare it with the expected pair.

Invariant: the stack holds the brackets that are open and not yet closed, in the order they were opened, with the last one on top. That is why a closing bracket is compared with the top only, not with the whole stack.

The string is invalid in three cases: the top does not match ("([)]"); the stack is empty when a closing bracket arrives ("())"); the string ends with a non-empty stack ("(()"). The second case also matters because Pop on an empty Stack<T> throws InvalidOperationException — check Count first.

A “closing → opening” dictionary answers with a single TryGetValue whether this is a closing bracket and hands you its pair. Time O(n), memory O(n) in the worst case "((((". Early exit: a string of odd length can never be valid.
flow: closing: stack empty or Pop() ≠ pair → false
end of string: is the stack empty?

cards.task: Step through "{[]}([)]". The rig stops twice and asks what the code does with the next bracket: look only at the top of the stack.

options.label: pop: “}” closes the “{” on top
return false: the stack still holds a bracket
push “}”

asks.q: “[]” has already closed. Now “}” arrives. What does the code do?
asks.explain: After popping “[” the top is “{” again — the pair for “}”. Pop it, and the stack is empty. A non-empty stack is an error only at the end of the string, not in the middle.

options.label: pop: there is a “(” somewhere in the stack
return false: “[” is on top
push “)”

asks.q: The stack holds “(” and “[”, with “[” on top. Now “)” arrives. What does the code do?
asks.explain: “)” can only close the last open bracket, and the last one opened is “[”. The “(” deeper down does not help: closing it before “[” would break the nesting. Pop gives “[” ≠ “(”, the answer is false.

cards.q: On "(()" this code returns true. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: The loop catches two of the three cases: a mismatched top and a closing bracket on an empty stack. The third — opening brackets that were never closed — is visible only after the loop. On "(()" one “(” stays in the stack, yet the code says true. It must be return stack.Count == 0.

cards.title: Min Stack: the minimum next to each element
cards.body:
Min Stack (LeetCode #155). A stack with Push, Pop, Top and GetMin, each in O(1). Values span the whole int range, Pop, Top and GetMin are only called on a non-empty stack, up to 3·10⁴ calls.

Naively: GetMin by scanning — O(n). Or a single min field: easy to update on Push, but if Pop removes the minimum itself, the previous one cannot be recovered without a scan.

The idea. The minimum of the stack depends only on what lies below the top, and what lies below an element does not change while that element is in the stack. So the minimum can be computed once on insertion and stored next to the element: a pair (val, min), where min is the minimum of this element and everything below it. Pop removes the pair — and the minimum “rolls back” by itself. Stack<(int val, int min)> stores the tuple struct directly in the array: no boxing, no object per element.

The two-stack variant: the values plus a separate stack of minimums that only receives “records”. The condition is x <= mins.Peek(), not <: otherwise a second copy of the minimum never reaches mins, and the first Pop of a two removes the minimum while the other two is still in the stack. Memory: pairs always take 2n numbers, two stacks take n plus the number of records (on descending input, the same 2n).

cards.q: Assemble Min Stack on (value, minimum) pairs.
cards.explain: Empty stack: the minimum is the element itself. Otherwise it is the smaller of the new value and the minimum of everything below — which is already stored in the pair on top: stack.Peek().min. Comparing with stack.Peek().val is wrong — that is only the top element, not the minimum below it. Push (val, min) in the order the tuple fields are named.

cards.task: Step through push 4, 2, 2, 5, followed by a mix of pop and getMin. The rig stops twice before a pop and asks which minimum ends up on top.

options: min = 2
min = 4
min = 5
asks.q: The stack holds (4, 4), (2, 2), (2, 2). Pop removes one of the twos. What is the minimum on the new top?
asks.explain: Each two carries its own minimum. The upper one is gone — below it is (2, 2): the minimum is still 2, because the other two is still in the stack. The two-stack variant with x < mins.Peek() would fail here: the second two never reached mins, and this pop would take the minimum with it.

options: min = 2
min = 4
min = 5
asks.q: Left: (4, 4), (2, 2). Pop removes the last two. What is the minimum on the new top?
asks.explain: Below the two is (4, 4): when 4 was pushed the minimum was 4, and it did not change while 4 stayed in the stack. Nothing is recomputed — the minimum rolled back by itself, O(1).

cards.title: In a game: a screen stack and undo/redo
cards.body:
A UI screen stack. Main menu → settings → “Reset progress?”. Opening a screen is Push and show it; Back (a button, Escape, the Android system back) is Pop and show the top again. A popup over a screen is a stack element too: the screen below stays visible but takes no input. “How would you build menu navigation?” at a Unity interview is exactly this.

Undo and redo are two stacks of commands. A player or level-editor action is an object with Do and Undo. Run it — push it onto undo. Undo — pop from undo, roll it back, push onto redo. Redo — the other way round. A new action clears redo: history has branched, and the old “forward” is no longer reachable.

Stack<T> cannot cap the history at, say, a hundred steps: there is no way to drop the oldest entry from the bottom. For that you use a fixed-capacity ring buffer (like the deque from the window unit), where a new entry overwrites the oldest. Unity’s built-in Undo.RecordObject exists only in the editor — in the game you write the history yourself.
cards.deep:
Inside Stack<T>. The fields are an array _array, a size _size and a version counter _version. The parameterless constructor allocates no array; the first Push creates one for 4 elements, then capacity doubles — Push is amortized O(1). For reference types (and structs containing references) Pop clears the freed slot so the collector can reclaim the object; the array itself never shrinks — Clear() keeps the capacity, TrimExcess() gives the excess back. foreach goes from the top to the bottom, and modifying the stack during enumeration throws InvalidOperationException. TryPop and TryPeek exist since .NET Core 2.0 and in .NET Standard 2.1, so in Unity since 2021.2.

Without the heap. For brackets, Span<char> st = s.Length <= 1024 ? stackalloc char[s.Length] : new char[s.Length]; plus a top index top is enough: push is st[top++] = c, pop is st[--top]. The threshold is there because the thread stack is limited (often just 1 MB). Burst has no managed Stack<T>: use a NativeArray<T> of the right capacity and the same top index.

Min Stack with O(1) extra memory. Keep one min field and push the difference x − min taken before updating the minimum. A negative difference means “this element became the new minimum”, and on Pop the previous minimum is restored as min − diff. The difference of two ints from the full range does not fit in an int — the stack has to hold long, so in bytes it barely beats the pairs. At an interview this answers “can you do it without a second stack?”, not the default solution.

cards.q: Which statements are true? Select all.
options: The player did A, B, C, pressed Undo twice and then did D. Now Redo brings nothing back
Two-stack Min Stack with x < mins.Peek(): after push 2, push 2, pop, GetMin returns 2
stack.Pop() on an empty Stack<int> returns 0
Stack<(int val, int min)> does not create a heap object on every Push
Valid Parentheses: a string of odd length can be rejected right away
cards.explain: D is a new action, it clears redo: the undone B and C can no longer be redone. With < the second two never reached mins, popping a two removed the only record, and mins.Peek() on an empty stack throws — while the answer should be 2. Pop on an empty Stack<T> throws InvalidOperationException rather than returning default. The (int, int) tuple is a struct stored directly in the stack’s array. Every bracket needs a pair, and with an odd length one is left without it.

cards.q: You are solving Valid Parentheses out loud at an interview. Put the steps in order.
items: Clarify: only the characters ()[]{}, can the string be empty, what is the length
Name the naive approach: cut out pairs while you can — O(n²) and string garbage; counters cannot see order
Idea: only the last open bracket can be closed — a stack of open brackets
Write the code, stating the invariant: the stack holds open, unclosed brackets, the last one on top
Run "([)]" and "(()": a mismatched top and a non-empty stack at the end
State the complexity: O(n) time, O(n) memory in the worst case "(((("
Edge cases: a closing bracket on an empty stack, odd length
cards.explain: Agree on the problem, name the baseline and why it is bad, then the idea and the code with its invariant, a run on examples that catch two different errors, and finally the complexity and edge cases.

cards.q: Match the problem with the technique.
pairs: The last one opened closes first
Minimum in O(1), even after Pop
A (value, minimum) pair in one stack
Two command stacks, a new action clears redo
The Back button in a menu
A screen stack: Pop and show the top

lessons.title: Monotonic stack
lessons.sub: Daily Temperatures and Largest Rectangle in Histogram: the nearest greater and smaller in O(n)

cards.title: The problem and the “next greater” signal
cards.body:
Daily Temperatures (LeetCode #739). Given daily temperatures t, 1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁵, 30 ≤ t[i] ≤ 100. For each day, answer how many days you have to wait for a strictly warmer one; if there is none, 0.

This is the next greater element problem: for each element find the nearest one to the right that is larger. Signals in the statement: “the nearest greater or smaller to the left or right”, “how long to wait”, “how far does it extend”, “who blocks it first”. Related problems: Next Greater Element (#496, #503), Online Stock Span (#901) and Largest Rectangle in Histogram (#84) — the second problem of this lesson.

In a game: in a 2D terrain profile (the column heights of a tile map), for each column find the first one to its right that is taller: that is where a horizontal ray cast from its top will hit.
cards.code:
int[] ans = DailyTemperatures(new[] { 73, 74, 75, 71, 69, 72, 76, 73 });
// [1, 1, 4, 2, 1, 1, 0, 0]: after 75° you wait 4 days — until 76°

cards.q: Where does the “nearest greater or smaller” technique apply? Select all.
options: For each day — how many consecutive days, including this one, the stock price was not above today’s
For each tower on a line — the nearest taller tower to its right
For each histogram bar — how far left and right it extends before meeting a lower one
The sum of every k consecutive numbers
A pair of numbers adding up to target in a sorted array
cards.explain: The stock price is Online Stock Span (#901): the nearest earlier day with a higher price, and the distance to it is the answer. The tower is the next greater to the right in its purest form. The bar needs the nearest smaller on both sides — that is the histogram from the second half of the lesson. The sum of k in a row is a sliding window, the pair with a sum is converging pointers: neither asks about the nearest neighbour by value.

cards.title: The naive solution and its cost
cards.body:
For each day i walk right until you find a warmer day. If the warmer day is close, that is quick. But if there is none, the scan runs to the end of the array.

The worst case is many days that never get a warmer one: all temperatures equal or decreasing. Then each day scans the whole tail: n(n − 1)/2 comparisons, O(n²). For n = 10⁵ that is about 5·10⁹ — tens of seconds against a one-second limit.

Note that the narrow temperature range (30–100) does not save you here. It bounds the values, not the distance to the answer.

cards.q: n = 10⁵. On which input does the naive scan run longest?
options: Every day has the same temperature, say 50°
The temperature strictly rises every day
Random temperatures from 30 to 100
cards.explain: With equal temperatures nobody has a strictly warmer day, so every day scans the whole tail: about 5·10⁹ comparisons. With rising temperatures each day finds its answer on the very next day — O(n). With random temperatures a warmer day is usually close; only the hottest days search for long.

wrong.1: When temperatures rise, the answer is always the next day: the inner loop makes one comparison and exits. That is O(n).
wrong.2: With random values a warmer day is usually a few steps away. Only the days that nothing beats scan the whole tail, and there are few of them.

cards.title: The idea: a stack of those still waiting
cards.body:
What work does the scan repeat? It walks past the same days again and again. Look at the days that, by the time we reach i, are still waiting for a warmer one: their temperatures do not increase from left to right. If an earlier day were colder than a later one, the later day would already be its answer.

Keep these days in a stack of indices. Day i arrives: while the top is colder than t[i], the top has its answer — Pop and ans[j] = i − j. Then push i: now it waits too. Why look only at the top: it is the latest and the coldest of those waiting. If i is not warmer than the top, it is not warmer than anyone deeper either.

Invariant: the stack holds the indices of days without an answer, and their temperatures do not increase from bottom to top. Hence the name — a monotonic stack.

Why O(n) despite the inner while. Each index is pushed once and popped at most once: at most 2n stack operations in total, however long the while spins on a single step. Time is O(n) amortized, memory O(n). Store indices, not temperatures: t[j] gives the temperature, and the distance has to be computed from the index.
flow: while t[top] < t[i]: j = Pop(), ans[j] = i − j
at the end the stack holds days with no answer: ans = 0

cards.q: Assemble the monotonic stack solution.
cards.explain: Pop while the top is strictly colder: the statement says “strictly warmer”. With <= a day of the same temperature would close a waiting one, and on [70, 70, 75] the first day’s answer would become 1 instead of 2. The wait is i − j days: j comes before i. Push the index, not the temperature — otherwise you cannot compute the distance or know which cell of ans to write.

cards.task: Step through [73, 74, 75, 71, 69, 72, 76, 73]. The rig stops twice when 72° arrives and asks what the code does to the stack.

options.label: ans[4] = 1, pop
ans[3] = 2, pop
push 5

asks.q: Day 5, 72°. The stack holds days 2 (75°), 3 (71°), 4 (69°), with 4 on top. What does the code do?
asks.explain: The code compares with the top only: 69° < 72°, so day 4 got warmer after 5 − 4 = 1 day. It moves further down the stack on the next iteration of the while.

options.label: ans[3] = 2, pop
push 5: one day has been handled already
ans[2] = 3, pop

asks.q: ans[4] is written. The top is now day 3 (71°). What next?
asks.explain: The while keeps going: 71° < 72°, ans[3] = 5 − 3 = 2. The next top is day 2 (75°), which is warmer, so the while stops and 5 goes on top. One warm day closed two waiting ones: those pops are paid for by their earlier pushes — that is where O(n) comes from.

cards.title: Largest Rectangle: the nearest smaller on both sides
cards.body:
Largest Rectangle in Histogram (LeetCode #84, hard). Bars of width 1 with heights h, 1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁵, 0 ≤ h[i] ≤ 10⁴. Find the area of the largest rectangle that lies entirely inside the histogram. On [2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3] the answer is 10: height 5 over bars 2 and 3.

Naively: from each bar expand left and right while the neighbours are not lower — O(n²), up to 10¹⁰ steps on equal heights.

The idea. The height of the best rectangle equals the height of some bar j — otherwise it could be raised. A rectangle of height h[j] extends from the nearest lower bar on the left to the nearest lower bar on the right. A stack of indices with increasing heights gives both boundaries at once. When bar i arrives and is not taller than the top, it is the top’s right boundary. Pop the top; the new top is the nearest lower bar on the left, so the left boundary is left = top + 1, and if the stack is empty, left = 0 — the popped bar was the lowest since the start. The width is i − left.

The sentinel. The loop runs up to i == n with height 0: it is lower than everything and pops whatever is left. Without it, rectangles that nothing blocked on the right are never counted.

Equal heights. The >= condition also pops an equal bar too early — its width comes out short. That is not a bug: the last of the equal bars counts the rectangle of that height in full. Each index enters and leaves once: O(n) time, O(n) memory. The answer is at most 10⁵ · 10⁴ = 10⁹ — it fits in an int.

cards.q: The code popped bar j, and the stack is now empty. What width does it use for the rectangle of height h[j] at step i?
options: i: there is nothing lower to the left, the rectangle extends from index 0
1: just bar j itself
i − j: from the popped bar to the current one
cards.explain: An empty stack means there is no bar lower than h[j] to the left of j: everything to the left that was taller has already been popped. The rectangle of height h[j] starts at index 0 and ends before i — width i. For example, on [6, 5, 2] at i = 2 we pop the 5: width 2, area 10.

wrong.1: Width 1 happens only when the nearest lower bar on the left is right next to it. An empty stack says there is no lower bar on the left at all.
wrong.2: There may be taller bars left of j that were popped earlier: the rectangle extends over them too. On [6, 5, 2] the five has i − j = 1, while the correct width is 2.

cards.task: Step through [2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3]. The rig stops twice and asks which rectangle the code counts: look for the left boundary in the stack.

options.label: pop 5: width 2, area 10
pop 5: width 1, area 5
push 4: two is taller than one

asks.q: i = 4, height 2. The six has already been popped. The stack holds indices 1 (height 1) and 2 (height 5), with 2 on top. What next?
asks.explain: 5 ≥ 2 — pop it. The new top is index 1, so left = 2 and the width is 4 − 2 = 2: the five extends over indices 2 and 3. The six is taller and was popped earlier, but a rectangle of height 5 passes over it too. Area 10 is a new record.

options.label: width 4, area 8
width 2, area 4
width 1, area 2

asks.q: End of the array: i = 6, a sentinel of height 0. The three has been popped. The stack holds indices 1 (height 1) and 4 (height 2). Which rectangle does the code count for the two?
asks.explain: Below the two is index 1, so left = 2 and the width is 6 − 2 = 4: bars 2–5 are all at least 2 tall. Area 8 is less than 10, the record stands. Without the sentinel this rectangle would never be counted: nothing to the right pushed the two out.

cards.q: On [2, 1, 2] this code returns 4 instead of 3. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: The top below the popped bar is the nearest lower bar, and it is not part of the rectangle: the left boundary is top + 1. Here the width is one too large. At the sentinel i = 3 we pop the last two (index 2), and below it is index 1 of height 1: the code takes width 3 − 1 = 2 and area 4, although a height of 2 does not fit over the one.

cards.title: The link to rain water, and variations
cards.body:
Trapping Rain Water (solution 3 in the two-pointer unit) is the same skeleton mirrored: a stack of non-increasing heights, popped by a taller bar. The popped bar is the bottom of a puddle, the new top is the left wall, i is the right wall. The common scheme behind all these problems: a popped element learns both boundaries at once — the right one (who popped it) and the left one (who is below it in the stack).

Which stack to use. Looking for the nearest greater — the stack decreases and a greater element pops it. Looking for the nearest smaller — the stack increases and a smaller element pops it. The popped element gets its answer “to the right”; the element being pushed gets its answer “to the left”: the top after the pops.

A circular array (Next Greater Element II, #503): the first element follows the last. Walk indices 0…2n − 1 and take nums[i % n]; push only when i < n.

Maximal Rectangle (#85): a matrix of 0s and 1s, the largest rectangle of ones. For each row, heights[c] is how many ones in a row go up from it; every row becomes a histogram. Time O(rows · cols). In a game: the largest free rectangular plot for a building on a tile map is exactly this problem; a 256 × 256 map is 65,536 cells in one pass.
cards.deep:
Amortization, formally. Take the stack size as the potential. Step i does k pops and one push: the actual cost is k + 1, the potential changes by 1 − k, the amortized cost is 2. Summed over all steps that is at most 2n plus the initial potential of 0. It is the same accounting as for List<T>.Add with doubling: an “expensive” step is paid for by earlier cheap ones. Here every push prepays the future pop of its element — an element can be popped only once.

Two passes instead of one. You can compute prevLess[i] and nextLess[i] separately (two monotonic passes, left to right and right to left) and then take max(h[i] · (nextLess[i] − prevLess[i] − 1)). Also O(n), more memory, but each boundary is easy to check on its own. With equal heights one pass uses a strict comparison and the other a non-strict one — otherwise counting problems (Sum of Subarray Minimums, #907) count equal ranges twice.

Without allocations. new Stack<int>() on every call is an object and an array for the garbage collector; in LargestFreeArea above that is one allocation per row. Keep the stack in a field and call Clear(), or simpler, use an int[] st of length n + 1 and a top index. Such code moves unchanged into a Burst job over a NativeArray<int>: for a map that changes every frame, that is a fitting answer to “what about 1024 × 1024?”.

cards.q: You are solving Largest Rectangle in Histogram out loud. Put the steps in order.
items: Clarify: bars have width 1, heights ≥ 0, n up to 10⁵, the answer up to 10⁹ — fits in an int
Name the naive approach: expand sideways from each bar — O(n²)
Idea: the best rectangle’s height is some bar’s height, so you need the nearest smaller on the left and the right
A stack of indices with increasing heights: a popped bar learns its right boundary i and its left one — the new top
Write the code with a sentinel of height 0 at the end
Complexity O(n), memory O(n); edge cases: all heights equal, heights strictly increasing
cards.explain: The problem and the cost of the naive approach, then the observation about height and boundaries, from it the stack and the code, a run on the example, and the complexity at the end. Strictly increasing heights test the sentinel: without it nothing gets popped.

cards.q: Match the problem with the technique.
pairs: How many days until a warmer one
A stack of indices, ans[j] = i − j on pop
The largest rectangle in a histogram
Next greater in a circular array
A pass over 0…2n − 1 with nums[i % n]
The largest rectangle of ones in a matrix
A histogram of heights for each row
Rain water between bars with a stack
A non-increasing stack, water in layers

lessons.title: Reversing and merging lists
lessons.sub: Reverse Linked List and Merge Two Sorted Lists: three pointers, recursion and its stack, the dummy node

cards.title: The list node and the reversal problem
cards.body:
In LeetCode problems in C#, a list is made of ListNode class nodes with val and next fields; the last node points to null. A class, not a struct: a node refers to a node of its own type.

Reverse Linked List (LeetCode #206, core). Reverse a singly linked list and return the new head: 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 becomes 5 → 4 → 3 → 2 → 1. From 0 to 5000 nodes. The follow-up in the statement: do it both iteratively and recursively.

What is being tested here is not an algorithm but pointer hygiene. Almost every list problem at an interview is like this: rewire the links in the right order, do not lose the tail, do not forget the empty list and the single node. Signals: “in place”, “O(1) memory”, “rearrange the nodes, not the values”.

cards.title: Naive solutions: a stack of nodes and an array of values
cards.body:
A stack of nodes. Push all nodes onto a Stack<ListNode> and pop them, linking in order: the first one popped is the new head. O(n) time and O(n) memory. The trap at the end: the former head is now the tail, but its next still points to the second node — without tail.next = null you get a cycle.

An array of values. Copy the vals into an array and write them back in reverse. Also O(n) memory, and worse: it changes the values, not the nodes. If something outside refers to the nodes (an “id → node” dictionary, as in an LRU cache), or a node holds an object with data rather than a single number, such a “reversal” silently scrambles the data.

Both solutions are honest and worth naming as a baseline. But the interviewer will almost always ask for O(1) extra memory.

cards.q: Why is “copy the values into an array and write them back into the nodes in reverse” usually not accepted?
options: It takes O(n) memory, and it changes values rather than nodes: outside references to the nodes will point at someone else’s data
It is O(n²): writing a value into the k-th node means walking from the head every time
It breaks on negative values
cards.explain: The task is to rearrange the nodes with O(1) memory. The array is an extra O(n), and writing values instead of rewiring links breaks anything that holds a reference to a node: a node dictionary, data inside the node, another list sharing the tail.

wrong.1: You can write in a single pass from the head while reading the array from the end — that is O(n). The problem is memory and swapped values, not time.
wrong.2: The values are just copied; the sign does not matter.

cards.title: The idea: three pointers, one arrow per step
cards.body:
Walk the list once and reverse one arrow per step. You need three pointers: prev — the head of the part already reversed, cur — the first node not yet touched, next — a spare reference to the tail.

A step is four assignments, and their order matters: 1) next = cur.next — save the tail while the link to it is intact; 2) cur.next = prev — reverse the arrow; 3) prev = cur; 4) cur = next. Swap 1 and 2 and the only link to the tail is overwritten before it was saved.

Invariant: before each step prev is the reversed prefix, cur is the untouched suffix, and there are no arrows between them. The loop ends at cur == null, and the new head is prev. The empty list and a single node need no special cases. Time O(n), memory O(1).

cards.q: Assemble the in-place list reversal.
cards.explain: The loop runs while there is an untouched node: with cur.next != null the last node is never reversed. First save the tail with next = cur.next, then point the arrow at prev, then move on to the saved next. The new head is prev: by the end head points to the former first node, which is now the tail.

cards.task: Step through 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5. The rig stops twice: in the middle of the reversal and at the very end.

options: 3.next = 2
3.next = 4
3.next = null
asks.q: prev = 2, cur = 3. Where does the code point the arrow 3.next?
asks.explain: First next = 4 is saved, then 3.next = prev = 2. The reversed part grows: 3 → 2 → 1 → null; nodes 4 → 5 are still untouched, and the only link to 4 is in next.

options: return prev (5)
return cur (null)
return head (1)
asks.q: The last step reversed the arrow 5 → 4, and now cur = null. What does the code return?
asks.explain: cur == null marks the end, and the head of the reversed list is prev, node 5. head still points to 1, which is now the tail with 1.next = null: returning head means returning a one-node list.

cards.q: On 1 → 2 → 3 this code returns a list with the single node 1. Tap the line after which the tail of the list is lost.
cards.explain: cur.next = prev overwrites the only link to node 2 before it was saved. On the first step 1.next = null, then next = cur.next = null, the loop ends, and 1 is returned without its tail. The order is: first var next = cur.next, then cur.next = prev.

cards.title: The recursive version and its stack
cards.body:
The follow-up is “and recursively?”. The recursion first reverses the tail and then attaches the current node to the end of the reversed part. head.next is the former second node, now the last one in the reversed tail, so head.next.next = head. And head.next = null is mandatory: otherwise the first and second nodes point at each other.

The cost: O(n) time, but also O(n) memory — one call-stack frame per node. On 5000 nodes that is fine; on a list of 10⁶ nodes it is a StackOverflowException, which cannot be caught in .NET. C# does not promise to turn tail recursion into a loop, and this recursion is not even a tail call: there is work left after the call.

At an interview, write both and say why production code uses the iterative one: the same time complexity, O(1) memory and no limit on length.

cards.q: The line head.next = null was removed from the recursive version. What happens on 1 → 2 → 3?
options: The head is 3, but nodes 1 and 2 point at each other: walking the list never ends
The correct list 3 → 2 → 1: the line was redundant
NullReferenceException on head.next.next
cards.explain: The call for 2 sets 3.next = 2, while 2.next stays 3. The call for 1 sets 2.next = 1, while 1.next stays 2. Result: 3 → 2 → 1 → 2 → 1 … — a cycle. head.next = null at each level cuts the old forward arrow.

wrong.1: The old forward arrow does not go anywhere: without clearing it the former head has 1.next = 2, while 2.next is already 1.
wrong.2: head.next.next runs only when head.next != null — the base case guarantees it. There is no crash, there is a cycle.

cards.title: Merge Two Sorted Lists: the dummy node
cards.body:
Merge Two Sorted Lists (LeetCode #21). Two sorted lists of 0–50 nodes each; merge them into one sorted list made of their own nodes. This is the merge step of merge sort: compare the heads, attach the smaller one to the result, move on.

The dummy node. The awkward part is the head of the result: while nothing is attached there is nothing to attach to, so the first iteration would have to be written separately. Create a dummy before the future head and a tail pointer to the last attached node. Then every step is the same: tail.next = smaller; tail = tail.next, and the answer is dummy.next. The same trick removes the special case “delete the head itself” in the next lesson.

The remainder. Once one list runs out, attach the other whole, with a single link — tail.next = a ?? b, no loop: it is already sorted. On equal values take from a (<=) — the merge is stable, equal elements keep their order. An empty input list is not a special case either: the loop runs zero times and the other list is attached whole. Time O(n + m), memory O(1): no new nodes except one dummy.
cards.deep:
Without a dummy: a reference to a reference. C# has no pointer to a pointer, but it has ref locals, and since C# 7.3 they can be reassigned. ref ListNode link = ref head; is “the slot where the next node goes”: first the head variable itself, then the next field of the last node. A step is link = smaller; link = ref link.next;. No dummy node and no special case for the head; it compiles in C# 9, so in Unity too.

Recursive merge is shorter — if (a.val <= b.val) { a.next = Merge(a.next, b); return a; } — but costs O(n + m) stack. On 50 + 50 nodes it does not matter; on long lists it carries the same overflow risk as the recursive reversal.

Sorting a list (Sort List, #148) is merge sort: find the middle with fast and slow pointers (next lesson), sort the halves, merge them with this function. O(n log n) time and no copying into an array. LinkedList<T> in .NET has no sort — the usual way is to copy into an array, sort it and rebuild.

k lists (Merge k Sorted Lists, #23) use a heap of heads, O(N log k); that is the heaps unit.

cards.q: Assemble the merge of two sorted lists with a dummy node.
cards.explain: A node was taken from a — advance a. tail moves to the node just attached. After the loop at least one list is empty, and the rest of the other is already sorted: a ?? b attaches it with a single link (null would lose the tail). dummy is a helper node with value 0; the head of the result is dummy.next.

cards.task: Step through merging [1, 2, 4] and [1, 3, 4, 6, 8]. The rig stops twice: on equal heads and when list1 runs out.

options.label: 4 from list1
4 from list2
Either one: the values are equal

asks.q: tail is on node 3. The head of list1 is 4, and the head of list2 is 4 too. Which node does the code attach next?
asks.explain: a.val <= b.val holds for 4 = 4, so the node from list1 is attached — just as with 1 = 1 on the first step. That makes the merge stable: of two equal nodes, the one from the first list goes first. With plain numbers you cannot see the difference, but if a node holds a record with a sort key (a timestamp, a priority), a strict < would swap equal records — and merge sort is stable precisely because of this <=.

options.label: Three more loop iterations: 4, 6 and 8 one by one
tail.next = a ?? b: the whole rest with one link
Nothing: the rest already hangs after tail

asks.q: The 4 from list1 is attached, and list1 has run out: a = null. list2 still holds 4 → 6 → 8. What does the code do?
asks.explain: The loop while (a != null && b != null) stops at a = null — there will be no three more iterations, and none are needed: the rest of list2 is already sorted and linked, so one link does it, tail.next = a ?? b, which is b here. And the rest does not hang there by itself: tail is the last node of list1, its next is null, and without this line the answer would stop at 1 → 1 → 2 → 3 → 4.

cards.q: You are reversing a list out loud at an interview. Put the steps in order.
items: Clarify: the list is singly linked, may be empty, rearrange the nodes, not the values
Name the naive approach: a stack of nodes or an array of values — O(n) memory
Idea: one pass, reverse one arrow per step; prev is reversed, cur is untouched
Write the code: save next, reverse the arrow, move prev and cur
Run 1 → 2 → 3 on paper, arrow by arrow
State the complexity: O(n) time, O(1) memory; recursion costs O(n) stack
Edge cases: the empty list and a single node go through without special branches
cards.explain: First the problem and the baseline, then the idea with its invariant, the code with the right order of assignments, a run, the complexity of both versions, and edge cases.

cards.q: Match the problem with the technique.
pairs: Reverse a list in O(1) memory
prev, cur, next: save, reverse, advance
dummy and tail, the remainder with a single link
Delete a node that may turn out to be the head
A dummy node before the head

lessons.title: Fast and slow pointers
lessons.sub: Linked List Cycle, the cycle entry with a proof, and Remove Nth Node From End: one pass and O(1) memory

cards.title: A cycle in a list: the problem and the naive solution
cards.body:
Linked List Cycle (LeetCode #141). Given the head of a list, does it contain a cycle — a node from which following next brings you back to it? Up to 10⁴ nodes. On LeetCode the cycle is described by a number pos — the index of the node the tail links to (−1 means no cycle), but it is not passed to the function. The follow-up: O(1) memory.

Naively: remember visited nodes in a HashSet<ListNode>. Meet a node a second time — there is a cycle; reach null — there is not. O(n) time and O(n) memory. The comparison here is by reference: ListNode does not override Equals and GetHashCode, so the set tells objects apart, not val values — two nodes holding the same number stay different.

More generally: any sequence x → f(x) over a finite set eventually loops — a path of “a tail, then a ring”, shaped like the letter ρ. A list is a special case: f(node) = node.next. That is why the same technique works for numbers too: the “happy number” (#202, repeat “sum of squares of the digits”) and finding a repeat in an array (#287, jumps i → nums[i]).

cards.title: Floyd’s idea: the tortoise and the hare
cards.body:
Two pointers start at the head: slow moves one node at a time, fast moves two. With no cycle, fast hits null after n/2 steps. With a cycle, both end up in the ring sooner or later, and there fast gains on slow by one node per step.

Why it cannot jump over. Say that in the ring fast is d nodes behind slow. In one step slow moves 1 and fast moves 2: the gap becomes d − 1. It shrinks by exactly one and will reach zero — zero cannot be skipped. And d is less than the ring length λ, so they meet within λ steps after slow enters the ring. In total O(μ + λ) = O(n), where μ is the length of the tail before the ring. Memory O(1).

The condition fast != null && fast.next != null checks both links that fast jumps through: without the second check, on an odd-length list fast lands on the last node and fast.next.next throws NullReferenceException.

The same pair finds the middle of a list (Middle of the Linked List, #876): when fast reaches the end, slow has covered half the way.

cards.q: Where do fast and slow pointers apply? Select all.
options: Find the middle of a list in one pass without counting its length
Decide whether “replace the number with the sum of squares of its digits” reaches 1 or loops forever
In an array of n + 1 numbers from 1 to n, find the repeated one without modifying the array and with O(1) memory
Find the k-th largest element of an array
Check that the brackets in a string are balanced
cards.explain: The middle: fast at the end means slow is in the middle. The sum of squares of digits is a sequence x → f(x) over a finite set: it either reaches 1 or loops (#202). An array of 1…n of length n + 1 is the same kind of sequence, i → nums[i], and the repeat is the entry of its cycle (#287). The k-th largest and the brackets are not about a sequence of jumps: they need a heap and a stack.

cards.task: Step through 8 nodes where the tail 7 links back to node 2. The rig stops twice and asks where the pointers move.

options.label: slow → 4, fast → 2
slow → 4, fast → null: the list ended
slow → 4, fast → 8

asks.q: slow is on node 3, fast on 6. The tail of the list is node 7, and it links to 2. Where do the pointers move?
asks.explain: fast jumps over two links: 6 → 7 → 2. There is no node 8, and there will never be a null: the tail 7 links back to 2. Now fast is behind slow in the ring and starts catching up.

options.label: They meet at node 6
fast jumps over: slow → 6, fast → 7
slow → 6, fast → 5: the gap stays the same

asks.q: slow is on 5, fast on 4 — one node behind. What happens on the next step?
asks.explain: slow: 5 → 6, fast: 4 → 5 → 6. The gap was 1 and shrank by exactly 1 — to zero. It cannot jump over: every step closes the gap by one, so it cannot pass zero.

cards.title: The cycle entry (#142) and the proof
cards.body:
Linked List Cycle II (LeetCode #142): return the node where the cycle begins, or null; the list must not be modified, memory O(1). Naively a HashSet finds the entry too: the first node met a second time is the entry. But that is O(n) memory.

Let μ be the number of steps from the head to the entry and λ the ring length. Say they meet after k steps: slow has followed k links, fast 2k. Both stand on the same ring node, so the difference 2k − k = k is a whole number of laps: k is divisible by λ.

Now the key part. From the meeting point take μ more steps — that makes k + μ from the head. The first μ of them led to the entry, the remaining k are whole laps that bring you back to the same place. So μ steps after the meeting point you are at the entry. And μ steps from the head is the entry too. Put one pointer at the head, leave the other at the meeting point and move both one step at a time: they coincide exactly at the entry. You never need to know μ in advance.

On the trace: the tail 7 links to 2, so μ = 2 and λ = 6. They meet at node 6 after k = 6 steps — exactly one lap. From the head: 0 → 1 → 2; from the meeting point: 6 → 7 → 2. The entry is node 2. Time O(n), memory O(1).
flow: phase 1: slow +1, fast +2 until they meet
k is a multiple of λ
p = head, slow stays at the meeting point

cards.task: A different list: the tail is longer than the ring. 8 nodes, node 7 links back to 5, so μ = 5 and λ = 3. Step through both phases; in the second one the rig stops and asks where the pointers meet.

options.label: The loop ends: slow is on the entry, and the code returns it
They keep walking and meet at 6, the meeting point, after λ = 3 steps
They keep walking and meet at 5 three steps later, after μ = 5 in total

asks.q: Phase 2, step 2: p is on node 2, and slow has just reached 5 — the cycle entry. What happens next?
asks.explain: The code does not know where the entry is: it only compares p and slow, and p is still on 2. slow runs past the entry because the meeting took k = 6 = 2λ steps: from the meeting point to the entry is 2 steps, but μ = 5 = 2 + λ, so slow makes one more lap 6 → 7 → 5 and reaches the entry exactly when p does, on step 5 of phase 2. Neither pointer returns to the meeting point, and λ alone says nothing about where they coincide.

cards.title: Remove Nth Node From End: a gap of n + 1
cards.body:
Remove Nth Node From End of List (LeetCode #19). Remove the n-th node from the end and return the head; 1–30 nodes, 1 ≤ n ≤ length. The follow-up: in one pass.

The naive way is two passes: count the length L, walk to the node before the (L − n + 1)-th and cut out the next one. That is O(L) and acceptable, but one pass is requested.

The idea — a fixed gap. fast runs n + 1 steps ahead, then both move together. When fast becomes null, slow is exactly n + 1 behind the end — that is, it stands before the node to delete, and slow.next = slow.next.next cuts it out. Why n + 1 and not n: to cut a node out of a singly linked list you need its predecessor.

Why a dummy. If n equals the length, the head itself must go, and it has no predecessor. A dummy node before the head always provides one: both pointers start at dummy, and the answer is dummy.next. Time O(L), memory O(1).

cards.q: Assemble the one-pass removal of the n-th node from the end.
cards.explain: fast runs n + 1 ahead: then slow stops before the target. Move while fast is not null. Cut it out: slow.next = slow.next.next (null would chop off the whole tail). Return dummy.next, not head: if the head was removed, head points to the node that was cut out.

cards.task: Step through 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 with n = 5 — remove the fifth from the end, which is the head. The rig stops right before the cut.

options.label: D.next = 2: removes the head 1
Nothing: slow never moved, there is nothing to remove
NullReferenceException: the head has no predecessor

asks.q: fast has run n + 1 = 6 steps and is already null, while slow is still on D. What does the code do?
asks.explain: The while never ran, but slow is already where it needs to be: before the fifth from the end, that is, before the head. slow.next = slow.next.next cuts out 1, and the answer is dummy.next = 2. Without the dummy the head would have no predecessor, and you would need a separate case.

cards.q: A version without a dummy. On [1, 2] with n = 2 it crashes with a NullReferenceException. Tap the line where that happens.
cards.explain: After the for loop fast has passed both nodes and become null, and fast.next on null throws. This is exactly the “remove the head” case: n equals the length, and the target has no predecessor. The cure is a dummy node before the head (or a separate check if (fast == null) return head.next).

cards.title: Floyd beyond lists, and where it shows up in games
cards.body:
A repeat in an array (Find the Duplicate Number, #287): n + 1 numbers from 1 to n, do not modify the array, O(1) memory. Treat the array as a list: index i links to nums[i]. The repeated number is a node with two or more incoming arrows (the repeat may occur more than twice), and on a ρ-shaped path there is exactly one such node — the cycle entry. No arrow leads into index 0 (there are no zero values), so the tail starts there. The rest is exactly the two phases of #142.

In a game. Data linked by a “next” reference: a patrol route of waypoints, each with a next field; a chain of quests or dialogue lines. Is the route closed, and at which waypoint does the loop start — that is #141 and #142. In an editor tool a HashSet is simpler: memory is not tight, and the code is obvious. Floyd is needed when the “nodes” are not objects but values of a function with nowhere to store them: the period of a pseudo-random number generator, for example, is found exactly this way.

At an interview it pays to name both versions and what each costs: a HashSet takes O(n) memory and a hash on every step, Floyd takes O(1) memory but roughly three times as many link traversals.
cards.deep:
Why speeds 1 and 2. What matters is the difference in speed: it is 1, so the gap in the ring shrinks one at a time. With speeds 1 and 3 the gap shrinks by 2 per step: with an even λ and an odd initial gap the pointers never meet. Speed 2 is the slowest that still catches up, and the cheapest in link traversals.

The cycle length. After the meeting, keep one pointer in place and walk the other one step at a time until it comes back: the number of steps is λ. That is the follow-up “and how long is the cycle?”.

Brent’s algorithm. One pointer stands still, the other walks; after 1, 2, 4, 8 … steps the standing one is moved to where the walker is. The meeting gives λ directly, and μ is then found by a second pass with a gap of λ. It usually makes fewer link traversals (evaluations of f) than Floyd — that matters when f is expensive, like a generator step or a hash function. The complexity is the same: O(μ + λ) time, O(1) memory.

The cost of HashSet<ListNode>. The hash of a reference object without an overridden GetHashCode is RuntimeHelpers.GetHashCode: it is assigned to the object on the first call and lives in its header or in an auxiliary runtime structure. For 10⁴ nodes that is nothing; but at an interview what matters is that you understand what is compared — the reference, not val.

cards.q: Which statements are true? Select all.
options: fast at speed 2 cannot jump over slow in the ring: the gap shrinks by exactly 1 per step
To find the cycle entry you first have to compute the tail length μ
HashSet<ListNode> tells nodes apart by reference, even if they have the same val
In #19, if n equals the list length, without a dummy you need a separate case for removing the head
The condition while (fast.next != null) is enough for HasCycle
cards.explain: The gap shrinks one at a time and passes through zero — no jumping over. You do not need μ: two pointers, from the head and from the meeting point, converge at the entry after μ steps on their own. ListNode does not override Equals, so the set compares references. With n equal to the length the head is removed, and it has no predecessor — the dummy provides one. Without the fast != null check, after a jump fast.next.next = null the next check of fast.next throws NullReferenceException.

cards.q: You are solving Linked List Cycle II out loud. Put the steps in order.
items: Clarify: return the entry node or null, do not modify the list, O(1) memory
Name the naive approach: a HashSet of visited nodes — the first repeat is the entry, O(n) memory
Phase 1: slow by 1, fast by 2; if they meet there is a cycle, if fast hits null there is not
Prove it: the step count to the meeting, k, is a multiple of λ, so μ steps from the meeting lead to the entry
Phase 2: one pointer at the head, the other at the meeting point, both one step at a time until they coincide
Run the example: μ = 2, λ = 6, they meet at node 6, the entry is node 2
Complexity O(n), memory O(1); edge cases: an empty list, a single node looping to itself
cards.explain: The problem and the baseline, then the two phases, with the proof between them: it explains why the second phase works. Then a run and the complexity. A node looping to itself: they meet on it, and p == slow right away — the entry is found with no steps.

cards.q: Match the problem with the technique.
pairs: Is there a cycle, O(1) memory
slow by 1, fast by 2: a meeting means a cycle
The head and the meeting point, both one step at a time
The middle of a list in one pass
fast at the end — slow in the middle
The n-th node from the end in one pass
A gap of n + 1 from a dummy
A repeat in an array of 1…n with no extra memory
Floyd on the jumps i → nums[i]

lessons.title: Lists in .NET and in the engine
lessons.sub: Reverse Nodes in k-Group, LinkedList<T> from the inside, and an index-based list with no allocations

cards.title: Reverse Nodes in k-Group: the problem
cards.body:
Reverse Nodes in k-Group (LeetCode #25, hard). Reverse the list in groups of k nodes; if fewer than k nodes remain at the end, that tail stays as it is. Only links may change, not values; 1 ≤ k ≤ n ≤ 5000. The follow-up: O(1) extra memory.

There is no new technique here: it is the reversal from the lists lesson applied to a piece, plus a dummy node. The difficulty is in the boundaries: where the group ends, what its new head attaches to, and where its new tail will point. The problem is hard not because of the idea but because on a whiteboard it is easy to lose a single link. The interviewer watches how you keep four pointers in your head and check them on an example.
cards.code:
// 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5
ReverseKGroup(head, 2);   // 2 → 1 → 4 → 3 → 5   (5 is a tail shorter than k)
ReverseKGroup(head, 3);   // 3 → 2 → 1 → 4 → 5   (4 → 5 is left alone)
ReverseKGroup(head, 1);   // unchanged

cards.q: The list 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 → 6 → 7 → 8, k = 3. What does ReverseKGroup return?
cards.explain: The two full groups [1, 2, 3] and [4, 5, 6] are each reversed in place. The remainder 7 → 8 is shorter than k = 3 and, by the statement, stays as it is.

wrong.1: The tail 7 → 8 is shorter than k = 3: by the statement it is not touched, even if it is “almost a group”.
wrong.2: That is reversing the whole list. Groups are reversed separately, and the order of the groups does not change.

cards.title: Four pointers per group
cards.body:
Before the head there is a dummy, and groupPrev is the node before the current group (initially dummy). One iteration:

1. Count k nodes from groupPrev: kth is the last node of the group. Not enough nodes — stop, leave the tail alone.
2. groupNext = kth.next — the first node after the group.
3. Reverse the group with the same prev/cur/next loop, but prev starts at groupNext instead of null. Then the former first node of the group points to the next group right away — the tail is attached by itself.
4. Attach the head: groupPrev.next = kth — the former last node is now first.
5. groupPrev = first — the former first node of the group is now its last and stands before the next group.

Invariant: before each iteration everything up to and including groupPrev is done, and everything after it is untouched. Each node is touched twice (counting and reversing): time O(n), memory O(1).
flow: kth = groupPrev + k steps (not enough — stop)

cards.q: Assemble the reversal in groups.
cards.explain: Counting follows the links: kth = kth.next. The reversal starts with prev = groupNext so that the former first node of the group points to the next group right away. first is remembered before attaching: it is the former head of the group, which has become its tail. groupPrev.next = kth attaches the new head, and groupPrev = first sets the boundary before the next group.

cards.task: Step through 1 → … → 8 with k = 3. The rig stops before the second group and before the tail.

options: 1.next = 6
1.next = 4
1.next = 7
asks.q: The first group is done: 3 → 2 → 1 → 4 → … The second one is [4, 5, 6]. Where will 1.next point once it is reversed and attached?
asks.explain: 1 is the former first node of the first group, now its tail and groupPrev. Attaching with groupPrev.next = kth points it at 6: the former last node of the second group has become its head. And after the reversal 4 points to 7 — prev started at groupNext.

options.label: Leaves 7 → 8 as it is
Reverses it into 8 → 7
Cuts the tail off: 4.next = null

asks.q: 7 → 8 is left, k = 3. What does the code do?
asks.explain: Counting from groupPrev = 4 hits null on the third step: kth == null, break. By the statement a tail shorter than k is not touched, and 4.next already points to 7 — the reversal of the second group attached it.

cards.q: On 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 → 6 with k = 2 this code returned 2 → 1. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: The reversal starts with prev = null, as for a whole list — and the former first node of the group points nowhere: 1.next = null, and the rest 3 → 4 → 5 → 6 is cut off. The next count from groupPrev = 1 hits null at once, and the loop ends. It must be prev = groupNext.

cards.title: LinkedList<T> from the inside
cards.body:
The collections unit covered the essentials: LinkedList<T> is a doubly linked circular list, operations on a node are O(1), search is O(n). Now — how it is built in the dotnet/runtime sources and what follows from that.

Fields. The list has head, count, version and a helper field for serialization; there is no “tail” field. A LinkedListNode<T> node stores list (whose node it is), next, prev and item. The ring: head.prev is the last node, so Last is simply head?.prev, O(1), and AddLast is an insertion before head. The ring is hidden from the outside: Next of the last node and Previous of the first return null.

Whose node. The list field catches mistakes: Remove(node) with a node from another list throws InvalidOperationException, and so does AddFirst(node) with a node that still belongs somewhere. After Remove the node is detached (list, next, prev are cleared), and it can be inserted again with no new allocation. The new LinkedListNode<T>(value) constructor is public: nodes can be prepared in advance and kept in a pool.

Version. Every change increments version; the enumerator is a struct, and if the list is modified in the middle of a foreach, the next MoveNext throws InvalidOperationException. Count is stored — O(1); Contains and Find walk the ring with EqualityComparer<T>.Default — O(n). There is no indexer.

Node size on 64 bits: a 16-byte object header, three 8-byte references and the value — 44 for an int, 48 bytes with alignment, for 4 bytes of data.
cards.deep:
Why a ring rather than head and tail. One head field instead of two: Last = head.prev, and inserting at the front and at the back is the same operation, “insert before head”, except that in the first case head then moves to the new node. Fewer branches, fewer empty-list special cases. The price is that Next and Previous have to compare with list.head to hide the ring, so every node needs a reference to its list.

Then and now. In .NET Framework (since 2.0) the list is built the same way: a ring, a single head field and the same four node fields — so a node costs the same. The struct enumerator does not allocate in a foreach over a variable of type LinkedList<T>; casting to IEnumerable<T> boxes it — the same trap as with List<T>.

In Unity the object header on 64 bits is also 16 bytes — in both Mono and IL2CPP (a pointer to the type description — the vtable in Mono, the class in IL2CPP — and a monitor field), so the order of the cost is the same: tens of bytes and an allocation per element. During a collection the Boehm GC visits every node, and the non-moving heap never gathers them back into a dense block.

cards.q: Which statements about LinkedList<T> are true? Select all.
options: list.Last is O(1): it is head.prev in the ring
list.Remove(node), where node is from another list, throws InvalidOperationException
A removed node can be inserted again with AddFirst(node) and no new allocation
LinkedList<T> has an O(1) indexer list[i]
list.Last.Next returns list.First, because the list is circular
cards.explain: There is no tail field, but the tail is always head.prev — O(1). The node’s list field lets the list check that the node is its own, and a foreign one is rejected with an exception. After Remove the node is detached, and AddFirst(node) inserts the same object. There is no indexer at all — only a walk. The ring is internal: Next of the last node returns null.

cards.title: Why you almost never need a linked list
cards.body:
“I’ll use a LinkedList — insertion is O(1)” is a common interview mistake. It is O(1) only when you already hold the node. Finding the place to insert is an O(n) walk, and walking nodes is slower than walking an array: each hop is a load from an arbitrary memory location and often a cache miss. List<T>.Insert in the middle is O(n) too, but it shifts a contiguous block with one memory copy — on thousands of elements that is often faster than getting to the spot through links.

Unity adds the garbage collector to this: every AddLast(value) is a new heap object, and the Boehm GC does not compact the heap, so the nodes stay scattered and every collection visits all of them.

When a list fits: you need order and O(1) removal or moving of a known node, with the nodes stored elsewhere — in a dictionary, for example. That is how an LRU cache works (the data-structure design unit). When it does not: order does not matter — List<T> and O(1) removal by swapping with the last element (the in-place arrays unit); you need a queue or a stack — Queue<T> and Stack<T>; you need a deque — a ring buffer.

cards.q: Unity, up to 2000 projectiles in flight. Every frame some hit and are removed, new ones are added; iteration order does not matter. What do you use?
options: List<Projectile> and removal by swapping with the last element
LinkedList<Projectile>: O(1) removal by node
Dictionary<int, Projectile> keyed by projectile id
cards.explain: Order does not matter, so remove by swapping with the last element: O(1), nothing shifts, the array is reused, and after warm-up there are no allocations. It is convenient to remove while iterating from the end, so the element moved into place has already been checked.

wrong.1: Removal by node is O(1), but every new projectile is a new heap node — garbage every frame — and iteration jumps around memory. Swapping with the last is O(1) too, with no allocations.
wrong.2: A dictionary is needed if projectiles are looked up by id. Here they are only iterated, iterating a dictionary is slower than an array, and enumeration order is not guaranteed.

cards.title: A list on indices in an array
cards.body:
Nodes do not have to be objects. A list can live in an array of structs struct Node { int value; int next; }: a “reference” is an index, “null” is −1. Freed cells are gathered into a free list through the same next field: allocating a node pops the head of the free list, freeing one pushes it back. Both operations are O(1).

What this buys you. Zero allocations once the array has grown to its working size. The nodes sit in one contiguous block — iteration is cache-friendly. An array of structs without references is unmanaged: you can put it in a NativeArray<Node> and walk it in a Burst job, where classes are not allowed. Indices survive array growth and are saved as plain numbers, while Unity’s serializer stores class fields by value by default: a graph of references between node objects does not get through it without [SerializeReference].

That is also how Dictionary works in .NET: bucket chains are next indices in the entries array, and removed entries are linked into a free list. Every technique in this unit carries over to indices one to one: cur.next becomes next[cur], and null becomes −1.
cards.deep:
Stale indices. If someone outside holds a node’s index, and the node is freed and its cell handed out again, the index silently points at someone else’s data. The cure is a generation: the cell keeps a version counter that grows on every free, and the external handle is a pair (index, version); a version mismatch means the handle is stale. That is exactly how Entity in Unity Entities works: Index and Version, with free entity indices reused.

In Burst. A NativeArray<Node> with Allocator.Persistent lives across frames, an IJob takes it as a field and follows next like any array; growing means a new NativeArray and a copy, with Dispose() on the old one. Inside NativeParallelMultiHashMap from Unity Collections you find the same chains: an array of next indices and an array of buckets.

The doubly linked variant adds a second field, prev: O(1) removal of a known node, like LinkedList<T>, but with no objects. That is the allocation-free LRU cache from the data-structure design unit.

cards.q: Reversing a list on indices: next[i] is the index of the next node, −1 is the end. Assemble it following the reference-based reversal.
cards.explain: The same reversal as with references: the end is −1, not 0 (0 is the real index of the first cell). First save the next one, nx = next[cur], then reverse the arrow, next[cur] = prev, then move on. Not a single object — an int array can be walked even in Burst.

cards.q: You are solving Reverse Nodes in k-Group out loud. Put the steps in order.
items: Clarify: leave a tail shorter than k alone, change only links, k may be 1 or n
The plan: a dummy, count k nodes, reverse the piece, attach it, move to the next group
Name the pointers: groupPrev, kth, groupNext, first — and what each one means
Reverse the group with prev = groupNext — the group’s tail attaches by itself
Attach: groupPrev.next = kth, then groupPrev = first
Run 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 with k = 2 and show that 5 stays in place
Complexity: O(n) time, each node twice; O(1) memory
cards.explain: The problem with its extreme k, the whole plan, then the pointers and their meaning — before the code, so the interviewer can follow them. Then the two attaching steps, a run with a tail shorter than k, and the complexity.

cards.q: Match the structure or operation with its cost.
pairs: About 48 bytes and an allocation per insert
O(n): a walk around the ring
Remove from List<T> when order does not matter

lessons.title: Final: stacks and linked lists
lessons.sub: New problems to recognize, a histogram trace with predictions, traps and explaining out loud

cards.q: New problems. Match the statement with a technique from the unit.
pairs: A stack of numbers: an operator pops two and pushes the result
The next greater element in a circular array
A monotonic stack over 0…2n − 1 with nums[i % n]
Is the list a palindrome? O(1) memory
The middle, reverse the second half, compare
A repeat in an array of 1…n, do not modify it
Floyd on the jumps i → nums[i]
A stack of folder names: “..” pops the top

cards.q: Implement Queue using Stacks (#232): Push goes onto stack in; Pop takes from stack out, and if out is empty, it first moves all of in into it. What does Pop cost?
options: O(1) amortized: each element moves from in to out at most once
O(n) always: every Pop moves the whole stack
O(log n): the transfer splits the stack in half
cards.explain: The transfer reverses the order: the top of out is the oldest element, just as a queue needs. An expensive Pop happens only when out is empty, and it pays for elements each of which travels in → out exactly once in its lifetime. The same argument as for the monotonic stack: at most 2n operations for n elements.

wrong.1: The transfer happens only when out is empty. After it, the following Pops take from out in O(1) until it runs dry.
wrong.2: The whole of in is moved at once; nothing is split in half. The cost is O(1) on average per element.

cards.q: Online Stock Span (#901): next(price) for each new day returns how many consecutive days, including today, the price was not above today’s. What do you keep on the stack so that next costs O(1) amortized?
options: (price, span) pairs: a new price pops every pair with a price not above its own and adds up their spans
All prices ever seen: the span is computed by scanning back
Only the highest price ever seen
cards.explain: This is “the nearest greater to the left”: the span is the distance to the last day with a higher price. Popped pairs are no longer needed: the new price is not below them, and any future day that covers it will cover them too — so their spans fold into its span. Each pair enters and leaves once.

wrong.1: Scanning back is O(n) per call, and O(n²) in total on rising prices. The monotonic stack removes exactly that repeated work.
wrong.2: The maximum does not tell you where the run ends: on prices 100, 60, 70 the answer for 70 is 2, and the maximum 100 does not show that.

cards.task: Step through Largest Rectangle in Histogram on [4, 2, 3, 3, 1]. The rig stops twice: on equal heights and on the last bar.

options.label: pop index 2: width 1, area 3
push 3: no need to pop an equal bar
pop index 2: width 2, area 6

asks.q: i = 3, height 3. The stack holds indices 1 (height 2) and 2 (height 3), with 2 on top. The heights are equal. What does the code do?
asks.explain: The >= condition pops an equal bar too. Below it is index 1, so left = 2, width 3 − 2 = 1, area 3 — undercounted. That is not a bug: the height-3 rectangle over indices 2–3 will be counted in full by index 3 when it is popped.

options.label: pop 2: width 4, area 8
pop 2: width 3, area 6
push 4: one is lower — wait

asks.q: i = 4, height 1. Index 3 has been popped: width 2, area 6. Only index 1 of height 2 is left in the stack. What does the code count?
asks.explain: 2 ≥ 1 — pop it. The stack is empty, so left = 0: there is no bar lower than 2 to the left — the four was popped back on the first step. Width 4 − 0 = 4, area 8 — a record and the answer.

cards.q: On [70, 70, 75] this code returns [1, 1, 0] instead of [2, 1, 0]. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: The day must be strictly warmer, but <= also pops a day with the same temperature: at i = 1 the second 70° day “closes” the first one, and ans[0] = 1. It must be t[stack.Peek()] < t[i] — then equal days wait together, and 75° closes both.

cards.q: Next Greater Element II (#503): a circular array; for each element, the nearest greater value, or −1.
cards.explain: The second lap goes over the same elements, hence nums[i % n]. The answer here is a value, not a distance, so ans = x. Push only the indices of the first lap: the second lap exists only so that elements near the end can see the start of the array.

cards.q: Palindrome Linked List (#234) with O(1) memory: find the middle with fast and slow pointers, reverse the second half, compare the halves. What does it cost, and what is worth telling the interviewer?
options: O(n) time, O(1) memory; after the check, reverse the second half back — the caller does not expect the list to change
O(n log n): reversing half the list is a sort
O(n) time and O(n) memory for a reversed copy
cards.explain: The middle takes n/2 steps, reversing the half n/2, comparing n/2: O(n). The reversal is in place, with three pointers — O(1) memory. But it modifies the input list, which may be referenced from outside: a careful solution restores the half with the same reversal.

wrong.1: A reversal compares nothing and orders nothing: it is one pass with three pointers.
wrong.2: No copy is needed: the second half is reversed in place by rewiring links.

cards.q: Game code and .NET. Which statements are true? Select all.
options: A UI screen stack: Back is Pop and show the new top
Recursively reversing a list of 10⁶ nodes in Unity is safe: IL2CPP turns the recursion into a loop
An index-based list struct Node { int value; int next; } can be walked in a Burst job
LinkedList<T>.AddLast(value) in every Update creates garbage
A Min Stack on pairs loses the minimum after push 3, push 3, pop
cards.explain: The screen below the top is the previous one, and that is what we show. Neither C# nor IL2CPP promises to turn recursion into a loop, and this reversal is not even a tail call — 10⁶ frames overflow the stack. An array of structs without references is unmanaged; NativeArray and Burst accept it. AddLast(value) is a new heap node on every call. Each three carries its own minimum in its pair: after the pop the top is (3, 3).

cards.q: You are solving Min Stack out loud at an interview. Put the steps in order.
items: Clarify: all four operations in O(1), the value range, no calls on an empty stack
Naive: GetMin by scanning — O(n); a single min field breaks when Pop removes the minimum
Idea: the minimum depends only on what lies below an element — store it next to the element on insertion
Code: Stack<(int val, int min)>, Push takes Math.Min(val, Peek().min)
Run push 2, push 2, pop: the minimum stays 2
Complexity: O(1) per operation, 2n numbers of memory
The two-stack variant and why it needs x <= mins.Peek()
cards.explain: The problem, the baseline and where it breaks, the idea and the code, a run on duplicates — the trickiest case, the complexity, and finally the variant you will be asked about next.

cards.q: Match the solution with its complexity.
pairs: Daily Temperatures with a monotonic stack
O(n): each index enters and leaves once
Pop on a queue built from two stacks

units.title: Binary search
units.blurb: Boundary invariants without off-by-one errors, the rotated array, searching on the answer, the median of two arrays. For games: a weighted loot table, a fair Fisher–Yates shuffle and seed determinism — System.Random versus UnityEngine.Random.

lessons.title: The boundary invariant
lessons.sub: What holds for lo and hi at every step: closed and half-open intervals, lower_bound, ~index in Array.BinarySearch and Span

cards.title: The problem and the invariant
cards.body:
Binary Search (LeetCode #704). The array nums is sorted in ascending order, its numbers are distinct, n ≤ 10⁴. Return the index of target or −1 — in O(log n).

You met the algorithm itself in the first unit. This lesson is about why it is correct and how to get the boundaries right in every variant of it. Signals of binary search: the data is sorted or the answer is monotonic (“the least x such that…”), and the constraints demand O(log n) per query.

Every variant rests on an invariant — a statement about lo and hi that holds before each iteration. For the closed interval it reads: if target is in the array, it is in nums[lo..hi]. At the start this is true — the whole array is a candidate. Each step preserves it: if nums[mid] < target, then everything left of mid is smaller too (the array is sorted), and lo = mid + 1 throws away only what certainly does not matter. The second obligation is that the interval shrinks by at least one element, so the loop terminates. Once lo > hi there are no candidates left — the answer is −1.

The rule for any variant: state the invariant first, then write the conditions. Every + 1, − 1, < or <= follows from it rather than being tuned against tests.

cards.q: In the closed variant someone wrote else hi = mid instead of hi = mid − 1. What happens?
options: On some inputs the loop never ends: with lo == hi and nums[mid] > target the interval stops shrinking
Nothing serious: mid is already checked, there will be one extra iteration
mid overflows on large arrays
hi becomes −1, and nums[mid] goes out of bounds
cards.explain: The first obligation still holds: nums[mid] > target, so the answer is not to the right of mid. The second one is broken — the interval must shrink. Example: [5], target = 3. lo = hi = mid = 0, 5 > 3, hi = mid = 0 — and the state never changes. In the closed variant mid has been fully checked, so it is discarded: hi = mid − 1.

wrong.1: It is not just one extra iteration: with lo == hi the new hi equals the old one, and the loop spins forever.
wrong.2: mid is computed as lo + (hi − lo) / 2, and how hi is moved has no effect on that.
wrong.3: hi cannot reach −1 here: hi = mid ≥ lo ≥ 0. The real trouble is that with lo == hi the interval stops shrinking.

cards.title: The half-open interval and lower_bound
cards.body:
Problems like “first occurrence”, “where to insert”, “how many numbers are less than x” look for a boundary, not an element. For them a half-open interval and a different invariant are more convenient.
