lower_bound(x) is the first index where a[i] ≥ x, or n if there is none. Invariant: everything left of lo is less than x, everything from hi on is not less than x. Only the band [lo, hi) is unknown. At the start lo = 0, hi = n: both known parts are empty, so the statement holds. Step: if a[mid] < x, mid joins the smaller ones — lo = mid + 1; otherwise it joins the not-smaller ones — hi = mid (it may be the answer, hence no − 1). End: lo == hi, nothing is unknown, and lo is the boundary itself.

Why this is robust: mid < hi always, so a[mid] never leaves the array, and both branches strictly shrink the band. One comparison per iteration and no equality check — which is why, with duplicates, you get the first occurrence.

upper_bound(x) is the first index where a[i] > x: the same code with <= instead of <. The two boundaries give you almost everything: x occurs upper − lower times, its last occurrence is at upper − 1, and the count of numbers in [L, R] is upper(R) − lower(L).

cards.q: Build upper_bound: the first index where a[i] > x.
cards.explain: The band [lo, hi) starts with hi = a.Length: if every element is ≤ x, the answer is n. The loop runs while the band is not empty: lo < hi. Elements equal to x go left together with the smaller ones — hence <=. In the else branch a[mid] > x, and mid may be the answer: hi = mid, no − 1.

cards.title: Array.BinarySearch and ~index
cards.body:
.NET already has binary search: Array.BinarySearch and List<T>.BinarySearch. Inside is the closed variant with a three-way comparison, as at the start of the lesson. What it returns:

Found — the index. But with duplicates it is some of the equal ones: the documentation does not promise the first. Need the first — write lower_bound.
Not found — a negative number ~i, where i is the insertion point: the index of the first element greater than the value, or Length if there is none. That is lo when the loop exits. The closed variant actually guarantees a stronger statement: everything left of lo is less than target, everything right of hi is greater; when lo = hi + 1, the two parts meet exactly at the insertion point.

~i is bitwise NOT, equal to −i − 1. Plain −i would not do: insertion point 0 would give 0, indistinguishable from “found at index 0”. The same ~ converts it back.

Details: the (array, index, length, value) overload takes a length, not an end; the array must be sorted with the same comparer, otherwise the answer is meaningless, and there is no exception. Inserting into a sorted List: the search is O(log n), but Insert shifts the tail — O(n).

In a game: level from experience. Level thresholds are sorted, and the level is the last threshold not greater than xp, that is upper_bound(xp) − 1. With Array.BinarySearch: the index if xp hit a threshold exactly, otherwise the insertion point minus one.
cards.code:
int[] xp = { 0, 100, 250, 500, 1000 };   // threshold of each level
int i = Array.BinarySearch(xp, 300);       // -4: absent, insertion point ~(-4) = 3
int level = i >= 0 ? i : ~i - 1;           // 2: 250 reached, 500 not yet

var sorted = new List<int> { 1, 4, 9 };
int j = sorted.BinarySearch(5);            // -3: insert at index 2
sorted.Insert(j >= 0 ? j : ~j, 5);         // [1, 4, 5, 9]

cards.q: a = [10, 20, 30, 40]. Which statements about Array.BinarySearch(a, x) are true? Select all.
options: On [10, 20, 20, 20, 30] with x = 20 it returns 1, the first occurrence
cards.explain: Not found means ~(insertion point). 5 is smaller than everything: point 0, ~0 = −1. 25 goes before 30, at index 2: ~2 = −3, while −2 would be ~1. 50 is greater than everything: point 4 = Length, ~4 = −5. With duplicates the first occurrence is not promised: in [10, 20, 20, 20, 30] the very first midpoint is index 2, it holds 20, and the method returns 2.

cards.title: Span: MemoryExtensions.BinarySearch
cards.body:
Span<T> and ReadOnlySpan<T> get the MemoryExtensions.BinarySearch extension methods — since .NET Core 2.1 and in .NET Standard 2.1, which means in Unity 2021.2+ as well. Same convention: the index or ~insertion point, but relative to the start of the slice. A slice AsSpan(start, length) copies nothing: this is how you search the filled part of a buffer and leave the rest alone.

You can search for more than a value. One overload takes an IComparable<T> — an object that compares itself with an element: the method calls comparable.CompareTo(element), and a positive result means “the target is to the right”. If the comparable is a struct, the generic overload BinarySearch<T, TComparable> kicks in, with no boxing.

In a game: snapshot interpolation in a networked game. The snapshot buffer is sorted by time, the frame is rendered slightly in the past — at renderTime — and you need the two snapshots around it. That is the insertion point: snapshot i is the first one later than renderTime, i − 1 is the last one not later.

cards.task: Search for 33 in [4, 9, 15, 21, 30, 42, 57, 63] — it is not there. Step through the trace; the rig will stop twice. Watch not mid, but what is known about the elements left of lo and right of hi.

options.label: lo = 5, hi = 4: no candidates, the loop ends
lo = 4, hi = 4: 30 gets checked again
hi = 3: we keep looking for 33 to the left

asks.q: One candidate is left, [4..4], and a[4] = 30 < 33. What happens to the bounds?
asks.explain: 30 < 33 — so everything left of index 4 is less than 33 too: lo = mid + 1 = 5. Now lo > hi, and the invariant says there are no candidates. Proving that 33 is absent took three comparisons out of eight possible.

options.label: lo = 5 is the insertion point of 33; Array.BinarySearch would return ~5 = −6
lo means nothing: 33 is absent, and Array.BinarySearch returns −1
The insertion point is hi = 4; Array.BinarySearch would return ~4 = −5

asks.q: The loop ends with lo = 5, hi = 4. What is true about lo?
asks.explain: When the closed variant exits, lo = hi + 1, and both halves of the invariant meet: a[0..4] = [4, 9, 15, 21, 30] are less than 33, a[5..7] = [42, 57, 63] are greater. So lo = 5 is the insertion point, and Array.BinarySearch encodes it as ~5 = −6. Index 4 is the last element less than 33, not the insertion point.

cards.q: LowerBound on [1, 3, 5]: with x = 4 it hangs, with x = 9 it throws IndexOutOfRangeException. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: The bounds are half-open, but the loop condition belongs to the closed variant. With lo == hi the band is empty, yet the loop keeps going. If hi = n, then mid = n and a[mid] is past the end (x = 9). If hi < n, the branch else hi = mid changes nothing — an infinite loop (x = 4: lo = hi = 2). One convention for the whole solution: [lo, hi) and while (lo < hi).

cards.title: Variations: where else a boundary hides
cards.body:
First and last occurrence (LeetCode #34, in O(log n)). first = LowerBound(x); if first == n or a[first] != x, x is absent and the answer is [−1, −1]; otherwise last = UpperBound(x) − 1. Two searches are still O(log n). Finding x and expanding outwards is O(n) when x fills the whole array.
Where to insert (#35) is exactly lower_bound.
Closest to x: i = LowerBound(x), and the candidates are a[i − 1] and a[i], if they exist.

Peak (Find Peak Element, #162). The array is not sorted, neighbours differ, and beyond the edges there is −∞; return any element greater than both neighbours, in O(log n). If a[mid] < a[mid + 1], there is definitely a peak to the right of mid: the slope goes up, and at the edge there is −∞. So lo = mid + 1, otherwise hi = mid. Invariant: there is a peak in [lo..hi].

The takeaway: binary search does not need a sorted array, it needs a question about the middle whose answer splits the candidates into “definitely not here” and “definitely here”. That is what the rest of this unit is about.

cards.q: You are solving First and Last Position (#34) out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
items: Clarify: is the order non-decreasing? What to return if x is absent? Can the array be empty?
Naive: find x and expand left and right — O(n) when x fills the whole array
Idea: look for two boundaries, not an element — lower_bound and upper_bound
Code with the invariant a[0..lo) < x ≤ a[hi..n) and the loop while (lo < hi)
Run [5, 7, 7, 8, 8, 10] with x = 8: boundaries 3 and 5, answer [3, 4]
Complexity: two O(log n) searches, O(1) memory
Edge cases: x absent, x below or above everything, an empty array
cards.explain: The same seven-step script. The example [5, 7, 7, 8, 8, 10] checks both boundaries at once, and x = 6 on the same array checks the [−1, −1] branch: LowerBound returns 1, and there is a 7 there.

cards.title: How many iterations, and when you don’t need binary search
cards.body:
Each iteration keeps at most half of the candidates, so there are at most ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 iterations: 20 for 10⁶, 30 for 10⁹. But in real code constants matter too.

A small array. With a few dozen elements a linear scan is often no slower: it reads memory sequentially, and the CPU almost never mispredicts its branches. Measure the threshold, don’t guess it.
Many queries over unchanging data — sort once in O(n log n) and answer each query in O(log n). If the data changes often, a sorted array with Insert costs O(n) per insertion — then use SortedSet from the first unit.
cards.deep:
A proof in two parts. Correctness: the invariant holds at the start and every branch preserves it. Termination: hi − lo strictly decreases and cannot decrease forever. If you cannot name both parts, there is an off-by-one somewhere.

Inside .NET. Array.BinarySearch<T> and List<T>.BinarySearch are the closed variant: midpoint lo + ((hi − lo) >> 1), a three-way comparison, ~lo on exit. For Span the midpoint is computed as (int)(((uint)hi + (uint)lo) >> 1): the sum in uint cannot overflow because both numbers are non-negative and below 2³¹. The untyped overload Array.BinarySearch(Array, object) takes the value as object, so it gets boxed, and for arrays of non-primitive structs every element it reads is boxed too; when the array type is known, C# picks the generic one.

Branchless. The “left or right” jump is unpredictable, and on large arrays every misprediction costs on the order of 15–20 cycles. The “base and length” variant tracks the start and size of the band instead of lo and hi, and the base update is written as a conditional assignment that the compiler can emit without a jump. Faster still on big data is a layout in tree traversal order (Eytzinger): nodes probed one after another sit next to each other, so there are fewer cache misses. This is for hot paths; in an interview it is enough to name it.

Unity. In com.unity.collections, NativeArray, NativeList and UnsafeList have BinarySearch with the same convention: the index or the bitwise complement of the insertion point. Inside it is exactly the “base and length” variant, and it works in Burst. The Java idiom (lo + hi) >>> 1 does not compile in C# 9 — the >>> operator arrived in C# 11.

cards.q: Match the task with the formula.
pairs: How many numbers lie in [L, R]
Where to insert x after Array.BinarySearch
Level from xp: the last threshold ≤ xp

lessons.title: Rotated sorted array
lessons.sub: One half is always sorted: search, minimum and rotation point — and why duplicates take O(log n) away

cards.title: The problem and why plain search breaks
cards.body:
Search in Rotated Sorted Array (LeetCode #33). An array of distinct numbers was sorted in ascending order and then rotated at an unknown point: [0, 1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 7] → [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2]. Find the index of target or −1 in O(log n); n ≤ 5000.

The signals — “sorted” and “O(log n)” — say binary search. But the plain version breaks. In [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2], searching for 0, the middle is 7; it is greater than zero, so plain search goes left, while the zero is on the right. The invariant “everything right of mid is greater” is false here, and comparing a[mid] with target no longer tells you the direction by itself.

The naive solution is a linear scan, O(n). It is correct and worth naming, but the problem explicitly asks for O(log n).

In a game a rotated array is a ring buffer — for example, a position history for lag-compensated hit checks: time keeps growing, but the data starts at the buffer head rather than at slot zero. If the head is known, the rotation is no obstacle: the index (head + k) % n turns the buffer into an ordinary sorted array. Problem #33 is the case where the head is unknown.

cards.q: nums = [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2], target = 0. What does the plain binary search from the previous lesson do?
options: mid = 3, 7 > 0 → hi = 2; then it searches [4, 5, 6] and returns −1
Finds 0 in three comparisons: the array is almost sorted
Throws IndexOutOfRangeException
Loops forever: 7 > 0, but 0 < 4
cards.explain: Plain search trusts the invariant “everything right of mid is greater than target”, but right of the 7 sit 0, 1, 2. It dutifully throws away the right half together with the answer and, not finding 0 in [4, 5, 6], returns −1. No runtime error — just a wrong answer, which is worse: a bug like this passes half the tests.

wrong.1: “Almost sorted” does not help: on the very first step 7 > 0 sends the search into the left half, and the zero is on the right.
wrong.2: mid always stays inside [lo..hi], and hi = mid − 1 does not leave the array: the search simply ends with −1.
wrong.3: The interval shrinks on every step, just as in plain search — the loop ends, but with a wrong answer.

cards.title: One half is always sorted
cards.body:
Cut [lo..hi] at mid into the halves [lo..mid] and [mid..hi]. A rotated array has exactly one place where the value drops (7 → 0) — the rotation point. It can land in at most one half, so the other one is sorted. Which one takes a single comparison: if a[lo] <= a[mid], there is no drop on the left and [lo..mid] is sorted; otherwise [mid..hi] is sorted.

In the sorted half you can check in O(1) whether target lies there — by its ends: for the left half, a[lo] <= target && target < a[mid]. If it does, go there. If not, target can only be in the other half, even though that one contains the drop. The invariant is the same as before: if target exists, it is in [lo..hi]. Each step discards half — O(log n).

Why <= and not <: with two candidates mid == lo, and the left “half” is the single element a[lo]. It is sorted, but a[lo] < a[mid] is false, so the code would decide the right half is sorted — and check target against the ends of a segment that contains the drop.
flow: a[lo] ≤ a[mid] → left sorted: target in [a[lo], a[mid]) ? left : right
otherwise right sorted: target in (a[mid], a[hi]] ? right : left

cards.q: Build the search in a rotated array.
cards.explain: The left half is sorted if a[lo] <= a[mid] — with equality for the lo == mid case. In it target lies in [a[lo], a[mid]): a[mid] is already checked, hence strictly less. In the right half it is (a[mid], a[hi]], right end included. Target is in the right half — go there: lo = mid + 1.

cards.task: Search for 53 in [41, 53, 55, 57, 58, 7, 8, 13, 20, 33, 37]. The rig will stop twice and ask which half the code treats as sorted and where it goes next.

options.label: Left [41..55] is sorted, 53 is in it → hi = mid − 1
Left [41..55] is sorted, 53 is not in it → lo = mid + 1
Both halves are sorted — the code cannot decide and does lo++

asks.q: The candidates are indices [0..4]: 41, 53, 55, 57, 58. mid = 2, a[mid] = 55. What does the code do?
asks.explain: a[lo] = 41 ≤ 55 — no drop on the left, the left half is sorted. 41 ≤ 53 < 55 — target is inside, so the right part is discarded together with mid: hi = 1. That the right half [55..58] happens to be sorted too does not matter to the code: it checks the left half first, and if target is not there, it goes right.

options.label: a[lo] <= a[mid] — left [41..41]; 53 is not in it → lo = 1
a[lo] <= a[mid] — left [41..41]; 53 is not in it → hi = −1
The else branch — right [41..53]; 53 is in it → lo = 1

asks.q: The candidates are [0..1]: 41 and 53. mid = lo = 0, a[mid] = 41. Which branch does the code take, and where does it move?
asks.explain: This is exactly the mid == lo case: the left “half” is the single element 41. The condition a[lo] <= a[mid] (41 <= 41) is true, 53 is not in [41, 41), so target is further right: lo = mid + 1 = 1. With < the code would take the else branch and here would happen to reach lo = 1 as well — but on another array it would go wrong.

cards.q: On nums = [3, 1] with target = 1 this code returns −1. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: lo = 0, hi = 1, mid = 0. 3 < 3 is false, so the code takes the else branch as if the right half [3, 1] were sorted — and that is precisely where the drop is. The check 3 < 1 is false → hi = −1, answer −1. With <= the single-element left “half” [3] counts as sorted, 1 is not in it → lo = 1 → found.

cards.title: The minimum and the rotation point
cards.body:
Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array (LeetCode #153): the same array without duplicates, find the minimum in O(log n). The minimum sits right after the drop, and its index is how far the array was rotated.

Compare the middle with the right end. If a[mid] > a[hi], there is a drop on (mid, hi] — the minimum is to the right: lo = mid + 1. Otherwise [mid..hi] is sorted, and the minimum is not to the right of mid: hi = mid. The invariant is the minimum is in [lo..hi]; the loop is while (lo < hi), as in lower_bound.

Why not the left end: a[mid] > a[lo] holds both in [3, 4, 5, 1, 2], where the minimum is to the right, and in the unrotated [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], where the minimum is a[lo] itself. Comparing with lo cannot tell these apart, comparing with hi can: if there is no drop on (mid, hi], then a[mid] < a[hi].

That gives a second solution to #33 — in two passes: find the index k of the minimum, then run a plain search in whichever of [0..k − 1] and [k..n − 1] covers target. Also O(log n), and easier to get right.

cards.q: FindMin was rewritten to compare with the left end: if (a[mid] > a[lo]) lo = mid + 1; else hi = mid. On which array does it return a wrong index?
cards.explain: The unrotated array: mid = 2, 3 > 1 → lo = 3, although the minimum is index 0, which was just thrown away. The code then returns 3. On the other two arrays it gets lucky: in [3, 4, 5, 1, 2] 5 > 3 → lo = 3, then 1 > 1 is false → hi = 3, answer 3; in [4, 5, 1, 2, 3] 1 > 4 is false → hi = 2, then 5 > 4 → lo = 2, answer 2. Both are correct.

wrong.1: Here it gets lucky: 5 > 3 → lo = 3, then 1 > 1 is false → hi = 3. Answer 3 — correct.
wrong.2: Correct here too: 1 > 4 is false → hi = 2, then 5 > 4 → lo = 2. Answer 2 — the index of the one.

cards.title: Duplicates: why O(log n) breaks
cards.body:
Search in Rotated Sorted Array II (LeetCode #81): the same, but values may repeat, and you only return true or false. The key rule stops working: if a[lo] == a[mid] == a[hi], you cannot tell which half is sorted. In [1, 1, 1, 2, 1] and [1, 2, 1, 1, 1] with lo = 0, hi = 4, both ends and the middle are ones, but the two sits in different halves.

What you can do: target ≠ a[mid] — that has been checked — so it is also ≠ a[lo] and ≠ a[hi], since they equal a[mid]. Both ends can go: lo++, hi--. The invariant survives, but this step discards two elements rather than half. As soon as at least one end differs from the middle, the “one half is sorted” rule works again.

The worst case is O(n), and that is not a weakness of the code but a property of the problem: in an array of ones with a single two anywhere, you cannot know whether the two is in a cell you have not looked at. Any algorithm that reads the cells of the array reads all of them in the worst case. That is the answer to the follow-up “how do duplicates affect complexity”.

cards.q: What is true about searching a rotated array with duplicates (#81)? Select all.
options: If a[lo] == a[mid] == a[hi], both ends can be discarded: they equal a[mid], and a[mid] ≠ target
The worst case is O(n), and no algorithm can do better
Replacing <= with < is enough to keep O(log n)
If the input has no duplicates, this code works like the #33 solution — in O(log n)
Sorting before the search brings the whole call back to O(log n)
cards.explain: The ends equal the middle, and the middle is not target, so dropping them loses nothing. The worst case is ones with a single two: any algorithm has to look into every cell. Without duplicates “all three equal” only happens when lo == mid == hi, and the code behaves like #33. A different comparison sign does not remove the ambiguity, and sorting alone is already O(n log n).

cards.q: You are solving Search in Rotated Sorted Array (#33) out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
items: Clarify: are the numbers distinct? Can the array be unrotated? What to return if target is absent?
Naive: a linear scan — O(n), while the problem asks for O(log n)
Idea: the rotation point lands in only one half, the other one is sorted
Code: pick the sorted half by a[lo] ≤ a[mid] and check target against its ends
Run [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2] with target = 0: 7 → right, 1 → left, answer 4
Complexity: O(log n) time, O(1) memory
Edge cases: one and two elements (mid == lo), an unrotated array, duplicates
cards.explain: The question about duplicates at the clarification step changes everything: with them the worst case is O(n), and that is worth saying upfront. The two-element case is your cue to explain the <= in the condition.

cards.title: The proof and related problems
cards.body:
A rotated sorted array is two sorted parts back to back, and every number of the second part is smaller than every number of the first. So any segment [lo..hi] contains at most one drop, and at least one half is free of it. With distinct numbers, a[lo] <= a[mid] is equivalent to lo and mid being in the same part — that is, no drop between them.

Minimum with duplicates (#154): if a[mid] == a[hi], the right end can be trimmed — hi--: the minimum is not lost, because the same value stays at a[mid]. The worst case is O(n) again, as in #81.

Search in a “mountain” (Find in Mountain Array, #1095): the array first rises, then falls. Find the peak with binary search, like Find Peak Element in the previous lesson, then run a plain search on each slope; on the descending one the comparison is reversed.
cards.deep:
One pass or two. Both are O(log n): two passes take up to 2·(⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1) iterations, one pass half as many, but with a more complex loop body. In an interview, pick the one you can talk through without mistakes: two passes reduce the problem to pieces you have already proven — FindMin and plain search.

A ring buffer with a known head. Searching the history by time is a plain binary search over the “virtual” index a[(head + k) % n]. A modulo on every step costs more than a comparison; if the capacity is a power of two, write & (n − 1). Or skip the arithmetic: the two sorted parts AsSpan(head) and AsSpan(0, head), compare target with a[0], the start of the newer part, and run MemoryExtensions.BinarySearch on the right one — with no copying.

Why #81 cannot beat O(n). An adversary argument: while the algorithm asks about cells, the adversary answers “1”. As long as at least one cell is unexamined, it may hold either 1 or 2 — both arrays are valid (they are rotations of [1, …, 1, 2]), yet the answers to “is there a 2” differ. So an algorithm that stops earlier is wrong on one of them.

Why there is no lower_bound here. A rotated array is not monotonic, so “the first element ≥ x” is not a boundary in it. What is monotonic is the predicate “the element belongs to the second part”, i.e. a[i] < a[0]: false…false, true…true. FindMin is a lower_bound over that predicate, except it compares with a[hi] so that an unrotated array works too.

cards.q: Match the condition with the technique.
pairs: Plain search over index (head + k) % n

lessons.title: Binary search on the answer
lessons.sub: No array, but a monotonic answer: the “least x such that true” and “greatest x” templates, an O(n) check and the bounds

cards.title: The problem and its signals
cards.body:
Koko Eating Bananas (LeetCode #875). There are piles of bananas piles and h hours. Each hour Koko picks one pile and eats up to k bananas from it; if the pile has fewer than k, she finishes it and rests for the rest of the hour. Find the minimum integer speed k at which she finishes within h hours. 1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁴, n ≤ h ≤ 10⁹, up to 10⁹ bananas per pile.

There is no array to search — but there are signals of binary search on the answer:

1. You are asked for the minimum or maximum value at which a condition holds.
2. For a fixed k the condition is easy to check: pile p takes ⌈p / k⌉ hours, the total takes O(n).
3. The answer is monotonic: if Koko makes it at speed k, she makes it at k + 1 too — no pile gets more hours.

Example: piles = [3, 6, 7, 11], h = 8. At k = 4 the hours are 1 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 8 — she makes it; at k = 3 it is 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 — she does not. The answer is 4.

cards.q: The naive solution tries k = 1, 2, 3, … until the first speed that works. How many operations is that in the worst case?
options: Up to 10⁹ speeds times 10⁴ piles — about 10¹³, too slow
About 10⁴: one check per pile
About 10⁹: one operation per speed
About 3·10⁵
cards.explain: With h = n the answer is the largest pile, up to 10⁹, and the scan goes all the way there. Each check walks over all piles — 10⁴ operations. That is 10¹³ in total: at the rule of thumb of 10⁸ operations per second, more than a day.

wrong.1: 10⁴ is a single check of a single speed. There are up to 10⁹ candidate speeds.
wrong.2: Checking one speed is not one operation: it sums the hours over all n piles.
wrong.3: 3·10⁵ is exactly the optimal solution: about 30 checks of 10⁴ each. A sequential scan makes up to 10⁹ of them.

cards.title: The template: the least x such that true
cards.body:
Write down fits(k) = “finishes within h hours” for every k in a row: false, false, …, false, true, true, …. Monotonicity means there is exactly one switch. What we want is the first true: that is lower_bound, only not over an array but over a predicate on the range of possible answers.

The “least x such that true” template: lo is the smallest possible value, hi a value where true is guaranteed. Invariant: everything below lo is false, fits(hi) is true. While lo < hi: if fits(mid), the answer is not to the right of mid — hi = mid; otherwise it is to the right — lo = mid + 1. When lo == hi, that is the answer. For Koko lo = 1 and hi = max(piles): at that speed every pile takes one hour, n hours in total, and n ≤ h.

The cost: log₂ 10⁹ ≈ 30 checks of O(n) each — about 3·10⁵ operations instead of 10¹³. In general — O(log(range) · cost of the check).

In games this is how balancing tools tune a parameter against a monotonic check: the least damage at which the boss falls within N turns (the check is a combat simulation run), the smallest buffer that fits the peak frame of a recorded session.

cards.q: Build the Koko Eating Bananas solution.
cards.explain: The upper bound is the largest pile: there fits is guaranteed to be true. piles.Sum() also gives true, but the range is wider, and with 10⁴ piles of 10⁹ the sum does not fit in int — LINQ adds ints with overflow checking and throws OverflowException. The loop runs until lo == hi. “Within h” means hours <= h, exactly h hours is fine too. A k that works may be the answer, so hi = k, no − 1.

cards.task: The example from the problem: piles = [3, 6, 7, 11], h = 8. The rig will stop twice and ask which speed the code checks and which bound it moves.

asks.q: k = 6 worked, hi = 6. The candidates are [1..6]. What is the next check, and how does it end?
asks.explain: mid = 1 + (6 − 1) / 2 = 3. At k = 3 the hours are ⌈3/3⌉ + ⌈6/3⌉ + ⌈7/3⌉ + ⌈11/3⌉ = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10 — too slow. By monotonicity every speed below 3 is too slow as well: lo = k + 1 = 4. hi = 3 would throw away the answer: false says nothing about speeds above k.

options.label: 8 ≤ 8 → hi = 4; lo == hi, answer 4
8 is not less than 8 → lo = 5; answer 5
fits(4) == true — return 4 right away without narrowing

asks.q: The candidates are [4..5]. At k = 4 it takes exactly 8 hours. What does the code do?
asks.explain: The condition is finishing within h hours, i.e. hours <= h: exactly 8 is fine. hi = k = 4, the interval [4..4] has closed, the loop ends, the answer is 4. The template cannot and should not return “right away”: fits(k) == true does not yet prove that k is minimal — only the closed interval proves that.

cards.title: The second template: the greatest x such that true
cards.body:
Sometimes it is the other way round: you need the greatest x at which the condition holds, and the predicate goes true, …, true, false, …. An example is Sqrt(x) (LeetCode #69): the integer part of the square root, i.e. the largest r with r² ≤ x; 0 ≤ x ≤ 2³¹ − 1.

The mirror template with the invariant “fits(lo) is true, everything above hi is false”: if fits(mid), the answer is not to the left of mid — lo = mid; otherwise hi = mid − 1. And here is the trap: the middle must be rounded up. With two candidates, hi = lo + 1, the usual middle equals lo, and if fits(lo), then lo = mid — the same value: the interval does not shrink, and the loop runs forever.

The rule: the branch that assigns mid without ± 1 gets the middle from the other side: hi = mid goes with the lower middle, lo = mid with the upper one. The upper middle is lo + (hi − lo + 1) / 2, but with lo = 0, hi = int.MaxValue the parenthesis overflows; hi − (hi − lo) / 2 is safer.

The comparison overflows too: mid * mid does not fit in int once mid exceeds 46,340. Compute (long)mid * mid or compare mid <= x / mid.

cards.q: This MySqrt hangs forever on x = 8. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: lo = 0, hi = 8: mid = 4, 16 > 8 → hi = 3; mid = 1 → lo = 1; mid = 2, 4 ≤ 8 → lo = 2. Now lo = 2, hi = 3, the lower middle is 2, and lo = mid changes nothing. The lo = mid branch needs the upper middle: hi − (hi − lo) / 2.

cards.title: Variations: same template, different check
cards.body:
Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days (#1011): packages ship strictly in order; find the minimum capacity that gets everything shipped within D days. The check is greedy: load while it fits, otherwise start a new day; were D days enough? Bounds: lo = max(weights) — with less the heaviest package does not fit, hi = sum(weights) — everything in one day.
Split Array Largest Sum (#410): split an array of non-negative numbers into k contiguous parts so that the largest part sum is minimal — the same check “are k parts with sum ≤ x enough” and the same bounds.
Minimum Number of Days to Make m Bouquets (#1482): search over the day, the check is a pass over the bloom days.
Magnetic Force Between Two Balls (#1552): place m balls at given positions so that the minimum distance is maximal. The check “is distance ≥ d possible”: put each next ball at the first position at least d away. If it works for d, it works for anything smaller — the maximum template.
Path With Minimum Effort (#1631, the pathfinding unit): the minimal largest height difference along a grid path — search over the difference with a grid traversal as the check.

The common signal: “minimise the maximum” or “maximise the minimum”, and checking a fixed answer is a greedy O(n) pass.

cards.q: Which problems are solved by binary search on the answer? Select all.
options: The minimum capacity to ship packages in order within D days
Split an array into k contiguous parts with the smallest possible largest sum
Place m towers at given positions so that the minimum distance between them is maximal
Check whether the array contains a duplicate
Count how many times each word of a text occurs
cards.explain: The first three are “minimise the maximum” or “maximise the minimum” with a monotonic greedy check: #1011, #410 and #1552 from the previous card. Duplicates and word counts are not about finding a value: there is nothing to guess, you need one pass with a hash map.

cards.q: Magnetic Force Between Two Balls (#1552): find the largest d such that m balls can be placed at least d apart. Which binary search template?
options: The greatest d such that true: fits(mid) → lo = mid, upper middle
The least d such that true: fits(mid) → hi = mid, lower middle
The greatest d: fits(mid) → lo = mid, lower middle as usual
None: the “can be placed” predicate is not monotonic
cards.explain: If the balls fit with distance ≥ d, they fit with any smaller distance too: the predicate is true…true, false…false, and we need the last true. The lo = mid branch needs the upper middle — otherwise with hi = lo + 1 the loop hangs, just like MySqrt on x = 8.

wrong.1: The first true here is d = 0 or 1: such a placement is always possible. We need the last true, not the first.
wrong.2: The template is right, but the lower middle with hi = lo + 1 gives mid = lo, and lo = mid does not move the bound — an infinite loop.
wrong.3: It is monotonic: a placement valid for d is valid for any smaller d — the distances are the same.

cards.q: You are solving Koko Eating Bananas out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
items: Clarify: is the speed an integer? Is h ≥ n guaranteed? How large are the piles?
Naive: try k from 1 upwards — up to 10⁹ speeds at O(n) each, about 10¹³ operations
Idea: fits(k) is monotonic — binary search for the first true on [1, max(piles)]
Code by the template: fits(mid) → hi = mid, otherwise lo = mid + 1; hours in long
Run [3, 6, 7, 11], h = 8: k = 6 yes, 3 no, 5 yes, 4 yes → answer 4
Complexity: O(n log max) — about 30 passes over the array
Edge cases: h == n — the answer is max(piles), one pile, piles of 10⁹ and sum overflow
cards.explain: The key sentence of the explanation is the proof of monotonicity: “if she makes it at k, she makes it at k + 1”. Without it binary search is a guess, not a solution.

cards.title: When binary search on the answer is correct
cards.body:
The method rests on the monotonicity of the check, and you must prove it, not assume it. For Koko: ⌈p / k⌉ does not grow as k grows, so neither does the sum. Without monotonicity, when the answer “jumps”, binary search returns some switch point rather than the minimum.

The bounds are part of the proof too: fits(hi) must be true. Tighter bounds mean fewer iterations, but the gain is only logarithmic. For Koko you can raise the lower one — nobody finishes slower than ⌈sum / h⌉ bananas per hour — but that saves a few iterations out of 30.

A real-valued answer — a speed in m/s, a radius — is searched not with while (hi − lo > eps) but with a fixed number of iterations, say 100: the reason is under “Go deeper”.
cards.deep:
Real-valued answers. When the answer is not an integer (a speed in m/s, a radius), run a fixed number of iterations: 100 halvings shrink the range by 2¹⁰⁰ ≈ 10³⁰ — far beyond the precision of a double (about 16 significant digits). The condition hi − lo > eps is riskier: for large values neighbouring doubles differ by more than eps, the middle rounds to one of the ends, and the loop never ends.

The cost of the check. The total is O(log(range) · cost of the check). If the check is a combat simulation or a level run, that is what is expensive: 30 runs instead of thousands. Binary search iterations are sequential — the next one depends on the result of the previous one — so it is the check itself that gets parallelised: for example, a thousand fights of one simulation spread across Jobs.

Path With Minimum Effort. The search over the difference with a grid traversal is O(E · log C), where C is the height range; Dijkstra with a maximum instead of a sum of weights is O(E log V). Both are accepted in interviews; we will cover the second one in the pathfinding unit.

The general idea. This is parametric search: an optimisation problem “find the best x” is turned into a decision problem “is x good enough”, and you search for the boundary. It works wherever checking is easier than optimising — and it is a common answer to “minimum of maximums”.

cards.q: Match the problem with its check and template.

lessons.title: Median of two sorted arrays
lessons.sub: Binary search over the cut position, not the value: the correctness condition, sentinels at the edges and O(log min(m, n))

cards.title: The problem and its signals
cards.body:
Median of Two Sorted Arrays (LeetCode #4, Hard). You get two sorted arrays: a of length m and b of length n, 0 ≤ m, n ≤ 1000, m + n ≥ 1. Return the median of their union as a double — in O(log(m + n)).

The median is the middle of a sorted list: for an odd length the middle element, for an even length the average of the two middle ones. [1, 3] and [2] → 2; [1, 2] and [3, 4] → (2 + 3) / 2 = 2.5.

Signals: both arrays are sorted, and the logarithmic requirement rules out even walking through them. So it is binary search — but not over values. We will search for the cut position.

This is the best-known Hard binary search problem. It is given to see how a candidate states the correctness condition and keeps the bounds straight; starting with the naive solution and naming its cost honestly is fine.
cards.code:
FindMedianSortedArrays(new[] { 1, 3 }, new[] { 2 });     // 2
FindMedianSortedArrays(new[] { 1, 2 }, new[] { 3, 4 });  // 2.5
FindMedianSortedArrays(new int[0], new[] { 5 });         // 5

cards.title: Naive: merge up to the middle
cards.body:
Merge the arrays as in merge sort and take the middle: O(m + n) time and memory. You can do it without memory: walk two pointers only up to the middle, remembering the last two numbers taken.

With m + n ≤ 2000 this is instant, but the problem asks for O(log(m + n)) — and this is exactly where the interviewer expects the key idea. Name the merge anyway: it is your baseline and the reference you check the fast solution against on random tests.

cards.q: Merging with two pointers up to the middle. What is its complexity, and why is that a problem here?
options: O(m + n) time, O(1) memory — while the problem asks for O(log(m + n))
O((m + n) log(m + n)): it is essentially a sort
O(log(m + n)): the pointers only cover half
O(m · n): every element is compared with every other
cards.explain: There are (m + n) / 2 + 1 steps, and half is still linear work: the constant 1/2 is dropped in O. Memory is two pointers and two numbers. It works and passes the tests, but the logarithmic requirement says plainly: you may not look at every element up to the middle.

wrong.1: There is no sorting: the arrays are already sorted, and merging is a single pass.
wrong.2: Covering half is (m + n) / 2 steps, i.e. O(m + n). A logarithm is when every step discards half of what is left.
wrong.3: Each step compares only the two current elements, one from each array.

cards.title: The key idea: the cut
cards.body:
The median splits the union into a left and a right part, with everything on the left ≤ everything on the right. Let the left part hold half = (m + n + 1) / 2 numbers — one more than the right when the total is odd. If we take the first i numbers of a, we must take j = half − i from b. Only i needs choosing — from 0 to m.

The cut is correct if everything on the left is no greater than everything on the right. Each array is already in order internally, so two cross comparisons are enough: a[i − 1] ≤ b[j] and b[j − 1] ≤ a[i]. Then the median is max(a[i − 1], b[j − 1]) for an odd total and the average of that maximum and min(a[i], b[j]) for an even one. Divide by 2.0: int / int in C# drops the fractional part.

Which way to move. If a[i − 1] > b[j], too much was taken from a — decrease i. If b[j − 1] > a[i], too little — increase it. As i grows, the edge a[i − 1] grows and b[j] shrinks, so “too much” is monotonic — that is a binary search over i on [0, m].

Sentinels. With i = 0 nothing from a is on the left — treat a[i − 1] = −∞, i.e. int.MinValue; with i = m nothing is on the right — a[i] = +∞, int.MaxValue. The same for b. The edges need no separate branches.

Why the shorter array. j = half − i must lie in [0, n] for every i in [0, m], and that is guaranteed only when m ≤ n. So if a is longer, swap the arrays. Hence the complexity — O(log min(m, n)).
flow: i from a, j = half − i from b
a[i − 1] > b[j] → took too many: hi = i − 1
b[j − 1] > a[i] → took too few: lo = i + 1
otherwise the cut is correct → median from the edges

cards.q: Build the solution with the cut.
cards.explain: The left part must hold half numbers: take half − i from b. To the right of the cut a is empty when i = m — the +∞ sentinel, int.MaxValue. a[i − 1] > b[j] means too many were taken from a: hi = i − 1. With an odd total the extra element is on the left, and it is the median: the largest of the left edges. (lo + hi) / 2 cannot overflow here: hi ≤ m ≤ 1000.

cards.task: a = [22, 35, 38, 39], b = [1, 2, 4, 25, 29, 34]: 10 numbers in total, 5 must end up on the left. Step through the trace; the rig will stop twice.

asks.q: i = 2 took too many: a[1] = 35 > b[3] = 25, so hi = 1. The candidates for i are [0..1]. What is the next cut?
asks.explain: i = (0 + 1) / 2 = 0 — integer division rounds down — and j = 5 − 0 = 5. Nothing from a is on the left, so the left edge of a is the −∞ sentinel (int.MinValue): an empty left part needs no special handling. Next it turns out that b[4] = 29 > a[0] = 22 — now too few were taken from a, and i moves right.

asks.q: The cut i = 1, j = 4 is correct: on the left 22 and 1, 2, 4, 25; on the right 35, 38, 39 and 29, 34. What is the median?
asks.explain: 10 in total — even: the average of the largest on the left and the smallest on the right. max(22, 25) = 25, min(35, 29) = 29, (25 + 29) / 2.0 = 27. 28.5 is (22 + 35) / 2: the edges of one array, not of the union.

cards.q: The function returns double, yet on a = [1, 2], b = [3, 4] it gives 2 instead of 2.5. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: (2 + 3) / 2 divides an int by an int, the result is 2, and only then does it become the double 2.0. It needs / 2.0 so the division happens in double. The cut itself is found correctly — i = 2, j = 0 — the bug is only in the final arithmetic.

cards.title: Edge cases and the k-th element
cards.body:
An empty array. If a is empty, m = 0: one iteration with i = 0, both edges of a are sentinels, and the median comes from b. No separate branch needed.
Sentinels never reach the answer. The left part holds half ≥ 1 numbers, so at least one of a[i − 1] and b[j − 1] is real — and so is the maximum. With an even total the right part also has at least one number — the minimum is real.
Without the swap, when m > n there is some i with j = half − i falls outside [0, n], and the access b[j] or b[j − 1] goes out of bounds.
Duplicates are fine: the conditions are non-strict, ≤.

The k-th smallest element of two arrays generalises this: the same cut, only with k numbers on the left, and i restricted so that j = k − i stays within [0, n]. The answer is the largest of the left edges.

The median of a stream is a different problem: numbers arrive one at a time, and the median is needed after each. That takes two heaps (the heaps unit), not binary search.

cards.q: What is true about the solution with the cut? Select all.
options: The search runs over the shorter array, hence O(log min(m, n))
Without swapping the arrays, j can become negative
The int.MinValue and int.MaxValue sentinels never end up in the answer
The solution is correct only if all numbers are distinct
The median of the union always equals the average of the two arrays’ medians
cards.explain: The search over i on [0, m] with m ≤ n gives a logarithm of the shorter length, and j = half − i stays in [0, n]; without the swap, when m > n, j goes negative. There is always a real number on the left, and with an even total on the right as well — so sentinels never reach the answer. The conditions are non-strict, duplicates are fine. Averaging medians does not work: [1, 2, 3] and [4] have medians 2 and 4, their average is 3, while the median of the union is 2.5.

cards.q: You are solving Median of Two Sorted Arrays out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
items: Clarify: can an array be empty? Return a double? Are there duplicates?
Naive: merge with two pointers up to the middle — O(m + n), while O(log(m + n)) is required
Idea: search for the cut — i numbers from a and half − i from b — with binary search over the shorter array
Code: the condition a[i − 1] ≤ b[j] and b[j − 1] ≤ a[i], sentinels at the edges, the array swap
Run [1, 3] and [2]: the shorter is [2]; i = 0 is too few (3 > 2), i = 1 is correct, median max(2, 1) = 2
Complexity: O(log min(m, n)) time, O(1) memory
Edge cases: an empty array, an even total and dividing by 2.0, duplicates
cards.explain: A dry run on a tiny example is especially valuable here: it immediately shows that the sentinels work (with i = 0 the left edge of a is −∞) and that the swap is in place.

cards.title: Why a correct cut always exists
cards.body:
Monotonicity. Call i “too large” if a[i − 1] > b[j]. Increasing i by one does not decrease a[i − 1] and does not increase b[j] (j went down) — so any larger i is too large as well. “Too small” is monotonic in the other direction. So the “too small” values of i form the start of [0, m] and the “too large” ones its end. It remains to show that at least one i in between is neither. The ends: i = 0 is never too large (a[−1] = −∞), i = m is never too small (a[m] = +∞). Neighbours: if i is too small, then b[j − 1] > a[i]; for i + 1 the right edge of b is that same b[j − 1] and the left edge of a is that same a[i], and a[i] > b[j − 1] is impossible. So a “too small” i is never directly followed by a “too large” one — there is a correct cut between them, and binary search over i finds it.

The cost. There are m + 1 candidates for i, so at most ⌊log₂(m + 1)⌋ + 1 iterations, each O(1): with m = 1000 that is 10 iterations versus a thousand merge steps.
cards.deep:
Overflow in the average. (Math.Max(al, bl) + Math.Min(ar, br)) / 2.0 adds in int and only then divides in double. On two arrays [int.MaxValue] this formula returns −1. Under LeetCode constraints (±10⁶) it does not matter, but noticing it is a senior trait.

The k-th element by elimination. Another solution for the k-th element: compare a[k/2 − 1] and b[k/2 − 1]. The smaller one and everything to its left in its array cannot be the k-th (at most k − 2 numbers are smaller than it: k/2 − 1 from its own array and fewer than k/2 from the other), so drop those k/2 and decrease k. O(log k) = O(log(m + n)) — enough for #4, but not O(log min(m, n)).

Binary search over the value. Yet another route is binary search on the answer from the previous lesson: find the least x such that the union has at least k numbers ≤ x. The check is two upper_bounds. O(log C · (log m + log n)), where C is the value range. Slower, but it generalises to k sorted arrays and to a matrix with sorted rows and columns (Kth Smallest Element in a Sorted Matrix, #378), where the check walks the matrix as a “staircase” in O(n).

Why (m + n + 1) / 2. With an odd total the extra element goes to the left, and the median is the left maximum; one half formula covers both cases. You can put the extra one on the right instead (half = (m + n) / 2) — then for an odd total the median is the right minimum. Just don’t mix the two.

cards.q: Match the situation in the solution with the action.
pairs: int.MinValue or int.MaxValue at the edge

lessons.title: Randomness for games
lessons.sub: A loot table on prefix sums and upper_bound, a fair Fisher–Yates shuffle, System.Random versus UnityEngine.Random and seed determinism

cards.title: A loot table: Random Pick with Weight
cards.body:
Random Pick with Weight (LeetCode #528). Given an array of weights w, the method PickIndex() returns index i with probability w[i] / sum(w). 1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁴, weights from 1 to 10⁵, up to 10⁴ calls.

This is the loot table of any game: a sword with weight 1, a potion with weight 3, gold with weight 2 — the potion drops half the time. The same goes for picking an enemy to spawn, an NPC line, a room for a procedural level. “How do you make a weighted drop, and how do you make it fast” is a frequent question at Unity interviews.

There are two naive solutions. Expand the table into an array where index i is repeated w[i] times and pick a random cell — O(1) per pick, but O(sum w) memory, up to 10⁹ cells. Or, for every pick, walk the weights subtracting them from a random number — O(n) per pick, no extra memory.

cards.title: Prefix sums of weights and upper_bound
cards.body:
Lay the weight segments end to end on a number line: item 0 takes [0, w₀), item 1 takes [w₀, w₀ + w₁), and so on. The right ends are the prefix sums prefix[i] = w[0] + … + w[i]; with weights ≥ 1 they strictly increase. A random r from [0, total) lands in item i’s segment with probability w[i] / total — the segment length over the length of the line.

Which segment r landed in: the first i with prefix[i] > r — that is upper_bound(r) over the prefix array. Building is O(n) once, a pick is O(log n), memory is O(n). The linear walk from the previous card does the same thing, only it finds the segment by scanning.

The boundary is strictly greater. With w = [1, 3, 2] the prefixes are [1, 4, 6]: item 1 owns r = 1, 2, 3, while r = 4 already belongs to item 2. The segments are half-open: the left end is your own, the right end is the neighbour’s. With Array.BinarySearch it is the same: the first prefix > r is the first prefix ≥ r + 1; if found — its index, if not — ~insertion point.

cards.task: Step through w = [3, 1, 4, 2] with r = 4. The rig builds the prefix sums and stops when the midpoint lands exactly on r, and again before the answer.

options.label: Right: lo = mid + 1 = 2
Left: hi = mid = 1
Nowhere: prefix[mid] == r, the answer is index 1

asks.q: prefix = [3, 4, 8, 10], r = 4, lo = 0, hi = 3. The midpoint is mid = 1, and prefix[1] = 4 — exactly r. Which way does the search go?
asks.explain: We want the first prefix > r, and 4 > 4 is false — so prefix[1] <= r and the answer lies to the right: lo = mid + 1. Index 1 owns [3, 4), and the right end is not its own: r = 4 opens the segment of index 2, [4, 8). Stopping on equality is an exact-match search, and hi = mid on equality is lower_bound, the first prefix ≥ r: with it every segment shifts by one, so index 0 would get 4 of the 10 values of r instead of 3, and index 3 one instead of two.

options.label: 2, with probability 1/4
1, with probability 1/10
2, with probability 4/10

asks.q: lo = hi = 2, the loop is over. What does PickIndex return, and how often does that index come out?
asks.explain: The answer is lo = 2: r = 4 lies in [4, 8). That segment owns 4 of the 10 whole values of r, and r is drawn uniformly from [0, 10), so index 2 comes out with probability 4/10 = w[2] / sum(w). 1/4 is a uniform pick of an index, with no weights at all. Index 1 is the last prefix ≤ r: its segment ends at r but does not contain it.

cards.q: Build Random Pick with Weight.
cards.explain: The total weight is the last prefix, and Next(total) gives r from [0, total). A segment with prefix[mid] <= r ended at or before r — the answer is further right: lo = mid + 1. Otherwise prefix[mid] > r, and mid may be the answer: hi = mid. This is the “least i such that prefix[i] > r” template with hi = n − 1: r < total, so the last item always qualifies.

cards.title: A loot table in Unity: float and zero weights
cards.body:
In Unity weights are often float and live in a ScriptableObject. Build the prefixes once — in OnEnable (and, in the editor, also in OnValidate after the weights are edited), not on every drop: otherwise it is O(n) and a new array per pick.

The float trap. UnityEngine.Random.value and Random.Range(float, float) return a number including both bounds: Random.Range(0f, total) can return exactly total. An upper_bound over the band [0, n) would then return n — past the end of the array. That is why the candidates are [0, n − 1], as in PickIndex: r == total goes to the last item. Random.Range(int, int), on the contrary, excludes the upper bound, like System.Random.Next.

Zero weights. A weight of 0 — an item temporarily disabled — breaks the strict growth of the prefixes: w = [1, 0, 2] → [1, 1, 3]. Your own upper_bound survives this: it looks for the first prefix > r, and a zero-length segment never matches. But Array.BinarySearch with duplicates returns some of the equal ones — for example, the disabled item. One gap remains in the float version: if the last item is disabled, r == total goes to it. The simplest fix is to leave zero-weight items out of the table when building it.

cards.q: What is true about a loot table on prefix sums? Select all.
options: Prefixes are built once, a pick is O(log n)
With zero weights Array.BinarySearch(prefix, r + 1) can return a disabled item
UnityEngine.Random.Range(0f, total) can return exactly total
The sum of 10⁴ weights up to 10⁵ does not fit in int
UnityEngine.Random.Range(0, n) for int can return n
cards.explain: The table does not change — prefixes are computed once, then it is only binary search. On w = [1, 0, 2] the prefixes are [1, 1, 3]; with r = 0 we search for 1, the very first midpoint is index 1 with weight 0, and the method returns it. The float version of Range includes both bounds. 10⁴ · 10⁵ = 10⁹ — less than int.MaxValue ≈ 2.1·10⁹. The int version of Range excludes the upper bound.

cards.title: The Fisher–Yates shuffle
cards.body:
Shuffle an Array (LeetCode #384): a class with Shuffle() — return a random permutation, with all n! equally likely — and Reset() — return the original order.

Fisher–Yates: go from the end; at step i pick j uniformly from [0, i] — including i itself — and swap a[i] and a[j]. After the step the tail [i..n − 1] is final. Why it is fair: the first step has n options, the second n − 1, …, so there are n · (n − 1) · … · 2 = n! equally likely paths, and different paths give different permutations — each with probability exactly 1/n!. O(n) time, in place.

Two classic mistakes. “Swap each element with a random one from all of them”, j = rnd.Next(n): there are nⁿ paths, and nⁿ is not divisible by n! for n ≥ 3. With three elements that is 27 paths for 6 permutations, so some permutations come up with probability 5/27 and others 4/27. The second mistake is j = rnd.Next(i), without i itself: that is Sattolo’s algorithm, it produces only cyclic permutations, and no element ever stays in place.

In a game: a deck of cards, the Tetris piece “bag” (the seven pieces are shuffled and dealt in order, so there are no long droughts of the piece you need), a track queue, the order of waves.

cards.q: After this shuffle the deck [A, B, C] only ever comes out as [B, C, A] or [C, A, B]: no card stays in its place. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: Next(i) gives j from [0, i − 1]: the element at position i is forced to move. That is Sattolo’s algorithm — on three cards it yields only two cycles out of six permutations. It must be Next(i + 1): j from [0, i], so “staying in place” is also one of the equally likely outcomes.

cards.task: Step through shuffling [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]. The j values are fixed in advance so the run is repeatable. The rig stops when j equals i, and again before the end.

options.label: Draws j again: swapping with itself achieves nothing
Swaps a[4] with itself: 5 keeps its place and becomes final
Takes j = i − 1 = 3: the element has to move

asks.q: i = 4, and j = 4 came out — i itself. What does the code do?
asks.explain: j = i is one of i + 1 = 5 equally likely outcomes, and there is no special branch for it: (a[4], a[4]) = (a[4], a[4]) leaves 5 where it is, and nothing touches index 4 again. Redrawing j or shifting it forbids “stay in place” — the same bug as Next(i) in the previous card: you get Sattolo’s algorithm, and every permutation with 5 at index 4 disappears.

asks.q: Only i = 0 is left, and it has nothing to choose from. How many equally likely j sequences does a shuffle of six elements have?
asks.explain: At step i, j has exactly i + 1 choices: 6, 5, 4, 3, 2 — 720 paths in total, and different paths give different permutations. There are also 6! = 720 permutations, so each comes out with probability 1/720. 6⁶ paths belong to the naive shuffle with j = rnd.Next(n) at each of six steps: 46,656 / 720 = 64.8 is not a whole number, so the paths cannot split evenly. The same on three elements: 27 paths for 6 permutations, some get 5 and others 4.

cards.title: System.Random, UnityEngine.Random and determinism
cards.body:
UnityEngine.Random is a static class with one global state. InitState(seed) sets the seed, and the Random.state property lets you save and restore the state; call it from the main thread. Being global is the main problem: any code that also calls Random (effects, AI, a third-party plugin) shifts the sequence, and the loot for the same seed comes out different.

System.Random is an object: every instance has its own state, and new Random(seed) repeats its sequence. But the .NET documentation does not promise that the algorithm stays the same across versions: for saves and networked games a few-line generator of your own (xorshift, PCG) is more reliable. An instance is not thread-safe: concurrent calls from several threads corrupt its state. Random.Shared (.NET 6+) is thread-safe, but Unity does not have it. In .NET Framework a seedless new Random() takes its seed from a timer, and instances created back to back produce the same numbers. In .NET Core and .NET 5+ the default seed is random, and the Mono in current Unity versions takes this class from .NET Core and behaves the same way. Older versions and other platforms promise nothing, though, so the rule is simple: one instance per system, not a new Random() per roll.

Unity.Mathematics.Random is a struct with explicit state for Jobs and Burst; its seed must not be zero.

Seed determinism means the same seed and the same sequence of calls. It is broken by: one generator shared by several systems; calls in Update, whose number depends on FPS; a seed taken from string.GetHashCode() — in .NET Core and .NET 5+ a string hash differs from process to process, and even on Mono the documentation does not promise it is stable; iterating a HashSet or Dictionary — their order is not guaranteed and depends on key hashes and on the history of removals. The roguelike technique is a separate stream per system: map, loot, AI, each with its own seed derived from the world seed.

cards.q: A replay must reproduce a fight from its seed. What breaks reproducibility? Select all.
options: Loot, AI and particles all draw numbers from the same UnityEngine.Random
The crit chance is rolled in Update rather than in a simulation step
The fight seed is the arena name: new System.Random(arenaName.GetHashCode()) on .NET 5+
Loot has its own new System.Random(seed), called only by the loot system
The seed is saved in the replay file together with the player’s input
cards.explain: A shared generator: particles depend on graphics settings, and every extra particle shifts loot and AI. Update runs once per frame — at a different FPS there will be a different number of rolls. On .NET 5+ string.GetHashCode() differs in every process — the seed is different on every run. A separate generator per system and the seed in the replay file are exactly what makes it reproducible.

cards.q: You are solving Random Pick with Weight out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
items: Clarify: are weights integers? Can they be zero? Does the table change? How many picks?
Naive: walk the weights subtracting them from a random number — O(n) per pick
Idea: prefix sums of weights are the right ends of segments on a line; the pick is the first prefix > r
Code: prefixes in the constructor, in PickIndex — r = Next(total) and upper_bound
Run w = [1, 3, 2]: prefixes [1, 4, 6], r = 4 → index 2
Complexity: O(n) to build, O(log n) per pick, O(n) memory
Edge cases: one item, zero weights, sum overflow, float with an inclusive bound
cards.explain: The r = 4 example sits exactly on a segment boundary: it checks that the search uses “strictly greater”. The question “does the table change?” at the clarification step opens the conversation about the Fenwick tree and the alias method.

cards.title: When O(log n) is not enough: aliases and changing weights
cards.body:
If there are millions of picks and the table does not change, there is the alias method: O(n) to build and O(1) per pick. The table has n columns of equal height, each holding at most two items: its “own” with share prob[i] and a “neighbour” alias[i]. A pick is a uniform column plus one coin flip inside it.

If weights change between picks (an item ran out, a chance grows with every miss), rebuilding the prefixes costs O(n) per change. A Fenwick tree gives O(log n) for both a weight update and a pick.

In an interview prefixes and upper_bound are enough; aliases and Fenwick are a chance to show you know where to go next.
cards.deep:
Building the alias table. Multiply the probabilities by n — the average column becomes exactly 1. Columns below 1 (“small”) are topped up from columns above 1 (“large”): take a small s and a large l, set prob[s] = p[s], alias[s] = l, and subtract the missing 1 − p[s] from l; if l drops below 1, it moves to the small ones. Each step closes one column, so building is O(n). Because of float rounding, whatever columns remain at the end are set to 1.

A Fenwick tree stores partial sums of the weights so that updating one weight and finding “the first prefix greater than r” by descending over the bits of the index are both O(log n). It is the choice for tables that change on every drop.

The modulo is biased. rng() % n is uniform only if the number of possible generator values is divisible by n: with 2³² values and n = 3, remainder 0 comes up for one more value than the others. The skew is tiny, but there is no reason to write the modulo yourself: Next(n), Random.Range and NextInt(min, max) take the range directly.

Shuffling and the seed. If the generator is seeded with an int, there are at most 2³² distinct sequences, and 13! already exceeds 2³². So even a fair Fisher–Yates cannot produce every permutation of a 52-card deck — most of them are unreachable. For a real-money card game that matters; for a Tetris bag it does not.

Pseudo-random distribution. “Fair” randomness in games often feels unfair: three misses in a row at a 50% chance are annoying. So the chance grows with each miss and resets on success: the average frequency stays the same, but long streaks disappear. The Tetris bag solves the same problem for ordering.

cards.q: Match the task with the technique.
pairs: A loot table with fixed weights
Millions of picks from a fixed table
A fair permutation of a deck
A generator of its own per system

lessons.title: Final: binary search
lessons.sub: Spot a boundary or a search on the answer, predict a trace, find the overflow, explain out loud

cards.q: First Bad Version (#278): versions 1..n, n up to 2³¹ − 1. isBadVersion(v) is an expensive request to the build server; after the first bad version all later ones are bad too. Find the first bad one with the fewest requests. Which technique?
options: The “least x such that true” template on [1, n]: about 31 requests
Scan from the end while versions are bad
Two pointers moving towards each other from both ends
A hash set of already checked versions
cards.explain: isBadVersion is monotonic: false…false, true…true, and we need the first true — a lower_bound over a predicate. log₂(2³¹) = 31 requests. The middle must be lo + (hi − lo) / 2: with n near int.MaxValue the sum lo + hi overflows.

wrong.1: If the very first version is bad, scanning from the end makes 2³¹ requests. Monotonicity lets you discard half per request.
wrong.2: Converging pointers move one step at a time — O(n) requests. What is needed here is the middle, not the ends.
wrong.3: Versions are never re-checked anyway; the request count is set by the strategy, and a scan stays O(n).

cards.q: New problems. Match the problem with the technique.
pairs: How many events of a sorted log fall into [t1, t2]
By how many positions a sorted array was rotated
Index of the minimum: a[mid] versus a[hi]
The least divisor d such that Σ ⌈a[i] / d⌉ ≤ threshold (#1283)
The k-th strongest player across two sorted tables
Cut: i from one, k − i from the other
Which enemy to spawn by weight

cards.task: A new array: search for 9 in [20, 26, 30, 33, 48, 53, 58, 59, 1, 6, 17] — it is not there. Step through the trace; the rig will stop once and ask what the code does.

options.label: Right [1..17] is sorted, 9 is in it → lo = mid + 1
Right [1..17] is sorted, 9 is in it → hi = mid − 1
Left [58..1] is sorted, 9 is in it → hi = mid − 1

asks.q: The candidates are indices [6..10]: 58, 59, 1, 6, 17. mid = 8, a[mid] = 1. What does the code do?
asks.explain: a[lo] = 58 > 1 — the drop is on the left, so the right half [1, 6, 17] is sorted. 1 < 9 ≤ 17 — target can only be in it, without mid: lo = 9. In [6, 17] there will be no nine: lo overtakes hi, and the code returns −1 — after four probes out of eleven elements.

cards.q: Koko Eating Bananas: up to 10⁴ piles, each up to 10⁹. On large tests the function sometimes returns a speed that is too small. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: For a small k the hours reach 10⁴ · 10⁹ = 10¹³, while int holds 2.1·10⁹: the sum wraps around and can turn negative. Then hours <= h holds for a speed that actually does not make it, and hi moves left past the answer. It needs long hours: the check stays monotonic only if it is computed honestly.

cards.q: Experience thresholds per level: [0, 100, 250, 500, 1000]. The player has exactly 500 xp. What is their level (threshold index), and which formula gives it?
options: 3: UpperBound(500) − 1
2: LowerBound(500) − 1
4: UpperBound(500)
3: ~Array.BinarySearch(xp, 500) − 1
cards.explain: The level is the last threshold not greater than xp. UpperBound(500) = 4 — the first threshold greater than 500, which is 1000; one to the left is 500, index 3. Exactly on the threshold the level is already reached.

wrong.1: LowerBound(500) = 3 — the first threshold ≥ 500, the threshold itself. Minus one gives 2: the formula is wrong exactly at the boundary.
wrong.2: UpperBound is the first threshold greater than xp, i.e. the next level, not the current one.
wrong.3: 500 is in the array, so Array.BinarySearch returns 3 — a non-negative number. ~3 − 1 = −5: “insertion point minus one” is only for a miss.

cards.q: A replay: loot must match by seed, but AI and particles also call UnityEngine.Random. What do you do?
options: Give loot its own generator seeded from the replay — System.Random or Unity.Mathematics.Random
Call UnityEngine.Random.InitState(seed) in Start
Use the float version of Random.Range instead of the int one
Roll loot in LateUpdate instead of Update
cards.explain: UnityEngine.Random has one sequence for everyone: however many numbers AI and particles take, that is how far loot shifts. An instance with explicit state called only by the loot system makes the same seed and the same input produce the same drop.

wrong.1: InitState only sets the start of the sequence. Particles and AI still take numbers from the same stream afterwards.
wrong.2: The type of the returned number does not change the fact that the stream is shared.
wrong.3: LateUpdate also runs once per frame and uses the same shared generator — it fixes neither the order nor the number of calls.

cards.q: Split Array Largest Sum (#410): split an array of non-negative numbers into k contiguous parts so that the largest part sum is minimal. What are the bounds for the search on the answer?
options: lo = max(nums), hi = sum(nums)
lo = 0, hi = max(nums)
lo = 1, hi = sum(nums) / k
lo = min(nums), hi = max(nums)
cards.explain: A part cannot weigh less than the heaviest element — it lands in some part whole. And at x = sum(nums) one part is enough, so fits(hi) is guaranteed to be true. These are the same bounds as for packages within D days.

wrong.1: At x = max(nums) more than k parts may be needed — fits(hi) is not guaranteed, and the template returns a wrong answer.
wrong.2: sum / k is a lower estimate of the answer, not an upper one: at x = sum / k a split into k parts can be impossible.
wrong.3: The answer is often above max(nums) — a part usually holds more than one element — and then it is outside the range: fits(hi) is not guaranteed.

cards.q: A new problem: Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days (#1011). Put the steps of the out-loud explanation in order.
items: Clarify: is the package order fixed? Can a package be split? What are n and the weights?
Naive: try capacities from max to sum, checking each in O(n)
Idea: “is cap enough” is monotonic — search for the first true on [max, sum]
Code: a greedy check by days and the template hi = mid, lo = mid + 1
Run weights 1..10 with D = 5: the answer is 15
Complexity: O(n log(sum)) time, O(1) memory
Edge cases: D = 1 — the answer is sum, D = n — the answer is max, a single package
cards.explain: The same script as for Koko — only the check changes. The edge cases D = 1 and D = n also verify the bounds: the answer can coincide with either of them.

cards.q: What is true about complexity? Select all.
options: lower_bound in an array of 10⁹ elements takes about 30 iterations
Koko Eating Bananas is O(n log max(piles))
Median of two arrays with the cut is O(log min(m, n))
Search in a rotated array with duplicates is O(log n) in the worst case
Fisher–Yates is O(n log n)
A loot table on prefix sums: building O(n), a pick O(log n)
cards.explain: log₂ 10⁹ ≈ 30. Koko is about log₂ max checks of O(n) each. The cut is searched over the shorter array. With duplicates the worst case is O(n): in ones with a single two every cell has to be inspected. Fisher–Yates is a single pass of swaps: O(n). Prefixes are one pass, a pick is one upper_bound.

units.title: Sorting, intervals and greedy
units.blurb: What Array.Sort guarantees and when you need no sort, a ulong sort key for rendering, merging and inserting intervals, a sweep for a sound timeline, one-pass greedy, Kadane, and how to prove a greedy solution is correct.

lessons.title: Sorting in .NET
lessons.sub: What Array.Sort promises, stability and its price, comparers, a ulong render key and sorting without comparisons

cards.title: What Array.Sort promises — and what it does not
cards.body:
In the lesson on common mistakes we saw that Array.Sort and List<T>.Sort are an introspective sort (List.Sort just sorts its internal array). Now for what that means in an interview. There are three guarantees:

1. O(n log n) in the worst case — on any input, even one crafted against quicksort. 10⁶ elements take about n·log₂ n ≈ 2·10⁷ comparisons; 10⁴ sprites take about 1.3·10⁵.
2. In place: no copy of the array, only O(log n) of recursion stack on top.
3. Unstable: elements with equal keys may come out in a different order from the one they went in.

The third one is sneaky. Ranges of 4 to 16 elements are finished with insertion sort, and insertion sort keeps equal elements in order. So a test on five units "shows" stability, while on a thousand the equal ones get shuffled: partitioning around the pivot moves them across the whole array. Never rely on the order of equal elements after Sort.
cards.deep:
How introsort works in .NET (ArraySortHelper in dotnet/runtime). The pivot is the median of three: first, middle and last. After partitioning, it recurses into the right part and handles the left part in the same loop. The depth limit is 2·(⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1); once it runs out, heapsort finishes that range — hence the O(n log n) worst case and an O(log n) bound on the stack. Ranges of up to 16 elements (IntrosortSizeThreshold) go to insertion sort, while ranges of 2 and 3 elements get a fixed chain of "swap if greater". That chain no longer keeps equals in order: [(1, a), (1, b), (0, c)] comes out as (0, c), (1, b), (1, a).

Why not merge sort. Merge sort is stable and also O(n log n), but it needs a buffer of n elements. The library chose "in place" over stability. OrderBy is stable for a different reason: it sorts an array of indices and breaks ties between equal keys by comparing the indices themselves.

Floating point. For float[] and double[] without a comparer, .NET 5+ first gathers all NaNs at the front and sorts the rest with direct comparisons. The result matches CompareTo: NaN is less than any number.

cards.q: What is true about List<T>.Sort in .NET? Select all that apply.
options: The worst case is O(n log n), even on a deliberately crafted input
It makes no copy of the list: it sorts the internal array in place
Elements with equal keys keep their original order
If equal elements kept their order on 5 elements, they will on 10⁵ as well
Sorting 10⁶ elements takes on the order of 2·10⁷ comparisons
cards.explain: Introsort switches to heapsort when quicksort recurses too deep, so there is no quadratic case. It works in place with an O(log n) stack on top. n·log₂ n for n = 10⁶ is about 2·10⁷. But the order of equals is not guaranteed: up to 16 elements insertion sort runs and equal elements usually stay put; on larger arrays partitioning shuffles them. A small test proves nothing here.

cards.title: When you need stability and how to get it
cards.body:
Stability matters when elements with equal keys already have a meaningful order: events with the same timestamp in arrival order (a replay must play back the same way), players with equal scores by who got there first, a table sorted by one column and then by another.

Option 1 — LINQ. OrderBy, ThenBy and their Descending versions are stable. The price is memory: the source is copied into a buffer, next to it go a key array and an index array, plus iterators and the resulting list. Fine for a sort while a level loads, not every frame.

Option 2 — remove equality. Append to the key something that tells any two elements apart: an arrival sequence number, a unique id. With no equal keys left, an unstable Sort has exactly one possible output — and no allocations.

The trap — two passes. "Sort by the second key, then by the first" only works with a stable sort: the second pass must keep the order the first pass built. List.Sort will destroy it.

cards.q: A leaderboard: by score descending, ties by name. Tests with five players pass; with 500 players the names among equal scores are scrambled. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: The second Sort is unstable and need not keep the name order among equal scores. With five players insertion sort runs and the order of equals survives; with 500 it does not. The fix is one pass with a composite comparer: compare scores, and on a tie compare names. Or OrderByDescending(p => p.Score).ThenBy(p => p.Name, StringComparer.Ordinal) if allocations do not matter.

cards.title: Comparers: the contract and the cost of a call
cards.body:
Compare(a, b) < 0 means "a goes before b", 0 means "equal", > 0 means "a goes after". The sort trusts the comparer and needs it to keep a contract: Compare(a, a) == 0; the sign of Compare(a, b) is the opposite of Compare(b, a); if a goes before b and b before c, then a goes before c. Break it and you get a wrong order or the exception "IComparer.Compare() method returns inconsistent results".

How people break it: a - b with overflow (from the lesson on mistakes); a < b ? -1 : 1 — it never returns 0, so an element is "greater than itself"; comparing float with < when NaN is around — every comparison with NaN is false. CompareTo gets all of this right. For descending order, swap the arguments: b.CompareTo(a); negating with -x breaks if the comparer returned int.MinValue.

Cost. Without a comparer, Array.Sort compares numbers directly: in .NET 5+ it is a plain < inside the sort code, in Unity (Mono and IL2CPP) a direct CompareTo call, again with no delegate. With a lambda, every comparison is an indirect delegate call that the JIT generally does not inline: ~n·log₂ n calls, 2·10⁷ for a million elements. And a lambda that captures a local also creates a closure and a new delegate on every call of the method — garbage for the GC. Hence the trick: if the key can be reduced to a number, sort numbers.
cards.deep:
Under the hood. In dotnet/runtime a sort without a comparer (or with Comparer<T>.Default) goes through GenericArraySortHelper<T>: for int, long, ulong, float, double and other primitives the comparison is the built-in operator; for other T : IComparable<T> it is a direct CompareTo call. If you pass your own IComparer<T>, its Compare method is turned into a Comparison<T> delegate — a new object per Sort call and an indirect call per comparison.

Lambda allocations. A lambda that captures nothing is cached by the compiler, so repeated Sort calls produce no garbage. A lambda that captures a local (say, the player position to compare distances) creates a closure and a delegate on every call of the method. In hot code, precompute the distances into a key array — faster and capture-free.

Shuffling with a "random comparer" — Sort((a, b) => rnd.Next(-1, 2)) — breaks the contract: the result is biased and the sort is allowed to throw. A fair shuffle is Fisher–Yates from the binary search unit.

cards.title: Sort keys, not objects
cards.body:
A pair of arrays. Array.Sort(keys, items) sorts keys and applies the same moves to items. The keys are numbers, so comparisons are direct, no delegate; the data rides along, no tuples or comparers needed. The typical case is distances in a float[] and enemy indices in an int[].

Part of an array. The overloads Array.Sort(array, index, length) and Array.Sort(keys, items, index, length) sort only a range. That matters for pooled buffers: the array is 1024 long but only count elements are filled — sorting the whole array drags garbage from the tail to the front.

Span. .NET 5+ has MemoryExtensions.Sort: span.Sort(), span.Sort(comparison) and keys.Sort(items) for two Spans — handy for a stackalloc buffer or a slice of an array. Unity (.NET Standard 2.1) does not have these methods: AsSpan is there, but there is no Sort on the result. Sort the array with an index and a length instead.

NativeArray. In the com.unity.collections package, NativeArray<T> has Sort() for T : unmanaged, IComparable<T> and an overload taking your own comparer as a struct IComparer<T>. A struct is not a delegate: Burst knows its type at compile time, so the Compare call is direct and usually inlined.

cards.q: Unity, every frame: 10⁴ enemies in a pooled buffer (count filled), you need them ordered by distance to the player, with no GC garbage. What do you pick?
options: Distances in float[], indices in int[]: Array.Sort(dist, idx, 0, count)
enemies.OrderBy(e => (e.Pos - player).sqrMagnitude).ToArray()
Array.Sort(buffer, (a, b) => (a.Pos - player).sqrMagnitude.CompareTo((b.Pos - player).sqrMagnitude))
buffer.AsSpan(0, count).Sort()
cards.explain: The key is computed once per enemy rather than twice per comparison; float comparison is direct, no delegate; only the filled part is sorted; no new objects — dist and idx live in fields and are reused.

wrong.1: OrderBy is stable, but every frame it creates a buffer, a key array, an index array and the result array — garbage for the Boehm GC 60 times a second.
wrong.2: The lambda captures player — a closure and a delegate on every call of the method. The distance is computed in every comparison, about 2·n·log₂ n times instead of n. And the whole buffer gets sorted, stale tail past count included.
wrong.3: In Unity (.NET Standard 2.1) Span has no Sort method — that is .NET 5+. Besides, it is unclear what comparing enemies "by default" would mean: you need a separate key anyway.

cards.title: Unity: transparents by depth, sprites by layer — a key in a ulong
cards.body:
