What Unity does itself. Transparent objects are drawn back to front by the distance from the camera to the object's center — otherwise a near semi-transparent object gets painted over by a far one. Opaque ones go roughly front to back: near objects write depth first, and the depth test rejects hidden pixels before the shader runs — less overdraw. In SRP these are the flags SortingCriteria.CommonTransparent (with BackToFront) and CommonOpaque (with QuantizedFrontToBack). For 2D objects (sprites, tiles), Sorting Layer and Order in Layer come first, then the material's render queue, and only then distance to the camera; for a top-down view people set Transparency Sort Mode = Custom Axis (0, 1, 0) — sorting by Y.

When you sort yourself — your own instancing (Graphics.RenderMeshInstanced), particles of your own system, bullets in a bullet hell — a three-field comparer means branches and a delegate call per comparison. The engine trick: pack all keys into one number so that comparing numbers matches comparing tuples. The high bits hold the main key: 63–48 — layer, 47–32 — order in layer, 31–0 — depth.

Depth as bits. For a float ≥ 0, the IEEE-754 bit pattern read as a uint grows with the value — order is preserved. Back to front means far ones first: invert the bits, ~d. Order in Layer in Unity ranges from −32768 to 32767; adding 32768 makes it unsigned, 0..65535. Then Array.Sort(keys, ids, 0, count) on ulong: direct comparison.
cards.deep:
Negative floats. If the key can be negative (a Y coordinate for top-to-bottom sorting), the bits of negative numbers run the other way. The standard transform: for non-negative values flip the sign bit, for negative ones flip all bits: u = (bits & 0x80000000) != 0 ? ~bits : bits | 0x80000000. The result is a uint whose order matches the order of the numbers.

Quantization. Opaque objects do not need all 32 bits of depth: objects at similar depth barely overlap anyway. Depth is squeezed into 10–16 bits, and the freed bits go to a material or shader id — objects sharing a material end up next to each other, with fewer GPU state changes. That is what Quantized means in QuantizedFrontToBack.

Why transparents "flicker". Sorting is per object, not per pixel: for two intersecting transparent meshes, the center of one is sometimes nearer and sometimes farther, and the order jumps as the camera moves. The fixes are splitting the mesh, a depth prepass, or order-independent transparency techniques — sorting cannot fix it.

cards.q: A key for opaque objects: layer first, then the material id (fewer state changes), then depth — near ones first. Fill in the blanks.
cards.explain: The layer takes the top 16 bits: shift by 48. The material takes the next 16 bits, 47–32. Depth goes into the low 32 bits as is: for a float ≥ 0 the bits grow with the value, so a smaller key is nearer. Transparents used ~d because there far ones go first. The raw depth cannot go here: a float cannot be shifted or OR-ed with a ulong.

cards.title: When you need no comparisons: counting and radix sort
cards.body:
Any comparison sort needs at least log₂ n! ≈ n·log₂ n comparisons in the worst case: there are n! possible orders, and each comparison rules out at most half of them. The only way around the bound is not to compare.

Counting sort. The keys are integers in a small range [0, k): levels 0..99, an age, a layer number. Count how often each key occurs, use prefix sums to find where each key starts, and place the elements — left to right, so the sort is stable. Time O(n + k), memory O(n + k). In the heaps unit the same trick — buckets by frequency — will give top-K in O(n).

Radix sort (LSD). The key is wide — a uint, a ulong. Counting-sort by the lowest byte, then by the next one, up to the highest: 256 buckets, 4 passes for a uint, 8 for a ulong. It works because of stability: the pass on byte j does not disturb the order the lower bytes established among elements with an equal byte j. Time O(w·(n + 256)), where w is the number of bytes, plus a buffer of n.

When it pays off: n from tens of thousands, keys are fixed-width integers (like the key from the previous card). When it does not: small n — the overhead of 256 buckets outweighs the gain; keys that are compared in a complex way (culture-aware strings).
cards.deep:
Data alongside the key. In real code the object id travels with the key: either a second array permuted with the same indices, or the id in the low bits of the key itself if there is room (24 bits of depth + an 8-bit id and so on).

Skipping passes. If every element lands in one bucket (all share a layer, so the high bytes are equal), the pass changes nothing: count shows this before placing, and the pass can be skipped.

Nearly sorted data. Between consecutive frames, the depth order of particles barely changes. Insertion sort runs in O(n + inversions): on a nearly ordered array that is almost O(n) — faster than both radix sort and introsort. That is why particles are often re-sorted with insertion sort, starting from last frame's order.

Counting without placing. If the key is the value itself (an array of 0, 1, 2 with no attached data), there is nothing to place: count, then write the values out in order. That is the next card.

cards.title: Exercise: Sort Colors (#75)
cards.body:
The problem. An array of 0s, 1s and 2s (red, white, blue). Sort it in place without the library sort. Counting takes two passes: count each value, then rewrite the array. The interviewer will ask: can you do it in one pass?

Three pointers (the Dutch national flag problem). The array splits into four zones: [0, lo) — zeros, [lo, mid) — ones, [mid, hi] — not looked at yet, (hi, n − 1] — twos. Each step shrinks the unknown zone by one:

a[mid] == 0 — swap with a[lo]: a zero goes there, and a one comes back to mid (or the zero itself if lo == mid); advance both.
a[mid] == 1 — already in place, mid++.
a[mid] == 2 — swap with a[hi], hi--. Do not move mid: the element that came from hi has not been seen yet.

Stop when mid > hi: the unknown zone is empty. O(n), one pass, O(1) memory. In a game — partition an entity array in place into three groups: opaque, alpha-tested and transparent; alive, stunned, dead. The rig runs it next.

cards.task: Step through the trace on [1, 2, 0, 2, 1, 0]. The rig stops twice and asks what the code does next: answer from the zones and pointers on screen.

options.label: Swap with nums[5]; hi = 4, mid stays 1
Swap with nums[5]; hi = 4, mid = 2
Swap with nums[lo]; lo = 1, mid = 2

asks.q: lo = 0, mid = 1, hi = 5, nums[1] = 2. What does the code do?
asks.explain: The 2 goes to the twos: swap with nums[5], hi = 4. But mid stays: a 0 came from hi, and nobody has looked at it yet. With mid++ in this branch the zero would stay behind mid, among the ones, and the array would not end up sorted: on [1, 2, 0] that gives [1, 0, 2]. Swapping with lo has no such problem — what comes to mid from there is a 1 that was already checked.

options.label: 1 — [lo, mid) holds only ones
0 — a zero swaps with a zero
2 — it will be sent to hi later

asks.q: nums = [0, 1, 0, 2, 1, 2], lo = 1, mid = 2, nums[2] = 0 — swap with nums[lo]. What lands at mid?
asks.explain: The zone [lo, mid) holds ones, so nums[lo] = 1. After the swap the zero joins the zeros and the one moves to the end of the ones zone, at mid. That is why mid moves together with lo in this branch: the element that arrived is already checked. A 2 can never come from lo — every 2 found so far sits past hi.

cards.q: Sort Colors in an interview, out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
items: Clarify: only 0, 1 and 2? In place? Are two passes allowed?
Name the simple options: counting in two passes, O(n), or Array.Sort in O(n log n)
The one-pass idea: four zones and the pointers lo, mid, hi
Code it, stating the zone invariant; mid does not move after a swap with hi
Run [2, 0, 2, 1, 1, 0] step by step
Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) memory, one pass
Edge cases: empty array, one element, all equal, no ones at all
cards.explain: First the conditions and the simple counting solution — it is already O(n), and you should say so. Then what the problem is really about: the zone invariant and its one subtlety, mid after a swap with hi. The example [2, 0, 2, 1, 1, 0] exercises both swap branches.

cards.q: Match the task with the tool.
pairs: Order of equals matters, rare call
Every frame, no garbage, keys and data
Layer, order, depth in one comparison
Three values in place in one pass

lessons.title: Intervals
lessons.sub: Merging after sorting by start, inserting in O(n), greedy by end, and a sweep for a timeline of buffs and sounds

cards.title: Merge Intervals: the problem and the signals
cards.body:
Merge Intervals (LeetCode #56). You get an array of intervals [start, end]. Merge all overlapping ones and return non-overlapping intervals that cover the same points. n ≤ 10⁴, endpoints from 0 to 10⁴. The intervals are closed: [1, 4] and [4, 5] share the point 4 and merge into [1, 5].

Signals of the interval family: the input is "start — end" pairs (times, ranges, segments on an axis), and the question is to merge, insert, remove the fewest, or count how many overlap at once. The reflex is to sort: by start (merge, insert) or by end (pick as many non-overlapping ones as possible).

When two intervals overlap. It is easier to say when they do not: one ended before the other started. Negating that gives the condition: a.start ≤ b.end and b.start ≤ a.end. For half-open [start, end) it is the same with strict signs: touching [1, 4) and [4, 5) is no longer an overlap. Time in games is usually half-open: a buff from second 10 lasting 5 seconds is [10, 15), and at 15 it is gone. Ask which convention applies at the start.

cards.q: Do the intervals [5, 9] and [2, 5] overlap as closed intervals? And [5, 9) and [2, 5) as half-open ones?
options: Closed — yes, they share the point 5; half-open — no
Both pairs overlap
Neither pair overlaps
Closed — no; half-open — yes
cards.explain: Closed: 5 ≤ 5 and 2 ≤ 9 — both conditions hold, the point 5 belongs to both. Half-open: you need 5 < 5, which is false: [2, 5) ends exactly where [5, 9) begins and does not contain 5.

wrong.1: For half-open intervals the signs are strict: 5 < 5 does not hold. [2, 5) does not contain the point 5.
wrong.2: The closed ones do share the point 5: 5 ≤ 5 and 2 ≤ 9.
wrong.3: The other way round: closing adds the endpoints, so closed intervals overlap at least wherever half-open ones do.

cards.title: The idea: after sorting by start, only the last block matters
cards.body:
Naively you merge any two overlapping intervals while such a pair exists: one pass over the pairs is O(n²), and there can be up to n passes. With n = 10⁴ that is 10⁸ checks per pass — too expensive.

What sorting by start buys. Overlapping intervals end up next to each other. If the next interval starts after the end of the current block, so do all later ones: their starts are no smaller. So you only ever compare with the last block of the result.

Invariant: res holds non-overlapping blocks in ascending order; all but the last are final, and the last can still grow. On an overlap, extend the last block to the max of the ends: an interval may lie entirely inside the block and must not shorten it. No overlap — open a new block. Time O(n log n) for the sort plus O(n) for the pass, O(n) memory for the answer. res[^1] is the last element, an index from the end (C# 8, works in Unity).

In a game: shield durations during a fight — "for how many seconds was at least one shield active" is the total length of the merged blocks; occupied ranges on a sound track; invulnerability windows from several sources.
cards.deep:
Why it is correct. Let the intervals be sorted by start, and let the current block [S, E] be the union of intervals 0 through i−1 of this run. If start_i > E, every later interval has start ≥ start_i > E — none of them touches what is already collected, and the block is closed for good. If start_i ≤ E, interval i overlaps the block and the union is [S, max(E, end_i)]. Induction on i.

Without allocations. You can write the answer straight into the sorted array: keep the index k of the last block, on a new block do a[++k] = a[i], and at the end the first k + 1 elements are the answer. O(1) memory on top of the sort.

Not an array of arrays. An int[][] is n separate heap objects and a sort with a delegate. In your own code, keep intervals as struct Interval { public int Start, End; } or as two arrays starts and ends — then Array.Sort(starts, ends) from the previous lesson sorts by start with direct comparisons while the ends ride along. In Burst — a NativeArray of structs and a struct comparer.

cards.q: Assemble Merge Intervals. Here the endpoints can be any int values, not just 0..10⁴.
cards.explain: Sort by start with CompareTo: the difference a[0] − b[0] overflows on endpoints like int.MinValue and 1 and gets the wrong sign. The intervals are closed and touching ones merge: ≤. The block end is the max of the two: [4, 5] inside [1, 6] must not shorten the block to 5. And res gets a copy, new[] { iv[0], iv[1] }: otherwise extending a block would silently modify the input array.

cards.task: Step through the trace on [2, 6] [1, 3] [8, 10] [4, 5] [12, 15] [9, 12]. The rig first sorts the intervals by start, then stops twice and asks what happens to the last block.

options.label: The block stays [1, 6]: end = max(6, 5)
The block becomes [1, 5]: end = 5
A new block [4, 5] opens

asks.q: The last block is [1, 6]. The next interval is [4, 5]. What does the code do?
asks.explain: 4 ≤ 6 — an overlap, so the last block is extended. But [4, 5] lies entirely inside [1, 6]: max(6, 5) = 6, and the block does not change. Had the end simply been assigned, the block would shrink to [1, 5] and lose the point 6.

options.label: The block becomes [8, 15]: 12 ≤ 12
A new block [12, 15] opens: they only touch

asks.q: The last block is [8, 12]. The next one is [12, 15]. What does the code do?
asks.explain: The intervals are closed: the point 12 is in both, and iv[0] <= res[^1][1] holds. The block grows to [8, 15]. With half-open intervals the condition would be strict and [12, 15) would open a new block — which is why you ask about the convention up front.

cards.title: Insert Interval (#57): inserting in O(n) without sorting
cards.body:
The problem. The intervals are already sorted by start and do not overlap. Insert a new [s, e] and merge where needed. Appending it and calling Merge costs O(n log n) for the sort, even though the order is already there. One pass in three phases is enough:

1. Entirely to the left: the interval's end is strictly less than s — copy it as is.
2. Overlapping or touching: its start is ≤ e — absorb it: s = min(s, start), e = max(e, end).
3. Add [s, e] and copy everything left — it is entirely to the right.

The signs are where people slip: the intervals are closed and touching ones merge, so phase 1 uses a strict < and phase 2 a non-strict ≤. Time O(n), O(n) memory for the answer. You can find the phase boundaries with binary search in O(log n), but copying is still O(n).

In a game: a character holds a sorted list of windows during which an effect is active; a new application arrives — insert with merging instead of re-sorting the whole list. The example from the code runs on the rig next.

cards.task: Step through inserting [4, 8] into [1, 2] [3, 5] [6, 7] [8, 10] [12, 16] — the example from the code. The rig stops twice and asks which phase an interval falls into: compare its ends with s and e on screen.

options.label: Absorb it: s = 3, e = 8
Copy it as left: its start 3 < s = 4

asks.q: s = 4, e = 8, [1, 2] is already in res. Next is [3, 5]. What does the code do?
asks.explain: Phase 1 looks at the end, not the start: 5 < 4 is false, so [3, 5] is not entirely to the left. Phase 2 checks the start: 3 ≤ 8 — it overlaps the new interval, so we absorb it: s = min(4, 3) = 3, e = max(8, 5) = 8. Had the code compared the start with s, [3, 5] would go to the answer on its own and overlap [3, 8].

options.label: Absorb it: 8 ≤ 8, giving [3, 10]
End phase 2 and add [3, 8]

asks.q: The new interval has grown to [3, 8]. Next is [8, 10]. What does the code do?
asks.explain: The intervals are closed and point 8 belongs to both — touching merges. The phase 2 condition is non-strict: ivs[i][0] <= e, 8 ≤ 8, and e = max(8, 10) = 10. With a strict < the answer would hold [3, 8] and [8, 10] side by side, though they are one block. The next one, [12, 16], starts after 10 — phase 2 ends and [3, 10] goes into res.

cards.q: With ivs = [[1, 2], [5, 6]] and add = [2, 4] this code returns [[1, 2], [2, 4], [5, 6]], but the answer is [[1, 4], [5, 6]]. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: Phase 1 copies intervals that end before the new one starts. With ≤, [1, 2] gets in too: its end 2 equals s = 2, the intervals touch and by the problem statement must merge. It needs a strict ivs[i][1] < s — then [1, 2] goes to phase 2 and s becomes 1.

cards.title: Non-overlapping Intervals (#435): greedy by end
cards.body:
The problem. What is the minimum number of intervals to remove so that the rest do not overlap? Here touching does not count as overlapping: [1, 2] and [2, 3] coexist. Removing the fewest is the same as keeping the most pairwise non-overlapping intervals: the classic scheduling problem — one meeting room, as many meetings as possible.

The greedy choice: sort by end and take the interval that ends first; skip everything that starts before its end; repeat. The earlier it ends, the more room is left for the rest.

Why not by start. [1, 100], [2, 3], [4, 5]: by start you take [1, 100] first and throw out both others, while by end you keep [2, 3] and [4, 5] and remove one. Nor by length: [1, 5], [4, 7], [6, 10] — the shortest, [4, 7], blocks both neighbours, while by end you keep two. The rigorous proof — an exchange argument — is in the fourth lesson.

The code: end is the end of the last kept interval. A start ≥ end — keep it and move the line, otherwise remove it. O(n log n), O(1) memory on top of the sort. In a game: one announcer voice channel — as many lines as possible without overlap.
cards.deep:
Arrows and balloons (#452, Minimum Number of Arrows to Burst Balloons): balloons are intervals, and an arrow at point x bursts every balloon containing it. The minimum number of arrows is the same greedy: by end, shoot at the end of the first one, skip everything that starts no further right than that point. The difference from #435 is that touching counts here (an arrow at a shared point bursts both), so a new shot needs a strict start > arrow.

When greedy by end fails. If meetings have weights (a payoff) and you maximize the total rather than the count, the earliest end can crowd out one expensive meeting. That is DP: sort by end, for each meeting binary-search the last compatible one and take max(take, skip) — O(n log n). DP is in the backtracking and dynamic programming unit.

Why int.MinValue instead of the first interval. A starting line at "minus infinity" guarantees the first interval by end is taken and removes a separate branch for an empty array.

cards.task: Step through the trace on [1, 3] [2, 4] [3, 5] [1, 2] [5, 7] [4, 6]. The rig sorts the intervals by end and asks once what the code will do. Touching is not an overlap here.

options.label: Keep it: 2 ≥ 2, the line moves to 4
Remove it: its start 2 equals the line

asks.q: [1, 2] is kept and the line is at 2; [1, 3] has been removed. The next by end is [2, 4]. What does the code do?
asks.explain: [2, 4] starts exactly where [1, 2] ended — that is touching, and in this problem touching does no harm. iv[0] >= end: 2 ≥ 2 — keep it, the line moves to 4. Later [4, 6] is kept the same way (4 ≥ 4), while [3, 5] and [5, 7] start before the line and go: 3 removed, 3 kept.

cards.title: Unity: a timeline of buffs and sounds — the sweep
cards.body:
A timeline raises two different questions.

"For how many seconds was at least one buff active?" — merge the intervals as in Merge Intervals and add up the block lengths. An overlap of two buffs is not counted twice.

"How many sounds play at once at the peak?" (Meeting Rooms II, #253 — how many meeting rooms you need). This is a sweep: walk through time, each start is +1, each end is −1, and the answer is the maximum of the running sum. It is convenient to keep starts and ends in two sorted arrays and move two pointers over them. The subtlety is equal times: sounds are half-open [start, end), and a sound that ends at 2 does not overlap one that starts at 2. So at equal times ends are processed before starts — in the code that is e[j] <= s[i]. O(n log n).

Why this matters in Unity. The peak of simultaneous sounds is the size of your AudioSource pool: fewer and sounds get cut off, more and you hold idle objects. The engine has its own limit too: Max Real Voices in Project Settings → Audio, 32 by default; beyond it Unity makes voices virtual — the quietest and lowest-priority ones go silent.

cards.task: Step through the sweep for the sounds [0, 3) [1, 2) [2, 5) [3, 4). The rig calls them meetings and the AudioSources rooms R1, R2: a source whose sound has ended goes back to the pool and serves the next one. The counter is how many play right now, its peak is the pool size. The rig stops where an end and a start fall on the same time.

options.label: The end of [1, 2) first: 1 plays, R2 is free
The start of [2, 5) first: 3 play, a new peak

asks.q: [0, 3) and [1, 2) are playing, the peak is 2. At time 2, [1, 2) ends and [2, 5) starts. What does the code handle first?
asks.explain: At equal times ends go before starts: the sounds are half-open, and [1, 2) is already silent at time 2. The counter drops to 1, R2 is freed, and [2, 5) takes it — the peak stays 2. Handling the start first would count three sounds at once and add a spare AudioSource to the pool. At time 3 the same happens with [0, 3) and [3, 4): the peak never goes above 2.

cards.q: Merge Intervals in an interview, out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
items: Clarify: closed or half-open intervals, does touching merge, is the input sorted, may I modify the array
Naive: merge pairs while overlaps remain — O(n²) per pass
The idea: after sorting by start, an interval can only overlap the last block
Code it, stating the invariant: blocks in res do not overlap, only the last one grows
Run [1, 3] [2, 6] [4, 5] [8, 10] — an interval inside a block
Complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) for the answer
Edge cases: one interval, everything merges into one, touching endpoints, nested intervals
cards.explain: First of all, the boundary convention: the sign in the condition depends on it. The example with [4, 5] inside [1, 6] checks the max when extending, and touching endpoints check that very sign.

cards.q: Match the question with the technique.
pairs: By start, extend the last block
Three phases in O(n), no sorting
Remove the fewest so none overlap
By end, take the one ending first
How many AudioSources the pool needs
Seconds with at least one buff active
Merge, then add up the lengths

lessons.title: One-pass greedy
lessons.sub: The minimum so far, the farthest reachable point, and Kadane: "extend or start over"

cards.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock: what you need from the past at step j
cards.body:
Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock (LeetCode #121). prices[i] is the price on day i. Buy once and sell on one of the later days; find the largest profit, or 0 if no profit is possible. n ≤ 10⁵, prices up to 10⁴. Example: [7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4] → 5: buy at 1, sell at 6.

Naively you try every pair "buy on i, sell on j > i": O(n²), about 5·10⁹ for n = 10⁵ — too slow.

The question that unlocks one-pass greedy: what do I actually need from the past at step j? To sell on day j you do not need the whole history, just one number — the lowest price before j. If the past boils down to one or two numbers (a minimum, a maximum, the farthest point), you update them on the fly, and the solution is O(n) time and O(1) memory.

Signals in the problem: the answer is built from pairs i < j or from a prefix, the order of elements is fixed (days, indices), and "the best so far" does not depend on what comes later.

cards.q: In which problems is everything you need from the past just one or two numbers updated on the fly? Select all that apply.
options: The largest difference a[j] − a[i] with i < j
Whether the array contains two equal numbers
The largest health drawdown: the peak so far minus the current value
How many times each word of a text occurs
The second largest element of an array
cards.explain: The difference is the stock problem again: the minimum so far. The drawdown is the mirror image: the maximum so far minus the current value. The second largest is two numbers, the first and second maximum. Duplicates and word counts cannot be reduced to a couple of numbers: you have to remember everything seen — a set or a dictionary from the hash table unit.

cards.title: The idea: the minimum so far
cards.body:
Walk the days keeping two numbers. minPrice is the lowest price among the days seen: the best buy day for any sale from now on. best is the best profit among the sales that could already have happened.

Invariant: after step j, minPrice = min(prices[0..j]) and best is the maximum of prices[b] − prices[a] over all a ≤ b ≤ j. A new day either updates the minimum or yields a candidate p − minPrice.

A new minimum does not reset best: the earlier deal is already counted, and the minimum only serves future sales. The order of the two lines in the loop does not affect the answer: if you update the minimum first, selling on the same day gives 0, which does not spoil the maximum.

In a game: telemetry — the largest FPS drop from a previous peak (maximum so far), or the largest rating gain between two matches (minimum so far). One pass over the history, no pairs.
cards.deep:
It is Kadane on differences. Let d[i] = prices[i] − prices[i − 1]. The profit from buying at a and selling at b is the sum of d[a + 1..b], a subarray of differences. The maximum profit is the maximum subarray sum of d (or 0). Kadane's algorithm is further on in this lesson.

The proof in one sentence. The optimal deal (a, b) is considered at step b: by then minPrice ≤ prices[a], so the candidate prices[b] − minPrice is at least the optimum, and it cannot exceed the optimum because it is a real deal too.

int.MaxValue as the start. The first price is bound to become the minimum, and an empty array returns 0 without a separate branch. p − minPrice cannot overflow: by then minPrice is no greater than p.

cards.q: Assemble the one-pass solution.
cards.explain: The minimum starts at int.MaxValue so the first price replaces it right away; starting at 0 it would never update. The minimum is Math.Min, the profit is sale minus purchase: p − minPrice. Starting at int.MinValue would break the minimum, and minPrice − p is a loss.

cards.task: Step through the trace on [4, 9, 2, 8, 1, 5]. The rig stops twice and asks what the code will do on the next day. Watch two numbers: the minimum so far and the best profit.

options.label: minPrice = 2, best stays 5
best resets to 0: the old purchase no longer counts
minPrice stays 4: you must buy before the best sale

asks.q: Days 0 and 1 are done: minPrice = 4, best = 5 (buy at 4, sell at 9). Day 2, price 2. What does the code do?
asks.explain: Two is a new minimum: the best purchase for every future sale. The profit of 5 is already earned and stays in best. The minimum serves the future and best records the past, so neither resets the other.

options.label: Profit 8 − 2 = 6 — a new best
Profit 8 − 4 = 4, best stays 5
Profit 9 − 2 = 7

asks.q: Day 3, price 8. minPrice = 2, best = 5. What does the code do?
asks.explain: A sale on day 3 is compared with the cheapest day before it — that is 2, not 4. 8 − 2 = 6 > 5 — a new best. 9 − 2 is not a deal: the nine came before the two, and you cannot sell before you buy. Later the minimum becomes 1, but 5 − 1 = 4 does not beat the record: the answer is 6.

cards.title: Jump Game (#55): the farthest reachable point
cards.body:
The problem. nums[i] is the longest jump from cell i (you may jump any distance from 1 to nums[i]). You start at 0. Can you reach the last cell? n ≤ 10⁴.

Naively you mark reachable cells: from every reachable i, mark i + 1 … i + nums[i]. That is O(n²): each cell may mark up to n neighbours.

The observation: the set of reachable cells is always a range [0, reach]. If you can jump to j, you can also land on any cell in between: a jump can be any length up to the maximum. So one number is enough — reach, the farthest reachable cell.

Invariant: before step i, all cells 0..reach are reachable and nothing beyond is. If i > reach, cell i cannot be reached, nor can anything to its right: the answer is false. Otherwise reach = max(reach, i + nums[i]). A zero in nums[i] is dangerous only if reach sits exactly on it: a zero inside the range is jumped over.

In a game: validating a procedurally generated corridor level where each point has its own dash range — can the level be completed? One pass instead of a path search.

cards.task: Step through the trace on [3, 2, 1, 0, 4]. There is a long jump at the end of the array, but the rig will stop and ask whether the code ever gets to it.

options.label: return false: i = 4 > reach = 3
reach = max(3, 4 + 4) = 8 — and true
It skips i = 4 and returns true at the end of the loop

asks.q: Cells 0–3 are done, reach = 3 — exactly on cell 3 with its zero, not beyond it. Next is i = 4, nums[4] = 4. What does the code do?
asks.explain: Each of the cells 0–3 reaches exactly 3: 0 + 3, 1 + 2, 2 + 1, 3 + 0. The four in nums[4] would jump to the end, but you cannot get into cell 4 itself: i > reach. The trap is a zero sitting exactly on the reach boundary: there is nothing to jump over it with. A zero left of the boundary would be harmless.

cards.title: Kadane (#53): extend or start over
cards.body:
Maximum Subarray (#53). The largest sum of a non-empty subarray. n ≤ 10⁵, numbers from −10⁴ to 10⁴. Trying all subarrays with prefix sums is O(n²), about 5·10⁹.

The idea. Ask for each position i: what is the best sum of a subarray that ends exactly at i? There are two options: extend the best one ending at i − 1, or start over with nums[i] alone. cur = max(nums[i], cur + nums[i]): if the running sum is negative, it only drags you down — better to start fresh. The answer is the maximum of cur over all i.

This is dynamic programming with a single cell: dp[i] = max(nums[i], dp[i − 1] + nums[i]), and only the last dp is needed — the array collapses into a variable. Dynamic programming is covered in depth in the backtracking and DP unit.

Start from nums[0], not 0: the subarray is non-empty, and in an all-negative array the answer is the largest of them. No overflow: |sum| ≤ 10⁵ · 10⁴ = 10⁹. In a game: the luckiest stretch of a run, when each round has a known income minus spending. The rig runs it next.
cards.deep:
Why it is correct. The best subarray ending at i is either nums[i] alone, or the best subarray ending at i − 1 plus nums[i]: if some non-best subarray ended at i − 1, swapping in the best one would not decrease the sum. That gives the recurrence, and the global answer is the maximum over all ends.

The subarray bounds. Remember the start whenever cur starts over (nums[i] > cur + nums[i], i.e. cur < 0), and copy the pair "start, i" whenever best improves.

Other solutions. Divide and conquer gives O(n log n) and sometimes comes up as a follow-up: "now without Kadane". Through prefix sums: max(P[j] − min P[i < j]) — the stock problem again, just on prefixes. All three are the same thing: "the best so far" in one number.

cards.task: Step through Kadane on [2, −5, 3, −1, 4, −10, 2]. The rig stops twice and asks whether the code extends the run or starts over. Watch two numbers: cur and best.

options.label: Start over: cur = 3
Extend: cur = −3 + 3 = 0

asks.q: i = 2, x = 3, cur = −3, best = 2. What does the code do?
asks.explain: cur = max(x, cur + x) = max(3, 0) = 3. The running sum −3 is negative and only drags down: a subarray ending at i = 2 is better off starting at x itself. The run is now [3], and best becomes 3 right away.

options.label: Extend: cur = 6 − 10 = −4, best stays 6
Start over: cur = −10

asks.q: i = 5, x = −10, cur = 6, best = 6. What does the code do?
asks.explain: max(−10, 6 − 10) = −4: extending still beats starting at −10 — the comparison is with x alone, not with zero. cur falls to −4, but best remembers 6: the answer is the maximum over the whole pass, not the last cur. On the next step the negative cur loses to x = 2 and the code starts over — but best no longer changes.

cards.q: On [-3, -1, -2] this code returns 0, but the answer is −1. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: Math.Max(0, …) allows an empty subarray with sum 0, while the problem requires a non-empty one. On all-negative input cur becomes 0 every time, and best = 0. Starting over means starting from x itself: cur = Math.Max(x, cur + x). Then cur = 0 at the start is harmless: the first step gives max(x, x) = x.

cards.title: Variations: what else one pass solves
cards.body:
Stock with unlimited deals (#122). You may buy and sell any number of times, holding at most one share. The answer is the sum of all rises: every prices[i] − prices[i − 1] > 0 is a separate deal. A long rise over several days gives the same total as one deal from the bottom to the peak.

Jump Game II (#45). Reaching the end is guaranteed — find the minimum number of jumps. Greedy by "layers": curEnd is the boundary of cells reachable with the current number of jumps, farthest is how far you can get from them. When you reach curEnd, the layer is over: one more jump, and the new boundary is farthest. It is a breadth-first search without a queue, O(n).

Maximum product subarray (#152). Minus times minus is plus, so you keep two numbers ending at i: the maximum and the minimum. A negative nums[i] swaps their roles.

A circular array (#918). The best subarray either does not wrap around — plain Kadane — or it does, and then it is "everything minus the worst subarray": total − minSub. The exception is an all-negative array: there total − minSub corresponds to an empty subarray, and the answer is plain Kadane.
cards.deep:
Why layers give the minimum. The cells reachable in at most k jumps form a range starting at 0 (for the same reason as in Jump Game), and the next layer extends it up to farthest. It is a breadth-first search on the graph "cell → cells a jump can land on", where the layers are ranges, so no queue is needed. The loop runs to n − 2: there is no need to jump from the last cell.

When one pass is not enough. Stocks with a fee, with a one-day "cooldown" after selling, or with at most k deals involve several states: "holding a share" and "not holding" (and the deal number). That is DP over states, waiting in the DP unit. The sign: the answer at step i depends not on a single "best so far" but on which state you arrived in.

cards.q: Maximum Subarray in an interview, out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
items: Clarify: is the subarray non-empty? What are n and the values, is int enough?
Naive: all subarrays via prefix sums — O(n²)
The idea: the best sum ending at i — extend the previous one or start over
Code with the invariant: cur is the best sum ending at i, best is the best overall
Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) memory
Edge cases: all negative, one element, sum overflow
cards.explain: The question "is the subarray non-empty" at the start directly determines how cur and best start: nums[0], not 0. The "all negative" edge case at the end checks exactly that.

cards.q: Match the problem with what you keep in one pass.
pairs: The best sum ending at i
Max and min ending at i

lessons.title: Why greedy is correct
lessons.sub: Candy in two passes, a lower bound and the exchange argument — and where greedy breaks: coins 1, 3, 4

cards.title: Candy (#135): the problem and why one pass is not enough
cards.body:
Candy (LeetCode #135, hard). Children stand in a row, each with a rating. Everyone gets at least one candy; a child rated higher than a neighbour gets more candies than that neighbour. Find the minimum number of candies. n ≤ 2·10⁴.

Two subtleties in the statement. Equal ratings require nothing: [1, 2, 2] → 1, 2, 1 — 4 in total, the third child is fine with one. The rule is two-sided: a child is compared with both the left and the right neighbour. A left-to-right pass sees only the left one: on [3, 2, 1] it hands out 1, 1, 1 — not enough for the first two.

Naively you give everyone one candy and fix violations while any remain. On decreasing ratings each pass fixes one more position: up to n passes of O(n) — O(n²), 4·10⁸ steps for n = 2·10⁴.

The question of this lesson is wider than Candy: a greedy solution is easy to come up with and easy to get wrong. In an interview you are expected to explain why it is correct — or find a counterexample.

cards.q: Ratings [1, 3, 2, 2, 1]. What is the minimum number of candies?
options: 9: 1, 3, 2, 2, 1 — equal ratings, equal candies
5: one each
cards.explain: The first two is lower than the three on its left, and on its right is an equal two — no rules apply, one candy is enough. The three is higher than both neighbours, who have one each — it gets 2. The second two is higher than the one on its right — it gets 2. Equal ratings need not get equal candies: 1 + 2 + 1 + 2 + 1 = 7.

wrong.1: Equal ratings require nothing — neither more nor the same. These are extra candies.
wrong.2: That is what one left-to-right pass hands out: the second two is higher than its right neighbour but got the same amount.
wrong.3: The three is higher than its neighbours and must get more than them.

cards.title: The idea: two passes and a lower bound
cards.body:
Pass 1, left to right: if the rating is higher than the left neighbour's, give one more than the neighbour, otherwise 1. That is the minimal distribution satisfying all the "left" rules. Pass 2, right to left: if the rating is higher than the right neighbour's, raise it to max(own, right + 1).

Why max does not break pass 1. The second pass only increases. If child i is higher than its left neighbour, raising i keeps the "more than the left one" rule. If it is lower, the left neighbour comes next in pass 2 and will rise itself if needed. Plain assignment of right + 1 is not allowed: it could lower what pass 1 gave.

Why it is the minimum — a lower bound. Let L be the length of the longest run of neighbours with strictly rising ratings that ends at i (i is its L-th element). In any valid distribution, candies grow by at least one at each step of that run, so i gets at least L. The right side works the same way: if ratings strictly fall for R children going right from i, then i gets at least R. So in any solution i gets at least max(L, R) — and our two passes give exactly max(L, R), and the distribution is valid. You cannot do better.

Time O(n), memory O(n). Pass 1 computes L, pass 2 computes max(L, R) in place.
cards.deep:
O(1) memory. There is a one-pass solution over "slopes": track the length of the current ascent up and descent down. On an ascent add up + 1, on a descent add down (the whole descent shifts up by one), and when the descent grows longer than the preceding ascent, the peak grows by one too. Equal ratings reset both counters. It is more code and easier to get wrong; in an interview you give the two passes first and mention this version as a memory improvement.

The formula as a self-check. candies[i] = max(L[i], R[i]), where L and R are the lengths of the increasing runs reaching i from the left and from the right. Working out L and R on paper for a small example is a quick way to check your code in an interview.

cards.q: Assemble Candy in two passes.
cards.explain: Pass 1 gives one more than the left neighbour. Pass 2 starts at n − 2: the last child has no right neighbour, and starting at n − 1 the code would read ratings[n] and crash. And max rather than assignment: pass 2 must not lower what pass 1 gave.

cards.task: Step through the trace on [1, 2, 3, 4, 2, 5, 4, 3, 2]. The rig only shows steps where a candy count changes. It stops twice during the second pass and asks what comes next.

options.label: It stays 2: pass 1 already gave more than the left neighbour
3 — the same as the right neighbour

asks.q: Pass 2 has reached i = 5: rating 5, and on the right a rating of 4 with 3 candies. After pass 1, i = 5 has 2 candies. How many will it have?
asks.explain: Rating 5 is higher than the right neighbour, so it needs more candies than that neighbour: at least 3 + 1 = 4. Pass 1 gave 2 — enough only against the left neighbour. max(2, 4) = 4, and the left rule still holds: i = 4 has one candy.

options.label: i = 3 keeps 4 = max(4, 1 + 1), and the trace goes straight to the total
i = 3 gets 1 + 1 = 2
i = 3 gets 5: one more than before

asks.q: What is left is i = 4 (rating 2, lower than its right neighbour 5 — no rule applies) and i = 3: rating 4, higher than the 2 on its right; i = 3 has four candies, its right neighbour one. What does the code do?
asks.explain: i = 3 already has 4 > 1 — the right rule holds, max(4, 2) = 4, and the trace does not show this step: nothing changes. Had the code assigned 1 + 1 = 2, the child rated 4 would have fewer candies than the left neighbour rated 3 with three candies. The total is 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 1 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 21.

cards.title: How to prove a greedy solution in an interview
cards.body:
Three ways, most common first.

1. The exchange argument. State the greedy choice precisely. Take any optimal solution O. If its first choice differs from the greedy one, swap in the greedy choice and show the solution stays valid and is no worse. So some optimal solution starts with the greedy choice; what remains is the same problem, smaller — induction.

On Non-overlapping Intervals from the second lesson: the greedy choice g is the interval with the earliest end. Let o be the first interval by end in an optimal set. end(g) ≤ end(o), and all other intervals of the set start no earlier than end(o) — hence no earlier than end(g). Replacing o with g breaks nothing, and the size is the same.

2. "Greedy stays ahead". Show that after every step the greedy solution is at least as good as any other by some measure. Jump Game: after step i, reach is the farthest cell that any path through cells 0..i can get to.

3. A lower bound. Prove that every solution is at least X and exhibit a greedy one equal to X — as in Candy.

The same exchange works in Assign Cookies (#455): the least demanding child gets the smallest cookie that satisfies them. If in an optimum they got a bigger one, swapping with whoever got the smaller suitable cookie leaves no one worse off.
cards.deep:
When greedy works in general. For "pick a maximum-weight subset" problems there is an exact answer: if every subset of a feasible set is feasible too, greedy by decreasing weight is optimal for every choice of weights if and only if the family of feasible subsets is a matroid. Its key property is exchange: from a larger feasible set you can always add an element to a smaller one. An example is the minimum spanning tree: Kruskal's algorithm is greedy on the graphic matroid. But exchange is broader than matroids: sets of non-overlapping intervals are not a matroid — the maximal sets {[1, 100]} and {[2, 3], [4, 5]} differ in size, and greedy works there only in the right order, by end. You do not need the word "matroid" in an interview: an exchange argument for the specific problem is enough.

Scheduling as exchange. In the proof for #435, after replacing o with g you need induction: remove g and everything that starts before end(g), and apply the same reasoning to the rest. That is precisely what the loop with the end line does.

cards.q: In the proof for Non-overlapping Intervals, the first interval by end o of an optimal set is replaced with g, the interval with the earliest end. Why does the set stay free of overlaps?
options: g ends no later than o, and the other intervals of the set start no earlier than the end of o
g is shorter than o
g starts before all the other intervals
After the swap the set has fewer intervals
cards.explain: The other intervals of the set did not overlap o, so they start no earlier than end(o) ≥ end(g). They do not overlap g either. The size of the set is the same, so it is still optimal and now starts with the greedy choice.

wrong.1: Length is irrelevant: greedy by length breaks on [1, 5], [4, 7], [6, 10]. What matters is where the interval ends.
wrong.2: g may well start after o. For the intervals to the right, what matters is the end of g, not its start.
wrong.3: Swapping one for another does not change the size — that is why the set stays optimal.

cards.title: Where greedy breaks: coins 1, 3, 4
cards.body:
Making change: reach a sum with the fewest coins. Greedy takes the largest coin that fits. For 1, 5, 10, 25 (and for most real-world sets of coins and notes) this is optimal. For 1, 3, 4 and a sum of 6 it is not: greedy takes 4 + 1 + 1 — three coins, while 3 + 3 is two. The exchange fails here: no optimal solution starts with the four. Arbitrary denominations need DP, dp[s] = min(dp[s − c] + 1) — it is in the backtracking and DP unit.

Knapsack. Fractional — you may take part of an item — greedy by value per kilogram is optimal, and the proof is an exchange: if a kilogram of a cheap item is in the knapsack while a valuable one is left out, swapping kilogram for kilogram only raises the value. 0/1 — an item whole or not at all — it is not: capacity 50, items (10 kg, 60), (20 kg, 100), (30 kg, 120). By value per kilogram you take the first two — 160, while the optimum is the second and third, 220.

How to catch it in an interview. Before coding, try to break the greedy on 2–3 elements: odd denominations, a long cheap item against a short valuable one. If it does not break, look for a proof using one of the three methods. If it breaks, that is your signal for backtracking or DP.

In games greedy is often an honest heuristic rather than an exact algorithm: packing sprites into an atlas (the exact problem is NP-hard), fitting effects into a frame budget of milliseconds (that is a knapsack). Greedy by "value per millisecond" is fine, but say out loud that it is not optimal.
cards.deep:
Canonical coin systems. A set of denominations on which greedy is optimal for every sum is called canonical. You do not have to check every sum: it is known that if the set contains 1 and a counterexample exists, the smallest one is less than the sum of the two largest denominations. For 1, 3, 4 that is 6 < 7 — exactly our example. So the check is DP or brute force up to that bound.

Greedy inside exact algorithms. Dijkstra is a greedy choice of the nearest vertex, and it is correct only with non-negative weights: a negative edge breaks the argument "the nearest one is already final". Same pattern: a greedy choice plus the condition under which the exchange works.

cards.q: Where does the greedy choice give the optimum? Select all that apply.
options: Coins 1, 5, 10, 25: take the largest coin that fits
Coins 1, 7, 10 and a sum of 14: take the largest coin that fits
As many non-overlapping intervals as possible: take the one ending first
0/1 knapsack: take items by decreasing value per kilogram
Fractional knapsack: take items by decreasing value per kilogram
As many non-overlapping intervals as possible: take the shortest one
cards.explain: On 1, 5, 10, 25 greedy is optimal for every sum. On 1, 7, 10 it is not: greedy gives 10 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 — five coins, while 7 + 7 is two. The earliest end is proven by exchange. The fractional knapsack is exchange too: trade a kilogram of the cheap item for a kilogram of the valuable one. The 0/1 knapsack breaks on (10, 60), (20, 100), (30, 120) with capacity 50, and the shortest interval breaks on [1, 5], [4, 7], [6, 10].

cards.q: On [1, 2, 3, 4, 2] this code hands out 1, 2, 3, 2, 1 — 9 in total, but the answer is 11. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: After pass 1 the four has 4 candies. Pass 2 sees that 4 is higher than the two on its right and assigns 1 + 1 = 2 — a decrease. Now rating 4 has fewer candies than rating 3 on its left. It needs Math.Max(candies[i], candies[i + 1] + 1): pass 2 may only raise.

cards.q: Candy in an interview, out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
items: Clarify: do equal ratings require anything? What is n?
Naive: fix violations while any remain — O(n²) on decreasing ratings
The idea: a left pass fixes the left rules, a right pass with max fixes the right ones
Why it is minimal: i gets at least the length of the increasing run from the left and from the right
Run [1, 0, 2] — the answer is 5
Complexity: O(n) time, O(n) memory
Edge cases: one child, all equal, strictly decreasing ratings
cards.explain: For a greedy problem the "why it is minimal" step is a required part of the explanation, not a deep-dive extra: without it the interviewer cannot tell whether you guessed or understand. Strictly decreasing ratings check that pass 2 starts at n − 2 and lifts the whole chain.

cards.q: Match the problem with a way to prove (or refute) the greedy.
pairs: Lower bound: runs from left and right
Exchange: earliest end replaces the first
Exchange: least demanding gets the smallest

lessons.title: Final: sorting, intervals and greedy
lessons.sub: Recognize the technique from the statement, predict a merge, spot a wrong sort, test a greedy with a counterexample

cards.q: Meeting Rooms (#252): meetings [start, end), n up to 10⁴. Can one person attend all of them? Which technique?
options: Sort by start and compare neighbours: start[i] < end[i − 1] is a conflict; O(n log n)
Check every pair — you cannot beat O(n²)
Sort by length and check starting from the short ones
Kadane over the meeting durations
cards.explain: After sorting by start, only the previous meeting can overlap a meeting — the same thought as "only the last block matters" in Merge Intervals. Meetings are half-open, so the sign is strict: ending at 10 and starting at 10 is not a conflict.

wrong.1: Pairs are unnecessary: if meeting i does not overlap the previous one by start, it does not overlap earlier ones either — they ended even sooner, or a conflict has already been found.
wrong.2: Length does not determine who overlaps whom. Sorting by start is what makes meetings neighbours in time.
wrong.3: Kadane finds the subarray with the largest sum — it does not check overlaps in time.

cards.q: New problems. Match the problem with the technique.
pairs: How many meeting rooms all the meetings need (#253)
How many seconds a player was stunned, with overlapping stuns
Merge and add up the lengths
The best run of consecutive rounds by total score
Can a runner clear a corridor where each point has its own dash length
Fewest arrows to burst all interval balloons (#452)

cards.task: A new input: [5, 8] [1, 2] [6, 7] [2, 4] [10, 13] [13, 14] [9, 10]. Step through the trace; the rig sorts the intervals by start and asks once what the code will do.

options.label: A new block [5, 8]: 5 > 4
The block becomes [1, 8]: 4 and 5 are adjacent integers

asks.q: The last block is [1, 4]. The next by start is [5, 8]. What does the code do?
asks.explain: An interval is every point from its start to its end, not a set of integers: between 4 and 5 lies (4, 5), which belongs to no interval. The condition iv[0] <= res[^1][1] — 5 ≤ 4 — is false, so a new block opens. Next, [6, 7] falls inside [5, 8], while [9, 10], [10, 13] and [13, 14] merge by touching: the answer is [1, 4] [5, 8] [9, 14].

cards.q: Non-overlapping Intervals: on [[1, 100], [2, 3], [4, 5]] the code returns 2, but the answer is 1. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: Sorting by start: [1, 100] is taken first, the line moves to 100, and both short ones are removed. The greedy choice in this problem is the earliest end: a[1].CompareTo(b[1]). Then [2, 3] and [4, 5] stay and only [1, 100] is removed. The rest of the code is correct.

cards.q: Every frame, 2000 transparent particles of your own system must be sorted back to front; there are no layers, depth ≥ 0. What is cheapest?
options: The key is ~(depth bits) as a uint, then Array.Sort(keys, ids, 0, count)
particles.OrderByDescending(p => p.Depth).ToArray()
List.Sort with a lambda that computes the distance to the camera in every comparison
Two List.Sort calls: first by id, then by depth
cards.explain: For a float ≥ 0 the bits grow with the value, and inverting them gives "far ones first". The keys are uints: direct comparison without a delegate, only the filled part is sorted, no new objects.

wrong.1: OrderByDescending creates a buffer, key and index arrays and a result array every frame — garbage for the GC.
wrong.2: The distance is computed about 2·n·log₂ n times instead of n, plus a delegate call per comparison, and capturing the camera creates a closure.
wrong.3: The second Sort will not keep the id order — it is unstable. Nor is it needed: equal depths decide nothing for transparents.

cards.q: Coins 1, 6, 10, sum 12. What does greedy change-making ("the largest coin that fits") give, and what is the optimum?
options: Greedy gives 3 coins (10 + 1 + 1), the optimum is 2 (6 + 6) — you need DP
Greedy gives 2 coins — that is the optimum
Greedy gives 3 coins — and that is the optimum
Greedy finds no change at all
cards.explain: Greedy takes 10, and the remaining 2 can only be ones: three coins. But 6 + 6 is two. As with 1, 3, 4: no optimal solution starts with the largest coin, the exchange fails, so you need DP over sums.

wrong.1: After the ten, 2 is left, and a six does not fit into 2: only 1 + 1.
wrong.2: 6 + 6 = 12 is two coins, fewer than three.
wrong.3: There is a one, so greedy always covers the remainder — the only question is how many coins.

cards.q: Prices [3, 5, 1, 4, 2, 6], unlimited deals (holding at most one share). What is the largest profit?
cards.explain: The sum of all rises: 5 − 3 = 2, 4 − 1 = 3, 6 − 2 = 4 — 9 in total. Each rise is a separate deal, and the falls are skipped.

wrong.1: 5 is a single deal (buy at 1, sell at 6), problem #121. Here deals are unlimited.
wrong.2: That is two deals out of three: 3 + 4. The rise 3 → 5 is profitable too.
wrong.3: That is only the rise 1 → 4. There are also 3 → 5 and 2 → 6.

cards.q: A new problem: Meeting Rooms II (#253) — how many rooms meetings [start, end) need. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
items: Clarify: are meetings half-open? Do an end at 10 and a start at 10 share one room?
Naive: for each start, count the meetings in progress at that moment — O(n²)
The idea: a sweep — a start is +1, an end is −1, the answer is the peak of the sum
Code: starts and ends in two sorted arrays, two pointers, ends before starts
Run [0, 30) [5, 10) [15, 20) — the answer is 2
Complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) for the array copies
Edge cases: no meetings, all at once, back-to-back meetings
cards.explain: The answer to the back-to-back question decides the sign in the code: e[j] <= s[i], ends before starts. The example [0, 30) [5, 10) [15, 20) shows that the second and third meetings can share the same room.

cards.q: What is true about complexity? Select all that apply.
options: Merge Intervals is O(n log n), because of the sort
Insert Interval on sorted input is O(n)
Array.Sort is O(n²) in the worst case
Counting sort of 10⁶ values from 0 to 100 is O(n + k)
Two-pass Candy is O(n) time and O(1) memory
Kadane is O(n) time and O(1) memory
cards.explain: Merging is a sort plus a pass. Insertion needs no sort: three phases in one pass. Counting is n for the counters and k for the prefixes. Kadane keeps two numbers. But Array.Sort is introspective: on deep recursion it switches to heapsort, so the worst case is O(n log n). Two-pass Candy stores the candy array — O(n) memory.

units.title: Heaps and top-K
units.blurb: A size-k heap versus quickselect, frequencies and nearest points, merging k lists and a streaming median. PriorityQueue in .NET 6+ and your own heap for Unity.

lessons.title: A heap of size k
lessons.sub: The k-th largest in O(n log k), quickselect in O(n) on average, EnqueueDequeue and your own heap for Unity

cards.title: The problem and its signals
cards.body:
Kth Largest Element in an Array (LeetCode #215). Given an array nums and a number k, return the k-th largest element — the k-th in descending sorted order, not the k-th distinct value: in [3, 2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 5, 5, 6] with k = 4 the answer is 4, because the descending order is 6, 5, 5, 4. Constraints: 1 ≤ k ≤ n ≤ 10⁵, |nums[i]| ≤ 10⁴, and the statement explicitly asks you to do it without sorting.

Signals that a heap will help:

1. You need not the whole order, only the k best (or worst), or the k-th of them.
2. You need the current minimum or maximum of a changing set again and again: take the best one out, put a new one in.
3. The data arrives as a stream, and the answer is needed after every element or at any moment.

Here it is signal 1. In the related problem Kth Largest Element in a Stream (#703), signal 3 joins it.
cards.code:
int a = FindKthLargest(new[] { 3, 2, 1, 5, 6, 4 }, 2);          // 5
int b = FindKthLargest(new[] { 3, 2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 5, 5, 6 }, 4); // 4: 6, 5, 5, 4

cards.q: Which problems does a heap solve? Select all.
options: Once a second a server takes the job with the earliest deadline from a queue, and new jobs keep arriving
The top 10 scores out of a million leaderboard records
After each new number of a stream, report the third largest so far
Find two numbers in an array that add up to target
The longest substring without repeating characters
cards.explain: The job queue is signal 2: the minimum deadline, again and again, from a set that keeps changing. The leaderboard is signal 1: you need 10 out of a million, not the whole order. The third largest after each number is signals 1 and 3 — that is exactly #703. A pair with sum target is a partner by exact value, so a hash map. A substring without repeats is a sliding window.

cards.title: Naive solutions and their cost
cards.body:
Sort and take the element at index n − k. Array.Sort is O(n log n): for n = 10⁵ that is about 1.7·10⁶ comparisons, which by the rule of thumb of 10⁸ operations per second is milliseconds. Time-wise sorting passes, and you should say so out loud in the interview. It is rejected for other reasons:

1. Wasted work: all n elements get ordered, while you need one.
2. Array.Sort sorts in place and destroys the input — or you copy it, which is O(n) memory.
3. It does not work on a stream: every new element means sorting again or inserting into the middle of an array in O(n).

Find and strike out the maximum k times — O(n·k). Fine for a small k, but k can be anything up to n.

cards.q: n = 10⁵, k = n / 2. How many operations does “find and strike out the maximum k times” take, and what follows?
options: ≈ 5·10⁹ — tens of seconds, the solution will not pass
≈ 1.7·10⁶ — the same as sorting
≈ 10⁵ — a single pass over the array
cards.explain: Each maximum search is a pass over n elements, and there are k passes: n·k = 10⁵ · 5·10⁴ = 5·10⁹. At about 10⁸ operations per second that is around 50 seconds against a limit of 1–2. Sorting is thousands of times cheaper. A heap of k elements with k = n / 2 costs about as much as sorting — n log k ≈ 1.6·10⁶; it pulls ahead when k is small.

wrong.1: 1.7·10⁶ is n log n for sorting. Here you make k full passes over the array: n·k.
wrong.2: One pass finds one maximum. To get to the k-th you need k passes.

cards.title: The idea: a min-heap of k elements
cards.body:
The brute force searches for the maximum among everything every time, although you only need to remember the k best seen so far. Keep them in a min-heap (how it works is in the lesson on .NET collections: the minimum sits at the root, insertion and removal are O(log size)). The root is the worst of the best, the entry threshold into the top k. The priority is the number itself: Enqueue(x, x). With priority −x the same queue would become a max-heap.

Put every new x into the heap. If it now holds k + 1 elements, Dequeue removes the minimum: it is definitely not among the k largest, since there are k numbers above it.

Invariant: after i elements the heap holds exactly the min(i, k) largest of them, and the root is the k-th largest of those seen. So the answer is Peek() after the pass.

Cost: n insertions at O(log k) each — O(n log k), memory O(k). For n = 10⁶ and k = 10 that is about 3.3·10⁶ steps against 2·10⁷ for sorting. The arrival order does not matter, and you do not need the whole array at once — you can even read it from a file.

Why min and not max: what you need to know quickly is whom to throw out — the weakest of the strong. A max-heap over all n elements also gives the answer (k times Dequeue), but that is O(n) memory, and n insertions cost O(n log n).

In a game: the top 10 scores on a leaderboard, the k most dangerous threats for the AI, the k nearest targets.
flow: the root is the k-th largest

cards.q: Assemble the solution with a min-heap of k elements.
cards.explain: Priority x gives a min-heap with the smallest at the root; with −x the root would be the maximum, and the best elements would be thrown out. Remove once there are k + 1 elements: the condition is Count > k. With >= the heap would keep k − 1 elements, and Peek would return the (k − 1)-th largest. At the end the root is the k-th largest: Peek(), without removing it.

cards.task: Step through the trace on [4, 1, 7, 3, 8, 5, 9, 2], k = 3. The rig stops twice and asks what Dequeue will do. Watch the root: it is the entry threshold into the top three.

asks.q: 9 has arrived: the heap holds 5, 8, 7, 9, size 4 > k. The code calls Dequeue. What will the root be?
asks.explain: Dequeue removes the minimum 5. The last element of the array, 9, takes its place and sinks towards the smaller child: 7 < 8, so it swaps with 7. The heap is 7, 8, 9 with root 7. These are the top three seen so far, and 7 is the new threshold.

asks.q: 2 has arrived — below the threshold 7. The code still called Enqueue, and the 2 rose to the root: 2, 7, 9, 8. What will Dequeue remove?
asks.explain: Dequeue removes the minimum — the 2 itself. The heap is back to 7, 8, 9: the 2 came in and went out, paying for a sift up and a sift down, O(log k) twice. Such a number can be rejected by comparing it with the threshold before inserting — how PriorityQueue does that is in the next card.

cards.title: PriorityQueue: EnqueueDequeue and descending priority
cards.body:
EnqueueDequeue(x, p) (.NET 6) is “add, then immediately take the minimum” in one operation. If the queue is empty or p is not greater than the root’s priority, the method returns x right away and leaves the heap alone. Otherwise x takes the root’s place and sinks — one sift instead of two — and the old root is returned. For “the k best”: the first k elements go in with Enqueue, and from then on only EnqueueDequeue.

DequeueEnqueue(x, p) (.NET 8) is the other way round: it removes the root first and then adds x, even if x is worse. In “the k best” that is a bug: the threshold is thrown out even when x should not get in.

Descending priority means a max-heap. Two ways: the comparer Comparer<int>.Create((a, b) => b.CompareTo(a)), or priority −x with the normal comparison. −x is faster (why — in “Deeper” on the card about your own heap), but it breaks on int.MinValue: in unchecked arithmetic −int.MinValue == int.MinValue, so the smallest number gets the most urgent priority. The comparer b − a instead of b.CompareTo(a) overflows the same way.

Last Stone Weight (#1046): each turn, smash the two heaviest stones y ≥ x. If y = x, both vanish; otherwise a stone of weight y − x remains. Return the weight of the last stone, or 0. “The two maximums, again and again” is signal 2: a max-heap, O(n log n). Re-sorting on every turn is O(n² log n).

cards.task: Step through the Last Stone Weight trace on [2, 7, 4, 1, 8, 1]. The root of the max-heap is the heaviest stone. The rig will ask about the turn with equal stones.

options.label: Smashes two stones of 1: both vanish, one stone is left — the answer is 1
Smashes two stones of 1 and puts a stone of weight 0 back into the heap
Stops: all stones are equal, the answer is 0

asks.q: The heap holds three stones of weight 1. What does the code do on this turn?
asks.explain: y = x = 1, so the condition y != x is false — nothing goes back into the heap. One stone is left, Count = 1, the loop ends: the answer is its weight, 1. A zero in the heap would not spoil the answer (smashing against zero changes nothing), but it is an extra turn, and the code does not make it.

cards.title: Quickselect: O(n) on average
cards.body:
The k-th largest is the element that would land at index n − k after an ascending sort. Quickselect is half of quicksort: partition the range around a pivot and continue only into the part that contains that index.

Three-way partition: smaller than the pivot on the left, equal in the middle, greater on the right. If the index you need falls into the block of equals, you are done.

Cost. With good pivots the work is n + n/2 + n/4 + … ≈ 2n — O(n) on average. In the worst case the pivot is an extreme every time and the range shrinks by one element — O(n²), which for n = 10⁵ is 5·10⁹. That is why the pivot is chosen at random: the worst case does not disappear, but it becomes vanishingly unlikely. A “first element” pivot on already sorted input gives exactly the square.

Duplicates. A plain two-way partition (the Lomuto scheme) on an array of identical numbers cuts off one element at a time — O(n²) whatever the pivot. A three-way partition gathers all the equal ones in the middle in a single pass.

The price: it rearranges the input in place (a copy is O(n) memory), and it needs the whole array at once — it does not work on a stream. Array and List<T> have no ready-made “select the k-th”; you write it by hand.

cards.q: A game server receives 10⁷ match results a day and once a minute shows the top 100 of the day. What do you choose?
options: A min-heap of 100 elements: each result is one comparison with the root, plus O(log 100) if it gets in
Store all results and run quickselect once a minute: it is O(n), faster than a heap
Store all results and sort them once a minute
cards.explain: This is a stream (signal 3), and k is small. A heap of 100 elements is ready at any moment: the top 100 sit in it, and printing them costs 100 · log 100 operations. Memory is 100 records, not 10⁷. Quickselect and sorting need to keep everything and go over the whole backlog again every minute.

wrong.1: O(n) is per run over everything collected. Once a minute that is up to 10⁷ operations and 10⁷ records in memory, while the heap is updated in O(log k) per result and is always ready.
wrong.2: Sorting everything collected once a minute is O(n log n) over and over, plus memory for all 10⁷ records. And you only need 100.

cards.title: Unity: your own binary heap on an array
cards.body:
Unity (.NET Standard 2.1) has no PriorityQueue, so you write your own heap. In Unity interviews you are often asked to write one from scratch — and they expect code with no off-by-one bugs. What matters:

1. Indices. Node i has parent (i − 1) / 2 and children 2i + 1 and 2i + 2. The right child may be missing — hence the check c + 1 < n.
2. A “hole” instead of swaps. When sifting up, do not swap elements at every step: move the parent down and write x once at the end. Half as many writes.
3. Clear the slot. After Pop write a[n] = default: if T is a reference type, the stale reference would otherwise keep the object alive for the collector.
4. Zero allocations. The array grows by doubling; once warmed up, Push and Pop allocate nothing.
5. PushPop mirrors EnqueueDequeue: if x is not greater than the root, return it right away.

A max-heap is the same heap with a descending comparer.
cards.deep:
How .NET does it. PriorityQueue<TElement, TPriority> keeps a single array of tuples (TElement Element, TPriority Priority)[]; the constructor without a capacity starts with an empty array, and it grows by doubling, but by at least 4 elements. The heap is 4-ary (Arity = 4): parent (i − 1) >> 2, first child (i << 2) + 1. Sifting up and down uses the same “hole” as above, and the vacated slot is cleared only if the tuple contains references (RuntimeHelpers.IsReferenceOrContainsReferences).

Why −x is faster than a comparer. If TPriority is a value type and no comparer was passed (or Comparer<T>.Default was passed), the queue stores null instead of a comparer and takes a separate path with Comparer<TPriority>.Default.Compare — the JIT devirtualizes and inlines that call. A custom IComparer is an interface call on every comparison. The difference only shows on a hot path, but you should know the answer to “why”.

A struct comparer in your own heap. The same trick works for your heap: MinHeap<T, TCmp> where TCmp : struct, IComparer<T> with a field TCmp cmp. For a value-type TCmp the JIT compiles a separate copy of the code per type, and Compare is called directly, not through the interface; IL2CPP with IL2CPP Code Generation = Faster runtime (the default) also generates separate code for value-type arguments, so the call becomes direct; in Faster (smaller) builds mode generic code is shared across all arguments, and the gain may be lost.

Building in O(n). From an existing array the heap is built bottom-up: SiftDown for i from n / 2 − 1 down to 0. There are about n / 2ʰ⁺¹ nodes at height h, and each sinks at most h levels: the total n · Σ h / 2ʰ⁺¹ ≤ n. That is how the PriorityQueue constructor from a collection and EnqueueRange into an empty queue work.

What else is missing. Remove(element, out …) only appeared in .NET 9 and costs O(n): it searches for the element linearly. There is no priority update at all — lazy deletion replaces it, covered in the lesson on merging and the median. EnsureCapacity and TrimExcess exist since .NET 6.

cards.q: After a series of Pop calls, a custom heap of positive numbers returned 0, although nobody ever pushed a zero. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: The check c + 1 < n is missing: the last internal node may have only a left child. Then a[c + 1] is a[n] — the slot past the end of the heap, where Pop has just written default, that is 0. On the heap 1, 5, 3: Pop removes 1, n = 2, a[2] = 0; SiftDown sees a “child” 0 < 5, picks it and lifts 0 into the root, while 3 is pushed past the end. Hence the zero.

cards.q: You are solving Kth Largest Element out loud. Put the steps in order.
items: Clarify: k-th in sorted order or among distinct values, may the array be modified, what are n and k
Name sorting: O(n log n), it passes, but it is wasted work and fails on a stream
Idea: keep only the k best in a min-heap; the root is the entry threshold
Write the code, stating the invariant: the heap holds the k largest seen so far
Run [3, 2, 1, 5, 6, 4], k = 2, and show when the root gets removed
State the complexity: O(n log k) time, O(k) memory
Alternative: quickselect — O(n) on average, O(n²) in the worst case, destroys the input
cards.explain: First agree on the statement — “k-th among distinct values” is a different problem, and a ban on modifying the array rules out quickselect without a copy. Then the baseline, the idea with its invariant, the code, a dry run, the complexity. Quickselect comes last, as the answer to “can you do better?”, with its honest price.

lessons.title: Frequencies and nearest points
lessons.sub: A frequency map plus a heap of k, buckets in O(n), K Closest Points without a square root, and the k nearest enemies in Unity

cards.title: The problem: two stages in one
cards.body:
Top K Frequent Elements (LeetCode #347). Given an array nums and a number k, return the k most frequent elements in any order. Constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁵, |nums[i]| ≤ 10⁴, k is at most the number of distinct values, and the answer is unique — there are no ties at the edge of the top. The statement asks for something better than O(n log n).

The problem has two stages, each with its own signal:

1. “How many times” — counters: a map “value → frequency”, one pass, O(n). That is the reflex from the unit on hash maps.
2. “The k best” — the heap of k elements from the previous lesson, except the priority is the frequency, not the value itself.

From here on, m is the number of distinct values: m ≤ n, and the second stage works with m “value, frequency” pairs rather than n elements.
cards.code:
int[] a = TopKFrequent(new[] { 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3 }, 2);   // [1, 2]: ×3 and ×2
// the map after the first stage: { 1 → 3, 2 → 2, 3 → 1 }, m = 3

cards.q: Which problems need both stages — counters and picking the k best? Select all.
options: The 10 most frequent words in a chat log
A match log is a list of killer ids; find the 3 players with the most kills
The k longest words of a text
The first non-repeating character of a string
cards.explain: Frequent words and top killers: first a frequency map, then the top k by frequency. Longest words need only the second stage: a length does not have to be accumulated, it is known at once, so a heap of k by length is enough. The first non-repeating character needs only the first stage: counters and a second pass over the string — there is nothing to pick the k best from.

cards.title: The naive solution: sort the frequencies
cards.body:
Count the frequencies and sort the m pairs by descending frequency: O(n + m log m). In the worst case all values are distinct, m = n = 10⁵ — about 1.7·10⁶ comparisons, so it passes time-wise. But that is exactly the O(n log n) you are asked to beat: the whole map gets sorted, while you need k pairs.

The LINQ version is short, and in an interview you can name it as the baseline. The cost: OrderByDescending copies all m pairs into a buffer, plus iterator objects and the result array — in hot Unity code that is garbage for the GC on every call. In modern .NET the chain OrderBy(…).Take(k) internally orders only the first k (a partial quicksort), but that is an implementation detail: in an interview reason about O(m log m), and the buffer of m pairs is allocated anyway.

GetValueOrDefault is a dictionary extension from .NET Core 2.0 and .NET Standard 2.1, available in Unity: for a new key it returns 0, whereas the indexer count[x] would throw KeyNotFoundException.

cards.title: The idea: a min-heap of k by frequency
cards.body:
The second stage is the same “top k” as in the previous lesson. Walk over the map’s pairs and enqueue the value with the frequency as priority: Enqueue(x, f). If the heap now holds k + 1 pairs, Dequeue removes the rarest one.

Invariant: the heap holds the k most frequent of the pairs seen so far, and the root is the rarest of them, the entry threshold.

Cost: O(n) for the map and O(m log k) for the heap — O(n + m log k), memory O(m + k). With k = 10 and m = 10⁵ the heap is about 3.3·10⁵ steps against 1.7·10⁶ for sorting.

Answer order. Dequeue yields pairs from the rarest to the most frequent, so the array is filled from the end — the most frequent ends up first. The statement allows any order, but interviewers often ask “and in descending order?” — that is your answer.

Ties. PriorityQueue is not stable (the lesson on .NET collections): of two pairs with the same frequency either may be thrown out. Here that is safe — the statement promises no ties at the edge of the top. Without that promise, agree on how ties are broken and put it into the priority: (frequency, value).

cards.q: Assemble the solution: a frequency map and a min-heap of k.
cards.explain: For a new key the indexer count[x] throws KeyNotFoundException, while GetValueOrDefault returns 0. The priority is the frequency f: then the rarest pair sits at the root, and that is the one to remove. With priority x the heap would select by value, and with −f it would throw out the most frequent. Fill the array from the last index k − 1: the rarest of the k comes out first, the most frequent comes out last and lands in res[0]. With i = k the code would run past the end of the array.

cards.task: Step through the trace on [1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4, 4, 4, 5], k = 2. The frequencies are already counted; the rig asks twice whom Dequeue will remove. Watch the frequency at the root.

asks.q: 4 (×4) has arrived. The heap holds 2 (×2), 1 (×3), 4 (×4) — size 3 > k. Whom will Dequeue remove?
asks.explain: The priority is the frequency, and the root of a min-heap holds the smallest: ×2. So 2 leaves, and 1 (×3) and 4 (×4) remain. The new threshold is ×3: from now on only a value seen more than three times gets into the top.

asks.q: 5 (×1) has arrived and risen to the root: 5 (×1), 4 (×4), 1 (×3). Whom will Dequeue remove?
asks.explain: The 5 is rarer than the threshold ×3 — it entered the heap and left right away. That is the same wasted sift up and sift down as in the previous lesson; EnqueueDequeue would have returned it without any work. The result is 1 and 4, the most frequent.

cards.title: Buckets: O(n) without a heap
cards.body:
The frequency of any value is an integer from 1 to n. So instead of comparing by frequency you can distribute: an array buckets of length n + 1, where buckets[f] holds the values that occurred exactly f times. Then walk from f = n downwards and collect until you have k.

This is counting sort by frequency: the keys are small integers in a known range, and no comparisons are needed. Time is O(n): the map takes n, distributing takes m, the walk takes n + 1 buckets. Memory is O(n): the bucket array plus the lists.

When buckets lose to a heap. The bucket array has length n + 1 however many distinct values there are. If n is huge and m is small — 10⁸ events and 1000 distinct ids — buckets allocate 10⁸ references (800 MB on 64 bits), while the heap needs m log k ≈ 3300 steps and O(k) memory. Buckets are good when n is moderate and you want a true O(n). You can use length maxFreq + 1 instead of n + 1, but in the worst case it is the same thing.
cards.deep:
Quickselect on frequencies. Another O(m) on average: write the m distinct values into an array and run the quickselect from the previous lesson, comparing by frequency; the k most frequent end up on one side of position m − k. The worst case is O(m²) and the input gets rearranged, but you do not need a bucket array of length n.

SortedSet as a heap with removal. If the top keeps changing — frequencies go up and down, like a counter of popular items in a game store — a heap lacks priority updates. SortedSet<T> can Remove in O(log n), and Min and Max walk down to the extreme node, also O(log n). Updating a frequency means removing the old pair and inserting the new one.

The trap: equal elements collapse. A set treats elements with CompareTo == 0 as the same. A SortedSet<int> with a “by frequency” comparer returns false from Add on a second value with the same frequency — and the value silently disappears. The key is the pair (frequency, value): a tuple compares field by field, and no two pairs are equal as long as the values are unique. For elements without a natural unique field you add an id or an insertion number.

Ties by rule. In Top K Frequent Words (#692), among equal frequencies the word that comes first alphabetically ranks higher. For a min-heap of k that is the comparer “frequency ascending, then word descending”: the worst candidate must sit at the root, and the worst among equals is the one later in the alphabet. Compare strings with string.CompareOrdinal: the statement has only lowercase Latin letters, and culture-aware comparison is unnecessary here.
