cards.q: A server log holds 10⁸ events with 1000 distinct player ids. You need the 10 most active players. The frequency map is ready — what do you use for the second stage?
options: A heap of 10 by frequency: m log k ≈ 3300 steps, O(k) memory
Buckets: O(n) is always better than O(m log k)
Sort the 1000 pairs by frequency and take 10 — that is the same as buckets
cards.explain: The second stage works with m = 1000 pairs. The heap takes 1000 · log₂ 10 ≈ 3300 steps. Buckets set up an array of length n + 1 = 10⁸ + 1 — 800 MB of references for a thousand values. Sorting 1000 pairs is about 10⁴ comparisons, also instant, but that is neither buckets nor O(n).

wrong.1: The O(n) of buckets is a walk over n + 1 buckets and the memory for them. With n = 10⁸ and m = 1000, a heap over m pairs is orders of magnitude cheaper.
wrong.2: Sorting 1000 pairs is O(m log m), about 10⁴ comparisons: it works, but buckets distribute without comparisons and need an array of length n + 1. They are different techniques with different costs.

cards.title: K Closest Points: distance without a square root
cards.body:
K Closest Points to Origin (LeetCode #973). Given points points[i] = [x, y] and a number k, return the k points closest to the origin, in any order. Constraints: 1 ≤ k ≤ n ≤ 10⁴, |x|, |y| ≤ 10⁴.

No square root needed. The distance is √(x² + y²), and the square root is monotonic: if a² < b², then a < b. Compare squares — no Math.Sqrt and no double. The square is at most 2·10⁸, and int.MaxValue ≈ 2.1·10⁹ — it fits. With coordinates up to 10⁵ it no longer fits: 2·10¹⁰, so compute in long.

The heap mirrors the previous lesson. You need the k smallest distances, so you must throw out the farthest candidate: a max-heap by distance of k elements. The root is the farthest of the k closest, the entry threshold. O(n log k), memory O(k). The rule: for the k smallest use a max-heap, for the k largest a min-heap; the root always holds whoever gets thrown out first. In Unity, use the MinHeap<T> from the previous lesson with the same descending comparer.

Quickselect by distance also works — O(n) on average, at the same price: the input is rearranged and it does not work on a stream.

cards.task: Step through the trace on 7 points, k = 3. The max-heap holds at most k points, with the farthest kept one at the root. The rig asks twice who leaves the heap.

options.label: #1 (5, −1), d = 26 — the root of the max-heap
#3 (1, −2), d = 5 — the nearest
#0 (3, 3), d = 18 — the first to arrive

asks.q: Point #3 (1, −2) arrives, d = 5. The heap holds four points: d = 26, 18, 20 and 5 — that is k + 1. Whom does Dequeue remove?
asks.explain: The root of a max-heap is the farthest point: d = 26. It leaves, d = 18, 20 and 5 stay, and the new threshold is 20: from now on only a nearer point gets in. Removing the nearest one is the min-heap bug: you would be left with the k farthest.

options.label: The new point itself: #4, d = 25
#2 (−2, 4), d = 20 — the old root

asks.q: Point #4 (−4, −3) arrives, d = 25, and rises to the root: it is farther than every kept point (20, 18, 5). Whom does Dequeue remove?
asks.explain: The root is the farthest of the k + 1, and that is the new point itself: 25 > 20. It came in and went straight out; the kept points did not change. The threshold was known in advance: a full heap can compare a new point with the root and not insert it at all.

cards.q: This code returns the k farthest points instead of the closest. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: The default queue is a min-heap: the closest point sits at the root, and Dequeue throws exactly that one out every time. The heap is left with the k farthest. You need a max-heap: a descending comparer or priority −d (the square is at most 2·10⁸, so negation is safe).

cards.title: Unity: the k nearest enemies
cards.body:
A tower needs the k nearest enemies, an AI needs the k nearest pieces of cover. This is #973 in a game, with adjustments for the engine.

sqrMagnitude, not Distance. Vector3.Distance and magnitude take a square root; (a − b).sqrMagnitude does not, and the order is the same. Compare a radius squared too: d < r * r.

Small k — a buffer instead of a heap. For k up to 10–20, keep a sorted array of k: a new enemy is first compared with the worst of the best — almost always a rejection after one comparison — and if it passes, it is put in place by insertion. Worst case O(n·k), in practice O(n) with a tiny constant, and not a single allocation: the buffers are fields, and foreach over a List<T> uses a struct enumerator.

Positions. transform.position is a call into the native side of the engine, not a field read. With thousands of objects, keep positions in your own array and update them once per frame.

When you need a grid. One tower and 200 enemies — a plain pass, 200 comparisons. But if 1000 units look for neighbours every frame, the “everyone with everyone” pass is 10⁶ distances per frame. As a rough estimate that is a few milliseconds, more on a mobile CPU — a noticeable share of the 16 ms budget, and it grows quadratically: 3000 units already means 9·10⁶. Then you need a spatial grid or hash: candidates come only from neighbouring cells, and inside them the same buffer of k. Details are in the unit on pathfinding and space. If the enemies have colliders, Physics.OverlapSphereNonAlloc also gives you the candidates within a radius.

cards.q: Unity: 1000 units, and every frame each one needs its 5 nearest neighbours to avoid collisions. What do you do?
options: A spatial grid: candidates only from neighbouring cells, and inside them a buffer of 5
For each unit, a pass over all the others with a buffer of 5: that is O(n) per unit, linear
For each unit, a min-heap of all 1000 by distance and Dequeue 5 times
cards.explain: A pass over everyone is O(n) per unit, but there are n units: 10⁶ distances per frame — a few milliseconds of a 16 ms budget, more on mobile, and the growth is quadratic. A grid leaves each unit a few dozen candidates from neighbouring cells, and the same buffer picks the five. This is now a question of spatial partitioning, not of heaps.

wrong.1: O(n) is per unit. For all of them it is n², 10⁶ distances per frame: a few milliseconds out of 16, and four times more every time the number of units doubles.
wrong.2: A heap of all 1000 is the same quadratic work, plus n log n for the insertions. And k = 5 already makes a buffer cheaper than a heap.

cards.q: You are solving Top K Frequent Elements out loud. Put the steps in order.
items: Clarify: the answer order, whether there are ties at the edge of the top, what are n and k
Name the two stages: a frequency map in O(n), then picking the k best
Baseline: sort the m pairs by frequency — O(n + m log m)
Idea: a min-heap of k by frequency, the root is the rarest of the best
Write the code and run [1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3], k = 2
Complexity: O(n + m log k) time, O(m + k) memory
If asked for O(n): buckets by frequency — and say when they lose to a heap
cards.explain: The question about ties decides whether you need a composite priority. Naming the two stages up front shows that the problem breaks into familiar parts. Buckets answer “and in O(n)?”, together with their price: an array of length n + 1.

lessons.title: Merging streams and the median
lessons.sub: A heap of the heads of k lists in O(N log k), two heaps for a streaming median, and the median frame time in Unity

cards.title: The problem: k sorted lists
cards.body:
Merge k Sorted Lists (LeetCode #23, hard). Given an array of k linked lists, each sorted in ascending order, merge them into one sorted list and return its head. Constraints: 0 ≤ k ≤ 10⁴, up to 500 nodes per list, N ≤ 10⁴ nodes in total, values up to 10⁴ in absolute value. Empty lists and an empty array are valid input.

Signals for a heap of heads:

1. You have k already ordered sequences and need the overall order.
2. At every step you need the minimum of k candidates — one from each sequence — and once chosen, a candidate is replaced by the next one from the same sequence.

This is signal 2 from the first lesson — “the minimum of a changing set, again and again” — except the set is the heads of the lists. In real life this is how sorted chunks are merged in an external sort of files, how logs from several servers are merged by time, how replay records from several clients are combined.

cards.q: Where does a heap of the heads of k sequences work? Select all.
options: Merge 50 server logs, each sorted by time, into one
The k-th smallest element of an n×n matrix in which every row is sorted
The median of an unsorted array
The longest substring without repeating characters
cards.explain: The logs are exactly Merge k Sorted Lists. The matrix is the same n sorted sequences: the heap holds the row heads, you take the minimum k times and push the next element of the same row (that is #378). The median of an unsorted array is quickselect: there are no ordered pieces there. A substring without repeats is a sliding window: there is one sequence there, not k.

cards.title: Naive solutions and their cost
cards.body:
Collect everything and sort: O(N log N) time and O(N) memory for the array of values. It works, but it ignores the fact that the lists are already sorted, and it does not suit streams that do not fit in memory.

Merge one at a time: result ← merge(result, next list). Merging two is two pointers plus a dummy head dummy: it always has a tail to append to, so the first node needs no special case; the answer is dummy.next. The trouble is that the result grows and is walked again every time. Say there are k lists of n nodes: the merges cost 2n + 3n + … + kn ≈ k²n / 2 = N·k / 2.

Pairwise (divide and conquer): merge the lists in pairs, then pairs of pairs. There are log₂ k levels, each touching N nodes in total — O(N log k), like the heap, and with no extra memory if you merge in place.

cards.q: k = 1000 lists of 100 nodes, N = 10⁵. How many steps does merging one at a time take, and how many does the heap of heads take?
options: ≈ 10⁵ and ≈ 10⁵: both visit each node once
cards.explain: One at a time: N·k / 2 = 10⁵ · 1000 / 2 = 5·10⁷ — the early nodes are walked again in every later merge. The heap: N nodes, each one insertion and one removal at O(log k), log₂ 1000 ≈ 10, about 10⁶ in total. The difference is 50×, and it grows with k.

wrong.1: Only the heap (and pairwise merging, per level) visits each node once. When merging one at a time, the first lists are walked in each of the k merges.
wrong.2: 10⁸ is N·k without dividing by 2, and 1.7·10⁶ is N log N, the cost of sorting everything. A heap of k heads costs N log k.

cards.title: The idea: a heap of heads
cards.body:
The minimum of everything that remains is among the heads of the lists: each list is sorted, so its head is its minimum. It is therefore enough to keep one head from each non-empty list in a min-heap (the priority is the node’s value).

Step: take the smallest head, append it to the answer, push its next into the heap if there is one. A list that runs out simply drops out: the heap shrinks.

Invariant: the heap holds exactly one node from each non-empty list — the first one not yet taken. So the root is the minimum of everything that remains, and the answer grows in ascending order.

Cost: N nodes, each entering and leaving the heap once — O(N log k) time and O(k) memory, not O(N): nodes are not copied, we only relink next.

Equal values. PriorityQueue is not stable, and of two heads with the same value either may come out first. For numbers that does not matter. If you merge events by time and need source order for equal times, use the priority (time, listIndex).
flow: push the head of each list
cards.deep:
Pairwise merging versus the heap. Both are O(N log k). Pairwise merging allocates nothing and needs no heap, but it requires all lists to be at hand. The heap works with streams: it only needs the current head of each source, which is why sorted chunks on disk are merged this way in an external sort — memory holds k heads and read buffers, not N records.

Merging enumerators. The same code works on IEnumerator<T> instead of nodes: the heap holds an enumerator with its Current as priority; after yielding, call MoveNext(), and if it returns true, the enumerator goes back into the heap. The result can be produced with yield return — lazily, one element at a time.

Stability. If, for equal keys, the element from the lower-numbered list must come first, the priority is the tuple (value, listIndex): a tuple compares field by field, and no equal priorities remain. Within one source stability holds by itself — its elements enter the heap one at a time, the next only after the previous one.

Allocations. PriorityQueue<ListNode, int> keeps the pairs in a single array: once it has grown to k, there are no new allocations. Set the capacity in the constructor — new PriorityQueue<ListNode, int>(lists.Length) — and there will be no growth either.

cards.q: Assemble the merge of k lists with a heap of heads.
cards.explain: The priority is the node’s value, so the min-heap yields the smallest head; with −node.val the list would come out in descending order. The tail moves to the node just appended. The heap receives the next node of the same list, if there is one — that keeps the invariant “one head from each non-empty list”. The answer is dummy.next: dummy itself is a placeholder node with value 0.

cards.task: Step through the trace on L1 = [1, 4, 5], L2 = [1, 3, 4], L3 = [2, 6]. The rig asks twice what the code will do: track which list each head came from.

options.label: Takes 3 from L2 and pushes the next node of L2 — 4
Takes 3 from L2 and pushes the next node of L3 — 6
Takes 4 from L1: that head has been in the heap the longest

asks.q: The answer already has 1, 1, 2. The heap holds the heads 3 (L2), 4 (L1), 6 (L3). What does the code do?
asks.explain: The root is the smallest head, 3 from L2. After it, the next node of the same list goes into the heap, 4 from L2 — the invariant “one head from each list”. How long a head has been sitting in the heap does not matter: only the value decides.

options.label: Takes 4 from L2 and pushes nothing: 5 and 6 remain in the heap
Takes 4 from L2 and pushes null into the heap
Stops: one of the lists has ended

asks.q: The heap holds 4 (L2), 6 (L3), 5 (L1). L2 has no nodes after the 4. What does the code do?
asks.explain: The minimum is 4 from L2, and it gets appended. node.next == null, and the check before Enqueue lets nothing into the heap: L2 simply drops out, and the heap shrinks to two heads, 5 and 6. The loop runs while the heap is non-empty, not while all lists are alive.

cards.title: A streaming median: two heaps
cards.body:
Find Median from Data Stream (LeetCode #295, hard). The class MedianFinder: AddNum(x) adds a number, FindMedian() returns the median of everything added — the middle element or the mean of the two middle ones. Numbers range from −10⁵ to 10⁵, up to 5·10⁴ calls.

Naively: keep a sorted List<int> and insert with BinarySearch + Insert — the search is O(log n), but the insertion shifts the tail, O(n). In the worst case 5·10⁴ calls make n²/2 ≈ 1.25·10⁹ shifts: a shift is a fast memmove, but the growth is quadratic.

The idea: the median does not need the whole order — only the boundary between the smaller and the larger half. Split the numbers into two heaps: low is a max-heap of the smaller half (priority −x, safe since |x| ≤ 10⁵), high is a min-heap of the larger half. The roots face each other across the boundary.

Invariant: (1) everything in low ≤ everything in high; (2) |low| = |high| or |low| = |high| + 1. Then the median is the root of low for an odd count, or the mean of the two roots for an even count.

AddNum: put x into low if it is not greater than its root, otherwise into high — that keeps (1). Then, if the sizes have drifted apart, move one root to the other heap — that keeps (2). Adding is O(log n), the median is O(1). In Unity, use two MinHeap<int> from the first lesson of the unit, with a descending comparer for low.

cards.task: Step through the trace on the stream 5, 15, 1, 3, 8, 7, 9, 10. The rig asks twice what AddNum will do: check both parts of the invariant.

options.label: 3 → low; low is two larger than high — 5 moves to high; the median is 4
3 → low; the median is 3
3 → high, because high has fewer elements

asks.q: 3 has arrived. low = {1, 5}, high = {15}. What does AddNum do?
asks.explain: 3 ≤ 5 (the root of low), so it goes into low — otherwise “low ≤ high” would break. Now low has three numbers and high has one: a difference of two, so the root of low, 5, moves to high. low = {1, 3}, high = {5, 15} — equal sizes, and the median is the mean of the roots, (3 + 5) / 2 = 4. Where to put a number is decided by its value, not by the sizes: the second step evens the sizes out.

asks.q: 9 has arrived. low = {1, 3, 5}, high = {7, 8, 15}. What will the median be?
asks.explain: 9 > 5, so it goes into high, which now has four against three. The root of high, 7, moves to low: low = {1, 3, 5, 7}, high = {8, 9, 15}. Seven elements, an odd count — the median is the root of low, 7. Check: in order 1, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9, 15, the middle is 7.

cards.q: After AddNum(1) and AddNum(2) this FindMedian returns 1 instead of 1.5. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: Peek returns an int, the sum is an int, and dividing by 2 is integer division: 3 / 2 = 1. Only the result is converted to double. You need / 2.0 — then the sum is converted to double before the division. There is no overflow here: |x| ≤ 10⁵, but with values near int.MaxValue the sum of the two roots would have to be computed in long.

cards.title: Unity: the median frame time
cards.body:
A HUD or telemetry needs a “typical frame time”. The mean is dragged up by spikes — garbage collection, shader compilation, scene loading: 119 frames of 16 ms and one of 500 ms give a mean of 20 ms but a median of 16. That is why you show the median, and the spikes separately: p99 or the maximum.

A window of the last N frames. The two heaps of #295 accumulate everything from the start, while here an old frame has to leave. PriorityQueue cannot remove (Remove only since .NET 9, and in O(n)), and Unity does not have it at all. What people do:

1. N ≈ 120 — copy and sort. A ring buffer of N values; on request, copy into a preallocated array and call Array.Sort: about 120 · 7 ≈ 840 comparisons, a few microseconds, no new arrays.
2. A narrow range — counters. Frame times from 0 to 100 ms in 0.1 ms steps are 1000 counter buckets: adding and removing are O(1), a percentile is a walk over the buckets. This is the #295 follow-up: “all numbers are from 0 to 100” → an array of 101 counters.
3. A large window and an exact median — Sliding Window Median (#480): two heaps with lazy deletion. Do not search for the leaving element; record “delete x” in a dictionary, and when x reaches a root, remove it. Count the sizes of the halves by live elements only. Or two SortedSet<(int value, int index)>: the index keeps equal values from collapsing into one.
cards.deep:
Lazy deletion in detail. It is the same trick as in Dijkstra on PriorityQueue instead of decrease-key: the stale entry stays in the heap and is recognized and skipped when it comes out. For a window median: a dictionary delayed “value → how many copies to delete”; when an element leaves the window, delayed[x]++ and adjust the live-element counter of the half where x lives (compare with the root of low). After every operation, “clean” the roots: while a root is in delayed, pop it and decrement the counter. The heap may bloat with dead elements, but each one is physically removed once — amortized O(log n) per step.

Why not UnorderedItems. PriorityQueue has the UnorderedItems enumeration, but it goes in the order of the internal array — fine for debugging, and for finding an element it is still O(n).

SortedSet instead of heaps. Two SortedSet<(int value, int index)> give O(log n) removal directly, with no dead elements, while Max and Min walk down to the extreme node. The price is a tree node on the managed heap for every insertion: in Unity that is garbage every frame, so lazy heaps on arrays or counters are the better deal.

A percentile from counters. For the p-th percentile, walk the buckets accumulating a sum and stop once it exceeds p · count. The precision is the bucket width; spikes above 100 ms go into the last bucket, and the maximum is shown separately.

cards.q: A #295 follow-up: every number in the stream is an integer from 0 to 100. How do you speed up MedianFinder?
options: An array of 101 counters: AddNum is O(1), FindMedian is a walk over 101 buckets
You cannot: two heaps already give O(log n) and O(1)
A sorted List<int> with BinarySearch: insertion in O(log n)
cards.explain: The values are small integers in a known range, like the frequencies in the buckets of the previous lesson: no comparisons needed, counting is enough. Adding is count[x]++, the median is a walk over the buckets until the sum reaches the middle: 101 steps, independent of n, and no heaps at all.

wrong.1: Two heaps are good for arbitrary numbers. When the range is 101 values, counters give O(1) per addition and a constant for the median, without a single heap.
wrong.2: BinarySearch finds the position in O(log n), but Insert shifts the tail of the list — O(n) per insertion. That is the naive solution from the card on two heaps.

cards.q: You are solving Find Median from Data Stream out loud. Put the steps in order.
items: Clarify: how many AddNum and FindMedian calls, the range of the numbers, what to return for an even count
Naively: a sorted list with insertion — O(n) per AddNum
Idea: the median is the boundary between halves; low is a max-heap of the smaller half, high a min-heap of the larger
Invariant: low ≤ high and |low| − |high| is 0 or 1
Write AddNum: place by value, then even out the sizes with one move
Run 5, 15, 1, 3 and show 5 moving to high
Complexity: AddNum O(log n), FindMedian O(1), memory O(n); the follow-up on the range 0–100 means counters
cards.explain: Asking about an even count and the range fixes both the answer type (double) and the likely follow-up. The invariant is stated before the code — it shows why AddNum has two steps: the first keeps the halves ordered, the second keeps their sizes.

lessons.title: Unit final: heaps and top-K
lessons.sub: New problems, a k-th largest trace with duplicates, a threshold trap and explaining out loud

cards.q: New problems. Match each statement with its technique.
pairs: After each number of a stream, return the k-th largest (#703)
A min-heap of k, the answer is the root
The k pairs with the smallest sums from two sorted arrays (#373)
A heap of heads: after (i, j) comes (i, j + 1)
Rearrange the characters of a string by descending frequency (#451)
The k numbers closest to x in an unsorted array
A max-heap of k by |a − x|
The median of a stream of integers from 0 to 100

cards.q: Kth Largest Element in a Stream (#703): the constructor gets k and an initial array, and the method Add(val) returns the k-th largest after each number. Up to 10⁴ Add calls. What do you store?
options: A min-heap of k: while there are fewer than k elements — Enqueue, then — EnqueueDequeue; the answer is Peek
A max-heap of all numbers: on each Add remove k elements and put them back
A sorted List<int>: BinarySearch and Insert, the answer is an element from the end
cards.explain: It is a stream and “the k best” — signals 1 and 3. The root of a min-heap of k is both the threshold and the answer. Add is O(log k), and EnqueueDequeue returns a number below the threshold without touching the heap. Memory is O(k), however many numbers arrive. The initial array may be shorter than k — that is why it starts with a plain Enqueue.

wrong.1: k removals and k insertions on every Add are O(k log n) per call and O(n) memory. A min-heap of k keeps the answer at the root.
wrong.2: Insert shifts the tail — O(n) per call, and memory grows with the stream. You do not need to store everything: numbers below the threshold will never become the answer.

cards.q: Sticks of length [2, 4, 3]. Joining two sticks costs the sum of their lengths and produces one stick of that length. You must join everything into one at minimum cost; it is known that joining the two shortest is always optimal. Which structure?
options: A min-heap: remove the two shortest, put their sum back — O(n log n)
Sort once and join from left to right
A max-heap, as in Last Stone Weight
cards.explain: This is signal 2 from the first lesson — the two minimums of a changing set, again and again, only minimums instead of maximums. 2 + 3 = 5 (cost 5), 4 + 5 = 9 (cost 9), 14 in total. The new stick goes back into the set, so a single sort is not enough.

wrong.1: After a join the new stick lands in the middle of the order, and the sort goes stale. On [1, 1, 1, 1] left to right gives 2, 3, 4 — 9 in total, while the heap gives 2, 2, 4 — 8 in total.
wrong.2: Stones are smashed two heaviest at a time. Here it pays to take the shortest — you need a min-heap.

cards.task: Step through the trace on [3, 2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 5, 5, 6], k = 4 — the array has duplicates. The rig asks twice what the root will be after Dequeue.

asks.q: 4 has arrived: the heap holds 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, size 5 > k. Dequeue removes one of the twos. What will the root be?
asks.explain: There are two twos in the heap, and Dequeue removes one element. The second two stays and rises to the root: the heap is 2, 3, 3, 4. The heap keeps duplicates as separate elements — and that is right, since the k-th is counted in sorted order, not among distinct values.

asks.q: 6 has arrived: the heap holds 3, 4, 5, 5, 6. Dequeue removes 3. What will the root — and the answer — be?
asks.explain: What remains is 4, 5, 5, 6 — the four largest, root 4. In descending order the array is 6, 5, 5, 4, …: the two fives take two places, and the fourth largest is 4. If the heap collapsed equal values, the answer would shift.

cards.q: On nums = [3, 2, 1, 5, 6, 4], k = 2 this code returns 4, while the correct answer is 5. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: The code removes the root before it knows whether x gets in — that is how DequeueEnqueue behaves. The threshold is thrown out even when x is below it. On the last step the heap holds 5, 6 and 4 arrives: Dequeue removes 5, Enqueue adds 4 — that leaves 4, 6 and the answer 4. Add first, then remove the extra one (Count > k), or use EnqueueDequeue directly.

cards.q: Complexity of the unit’s solutions. Which statements are true? Select all.
options: The k-th largest via a min-heap of k — O(n log k) time and O(k) memory
Quickselect with a random pivot is O(n) even in the worst case
Merge k Sorted Lists via a heap of heads — O(N log k), where N is the total number of nodes
Top K Frequent with buckets — O(n) time, but a bucket array of length n + 1
In a MedianFinder on two heaps, FindMedian costs O(log n)
cards.explain: A heap of k is n operations at O(log k). Quickselect with a random pivot is O(n) on average, and the worst case stays O(n²), just unlikely. A heap of heads: each of the N nodes enters and leaves once, and the heap never exceeds k. Buckets are O(n), and their number does not depend on the number of distinct values. FindMedian only looks at the roots — O(1); it is AddNum that costs O(log n).

cards.q: Unity 2022: an AI event scheduler. Each event has a firing time; every frame you must run all events with time ≤ now, and for equal times — in the order they were added. What do you choose?
options: Your own MinHeap keyed by (time, seq), where seq is the insertion number: each frame pop while the root ≤ now
PriorityQueue<Event, float> by time
A SortedSet<float> of times and a dictionary “time → event”
A List<Event> sorted by time every frame
cards.explain: The task is “the minimum of a changing set, again and again” — a heap. Unity has no PriorityQueue, so it is your own heap from the first lesson. A heap does not preserve the order of equals, so the insertion number goes into the key: a tuple compares field by field, and no ties remain. Each frame — Peek and Pop while the root’s time ≤ now: O(log n) per event.

wrong.1: PriorityQueue appeared in .NET 6; Unity (.NET Standard 2.1) does not have it. And it is not stable: two events with the same time come out in any order.
wrong.2: A set collapses equal values: a second event with the same time is not added, Add returns false. And every insertion is a tree node on the managed heap.
wrong.3: Sorting every frame is O(n log n) again and again, although only a couple of events change. A heap does O(log n) per event.

cards.q: K Closest Points, but the centre is an arbitrary point (px, py), and all coordinates are up to 10⁵ in absolute value. What do you change in the solution with the squared distance in int?
options: Compute the square in long: the difference reaches 2·10⁵, the sum of squares up to 8·10¹⁰
Nothing: the squared distance always fits in int
Switch to Math.Sqrt and double to avoid overflow
cards.explain: dx = x − px reaches 2·10⁵, dx² = 4·10¹⁰, and with dy² it is 8·10¹⁰. That is almost 40 times int.MaxValue ≈ 2.1·10⁹ — you need long and a long priority. The square root is still unnecessary: it does not change the order.

wrong.1: In #973 it fit because coordinates were up to 10⁴ and the centre was at zero: the square ≤ 2·10⁸. Here the difference range is twice as wide and the values are 10 times larger — the square is 400 times larger.
wrong.2: The square root is monotonic and does not change the order — it only costs time. Overflow is cured by the type: a square in long is exact, while a square root would only add work and rounding.

cards.q: You are solving Kth Largest Element in a Stream out loud. Put the steps in order.
items: Clarify: k-th in sorted order or among distinct values, may the initial array be shorter than k, how many Add calls
Naively: keep everything sorted — O(n) per insertion and O(n) memory
Recognize the pattern: a stream and “the k best” — a min-heap of k, the root is the threshold and the answer
Write the code: while Count < k — Enqueue, then — EnqueueDequeue; the answer is Peek
Run k = 3, initial array [4, 5, 8, 2], then Add(3) and Add(5)
Complexity: Add is O(log k), memory O(k)
Unity: there is no PriorityQueue — your own heap with PushPop
cards.explain: The same script as in every lesson of the unit. The dry run: heap 4, 5, 8; Add(3) — 3 is below the threshold 4, the answer is 4; Add(5) — 5 pushes out 4, heap 5, 5, 8, the answer is 5. The question about a short initial array explains why the first elements go through Enqueue.

units.title: Trees
units.blurb: Recursion and level order, validating a BST, LCA and maximum path sum: return one thing, update another. Walking a Transform hierarchy without recursion.

lessons.title: Recursion and levels
lessons.sub: Tree depth in one line and level-by-level traversal with a queue

cards.title: A tree in a problem: the words and the signal
cards.body:
Maximum Depth of Binary Tree (LeetCode #104). Given the root of a binary tree, return its depth — the number of nodes on the longest path from the root down to a leaf. There are 0 to 10⁴ nodes with values from −100 to 100. An empty tree has depth 0, a single node has depth 1.

The vocabulary interviews use. The root is the node without a parent, a leaf is a node without children. The depth of a node is how many nodes lie on the path from the root to it; the height of the tree h is the largest depth. For a tree of n nodes, h is between ⌈log₂(n + 1)⌉ (a complete, even tree) and n (a chain: every node has one child). LeetCode encodes a tree as an array level by level, left to right, with null for a missing node.

The signal for recursion: the answer for a node is built from the answers for its subtrees. Depth is 1 plus the larger of the left and right subtree depths. Node sums, node counts, “are two trees the same” and “is the tree balanced” all work the same way.

cards.title: A node’s answer comes from its children
cards.body:
The solution is one line: an empty tree has depth 0, a non-empty one has 1 + the max of its children’s depths. The recursion goes down to null, and the answers travel bottom-up: a node returns its number only after both children have answered. The order “children first, then the node” is called post-order.

One template covers dozens of problems: (1) what to return for null; (2) ask the left and right subtrees; (3) combine the two answers into the node’s answer. Name steps 1 and 3 and the code writes itself.

Cost. Each node is called once — O(n) time. Memory is the call stack: at any moment it holds the path from the root to the current node, so O(h). On an even tree of 10⁴ nodes that is about 14 frames, on a chain it is 10⁴. The thread stack is small (see the lesson on C# and Unity in the first unit), so in an interview you say: “O(h) memory, O(n) on a degenerate tree”.

cards.q: A tree of 10⁴ nodes where every node has only a right child — a chain. How many MaxDepth calls sit on the stack at the deepest moment?
options: About 10⁴: the stack holds the whole path from the root, and a chain’s path has length n
About 14: recursion depth is log₂ n
Two: the call for a node and the call for its child
About 5000: recursion goes both ways, and half of the calls have already returned
cards.explain: Recursion depth equals the height of the tree, and a chain has h = n: 10⁴ frames on the stack plus the call for null at the very bottom. A MaxDepth frame in .NET on x64 is about 50–60 bytes, so 10⁴ frames take about 0.6 MB: it fits into a 1 MB stack, but the margin is thin. Chains of 10⁵–10⁶ nodes need an explicit stack or a level-by-level traversal.

wrong.1: log₂ n is the height of an even tree. A chain’s height is n.
wrong.2: A call cannot return until its child answers, and the child waits for its own child — frames pile up along the whole path down.
wrong.3: There are no left children: calls for null return at once. There is a single path down, and its length is n.

cards.task: Step through MaxDepth: root 3, on the left 9 with child 4, on the right 20 with children 15 and 7, and 7 has 8 on its right. Badges show what a node returned, the call stack is below. The rig will stop twice and ask what the code does next.

options.label: Enter 20: the root still needs the right answer
Return 1 + 2 = 3 from 3
Enter 4 again to check its children

asks.q: 9 returned 2 — the root’s left subtree is done. What does the code do next?
asks.explain: The call for 3 has evaluated only the first argument of Math.Max(MaxDepth(left), MaxDepth(right)). Until the right call returns, the root cannot answer: 3 stays on the stack and the recursion goes into 20. Each node is visited once — the code never comes back to 4.

asks.q: 15 returned 1, 7 returned 2. What does 20 return?
asks.explain: A node’s depth is one plus the larger of its children’s depths: a root-to-leaf path goes one way only. 1 + 1 + 2 is the number of nodes on a path that turns at 20, a different quantity (you will need it in the maximum path problem). The root then gets 2 from the left and 3 from the right and returns 4.

cards.title: Levels: a queue and queue.Count
cards.body:
Binary Tree Level Order Traversal (LeetCode #102). Return the node values level by level: a list of lists, each level left to right. For [3, 9, 20, null, null, 15, 7] the answer is [[3], [9, 20], [15, 7]]. Up to 2000 nodes.

Recursion goes deep: from 9 it dives into 9’s children before it ever reaches 20. That is depth-first search, DFS. To go wide you need a Queue<T> — first in, first out: take a node from the head, put its children at the tail. Nodes then come out exactly level by level — that is breadth-first search, BFS.

How do you separate one level from the next? The trick: at the start of a level, remember queue.Count and take exactly that many nodes. Invariant: before every iteration of the outer loop the queue holds exactly one level, left to right. Children join the tail and wait for their own iteration, and the count taken in advance never reaches them.

Cost. Each node enters and leaves the queue once — O(n). Memory is the widest level w: a complete tree has about half its nodes on the last level, so O(n) in the worst case.

cards.q: Assemble the level-order traversal.
cards.explain: An empty tree gives an empty list, not null. The level size is read once, in the for initializer: afterwards Count grows with the children, but k is already counting down exactly this level. Dequeue takes from the head of the queue (Pop belongs to Stack). Children go in left to right — and come out in the same order on the next level.

cards.task: Step through the level-order traversal on the same tree. The current level is highlighted, and the queue after it is shown below. The rig will ask what the next level takes.

options.label: Level [4, 15, 7], queue [8]
Level [4, 15, 7, 8], queue empty
Level [4, 15], queue [7, 8]

asks.q: Level [9, 20] is done, and their children 4, 15, 7 are in the queue. What does the next iteration return, and what stays in the queue?
asks.explain: size = queue.Count = 3 was read before the loop, so the for takes exactly 4, 15 and 7. When 7 is taken, its child 8 joins the tail, but k has already counted down to zero — 8 becomes level 4. An option with 8 inside is mixed levels: that is what you get when the level size is not fixed in advance.

cards.q: On [3, 9, 20, null, null, 15, 7] this code returns [[3, 9], [20, 15], [7]]. Tap the buggy line.
cards.explain: The condition k < queue.Count is re-read on every step, while the queue both shrinks (Dequeue) and grows (children). On the first level: 3 is taken, 9 and 20 join, Count = 2, k = 1 < 2 — and 9 lands in the root’s level. Read the level size once before the loop: for (int k = queue.Count; k > 0; k--) or int size = queue.Count.

cards.title: DFS or BFS: how to choose
cards.body:
Both traversals are O(n) time: every node is visited once. What differs is the order and the memory.

DFS (recursion or an explicit stack) — when a node’s answer is built from its subtrees’ answers: depth, sums, checking a property, a root-to-leaf path. O(h) memory.
BFS (a queue and queue.Count) — when the problem talks about levels or “the nearest”. Average of levels (#637) — the level sum divided by size. Right side view (#199) — the last node of every level, the one taken when k == 1. Zigzag (#103) — reverse every other level. Minimum depth (#111) — BFS stops at the very first leaf, while DFS walks the whole tree.

Memory on the extreme shapes. A chain of n nodes: DFS holds n frames, while the BFS queue always holds one node. A complete tree of 10⁶ nodes: the DFS stack is 20 frames, while the BFS queue reaches about half the nodes by the last level, on the order of 5·10⁵.

The minimum depth trap. A leaf is a node with neither child. The recursion 1 + Math.Min(MinDepth(left), MinDepth(right)) on a node with one child takes 0 from the empty side and returns 1, although that node is not a leaf: on [1, 2] the answer is 2, not 1. An empty side must not enter the minimum. In BFS the leaf check is explicit.
cards.deep:
An explicit stack and the three DFS orders. Pre-order (node, left, right) on a Stack<TreeNode>: pop a node, push the right child before the left so the left comes out first. In-order (left, node, right): go left as far as possible pushing nodes, pop the top one, move into its right subtree. Post-order is the hardest: two stacks or a “children done” mark; it is often easier to do pre-order as “node, right, left” and reverse the result.

O(1) memory. Morris traversal does in-order with no stack and no recursion: it temporarily rewires the right pointer of the rightmost node of the left subtree to the current node and restores it on the second pass. O(n) time, O(1) memory, but the tree is modified during the walk — unacceptable in multithreaded code. In an interview it is enough to know it exists.

The queue in .NET. Queue<T> is a ring buffer; when full it doubles and never shrinks on its own. A queue kept in a field and reused between traversals is usually what you want; after a one-off traversal of a huge tree, call TrimExcess().

A tree for Burst. Node classes with references cannot go into Burst or Jobs. The tree is stored as index arrays: NativeArray<int> for left and right children, −1 for no child, values in a parallel array. A complete tree needs no links at all: the children of node i are at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, as in a heap. The traversal is the same loop with an explicit stack in a NativeList<int>.

cards.title: Unity: walking the Transform hierarchy
cards.body:
The scene hierarchy is a tree too, just not a binary one: a Transform has parent, childCount and GetChild(i). “Visit all descendants” in a Unity interview checks two things: recursion depth and garbage.

Hierarchies are usually tens of levels deep, so the stack will not run out. But recursion via foreach (Transform child in t) creates garbage: Transform implements the non-generic IEnumerable, and GetEnumerator returns a new enumerator object — an allocation per node. A loop over GetChild(i) plus a stack or queue kept in a field (with Clear() before each walk) gives a garbage-free traversal. Need the nearest object with a tag by level — use BFS: it finds the shallowest descendant, while DFS finds the first one along a branch. Note that Transform.Find(name) searches only direct children (or a path with “/”), not the whole subtree.

GetComponentsInChildren<T>() walks the object itself and all descendants depth-first, and every call creates a new array; it skips inactive descendants unless you pass includeInactive: true (the object itself is always checked). The list overload, GetComponentsInChildren(list), fills the List<T> you pass, replacing its previous contents: no new array (the list’s internal buffer grows only while its capacity falls short), but the traversal and the engine calls remain. The rule: do not call it in Update; collect once in Awake and rebuild when the hierarchy changes.
cards.deep:
Strings from the engine. t.name and t.tag create a new managed string on every read: comparing names in a loop over thousands of objects is garbage every frame. CompareTag compares without allocating. If you must search by name, put the names into a Dictionary<string, Transform> once.

Flat hierarchies. Changing a transform’s position marks all of its descendants as changed, while hierarchies under different roots can be processed by Unity independently, including in parallel. That is why Unity advises against keeping thousands of moving objects under one “folder” parent and against nesting objects without a reason.

Jobs. To work on the positions of many objects in parallel there are TransformAccessArray and IJobParallelForTransform: the job gets access to the transforms without walking the hierarchy on the main thread.

cards.q: Each of 200 units calls GetComponentsInChildren<Renderer>() in Update to highlight its model. The profiler shows GC Alloc every frame. What do you do?
options: Collect the array once in Awake and reuse it; rebuild only when the hierarchy changes
Replace it with your own recursion using foreach over Transform — no array, no garbage
Walk breadth-first instead of depth-first: BFS does not allocate
Nothing: the arrays are small, and the young GC generation is cheap to collect
cards.explain: Every call to GetComponentsInChildren<T>() creates a new array: 200 arrays per frame. The set of renderers changes only together with the hierarchy, so collect it once and update it on that event. If rebuilds are frequent, use the list overload — it creates no array.

wrong.1: foreach over Transform creates an enumerator at every node — there will be more garbage, not less.
wrong.2: The garbage comes from the API, not the traversal order: a new array on every call.
wrong.3: Unity’s collector is Boehm, with no generations: every collection walks the whole heap, and garbage every frame brings the next one closer.

cards.q: You are solving Level Order Traversal out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
items: Clarify: what to return for an empty tree, the order inside a level, how many nodes
Say why plain recursion does not fit: it goes deep, and we need levels — so a queue
Idea: at the start of a level remember queue.Count and take exactly that many nodes
Write the code while stating the invariant: the queue holds exactly one level
Complexity: O(n) time, O(w) memory — up to n/2 on a complete tree
Edge cases: an empty tree, a single node, a chain
cards.explain: First the problem, then the choice of traversal and why, then the invariant and the code, a dry run, and only then complexity and edge cases. On a chain the queue holds a single node — a good moment to compare memory with recursion.

cards.q: Match the problem with the technique.
pairs: A queue, queue.Count at the start of a level
The last node of every level
An explicit stack instead of recursion

lessons.title: The BST property
lessons.sub: Bounds from the ancestors versus in-order, and why comparing with children is not enough

cards.title: The problem and the BST property
cards.body:
Validate Binary Search Tree (LeetCode #98). Given the root of a binary tree, check that it is a binary search tree (BST): for every node, all keys in its left subtree are strictly less than the node’s key, all keys in its right subtree are strictly greater, and both subtrees are BSTs too. There are 1 to 10⁴ nodes, and the values span the whole int range, from −2³¹ to 2³¹ − 1.

The property is about whole subtrees, not children. Everything a BST is good for rests on it: a search follows one branch and costs O(h), the minimum is the leftmost node, and the walk “left subtree, node, right subtree” yields the keys in ascending order.

Example: [2, 1, 3] is a BST. [5, 1, 4, null, null, 3, 6] is not: 4 lies in the right subtree of 5, and 4 < 5.

cards.title: Naive: compare with the children — and why it is wrong
cards.body:
The first idea: at every node check that the left child is smaller and the right child is larger, then go down. The code is short, O(n) — and wrong: it checks children, while the property is about the whole subtree. On [5, 4, 6, null, null, 3, 7] node 6 has children 3 and 7, everything looks fine locally, but 3 lies in the right subtree of 5 and is smaller than 5. This is the main trap of the problem, and the interviewer expects you to come up with such a counterexample yourself.

The honest naive solution: for every node find the maximum of the left subtree and the minimum of the right one and compare them with the node. It is correct, but every subtree is walked again for each of its ancestors: O(n·h), O(n²) on a chain — on the order of 5·10⁷ steps for n = 10⁴.

We need every node checked once, but against all of its ancestors.

cards.q: The tree [10, 5, 15, null, null, 6, 20]. What does the “children only” check return, and what is actually true?
options: It returns true, but this is not a BST: 6 lies in the right subtree of 10
It returns false: 6 is less than 15
It returns true, and this is a BST: every node’s left child is smaller and right child larger
cards.explain: 10 has children 5 and 15, 15 has 6 and 20: every parent–child pair is in order, so the check returns true. But 6 lies to the right of 10, and the whole right subtree of 10 must be greater than 10. A local check cannot see violations that skip a level.

wrong.1: 6 is the left child of 15, and 6 < 15: for a left child that is exactly right.
wrong.2: The BST property is about the whole subtree: 6 cannot appear to the right of 10, at any depth.

cards.title: Bounds passed down
cards.body:
Every ancestor constrains a node. Go left from an ancestor and the node must be smaller than it; go right and it must be larger. All the constraints along the path collapse into one open interval (lo, hi): lo is the nearest ancestor we went right from, hi is the nearest one we went left from.

So the recursion carries the interval down. The root gets (−∞, +∞); the left child of a node gets (lo, node.val) — the top narrows; the right child gets (node.val, hi) — the bottom narrows. Invariant: the tree is a BST if and only if every node lies strictly inside the interval that came from above. Every node is checked once: O(n) time, O(h) stack. The && gives an early exit: if the left subtree is broken, the right one is never walked.

How to represent ∞. The values span the whole int, so int.MinValue cannot play “−∞”: a node with the value int.MinValue would fail the “greater than lo” check. Keep the bounds in long — long.MinValue is strictly less than any int — or in int?, where null means “no bound”.

cards.q: Assemble the bounds check.
cards.explain: The root’s lower bound is long.MinValue: it is strictly less than any int, so a node holding int.MinValue passes. An empty subtree violates nothing — true. Equality is forbidden on both sides, hence <= lo and >= hi. Going left, the top narrows to node.val; going right, the bottom becomes node.val and the top stays the same hi.

cards.task: Step through the check on [5, 3, 8, 1, 6, 7, 9]. Each checked node is labelled with its interval. The rig will stop twice and ask what happens next.

asks.q: 3 ∈ (−∞, 5) — fine. The next node is 1, the left child of 3. Which interval does it get?
asks.explain: Going left narrows the top: the upper bound of 1 is its parent’s value, 3, and the bottom stays what came to 3, which is −∞. The bound 5 still applies, but 3 is tighter: (−∞, 3) lies entirely inside (−∞, 5).

options.label: 6 is outside (3, 5) — not a BST, the walk stops
6 is inside (3, +∞) — fine, 8 is next
6 is larger than its parent 3 — the right child is fine

asks.q: 1 is fine and has no children. Next is 6, the right child of 3. What does the check say?
asks.explain: 6 receives the interval (3, 5): the bottom is its parent 3 (we went right), the top is the root 5 (this whole subtree is on its left). 6 > 5 — a violation. Against its parent 6 compares fine, so the “children only” check would miss it. && keeps the walk out of the root’s right subtree: the answer is already false.

cards.title: In-order: a BST reads in ascending order
cards.body:
The second approach uses a consequence of the property: an in-order walk (left subtree, node, right subtree) visits a BST in strictly ascending order. So the tree is a BST if and only if every next in-order value is greater than the previous one. No need to store the whole list — a single prev is enough. The three depth-first orders differ only in when the node itself is handled: before its children — pre-order, between the left and right subtrees — in-order, after its children — post-order.

In-order is convenient to write without recursion, on an explicit stack: go left as far as possible pushing nodes; pop the top one — it is the next in ascending order; move into its right subtree. The stack holds at most h nodes: O(n) time, O(h) memory, and an early exit at the first neighbouring pair that does not increase.

The bound trap is the same: starting with int prev = int.MinValue breaks on a tree whose leftmost value is int.MinValue. Start with long prev = long.MinValue, or keep TreeNode prev = null and compare only once it is set.

cards.q: On the tree [-2147483648, null, 5] this code returns false, although the tree is a BST. Tap the buggy line.
cards.explain: The root, int.MinValue, is the first node popped in-order, and int.MinValue <= prev = int.MinValue — a false violation. “Less than everything” cannot be represented by a value from the same range. One line fixes it: long prev = long.MinValue (or TreeNode prev = null with a check). The <= comparison itself is right: duplicates are not allowed in this problem’s BST.

cards.q: What is true about the bounds solution and the in-order solution? Select all.
options: Both are O(n) time and O(h) memory
In-order finds a violation at the first pair of neighbouring values that does not increase
The children-only check is correct if the tree is balanced
A node holding int.MinValue breaks the solution with long bounds
If the root’s left subtree is broken, the bounds solution does not walk the right one
cards.explain: Both visit every node once, and the stack — call stack or explicit — holds a path no longer than h. In-order compares neighbours in ascending order: the first pair with prev ≥ val is the violation. Balance is irrelevant: [10, 5, 15, null, null, 6, 20] is balanced, and the children check still gets it wrong. long.MinValue is less than any int, so int.MinValue passes. && does not evaluate its right side when the left one is already false.

cards.title: SortedSet: a BST that does not degenerate
cards.body:
A plain BST without balancing depends on the insertion order. Insert keys 1, 2, …, n in ascending order and each goes to the right of the previous one: the tree becomes a chain, h = n, a search is O(n), n inserts are O(n²). It is easy to end up there by accident, for example by inserting enemy ids in spawn order.

A balanced tree fixes its shape with rotations after every insert and removal and keeps h = O(log n). SortedSet<T> and SortedDictionary<TKey, TValue> in .NET are a red-black tree (see the collections lesson in the first unit): h ≤ 2·log₂(n + 1), O(log n) operations in the worst case. That is the answer to “how is SortedSet built”: a BST with this lesson’s property plus balancing.

The in-order walk is the same here: foreach over a SortedSet yields elements in ascending order because its enumerator is an in-order walk on an explicit stack. The k-th smallest element of a BST (#230) is the same walk with a counter: stop at the k-th popped node, O(h + k).
cards.deep:
Inside the SortedSet enumerator. In the dotnet/runtime sources, SortedSet<T>.Enumerator is a struct, but its constructor creates a Stack<Node> with capacity 2·log₂(n + 1) — the maximum height of a red-black tree. So foreach over a SortedSet allocates a stack (an object and an array, about 200 bytes per walk over a thousand elements in .NET 8) even when the enumerator is not boxed — noticeable in a hot Unity loop. The internal InOrderTreeWalk works the same way.

Red-black versus AVL. AVL keeps the height difference of subtrees at most 1 — the tree is lower (about 1.44·log₂ n), lookups are slightly faster, but updates rotate more. Red-black allows height up to 2·log₂(n + 1), but an insert does at most two rotations and a removal at most three. Standard libraries (.NET, Java’s TreeMap, std::map in common implementations) choose red-black.

Unity and Burst. SortedSet is available in the .NET Standard 2.1 profile, but every node is a heap object: an allocation on every Add and cache misses on the way down. The com.unity.collections package has no ready-made balanced search tree — only hash tables, lists, queues and sorting; in Jobs you usually sort a NativeList<T> and binary-search it, and when the data rarely changes that is faster than a tree anyway.

cards.q: A hand-written BST without balancing. Enemies get ascending ids — 1, 2, 3, … — and are inserted in spawn order, 10⁵ in total. What about the cost?
options: The tree is a chain: the inserts cost about 5·10⁹ steps, Contains is O(n)
O(n log n) for all inserts: a BST search is always logarithmic
O(n): a new id always lands right of the previous one, so an insert is O(1)
cards.explain: Every new id is larger than all previous ones and goes to the far right end: the tree degenerates into a chain, h = n. The i-th insert walks i nodes, about n²/2 ≈ 5·10⁹ steps in total. The cure is balancing — SortedSet<int> gives O(log n) — or a dictionary if order does not matter.

wrong.1: Only a balanced tree is logarithmic. The height of a hand-written BST depends on the insertion order.
wrong.2: An insert starts at the root and walks down the whole chain: a BST has no pointer to its last node.

cards.q: You are solving Validate BST out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
items: Clarify: strictly less and greater or not, are there duplicates, what is the value range
Name the trap: comparing only with children misses violations across levels — counterexample [5, 4, 6, null, null, 3, 7]
Idea: pass the interval (lo, hi) from the ancestors down
Write the code with long bounds, saying: going left narrows hi, going right narrows lo
Run the counterexample: 3 gets (5, 6) and fails
Complexity: O(n) time, O(h) memory
Edge cases: int.MinValue and int.MaxValue in nodes, a single node, a chain
cards.explain: The problem, then a counterexample to the obvious solution — it shows you understand the property — then the idea, the code and a run on that same counterexample. Complexity and edge cases go last; int.MinValue is not a detail here but the reason to use long.

cards.q: Match the problem or question with the answer.
pairs: Interval (lo, hi) passed down from ancestors
Walk a BST in ascending order
“−∞” when values span the whole int

lessons.title: Return one thing, update another
lessons.sub: LCA and the maximum path: what the recursion hands to the parent and what it records as the answer

cards.title: LCA: the problem and the signal
cards.body:
Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree (LeetCode #236). Given the root of a binary tree and two of its nodes, p and q, find their lowest common ancestor — the deepest node whose subtree contains both p and q; a node counts as a descendant of itself. There are 2 to 10⁵ nodes, values are distinct, p ≠ q, and both are in the tree. The tree is a plain one, not a BST: there is no key order.

On the tree [3, 5, 1, 6, 2, 0, 8, null, null, 7, 4]: LCA(7, 8) = 3 — the paths to them split at the root; LCA(7, 4) = 2; LCA(5, 4) = 5 — p itself, because q lies below it.

The signal: the answer is about a pair of nodes, and what we know about them sits in subtrees. Each subtree can report upward what it has found, and the answer appears where two reports meet. In Unity this is the common parent of two objects in the hierarchy — say, to find which UI container holds both elements.

cards.title: Naive: two paths, or Contains at every level
cards.body:
The brute-force solution finds the path from the root to p and the path to q (a depth-first walk with a list holding the current path) and compares them from the start: the last common node is the LCA. That is O(n) time, but two passes and memory for the paths — O(h), O(n) on a chain.

A worse version, written without thinking: walk down from the root and at every node ask a Contains function whether p and q are both in the left subtree, and if not, both in the right one. Each Contains walks a subtree, O(its size), and there are two per level — one for p and one for q. On a chain of n nodes with p and q at the bottom that is 2·(n + (n − 1) + …) ≈ n²: 10¹⁰ steps for n = 10⁵.

The repeated work is plain: the same subtree is walked again at every level. We want each subtree walked once, reporting its result upward.

cards.q: The Contains solution: at every node ask whether p and q are both in the left subtree (if so, go left), otherwise whether both are in the right one. The tree is a chain of 10⁵ nodes, and p and q are the bottom two. Roughly how many steps?
options: ≈ 10¹⁰: at every level two Contains calls walk almost everything below again
≈ 10⁵: each node is visited once
≈ 1.7·10⁶: it is n log n
cards.explain: At depth i there are still n − i nodes below, and two Contains calls — for p and for q — walk them again: 2·(n + (n − 1) + …) ≈ n² = 10¹⁰. At about 10⁸ operations per second that is roughly 100 seconds. A single recursion that reports its findings upward visits each node once.

wrong.1: That is how the single-recursion solution behaves. Contains at every level walks the lower part of the tree all over again.
wrong.2: A logarithm would appear on an even tree, where subtrees halve. On a chain the subtree shrinks by just one node per step.

cards.title: One recursion and a contract on the return value
cards.body:
Let the function for a subtree return a single value with this meaning: null — neither p nor q is in the subtree; p or q — one of them was found; their LCA — both were found.

The rules. If the node is empty or is p or q itself, return it and do not look deeper. That is correct: if the other one lies below, this node is the answer; if it is in another branch, the other side will find it. Otherwise ask the left and right subtrees. Both sides returned non-null — p and q are on different sides, this node is where they split, and it is the answer. Otherwise pass up whichever is non-null.

Invariant: the return value says what the subtree contains; once both have been found somewhere, the answer rises to the root as the only non-empty side. Each node once: O(n) time, O(h) stack.
flow: null, p or q → return it

cards.task: Step through LCA for p = 7, q = 8 on the example tree. Badges show what each subtree returned. The rig will stop twice and ask what happens next.

options.label: Ask the right subtree — enter 1
Return 7: one finding is already there
Return 3: the root is everyone’s ancestor

asks.q: The root’s left subtree returned 7. What does the code do at the root, 3?
asks.explain: So far the root only knows about 7, and one side cannot tell where the other node is. The right call LowestCommonAncestor(root.right, p, q) always happens. Returning 3 “just in case” is wrong: if q were 4, the answer would be 2, and it would come from the left.

options.label: 3 — p and q split here
7 — the left side answered first
8 — the latest finding

asks.q: 7 came from the root’s left, 8 from its right. What does 3 return?
asks.explain: Both sides are non-null: p is on the left, q on the right. No node below the root has both in its subtree, so 3 is the deepest common ancestor. If there were nodes above 3, this answer would rise through them as the only non-empty side.

cards.title: Maximum path: two different quantities
cards.body:
Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum (LeetCode #124). A path is a sequence of nodes where neighbours are joined by an edge and each node appears at most once; it need not pass through the root, but it has at least one node. Find the largest sum of values along a path. Up to 3·10⁴ nodes, values from −1000 to 1000. For [-10, 9, 20, null, null, 15, 7] the answer is 42: the path 15 → 20 → 7. Naively, try every pair of nodes and add up the path between them: O(n²) pairs, and each path still has to be walked.

Every path has a topmost node — where the path “turns”. The sum of such a path is the best way down to the left + the node + the best way down to the right. But the parent cannot extend this path: a path through the parent can enter the node along one branch only — two branches plus the parent is a fork, not a path.

So a node has two different quantities. It returns to its parent the downward gain val + max(left, right) — a path that can continue upward. It updates the global answer with the turning path val + left + right. A negative branch gain counts as 0: it is better not to take that branch. And best starts at int.MinValue, not 0: the path is non-empty, so if all values are negative the answer is below zero. That is this lesson’s template — return one thing, update another. O(n) time, O(h) stack.

cards.q: Assemble the solution: what to return and what to update.
cards.explain: best starts at int.MinValue: the path is non-empty, and when all values are negative the answer is below zero. A negative branch gain is cut to 0. best gets the path turning at the node, both branches at once. Only one branch goes up, the better one: the parent continues the path through it.

cards.task: Step through the trace on [-10, 9, 20, null, null, 15, 7]. Badges show what a node returned upward, best is shown below. The rig will stop twice and ask what gets recorded and what gets returned.

options: best = 42; return 35
best = 42; return 42
best = 35; return 35
asks.q: 15 returned 15, 7 returned 7, best = 15. What does node 20 do?
asks.explain: The path turning at 20: 15 + 20 + 7 = 42 — a new best. But only one branch goes up: 20 + max(15, 7) = 35. Returning 42 is wrong: the parent −10 would attach itself to a path that has already forked at 20.

options: best = 42; return 25
best = 34; return 25
best = 42; return 34
asks.q: The root −10: 9 came from the left, 35 from the right. What next?
asks.explain: The turn at the root: 9 − 10 + 35 = 34 < 42, the best stays. Upward goes −10 + 35 = 25, even though nobody is above: one function serves every node. The answer is best, not what the root returned: 42, not 25.

cards.q: On the tree [-3] this code returns 0, but the answer is −3. Tap the buggy line.
cards.explain: A path has at least one node, so when all values are negative the answer is the largest of them, and it is below zero. Starting with best = 0 means “an empty path with sum 0”, which the problem does not allow. Start at int.MinValue, and assign it inside MaxPathSum so a repeated call does not inherit the old best. Cutting branches to 0 in Gain is a different matter: dropping a branch is allowed, but the node itself is always on the path.

cards.title: The same template: diameter, balance, LCA in a BST and in a hierarchy
cards.body:
Diameter (#543) — the length of the longest path in edges. Return the height, update best = max(best, hl + hr): the path turning at a node has hl + hr edges. The same pair as in the maximum path, only with ones instead of values.

Is it balanced (#110: at every node the subtree heights differ by at most 1). Naively, recompute the children’s heights for every node: each node is recounted at every level above it, O(n log n) on an even tree. In one pass: return the height, and −1 as a “no longer balanced” signal that rises to the root. O(n).

LCA in a BST (#235) — the key order decides: if p and q are both smaller than the node, the LCA is on the left; both larger — on the right; otherwise it is the node itself. One walk down, no recursion, O(h).

LCA with parent links. A Transform has parent, so there is no need to walk the whole tree: compute the depths, lift the deeper node to the other’s depth, and step up together until they meet. O(depth), zero allocations.

cards.q: You are solving Maximum Path Sum out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
items: Clarify: a path has at least one node, need not pass through the root, values can be negative
Naive: for every pair of nodes walk the path between them — O(n²) pairs, each walked too
Idea: a path has a top node; return the one-way gain to the parent, record the turning path in best
Write the code: negative branches become 0, best starts at int.MinValue
Run [-10, 9, 20, null, null, 15, 7]: 20 records 42 but returns 35
Complexity: O(n) time, O(h) memory
Edge cases: all values negative, a single node, a chain
cards.explain: Here the clarifications solve half the problem: “at least one node” and “negative values” are exactly the two traps in the code. Then the naive solution, the idea with two quantities, the code and a run that shows the recorded and returned values differ.

cards.title: Why it is correct, and where the stack runs out
cards.body:
Both solutions are post-order: a node decides after its children. Correctness follows from the meaning of the return value.

LCA. If p and q are in different subtrees of node x, no node below x contains both — so x is the lowest, and it is the first node on the way up where both sides are non-null. If q lies under p, the call for p returns p without going down, and at every ancestor the other side returns null — p rises to the root. The code relies on the condition “both are in the tree”: if q might be missing, it returns p as the answer.

Maximum path. Every path has exactly one topmost node, and there its sum is the best way down to the left + the node + the best way down to the right. best tries every top node, so it sees the best path too.

Depth. #236 has up to 10⁵ nodes; on a chain that is 10⁵ frames, and at 50–60 bytes per frame that is over 5 MB: it will not fit into a 1 MB thread stack. Below is a version without recursion: parents via an explicit stack, then p’s ancestors in a set.
cards.deep:
Nodes as keys. TreeNode does not override Equals and GetHashCode, so the dictionary and the set compare by reference — exactly what we need. The iterative version is O(n) time and memory but does not depend on the thread stack; the walk stops as soon as both nodes have a parent.

If a node may be missing (#1644, LCA of a Binary Tree II), the return value is not enough: you also need a count of found nodes, and the walk can no longer stop at p or q — the subtree must be walked to the end.

Many queries on one tree. Binary lifting: up[k][v] is the ancestor of v 2ᵏ levels up, O(n log n) preparation, O(log n) per query. For a Unity hierarchy this is usually overkill: depths are small, and climbing parent is enough.

Overflow and state. In #124 |sum| ≤ 3·10⁴ · 1000 = 3·10⁷ — int with room to spare; with values up to 10⁹ use long. The best field is object state: not thread-safe and in need of a reset. The alternative is ref int best in the recursion or an (int gain, int best) tuple as the return value: no field and no boxing.

cards.q: Match the problem with what the recursion returns and what it updates.
pairs: Return the finding; the answer is where both sides are non-null
Walk down by key order, O(h)
Return the gain down, update the turning path
Return the height, update hl + hr

lessons.title: Unit final: trees
lessons.sub: New problems to recognize, a BST check trace, an in-order trap and explaining out loud

cards.q: New problems. Match the statement with the technique.
pairs: The average node value on every level
The length of the longest path between two nodes
Return the height, update hl + hr
The k-th smallest value in a BST
The common ancestor of two nodes in a BST
Walk down by key order, O(h)
Is there a root-to-leaf path with sum target
DFS passing the remaining sum down

cards.q: Find Bottom Left Tree Value (LeetCode #513): return the leftmost value on the last level of the tree. How?
options: Level-order traversal: remember the first node of every level — after the loop it is the answer
Go left from the root while there is a left child
Level-order traversal, remembering the last node of every level
cards.explain: The first node of a level is the one taken first after reading queue.Count; the last one remembered is the leftmost on the last level. O(n) time, O(w) memory. There is also a trick: enqueue the right child before the left one — then the answer is the last node taken.

wrong.1: The leftmost node of the tree is not necessarily on the last level: on [1, 2, 3, null, null, 4] going left stops at 2, but the answer is 4.
wrong.2: The last node of a level is the rightmost: that is the right side view, and we need the leftmost.

cards.q: Count Good Nodes in Binary Tree (LeetCode #1448): a node is good if no value on the path from the root to it is greater than its own. Count the good nodes; up to 10⁵ nodes. How?
options: DFS passing the path maximum down: a node is good if val ≥ max
Level-order traversal: a node is good if it is not less than the maximum of its level
In-order: a node is good if it is not less than the previous one
cards.explain: The condition is about ancestors, and ancestors are the path from above. As with the interval in the BST check, a summary of the path travels down — here a single number, the maximum. Dfs(node, max): the count grows if node.val >= max, and the children get Math.Max(max, node.val). O(n) time, O(h) stack; for a chain of 10⁵ nodes, an explicit stack of (node, max) pairs.

wrong.1: A level is neighbours, not ancestors: the level maximum says nothing about the path from the root.
wrong.2: In-order neighbours are not ancestors: a node and the previous one in in-order may sit in different branches.

cards.task: A new tree: [8, 4, 12, 2, 6, 10, 14, 1, 3, 5, 9]. Step through the bounds check; the rig will stop twice and ask what happens next.

asks.q: The left subtree of 4 — nodes 2, 1, 3 — is fine. Next is 6, the right child of 4. What is the interval of 6?
asks.explain: Going right from 4, the bottom becomes 4, and the top stays what came to 4 — 8: this whole subtree is to the left of the root. (4, +∞) would forget the root — that is exactly the “compare only with the parent” mistake.

options.label: 9 is outside (6, 8) — not a BST
9 is inside (6, +∞) — fine, the tree is valid
9 is larger than its parent 6 — the right child is fine

asks.q: 5 ∈ (4, 6) — fine. The last node is 9, the right child of 6. What does the check say?
asks.explain: 9 receives (6, 8): the bottom is its parent 6, the top is the root 8. 9 > 8, although 9 lies to the left of the root. Against its parent 9 compares fine, so the “children only” check would call the tree valid. The root’s right subtree — 12, 10, 14 — is never checked.

cards.q: The k-th smallest in a BST. On the tree [5, 3, 6, 2, 4] with k = 1 this code returns 5 instead of 2. Tap the buggy line.
cards.explain: A node is counted before its left subtree — that is pre-order, so the root 5 is counted first. A BST reads in ascending order in-order: first Walk(node.left), then count the node, then Walk(node.right). The --k line belongs between the two calls.

cards.q: Checking “is it balanced”. The naive solution computes Height(left) and Height(right) with a separate recursion at every node. The one-pass solution returns the height or −1. What does it buy?
options: O(n) instead of O(n log n) on an even tree: every height is computed once
Nothing in time: both are O(n)
O(1) memory instead of O(h)
cards.explain: The naive one recomputes the heights of everything below at every level: on an even tree that is log n levels of n work — O(n log n). One pass hands the height to the parent, and −1 cuts the checks above short at once. Memory is the call stack in both, O(h).

wrong.1: Height(left) is itself a walk of the subtree. Calling it from every node walks each node as many times as it has ancestors.
wrong.2: The recursion stays — and so does the O(h) stack. The gain is in time, not memory.

cards.q: Unity: a scene has 10⁴ transforms, and two objects sit about 20 levels deep under the same root. You need their common parent. What do you do?
options: Climb via parent: equalize the depths and step up together — tens of steps
GetComponentsInChildren<Transform>() on the root and a recursive LCA over the tree — O(n)
Breadth-first search from the root to both objects, then compare the paths
cards.explain: A Transform links to its parent, so the answer lies on two upward paths: depths of 20, equalizing and climbing — tens of steps and zero allocations. A top-down walk is only needed when there are no parent links, as with LeetCode’s TreeNode.

wrong.1: That is a new array of every transform under the root and a walk of the whole subtree — for an answer that lies on two short upward paths.
wrong.2: A top-down walk visits the whole subtree. Climbing via parent walks only two paths as long as the depth.

cards.q: You are solving Count Good Nodes out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
items: Clarify: is an equal value a good node? How many nodes, can the tree be empty
Naive: for every node walk the path from the root again — O(n·h)
Idea: pass the maximum of the path from the root down
Write the code: Dfs(node, max), good if val ≥ max, children get Math.Max(max, val)
Run [3, 1, 4, 3, null, 1, 5]: four good nodes — 3, 4, 5 and the lower-left 3
Complexity: O(n) time, O(h) memory
Edge cases: a single node, all values equal, a chain of 10⁵ — an explicit stack
cards.explain: The same order as throughout the course: the problem, a baseline, the idea, the code while talking, a dry run, complexity, edge cases. The run shows that the 1 under the root 3 is not good, while the 3 under that 1 is: the maximum on its path is 3.

cards.q: Complexity of this unit’s solutions. What is true? Select all.
options: Recursive MaxDepth is O(n) time and O(h) memory; on a chain h = n
Level-order traversal is O(n) time with O(w) memory; on a complete tree w is about n/2
The BST bounds check is O(n log n): the intervals narrow at every level
LCA in a plain binary tree is O(h): we only go down one side
The maximum path is O(n): each node returns a value once and updates best once
cards.explain: Every traversal in this unit visits each node once. Narrowing an interval is O(1) per node, so the BST check is O(n). Going down one side only works in a BST, where the key order decides; in a plain tree LCA does not know which way to go and walks both subtrees — O(n).

units.title: Graphs: traversal, connectivity, order
units.blurb: A grid as a graph, multi-source BFS, topological sort, state-space graphs and Union-Find. Tile flood fill, distance maps, system initialization order and procedural caves.

lessons.title: A grid is a graph
lessons.sub: Flood Fill and Number of Islands: a cell is a vertex, a neighbor is an edge, recursion versus an explicit stack

cards.title: The problem and the graph you don't see
cards.body:
Flood Fill (LeetCode #733). An image is an m×n grid image, with m and n up to 50. You are given a start (sr, sc) and a color. Repaint the start pixel and every pixel of its color that can be reached from it by steps up, down, left and right. It is the paint bucket from any image editor.

Graph traversal signals: “can be reached”, “connected”, “region”, “adjacent cells”. No graph is drawn here, but there is one: a cell is a vertex, sharing a side is an edge. There are m·n vertices, each with at most four neighbors, so at most 2·m·n edges. No adjacency lists are needed: offsets give the neighbors, as in u3.l5.

Depth-first search (DFS): paint the cell and call yourself on its four neighbors. A call that steps off the edge or lands on another color returns at once. Repainting doubles as the “visited” mark: a painted cell no longer has the original color, so nobody enters it twice. Each cell is painted once and checked from at most four neighbors — O(m·n) time.

cards.q: The start != color check was removed from FloodFill, so Fill is always called. What happens on image = [[1, 1]], sr = 0, sc = 0, color = 1?
options: Fill paints (0, 0) from 1 to 1, goes to (0, 1), from there back to (0, 0) — on and on until the stack overflows
The same image comes back: repainting 1 as 1 does nothing
Fill repaints both cells once each and returns
The compiler warns that from and to may be equal
cards.explain: The “visited” mark here is the change of color. If from == to, a painted cell keeps the color from, and the img[r][c] != from check doesn't stop it: (0, 0) → (0, 1) → (0, 0) → … The depth grows until the stack runs out, and StackOverflowException cannot be caught in .NET — the process terminates (u1.l3). A separate visited array would survive even this, but in this problem it is simpler to return right away.

wrong.1: A single repaint would do nothing, but recursive calls follow it. They can't tell the cell was visited: its color didn't change.
wrong.2: Only the mark guarantees “once each”. When the color doesn't change there is no mark, and the cells are visited again and again.
wrong.3: The code is valid as far as the language goes: the compiler doesn't check whether two int parameters are equal. The bug shows up only at run time.

cards.title: Number of Islands: how many times the traversal started
cards.body:
Number of Islands (LeetCode #200). An m×n grid, up to 300×300, of the characters '1' (land) and '0' (water). An island is land connected through sides; diagonal cells are not neighbors. Count the islands.

Idea. An outer loop visits every cell. When it meets land that no traversal has touched yet, that is a new island: count++, and the DFS Sink “sinks” the whole island by writing '0', so the loop doesn't count its cells again. The answer is the number of DFS launches, that is, the number of connected components of the land graph.
