Invariant: whenever the outer loop stands on a cell, every island it has already counted is fully sunk. So any '1' under the loop belongs to a new island.

Cost. The loop walks m·n cells, Sink enters each land cell once — O(m·n) time. The input gets destroyed along the way; if that's not allowed, keep a bool[,] visited. Whether the grid may be modified is a question for the interviewer.

cards.q: Assemble the island counter.
cards.explain: The counter grows on every Sink launch — one launch sinks one island. The grid has g.Length rows and g[0].Length columns: on a non-square map, swapped bounds index out of the array. Compare with the character '1', not the number 1: a char in C# is a number, and '1' equals 49. The mark is writing '0'; after it the loop no longer sees the cell. The four calls go down, up, right, left.

cards.task: Step through the trace on a 5×6 map. Color is the island number; below is the stack of Sink calls. The rig will stop twice and ask what the code does next: keep track of who is running — the outer loop or the recursion.

options.label: Sink(1, 0) returns to Sink(0, 0), which goes right and sinks (0, 1)
The outer loop finds (0, 1): that is island #2
Island #1 is done: it has two cells, (0, 0) and (1, 0)

asks.q: Sink(1, 0): water below, (0, 0) above is already sunk, water to the right, the edge to the left. What next?
asks.explain: Sink(1, 0) has returned, but Sink(0, 0) isn't finished: it checked down (that's where it went) and up (the edge), and right is next — (0, 1), land of the same island. The outer loop regains control only once the whole island is sunk, so it will never see (0, 1) as new land.

options.label: (4, 0) — island #5
(4, 4) — island #5
Nothing: there are 4 islands

asks.q: Island #4 is sunk: (3, 5), (4, 5) and (4, 4). The outer loop continues row by row. What will it find?
asks.explain: (4, 4) is land on the original map, but the DFS from (3, 5) reached it through (4, 5) and sank it. The loop finishes row 3, starts row 4 and immediately meets (4, 0) — untouched land: count = 5, and Sink will sink (4, 0) and (4, 1). That's the invariant at work: whatever is still '1' under the loop is a new island.

cards.title: Recursion depth: 50×50 is fine, 300×300 is not
cards.body:
The stack holds the current chain of DFS calls — from the cell where the traversal began to the cell it is handling now. On solid land Sink snakes: down to the edge, one step right, up to the edge, right again… No call returns until every cell is covered, and the depth equals the number of cells in the region. Small islands on a huge map are safe, though: the depth is bounded by the size of the island, not of the grid.

The numbers. In u10.l3 a recursive frame was estimated at 50–60 bytes; Fill and Sink take more parameters, and on x64 their frame comes out at 50–100 bytes, so a 1 MB stack holds on the order of 10⁴–2·10⁴ frames. Flood Fill at 50×50 is at most 2500 frames, 150–250 KB: safe. Number of Islands at 300×300 of solid land is 9·10⁴ frames, 5–9 MB: it doesn't fit in 1 MB. (On Linux the main thread usually gets 8 MB, which is why such a solution sometimes passes on a judge — don't count on it.) A 1000×1000 tile map is 10⁶ frames. A stack overflow cannot be caught (u1.l3), and a recursive fill launched from an editor tool can take the Unity Editor down along with the unsaved scene.

The cure from u1.l3 is an explicit stack on the heap. One detail: mark a cell when you push it, not when you pop it. Then each cell enters the stack once, and the stack never exceeds m·n. If you mark on pop, each of the four neighbors may push the same cell before its turn comes.

cards.q: The stack is 1 MB and a frame of the recursive traversal is 50–100 bytes. On which inputs is recursive DFS safe? Select all.
options: Flood Fill #733: an image up to 50×50
Number of Islands #200: 300×300, almost all land
A 1000×1000 map whose islands have at most 100 cells each
A 1000×1000 map with a one-cell-wide snake road half a million cells long
A 2000×2000 map of solid water
cards.explain: The depth equals the size of the region being filled. 50×50 is at most 2500 frames. Islands of 100 cells go no deeper than 100, however big the map is. On solid water Sink is never called at all. Almost solid land at 300×300 is up to 9·10⁴ frames, 5–9 MB; the snake is 5·10⁵: neither fits in a megabyte.

cards.title: BFS and DFS: one template, two structures
cards.body:
Replace Stack with Queue in the explicit traversal, and the same loop becomes breadth-first search, the BFS from u10.l1. Both work for filling and for counting islands, both are O(m·n): all that matters is that each cell is processed once. What differs is order and memory.

DFS follows one line as far as it goes and only then backs up: the fill crawls like a snake (you'll see it on the rig next). On a snake the explicit stack holds up to m·n cells.
BFS moves in waves: first every cell one step from the start, then two steps… Cells leave the queue in order of distance, so BFS also gives the shortest number of steps. The queue holds only the wave front: on an open map that is on the order of m + n cells (about 2000 from the center of 1000×1000), although on a tangled map the worst case is O(m·n) as well.

Rule: if you only need connectivity or the region itself, any traversal works — without recursion on a big grid. If you need “nearest” or “fewest steps”, only BFS: the path along which DFS reached a cell need not be the shortest.

cards.task: Step through the recursive fill from (1, 1): every connected 1 becomes a 2. The rig will ask twice what the code does next. Keep the call order in mind: down, up, right, left.

asks.q: (0, 2) is painted. Its neighbors: 0 below, the edge above, 0 to the right, (0, 1) to the left — already 2. Which cell will the code paint next?
asks.explain: Fill(0, 2) returns empty-handed, and control comes back to Fill(0, 1): down, up and right are checked there, left remains — (0, 0). (1, 0) is a neighbor of the start itself: BFS would paint it in the very first wave, but DFS reaches it only from (0, 0). (1, 2) is 0, not the original color.

options.label: All calls return: 6 cells repainted
Paint (3, 1): it is diagonal from (2, 0)
Find the next region of ones and repaint it

asks.q: (2, 0) is painted. 0 below, already 2 above, 0 to the right, the edge to the left. What next?
asks.explain: From (2, 0) you can reach (3, 1) only diagonally, and neighbors share a side. The ones at the bottom right are another region, and Flood Fill leaves it alone: there is no outer loop here, unlike in islands. The calls unwind back to the very first one; 6 cells are repainted, each once.

cards.q: On the map from the rig (5 islands) this code returns 13 — the number of land cells on it. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: g[r][c] is a char, and compared with the number 1 it turns into its code: '1' is 49, and 49 != 1 is always true. Sink returns immediately without sinking anything, and the outer loop counts every land cell as a separate island. The code compiles without a warning — it needs the character: g[r][c] != '1'.

cards.title: In a game: tile fill and connected regions
cards.body:
Filling tiles. Tilemap has a built-in FloodFill(position, tile). But for game logic — “which cells will the water flood”, “which area has the player captured” — your own traversal over an array is handier: Tilemap is slow for logic (u3.l5).

Region labels. The same outer loop as in islands, but instead of '0' the traversal writes the region number into int[] region. Now “can I get from A to B” is region[a] == region[b], O(1) without any pathfinding. That's how unreachable targets are rejected before A* runs; otherwise it would comb the entire region before giving up. Recompute the labels when the map changes: a door opened, a wall collapsed.

Caves. After a cellular automaton the map falls apart into regions. Labels find the small ones — they get filled in — and the large ones, which are later joined by corridors (choosing the corridors is lesson 5).

Variations. Island area (#695): the traversal returns the number of cells. Eight-connectivity: eight offsets, and islands touching at a corner merge into one. Don't destroy the input: bool[] visited. The queue here is a plain int[] of w·h cells: each cell enters it once, so two indices, head and tail, are enough, with no allocations on repeated calls.
cards.deep:
No allocations. The local function Push captures count, tail and the arrays. As long as it isn't converted to a delegate, the compiler puts the captured variables in a struct on the stack — there is no heap object. Array.Fill exists since .NET Core 2.0 and in .NET Standard 2.1, that is, in Unity 2021.2 and later.

Jobs and Burst. The traversal itself is sequential, but it can move off the main thread: an IJob with NativeArray<int> instead of arrays, and Burst compiles the loop. Labeling can be parallelized by chunks: each chunk is labeled on its own, and labels that touch across chunk borders are merged with the disjoint-set structure from lesson 5 — the classic two-pass connected-component labeling.

Partial recomputation. Destroying a wall can only merge regions, so there is no need to relabel the whole map. Building a wall may cut a region in two — then relabel just that region.

Four or eight neighbors. If land counts as connected diagonally, water must be connected only through sides — otherwise two diagonals “cross”: land and water both pass through the same point. That's why image processing uses different connectivity for the background and for the objects.

cards.q: You are solving Number of Islands out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
items: Clarify: neighbors through sides or diagonals too, may the grid be modified, what are the sizes
Reduce to a graph: a cell is a vertex, a side neighbor is an edge, the answer is the number of land components
Idea: an outer loop; on every untouched land cell count++, and a traversal sinks the whole island
Code: mark a cell on entry; at 300×300 use an explicit stack instead of recursion
Run it on a small map where two islands touch at a corner
Complexity: O(m·n) time and O(m·n) memory in the worst case
Edge cases: all water, all land, a single row
cards.explain: Connectivity (4 or 8 neighbors) changes the answer, so it is clarified first. The reduction to a graph names the pattern; then the idea, the code with the depth caveat, an example with corners to check connectivity, and then the cost. “All land” is exactly the case where recursion crashes.

cards.q: Match the requirement to the technique.
pairs: The traversal returns the cell count
Islands touching at a corner are one
The grid must not be modified
An explicit stack or a queue

lessons.title: A wave from many sources
lessons.sub: Rotting Oranges, 01 Matrix and Pacific Atlantic: every source in the queue at once, and searching back from the borders

cards.title: The problem: rot spreads from everywhere at once
cards.body:
Rotting Oranges (LeetCode #994). An m×n grid, up to 10×10: 0 is empty, 1 is a fresh orange, 2 is a rotten one. Every minute a rotten orange infects its fresh side neighbors. After how many minutes are no fresh oranges left? If some orange will never be reached, return −1.

Signals: “every minute — to the neighbors” and “minimum time” mean level-order BFS from u10.l1: one level of the queue is one minute, and the level size is queue.Count at its start. Only one thing is new: there is more than one source. The rot spreads from all rotten oranges at once, and an orange rots in the minute the nearest wave reaches it.

In other words, the minute an orange rots is its distance to the nearest rotten orange (through fresh cells), and the answer is the largest of these distances.

cards.title: Naive: search from every cell
cards.body:
The same problem in its pure form is 01 Matrix (LeetCode #542): in a matrix of 0s and 1s (m·n ≤ 10⁴, at least one 0), find for every cell the distance to the nearest zero in side steps.

Naive: launch a BFS from every one and stop at the first zero — BFS yields cells in order of distance, so the first zero is the nearest. One BFS is up to m·n cells, there are up to m·n ones, O((m·n)²) in total. The same goes for the oranges: a BFS from every fresh orange to the nearest rotten one, or a simulation that scans the whole grid every minute — and there can be up to m·n minutes (oranges in a snake corridor), a square again.

The repeated work is plain to see: neighboring cells have answers that differ by at most 1, yet every BFS walks almost the same territory all over again.

cards.q: 01 Matrix at 100×100: a single zero in a corner, ones everywhere else. How much work does the naive “BFS from every one to the first zero” do, and what follows?
options: ≈ 10⁸ cells: from far-away ones the BFS covers almost the whole grid — right at the time limit, and the work is repeated
≈ 10⁴: each BFS finds a zero within a few steps
≈ 2·10⁶: each BFS only walks to the corner, at most 200 steps
cards.explain: There are 10⁴ − 1 ones. A BFS from a cell at distance d from the corner visits every cell closer than d — thousands of cells for the far half, about 0.7·10⁸ dequeues in total, and several times more counting the neighbor checks. At 10⁸ operations per second that's a second or more — all for answers that differ by 1 between neighbors.

wrong.1: There is one zero, and it's in the corner. Far cells are up to 198 steps from it, and on the way the BFS covers everything closer — thousands of cells.
wrong.2: The path to the corner is up to 198 steps long, but BFS doesn't walk a path: it visits every cell closer than the zero, because the wave expands in all directions instead of heading to the target.

cards.title: The key idea: every source goes into the queue at once
cards.body:
Turn the question around: not “where is the nearest source for this cell” but “how far does the wave from all sources reach”. Put all sources into the queue with distance 0 and run one BFS. It is the same as a BFS from an imaginary vertex connected to every source: each cell is claimed by the wave that arrives first, that is, from the nearest source.

Invariant: the queue holds cells at distance d followed by cells at d + 1, never anything else. So a cell's distance is final the moment it is first reached — mark on push, as in lesson 1. Each cell enters the queue once: O(m·n) instead of a square.

Oranges. The sources are the rotten oranges, a level is a minute, and the fresh counter tracks fresh ones. The loop runs while there is a queue and fresh oranges: after the level on which the last fresh orange rots, the queue isn't empty — it holds the last rotten ones — and without the fresh > 0 condition the loop would take one more level, infect nobody and add a minute. If the queue runs out while fresh > 0, someone can't be reached: the answer is −1. No fresh oranges at the start — the loop never runs, the answer is 0.

cards.q: Assemble Rotting Oranges.
cards.explain: Every rotten orange goes into the queue up front — that is the multi-source BFS. The loop lives while fresh oranges remain: otherwise an extra level adds a minute. The level size is taken from queue.Count before the loop. An infected neighbor becomes 2 when it is pushed, so nobody pushes it twice. If fresh oranges remain, the answer is −1.

cards.task: Step through the trace on a 4×5 grid with rotten oranges in two corners. One rig step is one minute, that is, one BFS level; the oranges that rotted during that minute are circled. The rig will ask twice what happens next.

asks.q: Minute 1: (1, 0), (0, 1), (2, 4) and (3, 3) rotted. How many oranges will rot in minute 2?
asks.explain: The next level is the fresh neighbors of these four: (1, 1), (0, 2), (2, 3) and (3, 2). (1, 1) is adjacent to both (1, 0) and (0, 1), but it rots once: (1, 0) meets it first and paints it 2, so for (0, 1) it is no longer fresh. Marking on push keeps it from being counted twice.

options.label: −1: the rot will never reach (0, 4)
4: (0, 4) rots next minute from (1, 3)
3: an unreachable orange doesn't count

asks.q: Minute 4 infected nobody: one fresh orange is left, (0, 4). The queue is empty. What does the code return?
asks.explain: The side neighbors of (0, 4) are (0, 3) and (1, 4), both empty; (1, 3) is diagonal. The wave can't cross empty cells, the queue is exhausted, and fresh = 1 — the answer is −1. The problem asks when all of them rot, so an unreachable orange can't just be dropped.

cards.title: 01 Matrix: a distance map
cards.body:
In 01 Matrix the sources are all the zeros. Put them in the queue with distance 0 and give the ones −1, “not known yet”. No separate visited is needed: −1 is the mark. Pop a cell, and every neighbor with −1 gets a distance one larger and joins the queue. The distance is set once, on push, and never changes: waves that arrive later won't be any closer.

There's no need to separate levels here: the distance is stored in the cell itself. Each cell enters the queue once — O(m·n) time and memory.

In a game this is a distance map: for every cell, how many steps to the nearest exit, cover or enemy. An agent that always steps to a neighbor with a smaller number reaches the nearest target without any pathfinding. Flow fields are built on this (u12.l4).

cards.task: Step through 01 Matrix on a 4×5 grid with three zeros. A cell shows the distance found so far, “?” means not known yet; below is the queue. The rig will ask twice what the code does.

options.label: Push nothing: the neighbors already have distances
Give (3, 1) a 2 and push it again
Overwrite (3, 1) with 1: (3, 0) is closer to a zero

asks.q: We pop (3, 0) at distance 1. What does the code do?
asks.explain: The neighbor above, (2, 0), is a zero. The neighbor to the right, (3, 1), got a 2 when (2, 1) was popped — before (3, 0). The dist != −1 check filters out both. There's nothing to overwrite: (3, 0) and (2, 1) are both at distance 1, so the wave from either gives that cell a 2, and (3, 1) can't have a 1 — it isn't next to a zero.

options.label: Nothing new: no unknown cells are left, the maximum is 2
One more wave: (0, 0) gets a 3
One more wave: (1, 2) gets a 3

asks.q: The queue holds 9 cells at distance 2. What will this level produce?
asks.explain: Count them: 3 zeros, 8 cells at distance 1 and 9 at distance 2 — all 20 cells. The “?” marks vanished from the grid when these 9 cells were pushed, because distance is set on push. Level 2 will only check neighbors and won't find a single −1. (0, 0) is two steps from the zero at (2, 0), and (1, 2) is two from (0, 3).

cards.q: On the grid [[2,1,1],[1,1,0],[0,1,1]] the code returns 5, but the answer is 4. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: In minute 4 the last orange, (2, 2), rots and joins the queue. The loop sees a non-empty queue and takes one more level: (2, 2) infects nobody, but minutes++ still runs — 5. It needs while (queue.Count > 0 && fresh > 0). “Subtract one at the end” breaks another case: on a grid without a single orange the answer is 0, and you'd get −1.

cards.title: Pacific Atlantic: search from the borders, not from the cells
cards.body:
Pacific Atlantic Water Flow (LeetCode #417). A height map m×n, up to 200×200. The Pacific touches the top and left edges, the Atlantic the bottom and right. Rain flows from a cell to a neighbor that is not higher. Find the cells from which water reaches both oceans.

Naive: from every cell, a “downhill” traversal and a check whether it touched both oceans — O((m·n)²), up to 1.6·10⁹ for 200×200.

Reverse search. Water from cell X reaches an ocean ⇔ you can climb from the ocean to X stepping against the flow: into a neighbor not lower than the current cell. The sources are all the cells on the ocean's edge — once again a single multi-source traversal per ocean. Two traversals give two maps, “drains to the Pacific” and “drains to the Atlantic”, and the answer is the cells marked in both. O(m·n).

The same reversal works whenever the question is “from every cell to one of the targets”: search from the targets. Surrounded Regions (#130) and Number of Closed Islands (#1254) are solved by a traversal from the border: whatever it reaches is connected to the border.

cards.task: Step through the reverse search on the 5×5 map from the LeetCode example: first the traversal from the Pacific (top and left edges), then from the Atlantic (bottom and right). A step goes only into a neighbor not lower than the current cell. The rig asks twice whom the traversal adds.

options.label: No: 4 is lower than 5 — water from (1, 4) will not flow into (0, 4)
Yes: water flows downhill, from 5 to 4
Yes: the traversal marks every neighbor, and heights are compared when the maps are intersected

asks.q: The Pacific traversal takes (0, 4), height 5. The neighbor below, (1, 4), height 4, is not marked yet. Will the traversal add it?
asks.explain: The traversal goes against the flow and answers “where can water come here from”. Water reaches a cell of height 5 only from a cell at least 5 high. So (1, 4) does not drain to the Pacific through (0, 4). It may drain another way — then the traversal will reach it from there.

options.label: Adds it: 4 is not lower than 4 — water from (1, 4) runs into (1, 3) and on to the Pacific
Does not add it: water does not flow over flat ground
Does not add it: (0, 4) already rejected it, a cell is not checked twice

asks.q: Now (1, 3), height 4. Its right neighbor is the same (1, 4), height 4, still unmarked. What now?
asks.explain: Water flows into a neighbor that is not higher — so over flat ground too. From (1, 4) it runs into (1, 3), from (1, 3) into (0, 3) of height 3 and on into the ocean. The rejection from (0, 4) forbade nothing: a cell stays unmarked until a suitable neighbor reaches it, and any neighbor may check it.

cards.title: Unity: influence maps and the basis of flow fields
cards.body:
Multi-source BFS is a workhorse of grid-based game AI. From all enemies you get a threat map: how many steps to the nearest enemy; a unit retreats to the neighbor with a larger number. From all exits, an evacuation map: a thousand agents step to the neighbor with a smaller number and reach the nearest exit. One BFS in O(cells) serves every agent at once, while A* per agent means a thousand separate searches. This is the basis of flow fields (u12.l4).

In practice. A 256×256 map is 65,536 cells and about 2.6·10⁵ neighbor checks per rebuild. Keep the dist array and an int[] queue of w·h cells (each enters once) in fields — no garbage. Rebuild when the sources move or every few frames, not in every Update.

Where BFS stops working. If cells cost different amounts (swamp 3, road 1), queue levels no longer equal distance: you need Dijkstra (u12.l1). If a diagonal step costs the same as a side step, BFS over eight neighbors still works.
cards.deep:
Why 01 Matrix isn't just “two DP passes”. There is also a queue-free solution: a pass from top-left to bottom-right and a reverse pass, dist = min(dist, neighbor + 1). It is correct on a grid without walls — a shortest path there can always be split into two monotone pieces. With walls (a level map) the path winds around, two passes aren't enough, while BFS works on any graph.

Jobs and Burst. BFS is sequential, but it can move off the main thread: an IJob with NativeArray<int> for dist and the queue, and Burst usually speeds such loops up noticeably. While the job computes the new map, agents read the old one — double buffering, as in Game of Life from u3.l5.

Influence, not distance. An “influence map” in strategy games is often a sum of contributions with falloff (enemy strength divided by distance, propagation with a per-step factor). That is no longer a minimum over sources, and a single BFS can't produce it: it is computed by propagation with decay across the grid, or by adding up maps per group. The BFS distance map is the special, cheapest case.

Partial updates. If one source moves, only cells whose distance could change need updating. For BFS maps it is simpler to rebuild the whole thing, but large worlds split the map into chunks and rebuild only those the wave of changes passed through.

cards.q: You are solving Rotting Oranges out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
items: Clarify: side neighbors, what to return if there are no fresh oranges at the start and if one is unreachable
Naive: a BFS from every fresh orange to the nearest rotten one — O((m·n)²)
Idea: all rotten oranges in the queue at once, one BFS, a level is a minute
Code: fresh counts the fresh ones, mark on push, loop while there's a queue and fresh > 0
Run the example minute by minute, check an orange with two rotten neighbors
Complexity: O(m·n) time and memory
Edge cases: no fresh oranges — 0, a fresh orange cut off by empty cells — −1
cards.explain: First agree on the edge answers (0 and −1) — the loop condition depends on them. Then the naive baseline, the multi-source BFS idea, the code with its two traps (the extra minute and double counting), the run-through and the cost.

cards.q: Match the problem to the technique.
pairs: After how many minutes all oranges rot
All rotten in the queue, a level is a minute
BFS from all zeros, dist set on push
Cells from which water reaches both oceans
Two traversals against the flow from the edges
A fresh orange cut off by empty cells
A thousand agents head for the nearest exit
One distance map from the exits
A swamp costs more than a road

lessons.title: Directed graphs and order
lessons.sub: Course Schedule: Kahn's algorithm and three colors; Clone Graph: an old → new dictionary

cards.title: Course Schedule: dependencies are a directed graph
cards.body:
Course Schedule (LeetCode #207). Up to 2000 courses numCourses and up to 5000 pairs prerequisites; the pair [a, b] means “to take a, first complete b”. Can you finish all the courses?

Signals: “depends on”, “first — then”, “build, load or initialization order”. This is a directed graph: the edge b → a means “b is needed for a”. You can finish everything exactly when the graph has no cycle: courses on a cycle wait for each other forever. An order in which every edge points forward is called topological.

The graph comes as an edge list — move it into adjacency lists, List<int>[], in O(V + E). At the same time count each vertex's in-degree: how many prerequisites the course has.

How a directed graph differs from a grid. In lesson 1, meeting an already visited cell meant nothing. Here, too, not every repeat meeting is a cycle: in the “diamond” 0 → 1 → 3 and 0 → 2 → 3, vertex 3 is reached twice, yet there is no cycle.

cards.q: Which problems need a topological order or cycle detection in a directed graph? Select all.
options: The build order of projects, each referencing others
Whether all quests can be completed when quests have required predecessors
The number of connected regions on a tile map
The distance from every cell to the nearest exit
The recalculation order of spreadsheet cells whose formulas refer to other cells
cards.explain: Builds, quests and formulas are all “this first, then that”: directed dependency edges, where a cycle makes the task impossible. Connected regions are undirected connectivity (lesson 1), and the distance to an exit is a multi-source BFS (lesson 2): no order is needed there.

cards.title: Kahn's algorithm: take whatever is already possible
cards.body:
A course's in-degree is the number of its unmet prerequisites. Courses with in-degree 0 can be taken right away — they go into the queue. Take a course from the queue: taken++, and every course that depends on it loses 1 from its in-degree. Whoever reaches 0 joins the queue.

Invariant: a course enters the queue only once all its prerequisites have been taken. So the order in which courses leave the queue is topological.

Why the leftovers are a cycle. If the queue is empty but taken < n, every remaining course has in-degree above 0 and is waiting for another remaining course. Walk from a course to its unmet prerequisite, from that one to its prerequisite… There are finitely many courses, so the walk closes — that's a cycle. Kahn doesn't loop forever: the courses of a cycle simply never enter the queue.

Cost: every vertex enters the queue once and every edge decrements an in-degree once — O(V + E) time and memory.

cards.q: Assemble Kahn's algorithm.
cards.explain: The pair [a, b] means “a requires b”, the edge b → a: p[0] goes into the list next[p[1]], and p[0]'s in-degree grows. Courses without prerequisites start. The prefix decrement --indegree[d] compares the already decremented value with zero; the postfix indegree[d]-- would compare the old one and miss the moment the in-degree became 0. The queue is always empty at the end — the answer comes from the taken counter.

cards.task: Courses 0–5: a diamond 0 → 1, 2 → 3, then 3 → 4 → 5, plus an edge 5 → 3 — course 3 also requires course 5. Badges show how many prerequisites a course is still waiting for. The rig will ask twice what the code does.

options.label: Course 3 will have 2 prerequisites left — it won't enter the queue
Course 3 enters the queue: one of its prerequisites is done
Course 3 is taken right after 1: it's next by number

asks.q: Course 1 is about to be taken — one of course 3's prerequisites. What happens to course 3?
asks.explain: Course 3 has three prerequisites — 1, 2 and 5 — so its badge is 3. Taking course 1 brings it down to 2. Only courses whose in-degree reaches zero enter the queue: one met prerequisite isn't enough. The course number doesn't set the order — the queue does.

options.label: false: courses 3, 4 and 5 wait for each other in a circle
true: everything that could be taken was taken
The code loops forever on 3 → 4 → 5

asks.q: Course 2 is taken and the queue is empty; 3 of 6 courses are taken. What does the code return?
asks.explain: taken = 3, while n = 6. Course 3 still has a badge of 1 (waiting for 5), course 4 has 1 (waiting for 3), course 5 has 1 (waiting for 4): none of them will reach zero — that is the cycle 3 → 4 → 5 → 3. Kahn can't loop forever: the courses of a cycle simply never enter the queue, and the while loop ends.

cards.title: DFS and three colors
cards.body:
The second way to find a cycle is DFS, but with three vertex states. White (0): not visited yet. Gray (1): the vertex is on the current recursion path — we entered it and haven't left. Black (2): fully explored, no cycle leads out of it.

An edge into a gray vertex points back to an ancestor on the current path — that's a cycle. An edge into a black one isn't: in the diamond, vertex 3 turns black after the branch through 1, and the branch through 2 simply skips it. Two states aren't enough: a plain visited can't tell “I'm on this path” from “I was here earlier via another branch” and finds a cycle in the diamond.

Order. A vertex turns black after all its descendants. If you record vertices as they turn black, you get a topological order in reverse — reverse it, and you have the answer to Course Schedule II (#210).

Depth: up to V frames. For 2000 courses that's safe; for 10⁵ nodes use Kahn or an explicit stack (lesson 1). Time is O(V + E), the same as Kahn.

cards.q: On the diamond n = 4, [[1,0],[2,0],[3,1],[3,2]] this code finds a cycle, though there is none. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: HasCycle(0) goes to 1 and from there to 3: 3 has no edges, so it returns. Then 0 goes to 2, and 2 sees visited[3] = true and declares a cycle. But 3 isn't on the current path 0 → 2 — it was finished earlier, via another branch. Three states are needed: only an edge into a gray vertex is a cycle, and a black one is skipped.

cards.title: Order in a game: systems, bundles, tech trees
cards.body:
System initialization. [DefaultExecutionOrder] and Script Execution Order in the project settings give MonoBehaviours an order by hand, with numbers. When there are thirty services, each with declared dependencies, Kahn produces the order, and on a cycle a clear error listing the stuck ones: the cycle and everything that depends on it. Entities does the same: systems inside a group are sorted by [UpdateBefore] and [UpdateAfter], and a cycle makes the sort fail with an error.

Bundles. AssetBundleManifest.GetAllDependencies(name) returns all of a bundle's dependencies, direct and indirect. Unity doesn't care in which order the bundles themselves are loaded: what matters is that the dependencies are loaded before you load an asset from the bundle that needs them. Addressables does this for you. Kahn belongs in the build script here — to check that the bundle graph has no cycle.

Tech trees. A technology becomes available when all its prerequisites are researched — that's in-degree 0. Research one, and its dependents lose 1: Kahn stretched over a whole match.

Waves. Kahn by levels, with queue.Count at the start of a level as in u10.l1: a level is the set of systems that can be initialized in parallel, and the number of levels is the length of the longest dependency chain (Parallel Courses, #1136).

Determinism. The order from a Queue depends on the order of the input. If you need a stable one, “ascending id”, use a min-heap instead of the queue: PriorityQueue in .NET 6+, SortedSet<int> in Unity. The cost is O(V log V + E): each vertex enters and leaves the heap once, and edges still cost O(1).
cards.deep:
Showing the cycle itself. The list of stuck nodes is the cycle plus everything depending on it. To print exactly the cycle you need DFS with three colors and a path stack: when you meet a gray vertex d, the cycle is the stack's vertices from d to the current one.

Kahn or DFS. Both are O(V + E). Kahn has no recursion, yields levels naturally and is easy to make incremental (the tech tree). DFS is shorter for “is there a cycle” and finds the cycle right away. For an order with the smallest id first only Kahn with a heap works — DFS gives some valid order, but not the lexicographically smallest one.

Bundle dependencies. It pays to check the dependency graph in the build script with the same Kahn. A cycle between bundles means they can only live in memory together: unload one and the other loses assets it references. It usually signals that a shared asset should move into a bundle of its own.

Unity and Awake order. The order of Awake calls between objects in one scene is not guaranteed unless you set it. An explicit service dependency graph plus a single bootstrap object that initializes them in topological order is the usual answer to “how is your bootstrap built”.

cards.q: A system loader: dependencies are known, and everything that doesn't depend on each other should initialize in parallel, in waves. How do you find the waves, and how many will there be?
options: Kahn by levels: take queue.Count at a time; there are as many waves as the longest dependency chain
DFS with three colors: as many waves as vertices that turn black
As many waves as systems without dependencies: each one opens its own wave
One wave: Kahn gives an order, and the order is a single wave
cards.explain: A Kahn level is all systems whose dependencies were finished on earlier levels, and they don't depend on each other. A system lands on level k if the longest chain leading to it is k steps, so there are as many levels as the longest chain.

wrong.1: Every vertex turns black, so that's just n. Colors find cycles; they don't separate levels.
wrong.2: The systems without dependencies all form the first wave. After that, the chain lengths decide the waves.
wrong.3: Kahn's order is sequential: inside it, systems of one level simply stand next to each other. The waves become visible only if you take a whole level at a time.

cards.title: Clone Graph: an old → new dictionary
cards.body:
Clone Graph (LeetCode #133). You get a node of a connected undirected graph (up to 100 nodes): a Node with a value and a list of neighbors. Return a deep copy — new nodes with the same connections.

Two traps. Cycles: an undirected edge is a reference in both directions, and a naive “copy the neighbors” recursion runs in circles forever. Shared neighbors: if two nodes point to a third, the copy must also have one third node, not two.

A Dictionary<Node, Node> “original → copy” solves both. It is both visited and the way to find a copy that already exists. The key rule: put the copy into the dictionary before visiting the neighbors. Then a neighbor that points back finds the ready copy. Time is O(V + E). Node doesn't override Equals, so keys are compared by reference — exactly what we want.

In Unity this is how Object.Instantiate works: when an object is copied with all its children, references inside the copied hierarchy are redirected to the copies, while references pointing outside stay as they were. You need the same dictionary when copying a graph stored in ScriptableObjects — dialogues, quests, behavior nodes.

cards.task: Step through copying the square 1 — 2 — 3 — 4 — 1 with BFS and an old → new dictionary. The rig asks twice what the code does with the next neighbor: create a copy or only add a reference.

options.label: Only a reference: 1′ exists — add it to the neighbors of 2′
Creates another copy of 1 and puts 1 into the queue
Nothing: 1 is processed, the edge 1 — 2 is already copied

asks.q: 2 has been taken; 1′, 2′ and 4′ are already in the dictionary. The first neighbor of 2 is node 1. What does the code do?
asks.explain: copy.ContainsKey(1) is true: 1′ was created at the very start. No new node is needed, but the copy needs the edge: 2′ must point to 1′. The edge 1 — 2 is two references, 1 → 2 and 2 → 1; from the side of 1 only the first was written. A second copy of 1 would split the graph: 2′ would point to a “1” that nobody else knows about.

options.label: Only a reference: 3′ was created when 2 first met 3
Creates 3′: node 3 has not been processed
Skips it: 3 will add the 4′ → 3′ reference itself when it is taken

asks.q: 4 has been taken, and the reference to 1′ is added. The second neighbor is 3: it is still in the queue, nobody has looked at its neighbors. What does the code do?
asks.explain: A copy is created at the first meeting, not when the node leaves the queue: 3′ went into the dictionary while 2 was being processed. So for 4 the first-meeting branch does not fire — only 3′ goes into the neighbors of 4′. When 3 is taken, it adds the back references 3′ → 2′ and 3′ → 4′: each node fills only its own neighbor list.

cards.q: On a graph of two connected nodes 1 — 2 this code crashes with StackOverflowException. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: The copy reaches the dictionary only after the neighbors are visited. Clone(1) creates a copy and goes into Clone(2); 2 points to 1, and 1 isn't in the dictionary yet — Clone(1) starts over, and so on forever. The line copy[node] = c must move up right after new Node: then Clone(1) called from Clone(2) returns the ready copy.

cards.q: You are solving Course Schedule out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
items: Clarify: what the pair [a, b] means, whether there are duplicates and courses without prerequisites
Reduce to a graph: the edge b → a; everything can be finished if there is no cycle
Idea: Kahn — take courses with in-degree 0, decrement the in-degree of dependents
Code: adjacency lists and in-degrees in O(V + E), a queue, a taken counter
Run it on a diamond and on a small cycle 0 → 1 → 0
Complexity: O(V + E) time and memory
Variants: DFS with three colors, the order for #210, the order by ascending id
cards.explain: The direction of the pair is the main trap of the statement, so it is clarified first. Then the reduction to cycle detection, Kahn's idea, the code, a run on two graphs (the diamond checks in-degrees, the cycle checks the false answer), the cost and what else might be asked.

cards.q: Match the problem to the technique.
pairs: The order of leaving Kahn's queue
DFS: an edge into a gray vertex
A stable order by ascending id
A min-heap instead of the queue
Which systems can initialize in parallel
An old → new dictionary before visiting neighbors

lessons.title: State-space graphs
lessons.sub: Word Ladder and a path that breaks walls: a vertex is a state, and the size of the state space estimates the cost

cards.title: Word Ladder: a graph that isn't in memory
cards.body:
Word Ladder (LeetCode #127). You get beginWord, endWord and a list wordList — up to 5000 words of the same length, up to 10 lowercase Latin letters. Each step changes one letter, and every intermediate word must be in the list (the first one needn't be). Return the number of words in the shortest chain from the first word to the last, both included, or 0 if there is no chain.

Signals: “fewest steps”, and every step is a small change. That's a shortest path in an unweighted graph, i.e. level-order BFS. Vertices are words, and an edge joins words that differ in one letter.

What's new compared with a grid: the graph is not given. You have to find a word's neighbors yourself — and how you find them decides the whole cost. A vertex here is not a cell but a state of the problem; later in this lesson the state becomes composite too.

cards.title: Finding neighbors: all pairs or 26 letters
cards.body:
All pairs. Build the graph up front: compare every pair of words letter by letter. There are N²/2 pairs and a comparison is L characters: for N = 5000, L = 10 that's 5000²/2 · 10 ≈ 1.25·10⁸ — before the search even starts.

Generation. Don't look for neighbors among the words — create candidates: in each of the L positions put each of 26 letters and ask a HashSet whether such a word exists. That's L·26 candidates per word, each costing O(L): build the string and compute its hash. For the whole BFS, N · L · 26 · L = 5000 · 10 · 26 · 10 ≈ 1.3·10⁷.

The numbers decide which way wins: generation grows as N·L²·26, all pairs as N²·L. With a large list and short words (the usual case) generation wins; with a hundred long words, all pairs does.

The “visited” mark is removing the word from the set: words.Remove returns true only the first time. One set serves as both the dictionary and visited.

cards.q: The list has 5000 words of length 5. Roughly how much work do comparing all pairs and generating candidates take?
options: ≈ 6·10⁷ and ≈ 3·10⁶: generation is about 20 times cheaper
≈ 2.5·10⁷ and ≈ 6.5·10⁵: word length doesn't affect the cost
The same: both ways compare every word with every other
cards.explain: Pairs: 5000²/2 · 5 ≈ 6.25·10⁷ character comparisons. Generation: 5000 · 5 positions · 26 letters · 5 for the string and its hash ≈ 3.25·10⁶. The ratio of the costs is N/2 versus 26·L: 2500 versus 130, about 19 times.

wrong.1: Length enters both costs: comparing a pair is up to L characters, and each candidate is a new string of length L that also has to be hashed.
wrong.2: Generation doesn't compare words with each other: it builds L·26 candidates and asks the set, at O(L) each.

cards.title: Level-order BFS to the target
cards.body:
A plain level-order BFS from u10.l1. The level number is the number of words in the chain: the first word is level 1. Invariant: level k holds exactly the words whose shortest chain is k words long. So the moment the target word leaves the queue, its level is the answer, and there's no need to search further.

The answer is the number of words, not of transitions: one more than the edges in the path. It is a common off-by-one error.

If endWord isn't in the list, return 0 right away: you can't step into it. Remove the first word from the set if it's there — otherwise you can come back to it.

Cost: each word enters the queue once, and for each one L·26 candidates are generated at O(L) apiece — O(N·L²·26) time, O(N·L) memory for the set and the queue.

cards.task: Step through Word Ladder from hit to cog. One rig step is a new BFS level. The rig will ask twice what happens next.

options: [dot, lot]
[hit, dot, lot]
[dot]
asks.q: Level 2 is [hot]. What will be on level 3?
asks.explain: The words one letter away from hot are hit, dot and lot. dot and lot are in the list and haven't been seen yet. hit is the first word: it isn't in the list, and if it were, it would have been removed at the start — BFS must not go back to what it has covered. lot is as much a neighbor as dot: the loop tries every position, not only the first.

asks.q: Level 4 is [dog, log]. What does the code return?
asks.explain: cog is one letter away from both dog and log, so it lands on level 5, and the answer is 5: that's how many words the chain hit → hot → dot → dog → cog has. It has 4 transitions — that's exactly the off-by-one error. Going through log would give a chain of the same length: BFS answers with the level, not with a path.

cards.title: A state is not a cell: a path that breaks walls
cards.body:
Shortest Path in a Grid with Obstacles Elimination (LeetCode #1293). An m×n grid up to 40×40, 0 is empty, 1 is a wall. Go from the top-left corner to the bottom-right one in side steps; you may break at most k walls. Find the minimum number of steps or return −1.

Why visited per cell is wrong. You can arrive at a cell twice: earlier but having spent a break, and later having kept it. The second visit isn't a repeat: with breaks in reserve, paths open up that were closed to the first visit. Marking by cell throws it away, and the answer gets lost.

A vertex is a state (r, c, breaks left). A step into an empty cell keeps the reserve, a step into a wall spends one break; a reserve below zero means no move. The mark is bool[m, n, k + 1], over all three coordinates. A BFS level is one step, and the very first state in the target cell gives the answer.

The cost is the size of the state space: m·n·(k + 1). One more trick: if k ≥ m + n − 3, the answer is m + n − 2 right away — a shortest path has at most m + n − 3 intermediate cells, and you can break them all. So BFS is needed only for k < m + n − 3, and there are at most 40·40·77 ≈ 1.2·10⁵ states.

cards.task: Step through #1293 on the 5×3 grid from the problem statement, k = 1. A state is a cell plus the remaining breaks: the number in a cell is the step on which it was first reached, the small numbers in the corner are the reserves it was reached with. The rig will ask twice what the code does.

options.label: Add (0, 0)·0 and (2, 0)·0: with reserve 0 these states haven't been seen
Add only (2, 0)·0: (0, 0) is already visited
Break the wall (1, 1) to the right and add (1, 1)·0

asks.q: Next, (1, 0)·0 is popped — it was reached by breaking a wall. Above it is the start (0, 0), visited with reserve 1. What does the code do?
asks.explain: seen looks at the whole triple: (0, 0)·1 has been seen, but (0, 0)·0 hasn't, so it's a new state. A useless one — the cell was already visited with reserve 1, but this code doesn't notice that (how to prune such states comes later in the lesson). To the right is a wall and the reserve is 0: left = −1, no move. Below is the empty (2, 0) — the state (2, 0)·0.

options.label: The neighbor below, (4, 2), is the target: return 6
(4, 2) is the target, but BFS finishes the level in case there's a shorter path
Go nowhere: no breaks left

asks.q: Next, (3, 2)·0 is popped at step 5: this cell was reached by breaking a wall. What does the code do?
asks.explain: (4, 2) is an empty cell, no break is needed, left = 0. It's the target, so the code returns steps = 6 right away. Nothing shorter is possible: BFS goes level by level, and every path of 5 steps or fewer has already been explored. Reserve 0 forbids only steps onto walls.

cards.q: On the grid [[0,1],[0,0],[1,1],[1,0]] with k = 1 the code returns −1, but the answer is 4. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: The mark is per cell, not per state. Step 1: break the wall (0, 1) — state (0, 1)·0 — and go down to (1, 0)·1. Step 2: (0, 1)·0 reaches (1, 1) first and marks the cell. (1, 0)·1, with its unused break, is no longer let into (1, 1) — yet only it could later break the wall (2, 1) and reach the corner in 4 steps. It needs bool[rows, cols, k + 1].

cards.title: As many states, as much work
cards.body:
Before writing a BFS over states, count them: time and memory are on the order of the number of states times the moves out of each. Up to 10⁶–10⁷ BFS passes; beyond that you need a heuristic or a different idea.

Sliding Puzzle (#773): a 2×3 board, tiles 1–5 and an empty cell; a move slides an adjacent tile into the gap. The state is the whole board as a string like "412503". There are 6! = 720 arrangements, and 360 are reachable from a given one: BFS is instant. The 3×3 puzzle has 9!/2 = 181,440 states, still BFS. But 4×4 has 16!/2 ≈ 10¹³: that needs A* with a heuristic (u12.l3).

Keys and doors (#864): a state is a cell plus the set of collected keys. The set is stored as a mask: bit i of keys is 1 if key i is collected — keys | (1 << i) adds a key, (keys >> i & 1) == 1 checks one. With K keys there are 2ᴷ masks, and cells · 2ᴷ states.

Pruning. Sometimes some states can be thrown away up front. In #1293 BFS yields states in order of steps, and if a cell was already reached with no smaller reserve, the new state is no better. Keep the best reserve each cell was reached with, and accept a state only if its reserve is larger: memory is m·n instead of m·n·(k + 1).

Unity. Puzzles — sliding tiles, Sokoban, switches — are checked for solvability with the same BFS in the editor: a level generator discards unsolvable levels and learns the minimum number of moves for star ratings along the way.

cards.q: A puzzle: a 20×20 grid, 3 keys and 3 doors on the level, each door opened by its own key. You need the shortest path to the exit. What is the state, and how many are there?
options: (cell, key mask): 400 · 2³ = 3200 states, visited is bool[400, 8]
Just the cell: 400 states, with the keys kept in the queue item
(cell, order the keys were collected in): 400 · 3! = 2400 states
cards.explain: Future moves depend on where you stand and which doors you can open — that is, on the cell and the set of keys. A set of three keys has 8 masks. The collection order affects nothing: holding keys 1 and 2 is the same whichever was found first.

wrong.1: The queue item does carry the keys, but marking by cell discards a repeat visit with a new key — the same bug as with breaks in #1293.
wrong.2: The collection order distinguishes states that behave identically: doors open by the set of keys, not by history. Extra states are extra work for nothing.

cards.title: Bidirectional BFS
cards.body:
If both the start and the target are known and moves are reversible, BFS can run from both ends: one front grows from the start, the other from the target, and the answer is found when the fronts meet.

Why it's faster. With branching b and distance d, a plain BFS expands on the order of bᵈ vertices, and two opposing ones b^(d/2) each. For b = 10 and d = 6 that's 10⁶ versus 2·10³. To keep the fronts from growing needlessly, always grow the smaller one.

Where it works. Word Ladder: the “one letter” edge is symmetric. Sliding Puzzle: any move can be undone. In #1293 it's awkward: the target cell may be reached with any reserve, so it's unclear which state the backward front should start from — use a plain BFS there.

Fronts are handy to keep in a HashSet: “they met” is a check of the candidate in the opposite set in O(1).
cards.deep:
Patterns instead of 26 letters. Word Ladder has a third way to find neighbors: a “pattern → words” dictionary, where a pattern is a word with one letter replaced by *: h*t → [hot, hit]. Building it takes N·L patterns, and a word's neighbors are the union of L lists. It pays off when the alphabet is large (Unicode rather than 26 letters).

Allocations. Every candidate is a new string: for N = 5000 and L = 10 that's 1.3·10⁶ strings, all garbage. In hot code words are encoded as numbers: for L ≤ 12 a word of 26 letters fits in a long at 5 bits per letter, a candidate is made by replacing 5 bits, and a HashSet<long> produces no garbage.

Dominance in #1293, in code. Fill a best[r, c] array with −1, set the start best[0, 0] = k, and instead of seen[y, x, left] check left <= best[y, x]. Why no answer is lost: a state with the same or a larger reserve came on the same or an earlier level, and everything reachable for the new one is reachable for it too. Useless states like (0, 0)·0 from the rig then never appear at all.

When BFS over states isn't enough. With 10¹⁰ states or more — the 4×4 puzzle, Sokoban on a big level — you need a heuristic search (A*, IDA*) or a way to split the problem. That's u12.

cards.q: Branching b = 10, the shortest path is d = 6 moves. Roughly how many vertices do plain and bidirectional BFS expand?
options: ≈ 10⁶ and ≈ 5·10⁵: two fronts mean half the work
≈ 60 and ≈ 30: b vertices per move
cards.explain: A plain BFS to depth 6 expands on the order of 10⁶ vertices. Two opposing fronts each reach depth 3: 10³ + 10³. The gain isn't a factor of two but a square root: bᵈ versus 2·b^(d/2).

wrong.1: The work grows exponentially with depth, so half the depth means the square root of the work, not half of it.
wrong.2: Each level expands not b vertices but b times more than the previous level: 10, 100, 1000…

cards.q: You are solving #1293 out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
items: Clarify: side neighbors, the start and target are empty, what to return without a path
Notice: fewest steps without weights means BFS, but visited per cell loses visits with a larger reserve
Idea: the state (r, c, breaks left), a step onto a wall spends one
Code: level-order BFS, seen[r, c, rem], the answer is the first entry into the target
Run an example where arriving early at a cell wastes a break
Complexity: O(m·n·k), and for k ≥ m + n − 3 the answer is m + n − 2 at once
Improvement: keep the best reserve per cell instead of all k + 1 layers
cards.explain: First the agreement on the statement, then the pattern (BFS) and why its naive marking breaks, the idea of a state, the code, a counterexample as a check, the cost with the cutoff on k, and an answer to “can you save memory”.

cards.q: Match the problem to its state.
pairs: A word; neighbors are 26 letters per position
The board as a string, 360 reachable

lessons.title: Disjoint set union
lessons.sub: Union-Find: Number of Provinces, Redundant Connection and Kruskal — connectivity as edges arrive, in almost O(1)

cards.title: Connectivity that changes
cards.body:
Number of Provinces (LeetCode #547). Up to 200 cities and an n×n matrix isConnected: 1 means two cities are joined by a road. A province is a group of cities connected directly or through others. How many provinces are there? That's the number of connected components, and the DFS from lesson 1 solves it in O(n²) over the matrix.

Now make it online: edges arrive one at a time, and after each one you're asked “are a and b connected?” or “how many components are there now?”. A BFS per question is O(V + E); for 10⁵ edges and questions that's 10¹⁰. You need a structure that merges groups and answers “same group?” almost instantly.

Disjoint set union (Union-Find, DSU) is a forest: each group is a tree, its root is the group's representative, parent[x] is x's parent, and a root has parent[x] == x. Find(x) climbs to the root. Union(a, b) hangs the root of one tree under the root of the other. a and b are connected ⇔ Find(a) == Find(b). No adjacency lists, no traversal: just an int[n] array.

cards.title: Two improvements: rank and path compression
cards.body:
The naive version degenerates: if a big tree keeps getting hung under a single vertex, trees turn into chains, and Find costs O(n).

Union by rank. Each root stores a rank — an upper bound on the height of its tree; a single vertex has rank 0. The root with the lower rank goes under the root with the higher one, and the taller tree keeps its height. If the ranks are equal, hang either one, and the new root's rank goes up by 1. Rank r only arises from two trees of rank r − 1, so a tree of rank r has at least 2ʳ vertices, and the height is ≤ log₂ n. Union by size is the same rule comparing vertex counts instead: smaller tree under larger, the same height bound, and the group size is sometimes useful on its own. Either is fine in an interview; the rig below shows rank.

Path compression. Find walks the path twice: the first pass finds the root, the second re-hangs every vertex on the path directly onto the root. The next Find from any of them takes one step. Ranks are left alone during compression: heights only shrink, so a rank stays an upper bound. The same thing is often written as a one-line recursion: parent[x] == x ? x : parent[x] = Find(parent[x]). Shorter still is “skip one”, parent[x] = parent[parent[x]] in a single pass, with the same asymptotics.

Each improvement on its own gives O(log n) (compression in the amortized sense). Together — O(α(n)) amortized per operation, where α is the inverse Ackermann function: for any n that fits in memory, α(n) ≤ 4. In practice, a constant. Union returns a bool: false means “already in the same group” — it'll come in handy.

cards.q: The naive Union-Find from the first card: parent[Find(a)] = Find(b). We call Union(0, i) for i = 1, 2, …, n − 1 with n = 10⁵. Roughly how much work is that?
options: ≈ 5·10⁹: the tree is a chain 0 → 1 → 2 → …, and Find(0) walks all of it every time
≈ 10⁵: each Union is a single assignment
≈ 1.7·10⁶: the tree's height is at most log₂ n
cards.explain: Union(0, 1) sets parent[0] = 1, Union(0, 2) sets parent[1] = 2: the root of zero's group goes under the new vertex every time, and the path from 0 to the root grows by 1. At step i, Find(0) walks i links — n²/2 ≈ 5·10⁹ in total. With union by rank, the single vertex i (rank 0) goes under the group's root (rank 1), and Find(0) is one or two steps.

wrong.1: There is one assignment, but two Finds come before it, and Find(0) climbs the whole chain, which grows with every call.
wrong.2: log₂ n is the bound for union by rank or by size. Here neither is used, and the height reaches n − 1.

cards.q: Assemble Find and Union.
cards.explain: Find's second pass re-hangs every vertex on the path directly onto the root; up remembers where to go next. Equal roots mean one group already, so Union changes nothing and honestly returns false. After the swap ra is the root with the rank at least as high; the root rb goes under it, not the vertex b itself. The rank grows only when the ranks are equal, and only for the new root ra: the height of rb plus one could have caught up with ra's and exceeded it.

cards.title: Number of Provinces and Redundant Connection
cards.body:
#547: create a Dsu for n cities and call Union for every pair i < j with isConnected[i][j] == 1. Every successful merge lowers Count by 1 — the answer is dsu.Count. O(n²·α(n)).

Redundant Connection (LeetCode #684). A tree of n vertices (3 ≤ n ≤ 1000, numbered from 1) plus one extra edge — n edges in all. Return an edge whose removal leaves a tree; if several fit, the one that comes last in the list.

Walk the edges and call Union. false means the endpoints are already connected by another path, so this edge closes a cycle. There is one cycle, and any of its edges could be removed. The first false comes from the cycle edge that appears latest in the list: until it arrives, the cycle isn't closed. That's exactly the required answer. O(n·α(n)), with no traversal and no adjacency lists.

cards.task: Walk #684 on the edges 1-2, 3-4, 1-3, 5-6, 4-5, 2-6: a tree on six vertices plus one extra edge. An arrow points to the parent, the badge on a root is its rank (r0, r1…), and the parent array is at the bottom. Union by rank, and Find compresses the path. The rig will stop twice and ask what the code does next.

options.label: 3 goes under 1, and rank[1] becomes 2
3 goes under 1, and rank[1] stays 1: a hung subtree never changes the root's height
1 goes under 3: the second endpoint's root always becomes the new root

asks.q: Edge 1-3: the roots are 1 and 3, both of rank 1. What does the code do?
asks.explain: The ranks are equal, so there is no swap: rank[ra] < rank[rb] is false, and rb = 3 goes under ra = 1. The tree 1 — 2 of height 1 gets the subtree 3 — 4 of the same height, and the path 4 → 3 → 1 is one link longer than before: the height is now 2, and the rank goes up with it. Had the ranks differed, the lower tree would go under the higher one and the rank would not change — that is what happens on edge 4-5.

options.label: Find(2) = 1 and Find(6) = 1: the path is 6 → 5 → 1, and 6 is re-hung straight onto 1
Find(2) = 1 and Find(6) = 5: different roots, so 5 goes under 1
Find(2) = 2 and Find(6) = 6: these vertices have never been in the same edge

asks.q: Edge 2-6. What do the two Finds return?
asks.explain: On the previous edge, 4-5, root 5 (rank 1) went under 1 (rank 2), and 6 has hung from 5 since edge 5-6. Find(6) climbs 6 → 5 → 1 and on its second pass re-hangs 6 onto 1; Find(2) is one step to 1. The roots match: 2 and 6 are already connected by the path 2 — 1 — 3 — 4 — 5 — 6, the edge [2, 6] closes a cycle, and Union returns false — that is the answer.

cards.q: #684 on [[1,2],[1,3],[2,3]]: this code returns an empty array instead of [2,3]. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: It must hang the root, not the vertex itself. Union(1, 2): parent[1] = 2. Union(1, 3): Find(1) = 2, but the code writes parent[1] = 3 — so 1 leaves 2, and 2 stays a separate root. On [2,3], Find(2) = 2 and Find(3) = 3 — “different groups”, Union returns true, and the redundant edge is never found. It needs parent[ra] = rb.

cards.title: Union-Find or a traversal
cards.body:
The graph is given in full and never changes — components can be counted by DFS/BFS or by Union-Find, both O(V + E). Union-Find is handy because no adjacency lists are needed: edges in any order, one pass, O(V) memory.

Edges are added along the way, with questions in between — Union-Find: each operation is almost O(1), while a traversal would have to be repeated. Example: Number of Islands II (#305): land appears one cell at a time, and after each you need the number of islands. A vertex is the cell r·w + c; new land means Count++ and a Union with neighboring land.

What Union-Find can't do: delete edges or split groups, find paths and distances, respect edge direction. If walls are both built and destroyed, region labels are recomputed with a traversal (lesson 1).

Edges in increasing weight order — “at what moment did a and b first end up together”. Minimum spanning trees (next) and minimax paths (u12.l2) are built on this.

In a game. A destructible level: a wall between rooms is destroyed — Union; “are the bases connected” — compare two Finds. Caves after a cellular automaton: the regions from labeling (lesson 1) are vertices, and corridors are dug until Count reaches 1.
cards.deep:
Offline deletions. If all queries are known in advance, edge deletions can be reversed: walk the queries from the end, and a deletion becomes an addition. That's how “edges disappear, how many components after each step” problems are solved.

Recursive Find. The short form parent[x] = Find(parent[x]) compresses the path as fully as the two passes do, but it is recursive. With union by rank or by size the depth is at most log₂ n, so the stack is safe. Without it, a chain of 10⁵ vertices means 10⁵ frames, and a recursive Find crashes exactly where the recursive traversal from lesson 1 does. The iterative versions are always safe.

Union-Find with data. The root is a convenient place for group data: size, sum, minimum, a member list. When merging, the smaller group flows into the larger — the same “smaller under larger” principle: each element moves at most log₂ n times, so member lists merge in O(n log n) total.

Jobs and Burst. Union-Find is two int arrays, that is, a NativeArray<int> with no references and no garbage. Merging groups from several threads at once isn't straightforward — the root write would have to be atomic; a single-threaded Burst job is usually enough.

cards.q: A destructible map: the player breaks walls between rooms, and after each destruction the game checks whether the two teams' bases are connected. Walls are never rebuilt. What do you do?
options: Union-Find over rooms: a wall breaks — Union; the check is Find(baseA) == Find(baseB)
A BFS from base A after each destruction: it stops as soon as it finds base B
Kruskal by wall strength: the minimum spanning tree shows which bases are connected
Union-Find, and if walls start being rebuilt, call Union in reverse
cards.explain: Edges are only added and questions come in between — exactly the Union-Find case: each event and each check is almost O(1). BFS gives a correct answer too, but at O(rooms + walls) per event.

wrong.1: While the bases aren't connected, BFS walks the whole component of base A — over and over, after every broken wall.
wrong.2: A spanning tree answers “how to connect everything most cheaply”, while here you need the current connectivity after each event.
wrong.3: There is no reverse Union: the structure doesn't remember which edge merged the groups and can't split a tree. If walls are rebuilt, connectivity is recomputed with a traversal.

cards.title: Kruskal: the minimum spanning tree
cards.body:
Min Cost to Connect All Points (LeetCode #1584). Up to 1000 points on a plane, an edge costs the Manhattan distance |x₁ − x₂| + |y₁ − y₂|. Connect all the points with the minimum total cost. That's the minimum spanning tree: n − 1 edges, all vertices connected, the smallest sum of weights.

Kruskal's algorithm: sort all edges by weight and go from light to heavy; take an edge if Union returns true — it joins two different groups. An edge inside one group would form a cycle — skip it. Stop when one group is left.

Why it's correct: Kruskal takes e = (u, v), the lightest of the edges between different groups. Suppose some minimum spanning tree contains every edge taken so far but not e. Add e to it — a cycle appears. The cycle leaves u's group and comes back, so it contains another edge f leading out of u's group. f hasn't been taken yet and joins different groups, so f is no lighter than e. Swap f for e — the result is still a spanning tree, and the sum doesn't grow.

Cost. The graph is complete: n(n − 1)/2 ≈ 5·10⁵ edges, sorting is O(E log E) ≈ 10⁷ — it passes.

Unity: a dungeon. Rooms are points, possible corridors are edges with a length. The spanning tree connects every room with the smallest total corridor length, but it's a tree — all dead ends. So after Kruskal some rejected edges are added back, say every tenth one, to create loops.
cards.deep:
Prim versus Kruskal. A complete graph has Θ(n²) edges, and Kruskal spends O(n² log n) time and O(n²) memory on their list. Prim without a heap — an array “distance to the tree” over n vertices; at each step pick the closest and update the rest — is O(n²) time and O(n) memory. For #1584 it's faster and doesn't hold 5·10⁵ tuples. Kruskal wins on sparse graphs, where E ≈ V.

Fewer edges. For Euclidean distance the minimum spanning tree always lies within the Delaunay triangulation, which has about 3n edges instead of n²/2. That's why dungeon generators usually triangulate the room centers, build the tree on that, and then add back a few edges for loops.

Overflow. In #1584 coordinates are up to 10⁶ in absolute value: one edge is up to 4·10⁶, and the crude bound 999 · 4·10⁶ ≈ 4·10⁹ doesn't fit in an int. But the tree can't be that expensive: it costs no more than any path through all the points, and all the points lie in a 2·10⁶ × 2·10⁶ square. Cut the square into 32 horizontal strips and snake through the points strip by strip: that is 32 · 2·10⁶ horizontally, at most 6.3·10⁴ vertically per edge inside a strip, plus the hops between strips — under 3·10⁸ in total. That is below int.MaxValue ≈ 2.1·10⁹, and LeetCode returns an int. With no such constraints, or if you don't remember them, sum in a long.

Sorting tuples. ValueTuple compares fields left to right, which is why the weight goes first. List.Sort is an introspective sort and isn't stable; for a spanning tree that doesn't matter: with equal weights any order works, and the sum is the same.

cards.task: Step through Kruskal on the points [[0,0],[2,2],[3,10],[5,2],[7,0]], numbered 0–4: all 10 pairs are edges, sorted by Manhattan distance. The rig asks twice whether Kruskal takes the next edge.

options.label: Skips it: 0 and 3 are already in one group, Union returns false
Takes it: it is the lightest edge left
Takes it: vertex 0 has only one edge so far

asks.q: 1–3 (3), 0–1 (4) and 3–4 (4) are taken, total 11. The next edge is 0–3 (7). What does Kruskal do?
asks.explain: After 1–3, 0–1 and 3–4 there is one group — {0, 1, 3, 4}. Find(0) == Find(3), and an edge inside the group would close the cycle 0 — 1 — 3 — 0. 0–4 and 1–4 are skipped the same way. Edges are skipped not for being heavy and not by vertex degree, but for lying inside a group.

options.label: Takes it: Union attaches point 2, total 20 — the tree is done
Skips it: it is heavier than every edge taken
Takes it, but 20 is not the answer yet: 3 edges remain

asks.q: 0–3, 0–4 and 1–4 were skipped. Next is 1–2 (9), the heaviest seen so far. What happens?
asks.explain: Point 2 is still alone in its group, so Union(1, 2) returns true: 11 + 9 = 20. That is the fourth edge, n − 1 = 4, Count == 1 — the loop breaks, and the remaining 3 edges are not even looked at. The answer for these points is 20.

cards.q: You are solving Redundant Connection out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
items: Clarify: vertices from 1, exactly n edges, if several fit return the last one
Observation: a tree plus one edge has exactly one cycle; the extra edge closes it
Idea: Union-Find over the edges in list order; the first Union that returns false is the answer
Code: a Dsu with union by rank and path compression, Union returns a bool
Run [[1,2],[1,3],[2,3]]: on [2,3] both Finds give the same root
Complexity: O(n·α(n)) — almost linear, O(n) memory
Why the first false is exactly the cycle's last edge in the list
cards.explain: After clarifying comes the property “tree + edge = one cycle”, then the idea, the code and the run. The proof that the first false matches “last in the list” finishes the answer: it's usually asked.

cards.q: Match the problem to the technique.
pairs: The redundant edge in a tree
The first Union that returns false
Islands appear one cell at a time
Connect all points as cheaply as possible
Walls are both destroyed and built
Find that never degenerates into a chain
Lower tree under the higher one (rank)

lessons.title: Unit final: graphs
lessons.sub: New problems to recognize, an islands trace, a Union-Find trap and explaining out loud

cards.q: New problems. Match the statement to the technique.
pairs: Walls and Gates (#286): distance from every room to the nearest gate
BFS from all gates at once
Course Schedule II (#210): return the order of courses
The order of leaving Kahn's queue
Max Area of Island (#695): the area of the largest island
The traversal returns the cell count
Accounts Merge (#721): accounts sharing an email belong to one person
Open the Lock (#752): 4 wheels of 10 digits, forbidden combinations
Surrounded Regions (#130): fill regions that don't touch the border

cards.q: Shortest Bridge (LeetCode #934): an n×n grid up to 100×100 with exactly two islands. What is the minimum number of water cells to fill in to connect them? How do you solve it in O(n²)?
options: Mark the first island with a traversal and put all its cells in the queue; BFS through water level by level up to the first cell of the second island
A separate BFS from each cell of the first island to the second, then take the minimum
DFS from the first island through water: the first path that reaches the second is the shortest
Union-Find: merge water cells with islands until the islands are in one group
cards.explain: This is lesson 1 plus lesson 2: a traversal finds the first island, and all of it becomes one source of a multi-source BFS. The wave moves through water, and the level at which it touches the second island is the number of filled cells plus one. Each cell enters the queue once — O(n²).

wrong.1: The answer is right, but an island has up to n² cells and each BFS is up to n²: O(n⁴) in total, up to 10⁸ at 100×100. That's exactly the repeated work a single BFS from all sources removes.
wrong.2: The path along which DFS reached the target need not be the shortest: DFS follows one line as far as it goes. Fewest steps means BFS only.
wrong.3: Union-Find answers “are they connected”, not “how many cells to fill”: it knows nothing about distances.

cards.q: Number of Operations to Make Network Connected (LeetCode #1319): up to 10⁵ computers and a list of cables. Any cable can be moved to another pair of computers. How many moves are needed to connect them all, or −1?
options: If there are fewer than n − 1 cables — −1; otherwise the number of components minus 1, which Union-Find gives
The number of cables on which Union returned false: each redundant one has to be moved
n − 1 minus the number of cables: that's how many a tree is missing
The number of components: each one needs to be attached with one cable
cards.explain: Connecting n vertices takes at least n − 1 edges — with fewer cables it can't be done. If there are enough, spare cables can always be found: k components are joined by k − 1 moves, one for each component except the first. Union-Find counts the components in one pass over the cables, Count at the end.

wrong.1: There can be more redundant cables than moves needed: one component may have several, while the number of moves is exactly the number of components to attach.
wrong.2: The number of cables doesn't tell you how many components there are. On 4 computers with a triangle 0–1–2 there are 3 = n − 1 cables, the formula gives 0, but computer 3 isn't connected: 1 move is needed.
wrong.3: The first component is already in place: the others need attaching, k − 1.

cards.task: A new 5×5 map with lots of corner contacts. Step through the island count; the rig will ask twice what happens next.

options.label: The calls return, and the loop finds (0, 3) — island #2
Sink sinks (2, 2): it touches (1, 1) at a corner
The loop finds (2, 2) — island #2

asks.q: (1, 1) is sunk. Below, right and left are water, above is the already sunk (0, 1). Diagonally, at (2, 2), there's land. What next?
asks.explain: Neighbors share a side only, so (2, 2) isn't part of island #1. Sink unwinds, control returns to the outer loop, and the loop goes row by row: row 0 comes before row 2, so the first untouched land is (0, 3).

options.label: The loop finds (4, 4) — island #6
(4, 4) is already part of island #4: it's diagonal from (3, 3)
The traversal is over: 5 islands

asks.q: (4, 2) is sunk, island #5 is done. What next?
asks.explain: The side neighbors of (4, 4) are (3, 4) and (4, 3), both water; it touches (3, 3) only at a corner. So island #4's DFS never reached it, it's still '1', and the loop finds it as island #6. With eight neighbors this whole map would be a single island.

cards.q: Counting components of an undirected graph (#323). On n = 3 with edges [[0,1],[1,2],[0,2]] the code returns 0, but the answer is 1. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: The counter drops on every edge, not on every merge. The third edge [0,2] joins vertices already in one group: a == b, there's no merge, but count-- runs anyway. It needs if (a == b) continue; before merging — that's the false of Union from lesson 5. On a tree the bug is invisible: every edge there merges.

cards.q: Open the Lock (#752): a lock of 4 wheels with digits 0–9, a move turns one wheel by ±1, the start is "0000", some combinations are forbidden. Fewest moves to the target. How much work does BFS do?
options: 10⁴ states with 8 moves from each — up to 8·10⁴ transitions: BFS is instant
10⁸: compare every combination with every other
4! = 24 states: the wheels can only be rearranged
Infinite: the wheels turn in circles, so BFS loops forever
cards.explain: Count the state space before coding: 4 wheels of 10 positions — 10⁴ strings, and from each, 4 wheels × 2 directions = 8 neighbors. Forbidden combinations go into visited up front, so they're never entered. Loops are harmless: visited keeps any state from being entered twice.

wrong.1: Nobody compares pairs: neighbors are generated — 8 per state, like the 26 letters in Word Ladder.
wrong.2: The wheels aren't rearranged but turned: a state is four digits, not their order.
wrong.3: There are finitely many states, and visited marks each one when it's pushed: every state enters the queue at most once.

cards.q: Unity, an RTS: a 512×512 map, 300 player units must retreat from the nearest of 200 enemies, and the enemies move. What do you compute?
options: One distance map, a BFS from all enemies at once every few frames; a unit steps to the neighbor with a larger distance
A BFS from every unit to the nearest enemy every frame
A* from every unit to the cell farthest from the enemies
Union-Find over cells: a unit moves into another component
cards.explain: “Distance to the nearest of many” is a multi-source BFS: 2.6·10⁵ cells in one pass serve every unit at once. The enemies move, so the map is rebuilt — but every few frames, not once per unit.

wrong.1: The answer is the same, but it's 300 traversals instead of one, each up to the whole map in the worst case: up to 300 · 2.6·10⁵ ≈ 8·10⁷ cells per frame.
wrong.2: The farthest cell still has to be found — with the same distance map — and then come 300 path searches. The distance map itself already says where to step.
wrong.3: Connected components don't depend on where the enemies are: units and enemies are almost always in the same component. You need distances, and Union-Find doesn't provide them.

cards.q: You are solving Shortest Bridge out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
items: Clarify: side neighbors, exactly two islands, the answer is the number of cells filled
Naive: a BFS from every cell of the first island — O(n⁴)
Idea: find the first island with a traversal and make all its cells the sources of a single BFS
Code: a traversal with marking, then a level-order BFS through water to a cell of the second island
Run it on a small grid where one water cell separates the islands
Complexity: O(n²) time and memory
Edge cases: islands touching at a corner, a one-cell island
cards.explain: First agree on connectivity and on what counts as the answer — the “minus one” at the end depends on it. Then the naive baseline, an idea built from two known parts, the code, a run-through, the cost and the edges: touching at a corner is not a connection.

cards.q: Complexity of the unit's solutions. What is true? Select all.
options: Number of Islands is O(m·n) time
Kahn's algorithm is O(V + E)
Union-Find with union by rank and path compression is almost O(1) per operation, amortized
A multi-source BFS from k sources is O(k·m·n)
#1293 is O(m·n): each cell enters the queue once
Recursive DFS on a 300×300 grid of solid land is safe with a 1 MB stack
cards.explain: Islands: each cell once; Kahn: each vertex and each edge once; Union-Find: O(α(n)), α ≤ 4. A multi-source BFS is one traversal: all sources in one queue, O(m·n) for any k. In #1293 the queue holds states, not cells: O(m·n·k). Recursion over 9·10⁴ cells of solid land takes 5–9 MB of stack.

units.title: Pathfinding and space in games
units.blurb: What game dev interviews actually ask: Dijkstra, minimax paths, A* on a grid, flow fields for crowds of units and spatial partitioning with grids, hashes and quadtrees. With Jobs and Burst where they belong.

units.title: Backtracking and dynamic programming
