units.blurb: Decision trees, pruning, from recursion to a table, the unbounded knapsack, DP on two strings and LIS in O(n log n). How to spot DP in a problem and name the state and the transition.

lessons.title: The decision tree
lessons.sub: Subsets and Permutations: choose and undo, saying 2ⁿ·n and n!·n out loud, subsets as bitmasks

cards.title: The problem and the “list them all” signal
cards.body:
Subsets (LeetCode #78). Given an array of distinct numbers nums, 1 ≤ n ≤ 10, return all of its subsets, including the empty one, in any order. For [1, 2, 3] there are eight: [], [1], [2], [3], [1, 2], [1, 3], [2, 3], [1, 2, 3].

The signal for exhaustive search is that the problem asks you to list all the options: all subsets, all permutations, all placements, all partitions. The answer itself is exponential: there are 2ⁿ subsets, and each has to be written out. So nothing can beat O(n·2ⁿ), and the “naive solution” here is the solution — the only question is how to walk the options without duplicates and without wasted work.

It is a different story when the question is how many options, the minimum, or is it possible. Then you don’t have to write out every option, and there is often a polynomial solution — dynamic programming, the second half of this unit. Brute force there is the baseline, not the answer.

Small limits are a signal too: n ≤ 10–20 almost always means “you can enumerate”.

cards.q: Where is enumerating every option the actual solution, not a naive baseline? Select all.
options: Print every way to arrange 8 items in 8 slots
Print every set of 12 perks whose total cost fits the budget
How many subsets of an array of 10⁴ numbers sum to k ≤ 1000
The minimum number of coins that make the sum 10⁴
Print every word of length 5 over the letters A–D
cards.explain: Arrangements, perk sets and words ask you to list every option: the answer itself is exponential (8!, up to 2¹², 4⁵), and only enumeration can write it out. “How many subsets” and “minimum coins” ask for a number, not a list: with n = 10⁴, enumerating 2ⁿ is impossible, while DP computes the answer in polynomial time — that is lessons 3–4.

cards.title: Take it or leave it: choose, recurse, undo
cards.body:
A subset is n decisions in a row: for each number, “take” or “skip”. Draw these decisions as a tree: at level i we decide the fate of nums[i], every node has two children, at depth n there are 2ⁿ leaves, and each leaf is one subset.

We walk the tree depth-first, keeping one shared list path — what was chosen on the way from the root. The step is always the same: make a choice → recurse → undo the choice. Undoing (backtracking) returns path to the state the next branch expects.

Invariant: on entry to Dfs(i), path holds exactly the chosen elements of nums[0..i−1], and it is the same after Dfs(i) returns. At a leaf (i == n) we add a copy to the answer: path itself will keep changing.

The recursion depth is n, so the call stack is no danger here (its limit was covered in the C# and Unity lesson of the first unit).
flow: Dfs(i): i == n? → copy of path to the answer

cards.q: Build Subsets: choose, recurse, undo.
cards.explain: A leaf is when all n numbers have been decided, i == nums.Length (with nums.Length − 1 the last number would never get its choice). The answer gets a copy: path keeps changing. The undo removes exactly the last added element; Clear would also wipe the ancestors’ choices. The “without nums[i]” branch also moves on to the next number: Dfs(i + 1), while Dfs(i) would loop forever.

cards.task: Walk the decision tree for [1, 2, 3]: the left branch is “take”, the right one is “skip”, the leaves are answers. The rig will stop twice and ask where the code goes next: answer from path and the order “take first, then undo and skip”.

options.label: Undo 3 and take the branch without it: [1, 2] — a leaf
Undo 2 and take 3: path = [1, 3]
Stop: all numbers have been used

asks.q: The leaf [1, 2, 3] is saved. What does the code do next?
asks.explain: The call Dfs(3) returned to Dfs(2) — the decision about the number 3. Its first branch (“take”) is done, so the code runs path.RemoveAt and the second branch Dfs(3) without the 3: another leaf, [1, 2]. The code gets back to the 2 only when Dfs(2) has returned completely.

options.label: Undo 1: path = [], next comes everything without the 1
Take 2: path = [1, 2] again
Take 3: path = [1, 3]

asks.q: All four leaves with the 1 — [1, 2, 3], [1, 2], [1, 3], [1] — are saved. What next?
asks.explain: The “take 1” subtree has been walked completely, and Dfs(1) returned to the root. The root undoes its choice — path is empty again — and starts the right half of the tree: the subsets without the 1. There are no duplicates: every leaf is its own set of yes/no decisions.

cards.title: The cost: 2ⁿ·n and how to say it
cards.body:
There are 2ⁿ leaves, and each copies path — up to n elements. There are fewer internal nodes than leaves, and they do O(1) work. In total O(n·2ⁿ) time. Memory: the stack and path are O(n), the answer is O(n·2ⁿ), but that is the output size, usually named separately.

How to estimate whether it fits (the rule of thumb is about 10⁸ simple operations per second):

2ⁿ: 2¹⁰ ≈ 10³, 2²⁰ ≈ 10⁶, 2³⁰ ≈ 10⁹. So n ≤ 20 is comfortable, n ≈ 25 is borderline, n = 30 is out.
n!: 8! = 40 320, 10! ≈ 3.6·10⁶, 11! ≈ 4·10⁷, 12! ≈ 4.8·10⁸. Permutations can be enumerated up to n ≈ 10–11.

Out loud it sounds like this: “there are 2ⁿ leaves, at each I copy up to n elements — O(n·2ⁿ); with n ≤ 10 that is about ten thousand operations, and it can’t be faster: that many elements are in the answer itself.”

cards.title: A subset as a bitmask
cards.body:
The same tree can be walked without recursion. Write a subset as a number mask: bit i is 1 if nums[i] is taken. For [a, b, c], mask 5 = 101 in binary: bits 0 and 2 are set — that is {a, c}.

Two operations make it work. 1 << n is a one shifted left by n places, that is 2ⁿ: masks from 0 to 2ⁿ − 1 visit every subset exactly once. (mask >> i) & 1 shifts the mask right by i and keeps the lowest bit with a bitwise AND: that is bit i.

The complexity is the same, O(n·2ⁿ), but there is no recursion and no shared path, and a subset can be stored as a single int — handy when sets need to be compared, used as dictionary keys or counted without allocations. The limit is the bit width: the loop mask < (1 << n) on int works up to n = 30 (1 << 31 is already negative), on long with 1L << n up to 62. But enumerating 2ⁿ stops fitting in time long before that. Bits in depth are in the bitwise operations unit.

In a game: picking, out of n ≤ 20 items, the most valuable set that fits a backpack by weight is 2²⁰·20 ≈ 2·10⁷ operations. On level load or in an editor tool that is fine; every frame in Update it is not.

cards.q: nums = [4, 7, 9, 2]. Which subset does mask = 6 stand for?
cards.explain: 6 = 0110 in binary: bits 1 and 2 are set (the lowest bit is bit zero, on the right). Bit i stands for nums[i], so we take nums[1] = 7 and nums[2] = 9.

wrong.1: [4, 7] is bits 0 and 1, mask 0011 = 3. The lowest bit of 6 is zero.
wrong.2: [9, 2] is bits 2 and 3, mask 1100 = 12. Looks like reading the mask left to right.
wrong.3: [4, 9] is bits 0 and 2, mask 0101 = 5.

cards.title: Permutations: place and take back
cards.body:
Permutations (LeetCode #46). Given an array of distinct numbers, 1 ≤ n ≤ 6, return all permutations. For [1, 2, 3] there are 3! = 6.

Now each level decides not “yes/no” but which number goes into the next position: any one not used yet. The first level has n options, the second n − 1, … — n! leaves. To avoid scanning path for “was it used”, keep a flag array used: an O(1) check.

The template is the same: place (used[i] = true, path.Add) → recurse → take back both changes. Forgetting to reset used[i] means losing that number for all later branches.

The cost: n! leaves, each with an n-element copy, and a loop over n at every node — O(n·n!). For n = 6 that is about 4 thousand operations, for n = 10 already 3.6·10⁷.

cards.task: Walk the permutation tree of [1, 2, 3]: each level takes any number not used yet, left to right. The rig will ask where the code goes after the first complete permutation.

options.label: path = [1, 3]: 3 and 2 were taken back, 3 goes into the second position
path = [1, 2, 3] again, but from another level
path = [2]: everything was taken back, start with the 2

asks.q: [1, 2, 3] is saved. What will path be on the next step?
asks.explain: The third level took back the 3; there are no other free numbers there, so the call ends. The second level takes back the 2 (used[1] = false) and continues its loop: the next free index is 2, the number 3. We get [1, 3], and then [1, 3, 2]. The 2 gets the first position only when the first level’s loop moves on.

cards.q: This Subsets returns eight empty lists on [1, 2, 3]. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: List<int> is a reference type: res.Add(path) puts eight references to one and the same list into the answer. By the end of the walk every undo has run and path is empty — so all eight “subsets” are empty. A leaf needs a copy: res.Add(new List<int>(path)) or path.ToList().

cards.title: Variations: duplicates, k elements, a loop instead of yes/no
cards.body:
The second way to build subsets: every tree node is an answer right away, and a loop picks the next element to the right of the last one taken: Dfs(start) adds a copy of path and tries i from start. The start index guarantees that elements go in increasing index order — so {1, 2} and {2, 1} never both appear. This template is the basis of every “combinations” problem.

Exactly k elements (Combinations, #77): the same loop, but a copy goes to the answer only when path.Count == k. There are C(n, k) leaves.

Duplicates in the input (Subsets II, #90; Permutations II, #47). Sort so that equal values sit next to each other. In subsets, skip a value equal to the previous one on the same level: i > start && nums[i] == nums[i − 1]. In permutations, skip nums[i] if it equals the previous one and the previous one is not used right now: that way equal numbers are always placed in the same order.

A product of choices (Letter Combinations of a Phone Number, #17): each position has its own set of letters, up to 4ⁿ leaves.

In a game: every combination of items to check crafting recipes, every order of applying 5 buffs (5! = 120), every layout of a small set of slots. While there are 10⁵–10⁶ options, enumeration in an editor tool or on load is an honest solution.
cards.deep:
The lower bound. The Subsets answer holds exactly n·2ⁿ⁻¹ numbers, Permutations — n·n!. No algorithm writes out an answer faster than its size, so O(n·2ⁿ) and O(n·n!) are optimal. The subset tree has 2ⁿ⁺¹ − 1 nodes; the permutation tree has the sum of n!/(n − k)! over k, about e·n!: there are e − 1 ≈ 1.7 times more internal nodes than leaves, but the order is the same.

Allocations. Every leaf is a new List<int>: 2ⁿ objects. If you don’t need to return the answer, only to check every option (the best set, whether a valid one exists), don’t materialize it: check at the leaf using path or the mask — zero allocations. A local function that captures the method’s variables doesn’t touch the heap by itself: the compiler puts the captured state into a struct and passes it by reference — as long as the function is not turned into a delegate and no lambda captures the same variables.

Gray code. The masks g = i ^ (i >> 1) for i = 0, 1, 2, … differ from their neighbour in exactly one bit. So the sum or weight of the set can be updated by one element per step: O(2ⁿ) instead of O(n·2ⁿ) — noticeable when checking a set is expensive.

Permutations without used. The swap version: at level k, swap nums[k] with each nums[i], i ≥ k, recurse and swap back. The only memory is the stack. The next permutation in lexicographic order can also be produced without recursion (Next Permutation, #31): find the first descent from the right a[i] < a[i + 1], swap a[i] with the rightmost element greater than it, reverse the tail after i. The .NET base library has no such function.

Unity. The recursion depth equals n — for exhaustive search it is never the problem: the exponent runs out before the stack does. The problem is time: 2·10⁷ operations take tens, even hundreds of milliseconds, that is anywhere from a few frames to a dozen. Heavy enumeration goes into an editor tool, onto loading, or into a Job: masks are plain ints, easy to hand out to threads in ranges in an IJobParallelFor.

cards.q: You are solving Subsets out loud in an interview. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
items: Clarify: are the numbers distinct? is the empty set needed? does order matter? what is n?
Point out that the answer itself holds 2ⁿ sets — so enumeration is the solution
Idea: a “take / skip” decision tree, one shared path and backtracking
Write the code, saying: at a leaf — a copy of path, after the recursion — RemoveAt
Complexity: O(n·2ⁿ) time, O(n) for the stack and path plus the answer itself
Edge cases: n = 1, duplicates in the input — sort and skip equal values
cards.explain: Clarifying duplicates and the empty set changes the code, so it comes first. The argument “the answer itself is exponential” settles the question of a fast solution before the interviewer asks it. A run on two numbers checks both the undo and the copy.

lessons.title: Pruning
lessons.sub: Word Search, Combination Sum, N-Queens: mark and restore, sort and break, check a conflict in O(1)

cards.title: Word Search: a path where no cell is used twice
cards.body:
Word Search (LeetCode #79). Given an m × n grid of letters (up to 6 × 6) and a word of up to 15 letters, can you spell the word by moving between cells that share a side, never using a cell twice?

The signals of backtracking: we look for a path, every step has a choice (up to four neighbours), and there is a constraint that depends on the path walked so far — “the cell is not taken”. That is why flood fill doesn’t fit: there a cell is marked forever, while here a cell that failed one path may be needed by another.

The key word of this lesson is pruning: cut a branch of the decision tree as soon as it is clear there is no answer in it. Good pruning doesn’t change the worst-case complexity, but it removes almost the whole tree on real data. Here the pruning is the very first wrong letter: on the word “ABCCED” we don’t continue the path “AB…” from the cell “F”.

cards.title: Mark, go, restore
cards.body:
From every cell we start Dfs(r, c, i): “can the word be finished from letter i, standing at (r, c)”. Cheap checks come first — out of the grid and the wrong letter: that is the pruning. If the letter fits, we mark the cell (write '#' right into the board — that letter never appears in a word), go to the four neighbours with i + 1, and restore the letter.

Invariant: exactly the cells of the current path from the start are marked. Restoring the letter is the same undo as path.RemoveAt in subsets: after the call returns, the board is the same as before it.

|| between the calls is evaluated lazily: as soon as one neighbour returns true, the rest are not touched — an early exit.

Cost: m·n starts, the first step has up to 4 neighbours, later up to 3 (the cell we came from is marked). The worst case is O(m·n·3ᴸ), where L is the word length; for 6 × 6 and L = 15 that is up to 7·10⁸, but only on nasty boards like “all letters A, word AAA…AB”. Memory is the recursion depth L.

cards.q: In Word Search the line board[r][c] = saved was forgotten. What breaks?
options: Cells of a failed path stay '#', and another path that needs them can’t take them: false is possible when the word exists
One cell can enter a path twice, and the code finds words that aren’t on the board
Nothing: a failed path leads nowhere anyway, its cells are no longer needed
The code crashes with IndexOutOfRangeException on the '#' character
cards.explain: The mark is only needed while the current path lasts. Without the restore, a cell that a dead-end path went through is “taken” forever — but from another start or in another order it may be needed. The answer becomes a false negative: the word is there, and the code says false.

wrong.1: There is no double use: '#' matches no letter. The bug goes the other way — fewer cells are available than there should be.
wrong.2: A dead-end path leads nowhere from this point and in this order. Its cells one by one can still belong to another, successful path.
wrong.3: '#' is an ordinary character, the comparison board[r][c] != word[i] simply returns false. No index leaves the board.

cards.task: The same board, the word ECCB. The first E leads to a dead end, the second to the answer, and it will need the same C cells. Neighbours are tried in the order down, up, right, left; the rig doesn’t show marked cells or cells off the board. It will stop twice and ask what happens next.

options.label: Unmark (1,2) and return to (0,2) for its other neighbours
Return false right away: the path from this E failed
Take (0,2) again: it is a neighbouring C

asks.q: Path E(0,3) → C(0,2) → C(1,2). A B is needed, but the neighbours of (1,2) are E, S, F and the marked (0,2). What does the code do?
asks.explain: All four calls from (1,2) returned false, and the code restores the letter: board[1][2] = 'C'. The call returns to (0,2), which tries its remaining neighbours — to the left (0,1), a B, while a C is needed. (0,2) can’t be taken a second time: it is on the current path and marked.

options.label: (1,2) = “C” fits: it was unmarked on the way back
(1,2) is skipped: the first path already used it
The search ends: a cell can be taken once in the whole search

asks.q: A new start — E(2,2). Its neighbour above is (1,2) = C, which the first, dead-end path used. What will the rig show?
asks.explain: A mark lives while the cell is on the current path. The first path was undone completely, and the board is clean again — so (1,2) and then (0,2) fit again, and to the left of (0,2) lies a B. Without restoring letters this would be a false negative.

cards.title: Combination Sum: start, and break after sorting
cards.body:
Combination Sum (LeetCode #39). Distinct candidates from 2 to 40, a target up to 40. Return all distinct sets that sum to target; a number may be used any number of times. For [2, 3, 6, 7] and 7 that is [2, 2, 3] and [7].

No duplicate sets. [2, 2, 3] and [3, 2, 2] are one set. As with subsets built by a loop, we pass start down: from here on we only take candidates with index ≥ i. A set is always built in non-decreasing order — so each one comes out exactly once. The difference from subsets: we recurse into Dfs(i, …), not i + 1, because the same number may be taken again.

Pruning. Sort the candidates. If candidates[i] > remain, every candidate to the right is larger than the remainder too — so not continue but break: we cut the whole tail of the loop. Without sorting you can’t do that — you’d have to check each one.

Cost: the depth is up to target / min, the branching up to k candidates; roughly O(k^(T/min)). Nobody expects an exact bound here; say “exponential, bounded by the number of answers, and pruning cuts almost everything”.

cards.task: Walk the Combination Sum tree for [2, 3, 6, 7] and target = 7: the nodes show the remainder. The rig will stop twice and ask what the loop does: answer from start and the sorting.

options.label: 2 > 1 — break: only larger candidates follow
Take 2: remainder −1, the call comes back empty
Skip 2 and try 3

asks.q: path = [2, 2, 2], 1 left. What does the loop do?
asks.explain: The smallest candidate, 2, is already larger than the remainder 1. The array is sorted, so 3, 6 and 7 won’t fit either — break ends the whole loop with one comparison. The code never enters the pruned branch at all.

options.label: [3, 6]: break

asks.q: path = [3], 4 left. What is the next path?
asks.explain: The 3 was taken at index 1, and the recursion went into Dfs(1, 4): the loop starts at the 3 itself, the 2 is to the left and is no longer considered. Otherwise [3, 2, 2] would appear — the same set as the [2, 2, 3] already found. Then 3 > 1 — break.

cards.q: Combination Sum on [2, 3, 6, 7], target = 7 returns [2, 2, 3], [2, 3, 2], [3, 2, 2], [7]. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: The recursion gets start = 0: at every level the loop starts from the 2 again, and one set is built in every order — those are permutations, not combinations. It needs Dfs(i, …): from here on only candidates with an index no smaller than the current one. Dfs(i + 1, …) would forbid repeating a number and lose [2, 2, 3].

cards.title: N-Queens: a conflict in O(1)
cards.body:
N-Queens (LeetCode #51), n ≤ 9. Place n queens on an n × n board so that no two attack each other, and return all placements. For n = 4 there are 2, for n = 8 — 92.

The first pruning is in the formulation: every row holds exactly one queen, so we decide row by row: at level r we pick a column. Instead of n² cells per level there are n options, and “two in one row” is impossible by construction.

The second is checking a conflict in O(1) rather than by scanning the placed queens. A queen at (r, c) occupies column c, the “↘” diagonal, along which r − c is constant, and the “↙” diagonal, along which r + c is constant. We keep three flag arrays: cols[c], diag[r + c] and anti[r − c + n] (shifted by n so the index is never negative). Place — three flags to true, take back — to false.

Cost: without pruning there are nⁿ options, with “one per row and column” at most n!, and the diagonals cut even more: for n = 8 the code visits 2 057 nodes, while the tree “one queen per row and column” would have 8! = 40 320 leaves alone.
flow: Place(r): r == n → a placement is ready
for c: cols[c] or diag[r + c] or anti[r − c + n] → skip

cards.q: Build the loop that places a queen in row r.
cards.explain: The diagonals are checked by the same indices they are marked with: r + c and r − c + n. Without the shift, r − c goes negative as early as (0, 1) — IndexOutOfRangeException. Place — flags to true, take back after the recursion — to false. The next level is the next row, r + 1.

cards.task: Walk the placement of 4 queens: row by row, columns left to right, backtracking at a dead end. The rig will ask what to do when a row has no free cells left.

options.label: Remove the queen from (1,2) and try (1,3)
Remove the queen from (0,0) and start from (0,1)
Put a queen on (2,3): it has the fewest threats

asks.q: Queens at (0,0) and (1,2). In row 2 all four cells are attacked. What does the code do?
asks.explain: The loop of row 2 ended without placing anything, and Place(2) simply returns. Control is back in the loop of row 1, right after the recursion: it clears the flags of the queen at (1,2) and takes the next column, 3. Backtracking goes one level up, not to the start: the choice in row 0 may still work with a different choice in row 1.

cards.title: Variations and where this shows up in games
cards.body:
Combination Sum II (#40): each candidate once, but the input has duplicates. Recurse into Dfs(i + 1, …), and equal neighbours on one level are skipped: i > start && c[i] == c[i − 1] — the same trick as in Subsets II.

Generate Parentheses (#22): all valid bracket strings of n pairs. The pruning is in the rules of choice: “(” is allowed while fewer than n are open, “)” while fewer are closed than open. Invalid strings are never built at all.

Faster Word Search. Two prunings before any search: count the letters of the board and of the word — if some letter is missing, return false at once; if the word’s first letter is more common on the board than its last, search for the reversed word — fewer starts.

Word Search II (#212): many words on one board. Running a search per word is expensive; the words go into a prefix tree, and one walk from each cell follows the tree directly — a branch ends when no word has that prefix (prefix trees are in the last unit).

Sudoku Solver (#37): try digits 1–9 in an empty cell, check the conflict with row, column and box flags — just like the queens.

In a game: checking that a generated puzzle level is solvable; finding words on a letter grid in a word game; placing objects under constraints like “not closer than”, “not on one line”. Pruning decides everything here: without it the search doesn’t fit even into a level load.
cards.deep:
Queens on masks. The code on the card stores what is taken not in three arrays but in three numbers. cols is the taken columns. d1 and d2 are the cells of the current row attacked by diagonals from above: moving one row down, a “↘” diagonal shifts one column right and a “↙” one column left, hence << 1 and >> 1. ~(…) inverts the bits, & full keeps the low n — we get every free column of the row in one expression. free & -free isolates the lowest set bit (in two’s complement -x is ~x + 1). An iteration is a few cycles, with no arrays and no per-column checks; this is the classic fast variant of the n-queens search.

Word Search: why reversing helps. On an “all A” board and the word “AAA…AB”, every start builds a huge tree of A’s and is cut only at the last letter. The reversed word “BAA…A” starts with the rare B: a handful of starts, and counting letters up front rejects a board without a B entirely. On nasty boards this is orders of magnitude faster — interviewers love it as a follow-up.

Sudoku and the choice heuristic. The order in which cells are filled matters more than how fast the check is. Take the cell with the fewest allowed digits (minimum remaining values): mistakes surface at the top levels of the tree, where pruning cuts more. Stronger still is constraint propagation: having placed a digit, strike it from the neighbours right away and detect a cell with zero options before recursing.

Unity. Level solvability checks run in the editor or at generation time, not in a frame. If the search does run at runtime, give it a node budget per frame and continue in the next one (a coroutine, an explicit stack instead of recursion), or move it into a Job: flags and masks are unmanaged and can be passed to Burst. Keep the board in a flat array and change it in place with restore — no state copies at every node.

cards.q: You are solving Word Search out loud in an interview. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
items: Clarify: neighbours by side only? may the board be modified? board and word sizes
Say why it isn’t flood fill: whether a cell is taken depends on the current path
Idea: DFS from every cell, mark the cell, go to the neighbours, restore the letter
Write the code: bounds and letter checks first — that is the pruning — then the mark and the undo
Run a word where the first path hits a dead end — check that the undo gives the cells back
Complexity: O(m·n·3ᴸ) in the worst case, memory — depth L
Suggest speedups: count letters up front and search from the rarer end
cards.explain: First agree on adjacency and on whether the board may be modified: that decides between writing '#' and keeping a separate array. A run with a dead end is the best test of the undo. Speedups at the end show that you think about pruning, not just the template.

cards.q: Match each problem with the pruning that makes it fast.
pairs: Sort, and break when a candidate exceeds the remainder
Stop at the first letter that doesn’t match
Flags for the column and both diagonals
“)” only while fewer are closed than open
Skip an equal neighbour on the same level

lessons.title: From recursion to a table
lessons.sub: Climbing Stairs and Unique Paths: memoization, a table, two variables — and the five questions any DP is built from

cards.title: Climbing Stairs and the signals of DP
cards.body:
Climbing Stairs (LeetCode #70). A staircase of n steps, 1 ≤ n ≤ 45. Each move climbs 1 or 2 steps. In how many ways can you reach the top? For n = 3 — three: 1+1+1, 1+2, 2+1.

The signals of dynamic programming (DP):

1. The question asks for a number of ways, a minimum/maximum, or “is it possible” — not a list of options.
2. The answer is built from answers to the same problem of a smaller size: the last move was either 1 or 2, so the ways to reach n are the ways to reach n − 1 plus the ways to reach n − 2.
3. These smaller problems repeat — they are reached along different paths.

The first two points give a recursion, and it is correct. The third says that the recursion does the same work many times — and that is what DP cures.
cards.code:
// straight from the definition: correct, but exponential
int Climb(int n) => n <= 1 ? 1 : Climb(n - 1) + Climb(n - 2);

cards.q: How many calls does Climb(45) from the previous card make, and what follows from that?
options: ≈ 3.7·10⁹ — seconds of work, it won’t fit the limit
≈ 45 — one call per step, it’s instant
≈ 2 000 — 45², a fraction of a second
cards.explain: The number of calls is C(n) = 1 + C(n − 1) + C(n − 2) — it grows like the answer itself, about 1.618 times per step. Climb(45) = 1 836 311 903, and there are almost twice as many calls: 3 672 623 805. At the rule of thumb of 10⁸ operations per second, that is more than 30 seconds; a real call is cheaper, but even on .NET it takes seconds — no way to fit a 1–2 s limit.

wrong.1: One call per step would be the case if every step were computed once. Here Climb(43) is called from both Climb(45) and Climb(44) — and so on at every level.
wrong.2: The number of calls grows not like a square but exponentially: every call spawns two. The answer for n = 45 is almost two billion ways, and there are even more calls.

cards.title: Memoization: compute each step once
cards.body:
Draw the call tree for n = 5: Climb(3) appears twice, Climb(2) three times, Climb(1) five times. There are only n + 1 distinct subproblems — 0 to n — but exponentially many calls: the same thing is computed again and again. That is signal 3 — overlapping subproblems.

Memoization means remembering a subproblem’s answer the first time it is computed and returning it on every repeated call. The code stays a top-down recursion, but each step is computed once: O(n) time, O(n) memory for the array and O(n) for the call stack.

The array needs a “not computed yet” mark. Here 0 works: no step has zero ways. If 0 is a legitimate answer, use -1 or int?[]. If the states are sparse and large (a pair of coordinates, a string), use a Dictionary.

cards.title: A bottom-up table and the five questions of DP
cards.body:
Memoization computes subproblems in whatever order the recursion reaches them. If the order is known in advance — from small to large — the recursion is not needed: we fill a table with a loop. No stack, no “computed yet?” checks, and you can see which cells are needed.

Every DP is assembled from five answers, worth saying out loud before the code:

1. State — what a cell means: ways[i] is the number of ways to reach step i.
2. Transition — how a cell is expressed through smaller ones: ways[i] = ways[i − 1] + ways[i − 2].
3. Base — cells not derived by the transition: ways[0] = ways[1] = 1.
4. Order — everything the transition refers to is computed earlier: i ascending.
5. Answer — where it lies: ways[n].

And then — memory: the transition only looks at the two previous values, so two variables are enough. O(n) time, O(1) memory.

cards.q: Build the table version of Climbing Stairs.
cards.explain: The answer lies in ways[n], so there are n + 1 cells. The base: one way to stand on the ground and one way to reach the first step. The loop includes n: with i < n, ways[n] would stay zero. The transition is the last move of 1 or 2.

cards.task: Walk the table filling for n = 6. The rig will stop twice and ask what goes into a cell and what the code actually needed.

options: ways[4] = 5
ways[4] = 4
ways[4] = 6
asks.q: ways[2] = 2, ways[3] = 3. What goes into ways[4]?
asks.explain: Step 4 is reached from the third with a move of 1 or from the second with a move of 2: 3 + 2 = 5. 4 is “one way per step”, 6 is doubling ways[3]: that would happen if both moves led from every step to the same place.

options.label: Only ways[5] and ways[4]
All of ways[0..5]
ways[5] and ways[3]

asks.q: ways[6] = 8 + 5 = 13. Which cells did the code read on the last step?
asks.explain: The transition looks at exactly the two previous cells. Everything further left will never be needed again — that is why the table folds into two variables prev and cur: O(n) time, O(1) memory.

cards.q: The two-variable version returns 4 instead of 3 for n = 3. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: prev = cur overwrites the old prev before it is used: after that cur = cur + cur, and the values just double — 1, 2, 4. The window has to slide at once: (prev, cur) = (cur, prev + cur), or with a temporary int next = prev + cur; prev = cur; cur = next.

cards.title: Unique Paths: the same idea on a grid
cards.body:
Unique Paths (LeetCode #62). A robot stands in the top-left corner of an m × n grid (up to 100 × 100) and moves only right or down. How many paths lead to the bottom-right corner? The answer is guaranteed to be at most 2·10⁹.

The five questions. State: dp[r, c] is the number of paths to cell (r, c). Transition: a cell is entered from above or from the left — dp[r − 1, c] + dp[r, c − 1]. Base: the top row and the left column have one path each. Order: rows top to bottom, left to right within a row. Answer: dp[m − 1, n − 1]. Time and memory O(m·n). For 3 × 7 the answer is 28.

O(n) memory. A row only needs the previous row, and even that doesn’t have to be stored separately: in a one-dimensional row, before the update row[c] still holds the value from above, and row[c − 1] already holds the new one from the left. So row[c] += row[c − 1].

Combinatorics. Every path is m − 1 moves down and n − 1 moves right in some order, so the answer is C(m + n − 2, m − 1). It is computed in O(min(m, n)) with long. But the formula breaks under any change of the problem: obstacles (Unique Paths II, #63 — dp = 0 in a rock cell), cell costs (Minimum Path Sum, #64 — grid[r, c] + min(above, left)). The table survives all of them.

cards.q: Build Unique Paths with O(n) memory.
cards.explain: The top row has one path into each cell, hence Fill(row, 1). The left column is always 1 too, so c starts at 1 and row[0] is never touched. += adds the old row[c] (from above) to the new row[c − 1] (from the left); = would lose the path from above. The answer is the last cell of the row, row[n − 1].

cards.task: Step through Unique Paths on a 4 × 4 grid in row mode — the code you have just assembled: one array row is overwritten row after row. The rig asks twice what goes into a cell: keep in mind what row holds before the write.

options.label: 10: row[3] still holds 4 from above, row[2] = 6 is on the left
6: row[3] = row[2], the path from above is gone
7: 4 + 3 — row[2] from the previous row on the left

asks.q: Row 2: row = [1, 3, 6, 4], row[1] and row[2] are already updated. What goes into row[3]?
asks.explain: Before the write row[3] = 4 is still the value from row 1, the cell above. row[2] = 6 has already been updated in this row — the cell on the left. row[3] += row[2]: 4 + 6 = 10. With = instead of += the path from above is lost (6), and 7 uses the old row[2] = 3: taking it would need a second array, which is not needed.

options.label: row[1] = 3 + 1 = 4; row[0] stays 1
Clear row first: row[1] = 0 + 1 = 1
row[0] = 2: two paths lead to cell (3, 0)

asks.q: Row 2 is done: row = [1, 3, 6, 10]. Row 3 begins. What does the code write first?
asks.explain: The loop over c starts at 1: the left column always has exactly one path, so row[0] = 1 stays. row[1] adds itself (3, from above) and row[0] (1, from the left) — 4. Clearing the row would be wrong: the old values are exactly the "from above" part. Row 3 ends with row[3] = 20, which is C(6, 3).

cards.q: What is true about Unique Paths and its variations? Select all.
options: With obstacles it is enough to set dp = 0 in a rock cell — nothing else changes
The formula C(m + n − 2, m − 1) also works with obstacles if you subtract the rocks
In the one-dimensional version row[c] before the update is the value from above, and row[c − 1] is already from the left
Cells can be filled in any order — the transition doesn’t depend on it
Recursion without memoization won’t finish in reasonable time on a 100 × 100 grid
cards.explain: A rock is a cell with zero paths into it, and the transition carries that zero onward by itself. The formula counts all paths with no exceptions: a rock removes not one cell but every path through it, and you can’t “just subtract” those. The order must make sure above and left are computed first — that is the fourth DP question. Recursion without memory repeats subproblems, and it makes as many calls as there are paths — up to 10⁵⁸.

cards.title: Variations and where this shows up in games
cards.body:
Moves from a set {1, 2, 3} or any list: the transition is a sum over all moves, ways[i] = Σ ways[i − s]. That is already the coin problem — the next lesson.

Min Cost Climbing Stairs (#746): every step has a price, the minimum is needed. The transition is the same, but instead of a sum — cost[i] + min(dp[i − 1], dp[i − 2]). “How many ways” turns into “minimum” — only the operation changes.

House Robber (#198): you can’t take two adjacent houses, the sum must be maximal. dp[i] = max(dp[i − 1], dp[i − 2] + a[i]): house i is either skipped or taken together with the best up to i − 2. Two variables as well.

In a game: a table over a grid — when movement across it is simple (only forward and sideways: a runner, a conveyor, a row of tiles) and you need the minimum cost or the number of options. For an arbitrary path across a map that is pathfinding — Dijkstra and A* from the pathfinding unit. And in any per-frame code — a table or variables, not recursion with memo: no stack, no dictionary, zero allocations.
cards.deep:
Top-down or bottom-up. Memoization computes only the states the recursion actually reached — a win when there are many states but few are needed (for example, in turn-based games where most positions are unreachable). A table computes everything, but without recursion, without checks and with predictable memory access — on dense problems it is several times faster. In an interview it is fine to start with memoization (it follows directly from the recursion) and then say: “the order is known — I rewrite it as a table, and fold the table into two variables”.

Overflow. Climb(45) = 1 836 311 903 is the last value that fits in an int: Climb(46) = 2 971 215 073 > int.MaxValue. A long holds it up to n = 91. Beyond that — System.Numerics.BigInteger or the answer modulo 10⁹ + 7, as counting problems often ask.

O(log n). The transition is linear: the pair (cur, prev) is multiplied by the matrix [[1, 1], [1, 0]]. So ways[n] is an element of the n-th power of that matrix, and the power is computed by fast exponentiation in O(log n) 2 × 2 multiplications. That is the answer to “faster than O(n)?” — for DP with a linear transition and a huge n (10¹⁸ modulo something).

Combinatorics without overflow. In the Unique Paths formula the intermediate res * (total − k + i) reaches 2·10⁹ · 200, hence long. The division is exact at every step: after i steps res equals C(total − k + i, i) — an integer.

.NET and Unity. int[,] is convenient, but every access checks two bounds; in hot code keep the row in a one-dimensional int[] or Span<int> (for a small row — stackalloc). Array.Fill exists in .NET Core 2.0+ and .NET Standard 2.1 — in Unity since 2021.2; on the old profile — a plain loop.

cards.q: You are solving Climbing Stairs out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
items: Clarify: only moves of 1 and 2? what is n? is the answer needed modulo something?
Recursion on the last move: ways(n) = ways(n − 1) + ways(n − 2)
Its cost: subproblems repeat, there are exponentially many calls
The five questions: state, transition, base, order, answer
A bottom-up table, then two variables: O(n) and O(1)
Edge cases: n = 1, int overflow for n > 45
cards.explain: The recursion comes first — it explains where the transition comes from. Its cost explains why DP is needed. The five questions are the frame that shows the interviewer you are building the solution, not recalling it. The run on n = 4 checks the base as well.

cards.q: Match each problem with its transition.

lessons.title: Unbounded knapsack
lessons.sub: Coin Change: why greedy breaks, dp[s] = min(dp[s − c] + 1), and how loop order tells combinations from permutations

cards.title: Coin Change: the problem and the first idea
cards.body:
Coin Change (LeetCode #322). Given coin denominations coins (up to 12 distinct ones) and an amount up to 10⁴, with an unlimited supply of every coin, find the minimum number of coins that make exactly amount, or −1 if it can’t be done.

The signals: the question asks for a minimum, not a list; every item can be taken without limit; the remainder after choosing a coin is the same problem with a smaller amount. This is the unbounded knapsack: fill a “capacity” with items that each come in an infinite supply.

The first thing that comes to mind is greedy: take the largest coin that still fits into the remainder until the remainder is zero. For ordinary money — 1, 2, 5, 10, 50 — this really does give the minimum. The question an interviewer asks: and for arbitrary denominations?

cards.q: coins = [1, 3, 4], amount = 6. How many coins does the greedy code from the previous card use, and what is the optimum?
options: Greedy 3 (4 + 1 + 1), optimum 2 (3 + 3)
Both 2: 4 + 2
Greedy 2 (3 + 3), optimum 2
Greedy −1: after 4, the remainder 2 can’t be made
cards.explain: Greedy takes 4 and makes the remainder 2 out of ones: 4 + 1 + 1 — three coins. But 3 + 3 is two. The large coin is “good” only right now: it leaves a remainder that is expensive to fill. The decision at a step depends on everything after it — so you have to try the choices, not take one.

wrong.1: There is no 2 among the denominations: 4 + 2 can’t be made.
wrong.2: Greedy starts with the largest coin — 4, not 3. Only a search would find 3 + 3.
wrong.3: The remainder 2 is made of two ones — there is a 1, so greedy doesn’t get stuck. It can get stuck on denominations without a one: [3, 5] and the sum 9 — after 5 the remainder is 4, after 3 it is 1, while 3 + 3 + 3 exists.

cards.title: dp[s]: the minimum for every sum
cards.body:
Greedy may not find an answer at all: on [3, 5] and the sum 9 it takes 5, then 3 — and gets stuck on the remainder 1, although 3 + 3 + 3 exists. So the coin has to be chosen not by one rule but by trying the options.

Trying every choice is the decision tree from the first lesson, and it is exponential. But the subproblem “the minimum coins for sum s” depends only on s, not on how we got there: the remainder 2 after a 4 and the remainder 2 after 1 + 3 are the same problem. There are only amount + 1 subproblems — that is DP.

State: dp[s] is the minimum number of coins for the sum s. Transition: the last coin was some c, and before it — the optimum for s − c: dp[s] = min over c ≤ s of dp[s − c] + 1. Base: dp[0] = 0. Order: s ascending — every s − c is smaller than s. Answer: dp[amount].

Unreachable sums. They need an “∞”. int.MaxValue is dangerous: + 1 overflows. Use amount + 1 — you never need more than amount coins (even all ones), so this number works as infinity, and + 1 is safe. If at the end dp[amount] > amount, the sum is unreachable and the answer is −1.

Cost: O(amount·k) time — with 10⁴ and 12 coins that is 1.2·10⁵ steps; O(amount) memory.
flow: for every c ≤ s: dp[s − c] + 1

cards.q: Build Coin Change.
cards.explain: “∞” is amount + 1: int.MaxValue + 1 overflows. The base is zero coins for the zero sum. The transition is the last coin c, and before it the optimum for i − c; dp[i − 1] + 1 would mean “the last coin is always 1”. An unreachable sum is −1 by the problem statement.

cards.task: Walk the dp filling for coins = [1, 3, 4], amount = 6. The arcs are transitions from dp[s − c]. The rig will stop twice and ask what goes into a cell: compute from the table, not greedily.

asks.q: dp[1] = 1, dp[2] = 2. What goes into dp[3]?
asks.explain: Candidates: coin 1 — dp[2] + 1 = 3, coin 3 — dp[0] + 1 = 1. The minimum is 1: the sum 3 is one coin. Coin 4 is larger than the sum and isn’t considered. 3 is “all ones” — what you’d get looking only at dp[i − 1].

asks.q: dp[3] = 1, dp[4] = 1, dp[5] = 2. What goes into dp[6]?
asks.explain: Coin 1: dp[5] + 1 = 3. Coin 3: dp[3] + 1 = 2. Coin 4: dp[2] + 1 = 3. The minimum is 2, via the 3: 3 + 3. The greedy path 4 + 1 + 1 is the option through dp[2], and the table honestly counts it as three coins.

cards.q: Here “∞” is int.MaxValue. On coins = [2], amount = 3 the code returned −2147483648. Tap the line where that number came from.
cards.explain: dp[1] is unreachable and stays int.MaxValue. For i = 3, coin 2 gives dp[1] + 1 — an overflow in C#’s unchecked arithmetic: int.MaxValue + 1 = int.MinValue, and Math.Min happily picks it. The cure is “∞” = amount + 1, or checking dp[i − c] != int.MaxValue before the + 1.

cards.title: Which coins, BFS, and where this shows up in games
cards.body:
Recovering the set. Next to dp keep last[s] — the coin on which the minimum was reached. The answer is assembled from the end: s → s − last[s] until you reach zero. This is the standard trick for any DP: remember which transition won and walk those transitions back.

The same answer by breadth-first search. The sums 0…amount are vertices, a coin is an edge “+c”. The minimum number of coins is the shortest path from 0 to amount in an unweighted graph, and breadth-first search gives exactly that: a queue of sums, each visited once. The complexity is the same, O(amount·k), but BFS stops as soon as it reaches amount — earlier on “lucky” inputs.

In a game. Crafting from fixed-size resource bundles (bundles of 1, 3, 4 — make exactly 6 with the fewest bundles), giving change in an in-game currency with unusual denominations, picking a set of rewards worth exactly N points. A game designer sets the denominations — and nobody promises that greedy is correct for them. A table of 10⁴ cells is 40 KB and a fraction of a millisecond: it can be recomputed when the config changes and kept ready.

cards.title: The number of ways: loop order decides
cards.body:
Coin Change II (LeetCode #518): how many sets of coins make amount? Sets ignore order: 1 + 2 and 2 + 1 are one. The transition is “sum instead of minimum”: dp[s] += dp[s − c], with the base dp[0] = 1 — one way to make zero: take nothing.

But now the loop order matters. If coins are outside and sums inside — after processing coins coins[0..j], dp[s] holds the number of sets made of those coins only. Every set is built in one order — “all ones first, then all twos” — and counted once. That is the answer to #518.

If sums are outside and coins inside, then dp[s] = Σ dp[s − c] tries the last coin for every sum — and counts sequences: 1 + 2 and 2 + 1 separately. That is a different problem, Combination Sum IV (#377). For coins = [1, 2] and amount = 3 there are 2 sets and 3 sequences.

For the minimum the order doesn’t matter: the minimum over sets and over sequences is the same.

Each coin once (the 0/1 knapsack, Partition Equal Subset Sum, #416): coins outside, and sums inside descending. Then dp[s − c] hasn’t seen coin c yet, and it can’t be taken twice. Ascending — as in #518 — the same number can be taken again. Time O(n·W), where W is the capacity.

cards.task: This is Change from the previous card with the loops swapped: s from 1 to amount outside, foreach over the coins inside (order sums-outer on the rig). Step through it on coins = [1, 2], amount = 4. A table row shows how much a coin added to each dp[s]. The rig asks twice what gets added to dp[s].

options.label: Nothing: 1 + 2 was already counted as 2 + 1

asks.q: Sum 3. Coin 1 has already given dp[3] = 2: 1+1+1 and 2+1. Now coin 2 goes last. What does the code do?
asks.explain: dp[1] is already final and counts every sequence with sum 1 — just one: 1. Append the 2 — 1+2. As a set it equals 2+1, but the sums-outside code cannot tell them apart and counts both. dp[3] = 3, while there are only two sets for 3: {1, 1, 1} and {1, 2}.

options.label: 5: dp[2] = 2 gets added
4: only 2+2 gets added
3: everything ending in 2 is already counted

asks.q: Sum 4: coin 1 has given dp[4] = 3. Now coin 2. What does dp[4] become?
asks.explain: dp[2] = 2 — the sequences 1+1 and 2; with a 2 at the end they give 1+1+2 and 2+2. That makes 5: 1+1+1+1, 2+1+1, 1+2+1, 1+1+2, 2+2. Only three of them are distinct sets — {1, 1, 1, 1}, {1, 1, 2}, {2, 2} — and those are what the original Change with coins outside counts. Same formula, other loop order — and it is #377 now, not #518.

cards.q: What is true about the problems in this lesson? Select all.
options: For the minimum number of coins, the “coins/sums” loop order doesn’t change the answer
If the denominations are 1, 2, 5, 10, 50, greedy gives the minimum and DP isn’t needed
“∞” = amount + 1 is safe: dp[s − c] + 1 doesn’t overflow, and you never need more than amount coins
The greedy algorithm always finds some decomposition if one exists
In the 0/1 knapsack the inner loop over capacity goes downward
cards.explain: The minimum over sets and over sequences is the same — loop order only matters for counting ways. For “nice” denominations like ordinary money greedy is optimal, but not for arbitrary ones, and in an interview the denominations are almost always arbitrary. amount + 1 is an honest infinity. Greedy can get stuck: [3, 5], the sum 9. The descending loop in the 0/1 knapsack keeps an item from being taken twice.

cards.q: You are solving Coin Change out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
items: Clarify: unlimited coins? what to return if impossible? what are amount and the number of denominations?
Suggest greedy and immediately a counterexample: [1, 3, 4] and 6 — 4 + 1 + 1 versus 3 + 3
The state dp[s] and the transition: min over coins of dp[s − c] + 1
Base dp[0] = 0, “∞” = amount + 1, order — s ascending
Complexity: O(amount·k) time, O(amount) memory
Edge cases: amount = 0, an unreachable sum — −1
cards.explain: Greedy with a counterexample is a strong move: you show yourself why DP is needed before the interviewer asks. Then the five DP questions, a run over the table and the cost. amount = 0 is a common trap: the answer is 0, not −1.

cards.title: One table — four questions
cards.body:
Coin Change is the model of a whole family: “fill a capacity with items” (the knapsack). Minimum, maximum, number of ways or “is it possible” — only the operation in the transition changes: min, max, +, ||. A limit on how many of each item you may take changes the direction of the inner loop.

To “what if amount is up to 10⁹?” the answer is that the table won’t do: O(amount·k) depends on the magnitude of the number, not on the input size. Then you look for something else: the math of the denominations, BFS with pruning, limits on the number of coins.
cards.deep:
Correctness. Optimal substructure: if an optimal set for s contains coin c, the remaining coins are an optimal set for s − c. Otherwise we would replace them with a better set for s − c and get fewer coins for s than the “optimum”. So the minimum over the last coin covers every optimal candidate.

When greedy is correct. Coin systems for which greedy always gives the minimum are called canonical; ordinary coins and notes are like that. A system can be checked: if it contains a 1 and greedy is ever wrong, the smallest counterexample is below the sum of the two largest denominations — comparing greedy with DP on the sums up to that bound is enough. In an interview “not for arbitrary denominations, here is a counterexample” is enough.

Pseudo-polynomial time. O(amount·k) is polynomial in the value of amount, but a 30-bit number can be 10⁹: in terms of input length that is exponential. That is why the general knapsack stays a hard problem, and DP over capacity only works when the capacity is small. If the capacity is huge but there are only 20–40 items — enumerate subsets, or “meet in the middle” (enumerate each half of the items, then sort and binary search): O(2^(n/2)·n).

Top-down. A memoized recursion over s goes as deep as amount — 10⁴ frames with a coin of 1. That still fits in the stack (the first unit: thousands and tens of thousands of calls are fine), but the margin is small, and with amount 10⁶ the recursion would crash — one more reason to write the table.

.NET and Unity. int[amount + 1] for 10⁴ is 40 KB: allocate once and reuse it if you compute often. For small sums in hot code — Span<int> dp = stackalloc int[amount + 1] (keep amount small: a thread stack is on the order of a megabyte). Code with no reference types inside the loop maps well to a Burst job over a NativeArray<int>.

cards.q: Match the problem with how its loops are arranged.

lessons.title: DP on two strings
lessons.sub: LCS and Edit Distance: an (i, j) table over prefixes, three transitions, recovering the answer and O(min) memory

cards.title: LCS: the problem and the “two strings” signal
cards.body:
Longest Common Subsequence (LeetCode #1143). Given strings a and b of up to 1000 characters, find the length of their longest common subsequence. A subsequence is obtained by deleting characters without changing the order of the rest: “ace” is a subsequence of “abcde”, and “aec” is not. A substring, by contrast, is contiguous.

Naively — enumerate all 2ᵐ subsequences of a and check each one in b in O(n). With m = 1000 that is 2¹⁰⁰⁰ — pointless.

The signal of DP on two strings: two sequences, and the answer for the whole strings is built from answers for their prefixes — look at the last characters and cut off one or both. A subproblem is defined by a pair of lengths (i, j), and there are (m + 1)(n + 1) such pairs — about 10⁶ for m = n = 1000.

This signal identifies LCS, Edit Distance, pattern matching, Interleaving String and many others.
cards.code:
LongestCommonSubsequence("abcde", "ace");   // 3: "ace"
LongestCommonSubsequence("abc", "def");     // 0

cards.q: What is the LCS length of “abcde” and “aec”?
cards.explain: The common characters are a, c, e, but order matters: in “abcde” c comes before e, and in “aec” after it. Together with a you can take either c (“ac”) or e (“ae”), but not both. The answer is 2.

wrong.1: 3 would be the answer if order didn’t matter — that is the size of the intersection of the character sets. A subsequence keeps the order.
wrong.2: One letter is too little: “ac” appears in both strings in order.

cards.title: dp[i, j] and two cases
cards.body:
State: dp[i, j] is the LCS of the prefixes a[..i] and b[..j] (the first i and j characters). Base: an empty prefix — dp[0, j] = dp[i, 0] = 0. Answer: dp[m, n].

Transition — look at the last characters of the prefixes, a[i − 1] and b[j − 1]:

Equal — pair them up: dp[i − 1, j − 1] + 1 (the diagonal). This is safe: if an optimal LCS doesn’t use them, the last character of one of the strings in it can be swapped for this pair — the length won’t drop.
Different — at least one of them is not in the LCS. Cut either the character of a or the character of b: max(dp[i − 1, j], dp[i, j − 1]) — the maximum of the cell above and the cell to the left.

Order: rows top to bottom, left to right within a row — above, left and diagonal are all ready. Time O(m·n), memory O(m·n).
flow: rows top to bottom, left to right

cards.q: Build the LCS transition.
cards.explain: The table is shifted by one: dp[i, j] is about the first i characters, and the last of them is a[i − 1]. a[i] with i = a.Length would run past the string. A match adds a pair to the diagonal’s answer, a mismatch takes the better of the two ways to cut a character — the maximum, since we want the longest.

cards.task: Walk the LCS table for “abcde” and “ace”: rows are prefixes of abcde, columns are prefixes of ace. The rig will stop twice and ask what goes into a cell.

asks.q: Cell (3, 2): “c” and “c”. Diagonal dp[2, 1] = 1, above dp[2, 2] = 1, left dp[3, 1] = 1. What goes in?
asks.explain: The characters are equal — take the diagonal and add the pair: 1 + 1 = 2. That is “ac”: the “a” came from the diagonal, the “c” is the new pair. On a match we don’t look above or left.

asks.q: Cell (3, 3): “c” and “e”. Above dp[2, 3] = 1, left dp[3, 2] = 2, diagonal dp[2, 2] = 1. What goes in?
asks.explain: The characters differ — the maximum of above and left: max(1, 2) = 2. Left is “abc” versus “ac”, which already has “ac”. Diagonal + 1 can’t be taken on a mismatch: there is no pair.

cards.title: Recover the answer and squeeze the memory
cards.body:
The LCS string itself. The table holds lengths, but you can walk it back from (m, n): characters equal — that is a character of the answer, go along the diagonal; otherwise go where the maximum came from — up or left. Characters are collected from the end, so reverse at the end. The walk back is O(m + n). That is how the answer is recovered in any DP: repeat the winning transition.

O(min(m, n)) memory. A table row depends only on the previous row. Keep two rows prev and cur of length n + 1 and swap them after every i. If you make b the shorter one (swapping the strings — LCS is symmetric), the memory is O(min(m, n)). The price: the string itself can no longer be recovered from two rows — that needs the whole table or the clever algorithm in “Deeper”.

Numbers: 1000 × 1000 int is 4 MB; 10⁴ × 10⁴ is 400 MB, and there two rows are the only option.

cards.q: LCS on two table rows returns 2 instead of 1 for a = “ba”, b = “aa”. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: Arrays are reference types: prev = cur doesn’t copy the row, it makes both variables the same array. From the second row on, prev[j − 1] is already the new value of the current row, and one “a” from a pairs with both “a”s of b. It needs a reference swap (prev, cur) = (cur, prev): the old prev becomes the buffer for the next row.

cards.title: Edit Distance: three operations — three neighbours
cards.body:
Edit Distance (LeetCode #72), strings up to 500 characters. What is the minimum number of operations “insert a character”, “delete a character”, “replace a character” that turns a into b? “horse” → “ros” takes 3: replace h with r (rorse), delete r (rose), delete e (ros). This is the Levenshtein distance.

State: dp[i, j] is the number of edits that turn a[..i] into b[..j]. Base: dp[i, 0] = i — delete everything, dp[0, j] = j — insert everything.

Transition on the last characters. Equal — no edit needed: dp[i − 1, j − 1]. Different — 1 + the best of three operations, each one a neighbour:

↖ replace a[i − 1] with b[j − 1]: what remains is prefixes i − 1 and j − 1.
↑ delete a[i − 1]: what remains is turning a[..i − 1] into b[..j].
← insert b[j − 1] at the end: what remains is turning a[..i] into b[..j − 1].

O(m·n) time, and the memory squeezes to two rows the same way. In a game: a developer console with fuzzy command search — “spwn” finds spawn, “godmod” finds godmode: the names closest by distance. 300 commands of 15 characters is about 7·10⁴ cells per keystroke — a fraction of a millisecond.

cards.task: Walk the Edit Distance table for “horse” → “ros”. Under each cell — which transition won. The rig will stop twice and ask what goes in.

asks.q: Cell (2, 2): “o” and “o”. Diagonal dp[1, 1] = 1, above dp[1, 2] = 2, left dp[2, 1] = 2. What goes in?
asks.explain: The characters are equal — no edit needed, take the diagonal as it is: 1. “ho” → “ro” costs exactly as much as “h” → “r”, one replacement. Adding +1 on a match is a common mistake.

options.label: 3 by deleting “e”
4 by replacing “e” with “s”
2: take the cell above, no edit needed

asks.q: The last cell (5, 3): “e” and “s”. Diagonal dp[4, 2] = 3, above dp[4, 3] = 2, left dp[5, 2] = 4. What goes in?
asks.explain: The characters differ: 1 + min(3, 2, 4) = 3, and the cell above won — deleting “e”. Above is “hors” → “ros”, 2 edits; plus deleting the last “e”. Only the diagonal comes for free, and only for equal characters.

cards.q: What is true about DP on two strings? Select all.
options: Edit Distance takes the diagonal without + 1 when the characters are equal
LCS on two table rows can return both the length and the subsequence itself
The Edit Distance base is the first row 0, 1, 2, … and the first column 0, 1, 2, …
Memory can be squeezed to O(min(m, n)) by making the inner-loop string the shorter one
In LCS, equal characters require taking the maximum of three neighbours
cards.explain: Equal characters need no edit — the diagonal as it is. The base is “delete everything” and “insert everything”. A table row is as long as the inner-loop string, so that is the one to make short. Two rows give only the length: the walk back needs the whole table. In LCS a match only needs diagonal + 1 — it is never less than the neighbours, the character-swap argument proves it.

cards.q: You are solving Edit Distance out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
items: Clarify: which operations and their cost? letter case? string lengths?
Naively: enumerating edits is exponential, but a subproblem is a pair of prefixes
The state dp[i, j] — edits for a[..i] → b[..j]; the base — i and j
Transition: equal → diagonal, otherwise 1 + min(replace ↖, delete ↑, insert ←)
Run a small example: “ab” → “b” — one deletion
Complexity: O(m·n) time, memory down to two rows — O(min(m, n))
Edge cases: an empty string — the answer is the other’s length, equal strings — 0
cards.explain: The question about operation costs changes the transition (for example, a replacement costing 2), so it comes first. Explaining what each neighbour means matters more than writing the formula: the interviewer almost always asks “why is above a deletion?”.

cards.title: Variations, diff and fuzzy search
cards.body:
Longest Common Substring — contiguous: on a match dp[i − 1, j − 1] + 1, on a mismatch 0 (the substring breaks), and the answer is the maximum over the whole table.

Longest Palindromic Subsequence (#516) is the LCS of a string and its reverse. Delete Operation for Two Strings (#583) is m + n − 2·LCS: everything outside the common part gets deleted. Shortest Common Supersequence (#1092) is m + n − LCS, and the string itself comes from a walk back over the LCS table.

Diff. Comparing two versions of a file is LCS over lines: lines outside the common subsequence are exactly the deleted and added ones. In a game — showing a designer the difference between two versions of a config, dialogues or a localization table.

Fuzzy search. In a developer console or an asset search you usually need not the exact distance but “at most k”: then cells further than k from the diagonal don’t need computing, and a row can stop as soon as its minimum exceeds k.
cards.deep:
Recovery in O(min) memory. The LCS string or the list of edits can be obtained without the full table: compute the two-row table down to the middle of a top-down, and for the reversed strings bottom-up, find the column where the sum is maximal (minimal for edits) — the point the optimal path passes through — and solve the two halves recursively. The time stays O(m·n) (about twice as much), the memory is O(m + n). This is the classic technique when you need the answer itself and the table doesn’t fit in memory.

A band. If you only need the answer when the distance is ≤ k, cells with |i − j| > k are certainly greater than k: compute a band of width 2k + 1, O(k·n) instead of O(m·n). For console suggestions k = 2–3.

Swapped neighbours. The most common typos are transposed letters (“spanw”). The Damerau–Levenshtein distance adds a fourth transition: if a[i − 1] == b[j − 2] and a[i − 2] == b[j − 1], then dp[i − 2, j − 2] + 1.

Faster than O(m·n). In the worst case you can’t do substantially better (there are conditional lower bounds), but in practice diff tools use algorithms that run in O((m + n)·D), where D is the number of differences: on almost identical files that is almost linear. There are also bit-parallel variants of LCS and Levenshtein: one machine operation processes 64 cells of a column.

.NET and Unity. int[,] checks two bounds on every access; a flat int[] indexed by i * (n + 1) + j, or two rows, is usually faster. For suggestions on every keystroke keep two rows in a field and reuse them — don’t allocate a table per command; for short strings stackalloc works. The LINQ on the card allocates delegates with a closure, iterators, a sort buffer and a list — fine for a console, not for per-frame code. Compare case-insensitively with char.ToLowerInvariant up front, once per string, not in every cell.

cards.q: Match the problem with its transition or formula.

lessons.title: LIS and tricky transitions
lessons.sub: Longest Increasing Subsequence from O(n²) to O(n log n) via tails and binary search, Regular Expression Matching and DP for “is it possible”

cards.title: LIS: the problem and an O(n²) solution
cards.body:
Longest Increasing Subsequence (LeetCode #300). Given an array of up to 2500 numbers, find the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence — the elements need not be adjacent, but they keep their original order. For [10, 9, 2, 5, 3, 7, 101, 18] the answer is 4: for example, 2, 3, 7, 18.

A subsequence, as in the previous lesson, signals DP over prefixes. State: dp[i] is the length of the longest increasing subsequence that ends exactly at i. That makes it easy to extend: nums[i] can be appended to any subsequence that ends on a smaller number to its left.

Transition: dp[i] = 1 + max dp[j] over j < i with nums[j] < nums[i], or 1 if there is none. Answer — the maximum over all dp[i], not dp[n − 1]: the longest one doesn’t have to end at the last element.

Cost: for every i we scan everything to its left — O(n²). For n = 2500 that is 3·10⁶ comparisons, which fits. But the problem asks right away: and in O(n log n)?

cards.task: Walk the dp filling for [10, 9, 2, 5, 3, 7, 101, 18]. The rig will stop twice and ask which value the next number gets.

asks.q: dp = [1, 1, 1, 2] for 10, 9, 2, 5. The next number is 3. What goes into dp[4]?
asks.explain: Only a subsequence ending on a smaller number can be extended. To the left of 3 only 2 is smaller, and its dp = 1 — we get 2. The 5 with dp = 2 is larger than 3: 5, 3 isn’t increasing.

asks.q: dp[5] = 3 for 7, dp[6] = 4 for 101. The last number is 18. What goes into dp[7]?
asks.explain: Among the smaller ones to the left the best is 7 with dp = 3: 18 extends, for example, 2, 3, 7 — we get 4. 101 with dp = 4 is larger than 18 and doesn’t fit. The problem’s answer is the maximum over dp, also 4: two different subsequences of length 4 end on 101 and on 18.

cards.title: Tails: O(n log n) via binary search
cards.body:
What work does O(n²) repeat? For every number it searches all of the left part again for “the best thing to extend”. But for extending, what matters is not everything that came before, only one thing: which number a subsequence of a given length ends on. And of two subsequences of the same length, the one ending on the smaller number is better — more numbers can extend it.

Keep an array tails: tails[k] is the smallest last element among all increasing subsequences of length k + 1 found so far. Invariant: tails is strictly increasing (a subsequence of length k + 2 contains a subsequence of length k + 1 with a smaller end). So binary search works on it.

The step for a number x: find the first tails[k] ≥ x — that is lower_bound from the binary search unit. If there is none, x extends the longest one, append it. Otherwise set tails[k] = x: a subsequence of length k + 1 now ends on a smaller number. The length of tails at the end is the answer. Time O(n log n), memory O(n).

Important: tails itself is not an LIS. On [3, 4, 1] it becomes [1, 4], and there is no such subsequence: the 1 comes after the 4. Only the length matches.

Instead of your own lower_bound you can use List<int>.BinarySearch: in a strictly increasing list it finds an equal element, and if there is none it returns the ~index of the insertion point, like Array.BinarySearch.
flow: the answer is the length of tails

cards.task: Step through the tails on [2, 5, 3, 7, 11, 8, 10, 13, 6, 3]. The rig asks twice where x goes: look for lower_bound — the first tail ≥ x.

options.label: tails[3] = 8: the first tail ≥ 8 is 11
Append: tails = [2, 3, 7, 11, 8]
tails[2] = 8: replace the 7

asks.q: tails = [2, 3, 7, 11], x = 8. What does the code do?
asks.explain: 8 is not bigger than every tail, so it is not appended. lower_bound(8) = 3: the first tail ≥ 8 is 11. Length 4 can now end at 8, and the coming 10 and 13 will extend it. The 7 must stay: length 3 already ends at 7 < 8 — an 8 extends that run rather than improving it.

options.label: tails[2] = 6: replace the 7
Nothing: 6 comes after 13 and extends nothing
Append 6 at the end

asks.q: tails = [2, 3, 7, 8, 10, 13], x = 6 — near the end of the array. What does the code do?
asks.explain: lower_bound(6) = 2: the first tail ≥ 6 is 7, so tails[2] = 6. The code does not care where 6 sits in the array. The result is [2, 3, 6, 8, 10, 13] — same length, but no longer a subsequence of nums: 6 comes after 8, 10 and 13. Only the length is right — the answer is 6.

cards.q: Build O(n log n) LIS on List<int>.BinarySearch.
cards.explain: A negative BinarySearch result is the ~index of the insertion point, and ~k gives it back; −k would be one index too far. An insertion point past the end means x is larger than every tail — append. Otherwise x becomes the new, smaller tail of length k + 1. If x is already in tails, BinarySearch returns its index — replacing with an equal value changes nothing, and strict increase is preserved. The answer is the length of tails, not n.

cards.q: This LIS returns 3 instead of 1 on [2, 2, 2]. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: With <= the search finds the first tails[k] > x — that is upper_bound, and an equal number is appended at the end: [2] → [2, 2] → [2, 2, 2]. That computes the longest non-decreasing subsequence. A strictly increasing one needs lower_bound — the first tails[k] ≥ x, that is the condition tails[mid] < x.

cards.title: Regular Expression Matching: “is it possible” is DP too
cards.body:
Regular Expression Matching (LeetCode #10). A string s and a pattern p, up to 20 characters each. The pattern has letters, . — any single character, and * — zero or more copies of the preceding element. The whole string must match. “aab” and “c*a*b” — yes: c* takes zero c’s, a* — two a’s.

The answer is yes/no, there is nothing to minimize. But at every x* there is a choice: how many characters it eats. And what follows depends only on the position — how many characters of the string and the pattern have been consumed. A choice plus a subproblem by position is DP, where a cell holds a bool and the transition is an “or” over the options.

State: dp[i, j] — does s[..i] match p[..j]. Base: dp[0, 0] = true; the empty string matches a prefix like “a*b*”, so dp[0, j] = p[j − 1] == '*' && dp[0, j − 2].

Transition. If p[j − 1] is a letter or a dot, it must match s[i − 1], and the rest is the diagonal dp[i − 1, j − 1]. If p[j − 1] == '*', the pair x* has two options: zero copies — drop the pair, dp[i, j − 2]; one more copy — x matches s[i − 1], and that character is eaten by the same pair: dp[i − 1, j].

Time and memory O(m·n) — 441 cells for 20 × 20.

cards.task: Walk the table for s = “aab”, p = “c*a*b”: rows are prefixes of the string, columns are prefixes of the pattern, ✓ — matches, · — doesn’t. The rig will stop twice and ask what goes into a cell.

options.label: ·: the characters matched, but the diagonal is ·
✓: the last characters matched
✓: take the cell above

asks.q: Cell (2, 3): “aa” versus “c*a”. The last characters are “a” and “a”. The diagonal dp[1, 2] — “a” versus “c*” — is ·. What goes in?
asks.explain: A pattern letter eats exactly one character of the string, and the diagonal checks the rest: “a” versus “c*” doesn’t match, so neither does “aa” versus “c*a”. A single letter “a” in the pattern can’t cover two. Only the “*” transition looks at the cell above.

options.label: ✓: “a*” eats one more “a” — take the cell above
·: zero copies dp[2, 2] doesn’t fit
·: “*” isn’t a character, there is nothing to compare

asks.q: Cell (2, 4): “aa” versus “c*a*”. Zero copies — dp[2, 2] = ·, above dp[1, 4] = ✓. What goes in?
asks.explain: For “*” the two options are joined by “or”. Zero copies didn’t fit, but “one more copy” does: the “a” before the “*” equals s[1], and the cell above dp[1, 4] says “a” is already covered by the pattern “c*a*”. The same pair a* eats the second “a” too: ✓.

cards.q: Why does the “one more copy” option for “*” look at dp[i − 1, j] and not at dp[i − 1, j − 2]?
options: dp[i − 1, j] keeps the pair x* in the pattern, so it can eat more characters; dp[i − 1, j − 2] would allow it exactly one copy
dp[i − 1, j − 2] goes outside the table when j = 2
There is no difference: both options produce the same tables
dp[i − 1, j] is the “zero copies” option, and dp[i − 1, j − 2] is “one copy”
cards.explain: Cell (i − 1, j) has the same pair x* at the end of the pattern and a string one character shorter. If it is ✓, x* has already covered some characters, and s[i − 1] is one more. That way one formula allows any number of copies. With (i − 1, j − 2) the pair would eat exactly s[i − 1] and nothing else: “aaa” versus “a*” would become ·.

wrong.1: With j = 2 the index j − 2 = 0 is the legitimate column of the empty pattern. It is not about bounds but about the number of copies.
wrong.2: There is a difference: on “aaa” and “a*” the j − 2 option gives ·, although a* covers three a’s.
wrong.3: Zero copies is dp[i, j − 2]: the string doesn’t get shorter, the pair is dropped. dp[i − 1, j] shortens the string — that is a copy.

cards.title: How to recognize DP, and where else these transitions appear
cards.body:
“I see DP” — when three signs come together: the question asks for a count, a minimum/maximum or whether it is possible; every step has a choice; what follows depends on a small state (a position, a sum, a pair of indices), not on the whole history. Then out loud: “the state is …, the transition goes over the choice of …, there are so many cells, so much work per cell — in total …”.

Word Break (#139): can a string be cut into dictionary words? dp[i] — can the prefix of length i be split; dp[i] = true if there is j < i with dp[j] and the word s[j..i) in the dictionary.

Wildcard Matching (#44): ? is any character, * is any sequence. The star stands alone: dp[i, j − 1] || dp[i − 1, j] — empty, or it eats one more character.

LIS in problems: Russian Doll Envelopes (#354) — sort by width, and for equal widths by height descending, then LIS over the heights. A non-decreasing subsequence — upper_bound instead of lower_bound. n − LIS is the minimum number of elements to move (take out and reinsert elsewhere) to sort a list.

In a game: filters with * in a console or an asset search (“enemy_*”, “*_lod0”) are Wildcard Matching. When a list of UI elements is updated, an LIS over the new positions shows which elements can stay put — only the rest move (some UI frameworks minimize node moves exactly this way).
cards.deep:
Recovering an LIS in O(n log n). Store indices in tails instead of values, plus a parent array: when nums[i] lands at position k, its parent is the index that was in tails[k − 1]. At the end walk from tails[len − 1] along parent — you get the subsequence backwards. The number of distinct LIS (#673) can’t be counted this way — that needs the O(n²) version with a “length, count” pair, or a segment tree.

Why tails is correct. The invariant “tails[k] is the minimal end of length k + 1” is preserved: x extends a subsequence of length k (its end tails[k − 1] < x) and gives length k + 1 ending in x ≤ tails[k]; positions right of k are untouched: x can’t extend a subsequence of length k + 1, since its smallest end tails[k] ≥ x. This is related to dealing cards into piles (patience sorting): the number of piles equals the LIS length.

Regex top-down. A recursion Match(i, j) over the same transitions, memoized by (i, j), is also O(m·n) and often easier to explain. Without memory it is exponential in the worst case: the pattern “a*a*a*a*b” on a string of only a’s tries every way of distributing the characters among the stars, and each extra star multiplies their number by roughly the string length.

.NET Regex. The System.Text.RegularExpressions engine backtracks by default — like our recursion without memory — and on patterns like (a+)+$ time grows exponentially (catastrophic backtracking, the basis of ReDoS attacks). Protection: a timeout in the Regex constructor (the matchTimeout parameter, available since .NET Framework 4.5) and, since .NET 7, RegexOptions.NonBacktracking — linear time in the input length, without backreferences and lookarounds. Unity doesn’t have this mode (it arrived in .NET 7), so user input goes into Regex only with a timeout, or into your own simple matcher like the Wildcard DP. RegexOptions.Compiled does nothing in Unity: Unity’s class library comes from Mono, which ignores this flag — both on Mono and under IL2CPP, where generating IL at runtime isn’t possible anyway.

cards.q: What is true? Select all.
options: In Word Break dp[i] means the prefix of length i can be split into words
In Wildcard Matching “*” gives the transition dp[i, j − 1] || dp[i − 1, j]
After the pass, tails is one of the longest increasing subsequences
A non-decreasing subsequence needs upper_bound in tails
If the answer is yes/no, DP isn’t needed: there is nothing to minimize
cards.explain: Word Break is DP over prefixes with a bool in each cell. The Wildcard star is empty (the column to the left) or eats a character (the row above). tails holds the best ends for every length, but may not itself be a subsequence: [3, 4, 1] → [1, 4]. For non-decreasing, equal numbers must extend — upper_bound. “Is it possible” is as much a reason for DP as a minimum: a bool cell, an “or” transition.

cards.q: You are solving Regular Expression Matching out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
items: Clarify: must the whole string match or a part? what can precede “*”? lengths?
Naive recursion: at every x*, try every number of copies — exponential
The state dp[i, j] — does s[..i] match p[..j]; the base dp[0, 0] and the row for “x*”
Transitions: letter or dot — diagonal; “*” — zero copies dp[i, j − 2] or one more dp[i − 1, j]
Run “aa” and “a*”: ✓ via “one more copy” twice
Complexity: O(m·n) time and memory
Edge cases: the empty string versus “a*b*”, the pattern “.*”
cards.explain: Clarifying “the whole string” changes the answer for “aab” and “a”. The recursion explains where the transitions come from, the table how to get rid of the exponent. Running “aa” against “a*” checks the subtlest transition right away.

cards.q: Match the problem with its state or technique.
pairs: dp[i] — the longest one ending at i
dp[i, j]: zero copies or one more
dp[i] — the prefix splits into words

lessons.title: Unit final: exhaustive search and DP
lessons.sub: Recognize search or DP from the statement, predict a coin table without a one, find the bug in a 0/1 knapsack, explain out loud

cards.q: New problems. Match the statement with the technique.
pairs: All letter words that can be typed with phone digits
A decision tree: each digit gets its letters
Can the array be split into two parts with equal sums
LCS of the string and its reverse
All valid bracket strings of n pairs
Pruning: “)” only while fewer are closed than open
Maximum money without robbing two adjacent houses

cards.q: A game has 20 items, each with a weight and a value up to 10⁹, and a backpack capacity up to 10⁹ as well. You need the maximum value of a set that fits. How do you solve it?
