options: Enumerate subsets: 2²⁰·20 ≈ 2·10⁷ operations
0/1 knapsack over capacity: dp with 10⁹ + 1 cells
Greedy: take items by decreasing value per unit of weight
Unbounded knapsack: sums ascending
cards.explain: A table over capacity costs O(n·W) = 2·10¹⁰ operations and about 8 GB of memory (value sums up to 2·10¹⁰ need a long) — that is not a solution. But there are only 20 items, and enumerating every set with a mask is about 2·10⁷ steps, a fraction of a second. Which one is cheap — n or W — is decided by the limits.

wrong.1: O(n·W) depends on the magnitude of the capacity, not on the number of items: with W = 10⁹ that is 2·10¹⁰ operations and gigabytes of memory — a thousand times slower than enumerating masks.
wrong.2: Greedy by value per weight is correct only for the “fractional” knapsack, where an item can be cut. Here an item is taken whole, and greedy fails, as with coins 1, 3, 4.
wrong.3: Each item exists once: an unbounded knapsack could take it twice. And a table over capacity is still too big.

cards.q: Decode Ways (LeetCode #91): a string of up to 100 digits, “1” → A … “26” → Z. In how many ways can it be decoded? “226” — three: 2·2·6, 22·6, 2·26. How do you solve it?
options: DP like Climbing Stairs: the last “move” is one digit or two, dp[i] = dp[i − 1] + dp[i − 2] for the moves that are allowed
Enumerate every split of the string: 100 characters isn’t much
Greedily take two digits whenever they form a number up to 26
cards.explain: The last piece is one digit (if it isn’t “0”) or two (if they form 10–26), and the rest is the same problem on a prefix. It is a staircase with moves of 1 and 2, except a move isn’t always allowed. O(n) time, two variables of memory.

wrong.1: A string of 100 digits has 2⁹⁹ splits into pieces; even with pieces of only one or two digits there are about 6·10²⁰ — the same order as the calls of the naive staircase recursion. The subproblems “how many ways for the prefix of length i” repeat, and DP counts exactly those.
wrong.2: The question asks for the number of ways, not one way: greedy gives a single split, and on “2101” it is also wrong — “21” leaves “01”, which can’t be decoded.

cards.task: New coins — [2, 5], amount 11, and no coin of 1. Walk the table; the rig will stop twice and ask you to predict a cell. The rig shows unreachable sums as ∞.

asks.q: dp[1] = ∞, dp[2] = 1. What will dp[3] be?
asks.explain: Coin 2 leads from dp[1], and that is unreachable: “∞” + 1 = amount + 2 is not less than “∞” = amount + 1, so Math.Min keeps infinity. Coin 5 is larger than the sum. A 3 can’t be made from 2 and 5 — dp[3] stays ∞.

asks.q: dp[6] = 3, dp[9] = 3. What will dp[11] be?
asks.explain: Coin 2: dp[9] + 1 = 4. Coin 5: dp[6] + 1 = 4. The minimum is 4 — for example, 5 + 2 + 2 + 2. Greedy would take 5 + 5 and get stuck on the remainder 1, deciding it can’t be made; 3 coins would only be 5 + 5 + 1, and there is no coin of 1.

cards.q: Partition Equal Subset Sum: can the array be split into two parts with equal sums? On [1, 2, 5] the code returned true, although the answer is false. Tap the line with the bug.
cards.explain: The sums go up, and ok[s − x] already accounts for the number x: at x = 1 the code marks 1, 2, 3, 4 — the one is taken several times. That is the unbounded knapsack, while each number here exists once. It needs the reverse loop: for (int s = half; s >= x; s--) — then ok[s − x] hasn’t “seen” x yet.

cards.q: Two strings of 2·10⁴ characters each, only the LCS length is needed. How much memory does a full int table take, and what do you do about it?
options: ≈ 1.6 GB; two table rows are about 160 KB, the time is the same
≈ 160 MB; fine, leave it as is
≈ 1.6 GB; switch to memoization — it stores less
≈ 40 KB; the table grows like m + n
cards.explain: (2·10⁴ + 1)² ≈ 4·10⁸ cells of 4 bytes — about 1.6 GB. A table row depends only on the previous one, so two arrays of 2·10⁴ + 1 are enough — 160 KB. The time stays O(m·n) ≈ 4·10⁸ — a few seconds, but memory is no longer a problem.

wrong.1: 4·10⁸ cells are 4·10⁸ ints, 4 bytes each. The order is gigabytes, not hundreds of megabytes.
wrong.2: Memoization stores the same (i, j) — up to all 4·10⁸ — plus a recursion stack up to m + n deep. No less memory.
wrong.3: A table row grows like m + n, but the table has m·n cells.

cards.q: Unity: a developer console with 400 commands, names up to 20 characters. While typing, you need to show the closest ones by spelling. What do you pick?
options: Edit Distance to every command on two reused rows, with a threshold k = 2–3
LCS of the input with every command: the longer the common part, the closer
Build a Regex from the typed string and run IsMatch over all commands
Enumerate every string within 1–2 edits of the input and look each up in a HashSet
cards.explain: 400 commands · 20 · 20 is about 1.6·10⁵ cells per keystroke: on the order of a millisecond, unnoticeable while typing. Two rows kept in a field mean zero allocations; the threshold lets you drop distant names and stop a row once its minimum exceeds k.

wrong.1: LCS doesn’t penalize extras: “spawn” is entirely inside “spawn_all_enemies_debug”, and they would look “very close”. LCS also sees a substitution typo worse than Edit Distance does.
wrong.2: User input in a Regex risks exponential backtracking time and parse errors on characters like “*”. And Regex doesn’t forgive typos.
wrong.3: Strings within 2 edits of a 20-character input number in the hundreds of thousands and more (replacements, insertions, deletions with 26 letters at each position), while there are only 400 commands: comparing with each is cheaper.

cards.q: Partition Equal Subset Sum out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
items: Clarify: are the numbers positive? what are n and the sum? may the parts be any subsets?
Naively: enumerate subsets, 2ⁿ — impossible for n = 200
Reduce it: we need a part with the sum total / 2; an odd sum — false at once
The state ok[s] — can the sum s be made; each number once — sums descending
Run [1, 5, 11, 5]: half = 11, ok[11] = true via 11 or 1 + 5 + 5
Complexity: O(n·half) time, O(half) memory
Edge cases: a single element, an element larger than half — false at once
cards.explain: The reduction to “make half” is the key step, worth saying before the code. The loop direction explains that this is the 0/1 knapsack, not the unbounded one — exactly the bug from the card with the code.

cards.q: Which estimates are correct? Select all.
options: Subsets is O(n·2ⁿ), and it can’t be faster: that many elements are in the answer itself
Permutations is O(n·n!), for n = 11 that is already about 4·10⁸
Edit Distance on two table rows is O(m + n) time
LIS via tails and binary search is O(n log n)
Coin Change is O(amount·k) time and O(amount) memory
cards.explain: Enumeration is optimal by the size of the answer. 11!·11 ≈ 4.4·10⁸ — at the edge of the limit. Two table rows save memory, but there are still m·n cells — the time is O(m·n). tails is n steps of O(log n). The coin table has amount cells, each trying k denominations.

units.title: Data structure design and final exam
units.blurb: LRU and LFU, the trie, tree serialization, object pools and ring buffers, from the LeetCode problem to an asset cache in a game. Then the exam on the whole course.

lessons.title: LRU cache
lessons.sub: A dictionary finds, a list keeps the order: O(1) Get and Put, and the same cache on indices with no allocations

cards.title: The problem and the signals of a design task
cards.body:
LRU Cache (LeetCode #146). Design a class with a capacity capacity and two methods: Get(key) returns the value or −1, Put(key, value) inserts the key or updates its value. When there are more keys than capacity, evict the one that has gone unused the longest (least recently used). Both Get and Put count as a use: each makes the key the most recent. Both operations are O(1) on average. Constraints: capacity ≤ 3000, keys ≤ 10⁴, up to 2·10⁵ calls.

There is no input here — there are methods. This is a data structure design problem, and it has its own signals:

1. “Implement the class …”, a list of calls with expected outputs — choose the state first (which dictionaries, lists, counters), then write the methods.
2. “O(1) per operation” — no method may contain a single pass over the data.
3. “Evict the least …” — you need two structures: one that finds (a dictionary) and one that keeps order.

LRU is the most common design problem in both .NET and Unity interviews: every service and every engine has a cache.

cards.q: Capacity 2. Calls: Put(1, 1), Put(2, 2), Put(1, 10), Put(3, 3), Get(1), Get(2). What do the last two Gets return?
options: 10 and −1
−1 and 2
1 and −1
10 and 2
cards.explain: Put(1, 10) is an update and also a use: key 1 became more recent than key 2. Put(3, 3) does not fit and evicts the least recent key — 2. Get(1) returns the new value 10, Get(2) returns −1.

wrong.1: That would happen if an update did not count as a use: key 1 would stay the least recent. But by the statement a Put is a use too.
wrong.2: A Put on an existing key replaces the value: after Put(1, 10) it holds 10, not 1.
wrong.3: With capacity 2 there would be three keys: Put(3, 3) has to evict someone. That is key 2 — it was used least recently.

cards.title: Naive solutions and their cost
cards.body:
Dictionary + timestamp. Store key → (value, tick), where tick is the number of the last use from a global counter. Get is O(1). But to evict you have to find the smallest tick — a scan over all keys, O(capacity). If every Put evicts, that is 2·10⁵ · 3000 = 6·10⁸ operations — seconds.

Dictionary + a List<int> for order. The most recent key goes to the end of the list, the victim is list[0]. But using a key from the middle means list.Remove(key): a linear search and a shift of the tail, O(n). And RemoveAt(0) shifts the whole list as well.

SortedSet<(long tick, int key)>. The minimum is O(log n), a use is Remove of the old pair and Add of a new one, O(log n). A working answer, and worth saying out loud, but the statement asks for O(1), and every tree node is an allocation.

All three share one flaw: they search for the recency order instead of keeping it. We need a structure where moving a known element to the front and removing from the back cost O(1).

cards.q: The “dictionary + List<int> for order” solution: on every Get the key moves to the end — list.Remove(key), then list.Add(key). 2·10⁵ calls, capacity 3000. What is wrong?
options: Remove(key) searches for the key linearly and shifts the tail: O(capacity) per call, up to 6·10⁸ operations
Nothing: Remove and Add on a List<T> are O(1)
List<int> boxes every key, which creates garbage
Only RemoveAt(0) on eviction is a problem; Remove(key) is cheap
cards.explain: A List<T> is an array: Remove(key) first looks for the value linearly (IndexOf), then shifts everything to its right with Array.Copy. Both steps are O(n). Over 2·10⁵ calls with 3000 keys that is on the order of 6·10⁸ operations, and the task asked for O(1).

wrong.1: List<T> is O(1) only for Add at the end, the indexer and removing the last element. Remove(value) is a search plus a shift, O(n).
wrong.2: List<int> stores ints in an int[] without boxing. The problem is the scan, not garbage.
wrong.3: RemoveAt(0) is O(n) too, but Remove(key) is no cheaper: it searches for the key and shifts the tail.

cards.title: Dictionary + doubly linked list
cards.body:
A doubly linked list keeps the recency order: the most recent key at the front, the next one to go at the back. Moving a node to the front and removing the last one cost O(1) once the node is in hand. The dictionary key → LinkedListNode puts it in your hand: this is the pairing from the linked list unit, where nodes are stored outside the list.

Get: find the node in the dictionary → unlink it → insert it at the front → return the value.
Put: the key exists — unlink its old node. The key is new and the cache is full — remove the last node and delete its key from the dictionary. Then insert (key, value) at the front and store the node in the dictionary.

Two details people get wrong. The node stores the key as well: on eviction you hold the last node, and you must delete its key from the dictionary. And the order of checks: first “does the key exist”, and only for a new key — eviction; an update does not change the size.

Invariant: the dictionary and the list hold the same keys, and the list is ordered from most to least recent. Every method restores this before returning. Time is O(1) on average per operation (average because of the dictionary), memory is O(capacity).
flow: new key and full → drop the tail
tail's key → out of the dictionary

cards.q: Assemble Get and Put.
cards.explain: Remove(node) is O(1): the node comes from the dictionary. Remove(key) would not even compile here (the list holds tuples), and LinkedList<T>.Remove(value) is a scan. else if: evict only for a new key, an update does not change the size. The victim is the tail of the list, order.Last, and you delete its key from the dictionary, not its value.

cards.task: Walk the trace: capacity 3. The most recent key is on the left, the next to go is on the right. The rig will stop twice and ask what the code does.

options.label: Update the value and move 3 to the front: 3, 1, 2
Evict 2 from the tail, then insert 3
Change the value and leave 3 where it is: 1, 3, 2

asks.q: The list is 1, 3, 2. The cache is full, and put(3, 30) arrives — key 3 is already there. What does the code do?
asks.explain: The key exists, so this is an update: the size does not change and nobody needs to go. The code unlinks the old node 3 and inserts (3, 30) at the front: a Put is a use too. “Evict 2” is exactly the order-of-checks bug: eviction is only for a new key.

options.label: Key 1
Key 4
Key 3

asks.q: The list is 3, 4, 1. put(5, 5) is a new key and the cache is full. Whom does the code evict?
asks.explain: The victim is the tail of the list, order.Last: no search needed. It is key 1: it was last touched by get(1) at the very start, and since then 3 (update), 4 (insert) and 3 again were used. The node leaves the list, and its key 1 leaves the dictionary.

cards.q: Capacity 2: Put(1, 1), Put(2, 2), Put(2, 5), Get(1). Get returned −1, but it should return 1. Tap the buggy line.
cards.explain: Eviction is checked before “does the key exist”. Put(2, 5) sees a full cache and drops the tail — key 1 — even though it is an update and there is enough room. The fix is the order: TryGetValue first, and eviction in an else if, only for a new key.

cards.title: LinkedList<T> or your own list on indices
cards.body:
What the solution above costs. Every AddFirst((key, value)) is a new LinkedListNode object: a 16-byte header, three references and the tuple — 48 bytes on 64-bit. It is created both for a new key and on every update. The node can be reused: AddFirst(node) accepts a node that is already unlinked, and the value changes through node.Value. Then a new object is needed only for a new key, and on eviction you can take the removed tail. But the nodes are still scattered across the heap: every hop is a cache miss, and the Boehm GC walks all of them on every collection.

A list on indices (linked list unit): keys, values and the prev/next links live in arrays, and a “node” is a slot number. Slot 0 is a sentinel: next[0] is the most recent, prev[0] the least recent, and an empty list is the sentinel looped onto itself. There are no null checks at all. Eviction takes the tail's slot and gives it to the new key.

All the arrays and the dictionary are created in the constructor. A dictionary with a preset capacity does not grow, and it reuses removed entries through its own free list. So after the constructor there are zero allocations on any call. The arrays can move to a NativeArray, but the dictionary is managed: in Burst a NativeHashMap<int, int> replaces it.
cards.deep:
Threads. Two structures change together, so a ConcurrentDictionary does not help: between the dictionary edit and the list edit another thread sees them out of sync. You need one lock around the whole method — Get included: a read moves a node, so it writes. A reader–writer lock buys nothing here. Under load the cache is split into N independent shards by hash(key) % N, each with its own lock: the eviction order becomes approximate, but threads barely wait for each other.

.NET has no ready-made LRU. OrderedDictionary<TKey, TValue> from .NET 9 keeps insertion order in an array: moving a key out of the middle is a removal with a shift, O(n). MemoryCache from Microsoft.Extensions.Caching.Memory is not an LRU: if a new entry does not fit into SizeLimit, it is simply not added, and the cache compacts in the background by a CompactionPercentage share — expired entries first, then by priority, and only within a priority by recency.

Approximations. Strict LRU pays for a reorder on every read. The CLOCK algorithm keeps entries in a ring buffer with a “touched” bit: a read only sets the bit, and on eviction a hand walks the ring, clears bits and takes the first entry without one. Variants of CLOCK replace pages in operating systems and buffers in databases. Redis evicts by sampling: it picks a few random keys and removes the least recent of them.

cards.q: What is true about the two LRU implementations? Select all.
options: In the first version, a Put on an existing key creates a new node: order.AddFirst((key, value))
The node can be reused: change node.Value and insert the same node with AddFirst(node)
The index version allocates no memory on any call after the constructor
LinkedList<T>.Remove(value) is O(1) too, so storing the node in the dictionary is optional
The index version can be called from a Burst job as is
cards.explain: AddFirst(T value) always creates a new LinkedListNode, while AddFirst(node) inserts an existing one, and after Remove a node is free to be inserted again. In the index version all arrays and the dictionary with a capacity are created up front, and the dictionary reuses removed entries. Remove(value) is a scan, O(n). And Burst cannot touch a managed Dictionary: the arrays move to NativeArray, the dictionary to NativeHashMap.

cards.title: Unity: an asset cache evicts by memory
cards.body:
Games cache textures, meshes and audio loaded from Addressables or from disk. The limit here is not the number of entries but memory: a 4096×4096 RGBA32 texture is 64 MB (mipmaps add another third), a 64×64 icon is 16 KB. “At most 100 entries” guarantees nothing.

It is the same LRU, but each entry has a weight in bytes, and the cache keeps the total bytes and a budget. Insertion: add at the front, add the weight, then in a loop drop the tail while bytes > budget — several entries may go. An entry heavier than the whole budget is not cached at all: it would evict everything and still not fit.

What matters in Unity. You compute the weight yourself on load: width × height × bytes per pixel of the format (compressed formats use less than a byte per pixel). Profiler.GetRuntimeMemorySizeLong returns 0 when the profiler is not available — and a release build has none. Evicting means releasing: Addressables.Release(handle) for something loaded, Destroy for a texture created in code. The GC knows nothing about a texture's native memory: dropping the reference does not free it — the texture lives on until Destroy or Resources.UnloadUnusedAssets. And whatever is on screen right now is not kept in the eviction list: an entry goes there when its use count drops to zero.

cards.q: A texture cache has a 256 MB budget, 250 MB in use. At the tail of the list are three 4 MB textures, and in front of them one of 64 MB. A Put of a new 16 MB texture arrives. What happens?
options: The three 4 MB textures go: 266 → 254 MB
One texture goes — the least recent
The 64 MB texture goes: that frees the most
The new one is refused: it does not fit the budget right now
cards.explain: After the insertion it is 266 MB > 256. The loop drops the tail: 262, then 258 — still over budget — then 254, and the loop stops. The 64 MB texture is more recent, so it stays.

wrong.1: One entry is the count-based LRU rule. By memory you evict in a loop until the total fits the budget: 262 MB is still too much.
wrong.2: LRU picks by recency, not by weight. The heaviest entry may have been needed a frame ago.
wrong.3: Only entries heavier than the whole budget are refused. 16 MB is less than 256: eviction makes the room.

cards.q: You are solving LRU Cache out loud in an interview. Put the steps in order.
items: Clarify: what counts as a use, what to return on a miss, the capacity, whether several threads access it
Name the naive solution: a dictionary with timestamps, eviction by scan — O(capacity)
The idea: a dictionary finds the node, a doubly linked list keeps the recency order
Write Get and Put, stating the invariant: the dictionary and the list hold the same keys
Walk an example with capacity 2: a key update and a tail eviction
Complexity: O(1) on average per operation, O(capacity) memory
Edge cases: a Put on an existing key when the cache is full, capacity 1
cards.explain: Agree on the rules first (is a Put a use, what to return, threads), then the baseline, the two-structure idea, code with the invariant, a walk on a small example, complexity and edge cases. An example with an update on a full cache also catches the order-of-checks bug.

cards.q: Match each operation with how the LRU cache does it and at what cost.
pairs: Make a key the most recent
order.Last — the tail of the list
A texture cache with a budget
Drop the tail while bytes > budget

lessons.title: LFU cache
lessons.sub: Buckets by frequency, LRU inside a bucket, and a minFreq that is never searched for

cards.title: The problem: least frequent, and on a tie least recent
cards.body:
LFU Cache (LeetCode #460, hard). A cache of capacity capacity with Get(key) and Put(key, value), both O(1) on average. When there is no room, evict the key that was used least often (least frequently used). If several keys tie, evict the one among them that was used least recently, as in LRU.

A key's count is the number of Get and Put calls on it since it was inserted. A new key starts at 1. An evicted key's count is forgotten: if it comes back, it starts at 1 again. Constraints: capacity ≤ 10⁴, keys ≤ 10⁵, up to 2·10⁵ calls.

The signals are the same as for LRU: “implement the class”, O(1) per operation, “evict the least …”. But the order is now two-level — by frequency first, by recency within a frequency — and a single list cannot hold it: a key with count 5 cannot simply be “moved to the front” when keys with count 9 may be ahead of it.

cards.q: Capacity 2: Put(1, 1), Put(2, 2), Get(2), Get(1), Put(3, 3). Which key does Put(3, 3) evict?
options: None: 3 does not fit and is not inserted
Either one: their counts are equal
cards.explain: Keys 1 and 2 have two uses each — a frequency tie. Recency breaks it: key 2 was last touched by Get(2), key 1 later, by Get(1). Key 2 goes.

wrong.1: Key 1 was touched last (Get(1) came after Get(2)), so it is the more recent of the two.
wrong.2: A new key is always inserted: eviction makes room for it.
wrong.3: A tie is not arbitrary: the statement says to evict the least recent of the tied keys.

cards.title: Naive solutions and their cost
cards.body:
Dictionary + (freq, tick). For each key store the value, the count and the timestamp of the last use. Get and Put are O(1), but eviction scans all keys for the smallest (freq, tick) pair: O(capacity). In the worst case that is 2·10⁵ · 10⁴ = 2·10⁹ operations.

SortedSet<(int freq, long tick, int key)>. Tuples compare field by field from left to right — exactly the LFU rule with recency as the tie-breaker. The victim is Min, O(log n); a use is Remove of the old tuple and Add of a new one, O(log n). An honest solution, name it — but not O(1), and every Add is a tree node on the heap.

A PriorityQueue heap. It looks natural: “take the lowest frequency”. But a key's priority changes on every use, and PriorityQueue cannot change a priority (collections unit). Lazy deletion — enqueue the key again and skip stale copies — bloats the heap: there are as many copies as there were uses.

What repeats: every eviction searches for the minimum from scratch, although between evictions frequencies only grow by 1.

cards.q: Why is PriorityQueue<int, (int freq, long tick)> a poor fit for LFU?
options: A key's priority changes on every use, and it cannot change a priority — only enqueue copies
It cannot compare tuples
Removing the minimum is O(n) in it
It returns elements in insertion order
cards.explain: PriorityQueue is a heap without decrease-key, and finding an element in it takes a scan (Remove arrived only in .NET 9 and costs O(n)). Without a scan, the only way to update a key's frequency is lazy deletion: enqueue a copy with the new priority and skip the old one when it comes out. Every use adds a copy, so the heap grows with the number of calls, not with the capacity.

wrong.1: Tuples compare field by field through Comparer<T>.Default — that works.
wrong.2: Dequeue on a heap is O(log n). The trouble is updating a priority, not removing the minimum.
wrong.3: It is a heap: it returns the minimum by priority, and equal priorities in arbitrary order.

cards.title: Buckets by frequency and minFreq
cards.body:
Spread the keys over buckets: bucket f holds all keys that were used exactly f times. Inside a bucket is a list in recency order, the least recent first: that is an LRU for a single frequency. The dictionary map stores an entry per key: the value, the count freq and the node in its bucket's list.

A use (a Get, or a Put on an existing key): unlink the node from bucket f — O(1), it is in hand — and append it to bucket f + 1. Eviction: the first key of the bucket with the lowest frequency. To avoid searching for that bucket, keep a field minFreq.

minFreq changes in only two cases. A new key: minFreq = 1 — nothing is used less often than a new key. A use emptied bucket f and f was the lowest: minFreq = f + 1 — the key that left has just landed exactly there, and there is nothing below f. If a bucket above the lowest empties, minFreq stays. There are no other changes: a use moves one key up by one bucket, and an eviction is immediately followed by the insertion of a new key.

Without minFreq, eviction would look for a non-empty bucket by scanning frequencies from the bottom, and frequencies grow up to the number of calls — 2·10⁵. Invariant: minFreq is the number of the lowest non-empty bucket. Time is O(1) on average per operation, memory is O(capacity).
flow: node: bucket f → end of f + 1
f empty and f == minFreq → minFreq++

cards.q: Assemble the move between buckets and the eviction.
cards.explain: Remove(e.node) is O(1) by node. Remove(e.freq) compiles (the list holds ints), but it removes by value, with a scan, and the wrong element. minFreq grows only when exactly the lowest bucket empties. The victim is the first key of bucket minFreq, and after the eviction a new key with count 1 is inserted, so minFreq = 1.

cards.task: Walk the trace of the LeetCode example: capacity 2. Buckets go by use count, the least recent key in a bucket is on the left. The rig will stop twice: on minFreq and on a tie.

options.label: minFreq = 2 — no search at all
Scan the buckets from the bottom to find a non-empty one
Keep minFreq = 1 until the next put

asks.q: get(3) moved key 3 from bucket 1 to bucket 2, and bucket 1 is now empty. minFreq was 1. What does the code do?
asks.explain: Bucket 1 was the lowest and it emptied, and the key that left it landed in bucket 2 — so bucket 2 is non-empty and there is nothing below it. One comparison and an increment. Keeping 1 is wrong: the next eviction would reach into an empty bucket.

options.label: Key 1
Key 3
Both: the whole bucket is freed

asks.q: put(4, 4): the cache is full, minFreq = 2, bucket 2 holds keys 1 and 3. Whom does the code evict?
asks.explain: The frequencies are equal, so recency breaks the tie. Keys are appended to a bucket: 1 after get(1), 3 later, after get(3). The first in the list is the least recent: victims.First, key 1. Exactly one key is evicted — to make room for one new key.

cards.q: Capacity 2: Put(1, 1), Put(2, 2), Get(2), Get(2), Put(3, 3) — and Put throws a NullReferenceException. Tap the buggy line.
cards.explain: minFreq grows whenever any bucket empties, not only the lowest one. The second Get(2) empties bucket 2 while minFreq = 1 and key 1 is still in bucket 1 — and minFreq becomes 2. Put(3, 3) takes buckets[2], an empty list: First == null, and First.Value throws. The condition needs && minFreq == e.freq.

cards.title: Why it is O(1), and what it costs
cards.body:
Why O(1). Every operation is a dictionary lookup (O(1) on average), at most two list operations by node (O(1)) and one comparison for minFreq. Not a single loop over keys or buckets: everything we used to search for is now kept — the list keeps the order inside a bucket, minFreq keeps the lowest bucket.

Memory. Per key: an Entry object (32 bytes on 64-bit) and a LinkedListNode<int> (48 bytes), plus one LinkedList object per frequency. On a use the node moves between buckets by itself, without a new allocation: after Remove it is unlinked and can be inserted again.

Empty buckets. In the code above an emptied bucket stays in the buckets dictionary. Frequencies grow up to the number of calls, and the dictionary can pile up thousands of empty lists. You can remove a bucket when it empties — but then the list is created again the next time a key reaches that frequency. In an interview it is enough to name the trade-off and pick one.
cards.deep:
Buckets as a list, no frequency dictionary. The buckets can themselves form a doubly linked list ordered by frequency: each bucket knows its neighbours and its frequency. A use moves the key into the next bucket on the right — if its frequency is f + 1 — or creates that bucket between the current one and its neighbour. An emptied bucket is removed at once, and minFreq is just the first bucket. The same shape solves All O(1) Data Structure (#432): inc, dec, getMaxKey and getMinKey in O(1).

Without allocations. Just like LRU on indices: keys, values, frequencies and the prev/next links live in arrays of capacity plus sentinels; a bucket is a “head, tail” pair in an array indexed by frequency or in a freq → bucket number dictionary. After the constructor, not a single object.

Can the count overflow? An int is 2.1·10⁹ uses of one key. The problem has 2·10⁵ calls, and in a long-lived service counts age anyway (next card), so they never get near the limit.

cards.title: When LFU is worse than LRU
cards.body:
LFU remembers the past: a key that was used a lot an hour ago stays on its count even if it is no longer needed. That causes two problems.

1. Stale keys. The player has left the first biome: its sounds and textures racked up thousands of uses and now never get evicted, while the new biome's assets fight over what is left of the cache.
2. Newcomers go first. A new key starts at 1 and is evicted before everyone else, even if it will be needed constantly: it never gets the chance to build up a count.

LRU reacts to a change of pattern at once: whatever is not touched goes. That is why games default to LRU, and LFU pays off when popularity is stable: frequent lookups of reference data, shared UI resources.

The cure is aging. Every N operations, or on a level change, all counts are halved — old merit fades. That is O(n) once every N operations, cheap when amortized. Another option is a hybrid: a small LRU window for new keys, and only keys that have proven their frequency get into the main part. In an interview, naming both problems and aging is enough.

cards.q: A sound cache uses LFU. After a biome change the old biome's sounds are never evicted, while the new biome's sounds keep getting evicted and reloaded. What helps? Select all.
options: Aging: halve all counts on a biome change
Switch to LRU: sound popularity changes with the biome
Double the capacity — and the problem is gone for good
Reset minFreq to 0 on a biome change
Switch to a SortedSet by (freq, tick)
cards.explain: The problem is stale counts. Aging makes them fade, and LRU ignores past merit altogether — a good fit when popularity changes. A bigger capacity only delays the problem until the next biome. minFreq is the number of the lowest non-empty bucket, and setting it to 0 breaks the invariant. A SortedSet changes the cost of operations, not the eviction rule.

cards.q: You are solving LFU Cache out loud. Put the steps in order.
items: Clarify: what counts as a use, how a frequency tie is broken, what happens to an evicted key's count
Name the honest solution: a SortedSet by (freq, tick) — O(log n) per operation
The idea: buckets by frequency, recency order inside a bucket, plus a minFreq field
Explain why minFreq is never searched for: it is reset to 1 or grows by 1
Write Get, Put and Touch, then walk an example with a tie
Complexity: O(1) on average per operation, O(capacity) memory
Say when LFU is worse than LRU and what aging is
cards.explain: The tie and use rules come before the code: the structure depends on them. O(log n) is the baseline and a fallback. What interviewers want to hear on this hard problem is the minFreq argument: why it is enough and why it needs no search.

cards.q: Match each event in the LFU cache with what the code does.
pairs: From bucket f to the end of bucket f + 1
The first in the bucket is the least recent
Old keys hang on by their count

lessons.title: The trie
lessons.sub: A node is a prefix: next[26] and an end flag, O(word length) per operation, a child dictionary and nodes in an array

cards.title: The problem and the signals of a trie
cards.body:
Implement Trie (LeetCode #208). Implement a prefix tree (trie) with three methods: Insert(word); Search(word) — is exactly this word stored; StartsWith(prefix) — does any stored word begin with prefix. Words are lowercase a–z, up to 2000 long, up to 3·10⁴ calls.

Signals of a trie:

1. The question is about a prefix: “starts with”, autocomplete, suggestions while typing.
2. One dictionary and many queries against it.
3. Words are built letter by letter, and after each letter you want to know whether any word continues that way — for example, while walking a grid of letters.

If you only need whole words, a HashSet<string> is enough. A trie is for when the question is about the beginning of a word.

cards.title: Naive solutions and their cost
cards.body:
HashSet<string>. Search is O(L) on average: the string's hash is computed over all its characters, then compared. But StartsWith scans all words: w.StartsWith(prefix, StringComparison.Ordinal) for each, O(n · L) per query. The hash of a prefix has nothing to do with the words — it cannot find the words that start with it.

All prefixes in a HashSet. On insert, add every prefix of the word: “a”, “ap”, “app”… A query is O(L), but a word of length L gives L prefixes with about L²/2 characters in total: for L = 2000 that is 2·10⁶ characters for one word, and every prefix is a new string on the heap.

A sorted array + binary search. Words sharing a prefix are adjacent in it: the first one ≥ prefix is found in O(L · log n). Good for a dictionary that never changes, but an insertion is O(n), a shift.

What repeats: words with a common beginning store and compare that beginning each on their own.

cards.q: A dictionary of 10⁴ words in a HashSet<string>, 3·10⁴ StartsWith queries by scanning. How many string comparisons in the worst case, and what follows?
options: 3·10⁸ — that is seconds, a different approach is needed
3·10⁴ — one per query: the HashSet finds the prefix by its hash
10⁴ — each word is compared once across all queries
cards.explain: Every query with no match goes through all 10⁴ words: 3·10⁴ · 10⁴ = 3·10⁸ comparisons, each up to the prefix length in characters. At the rule of thumb of 10⁸ operations per second, that is seconds.

wrong.1: The hash of “app” has nothing to do with the hash of “apple”: a HashSet only answers questions about whole strings.
wrong.2: The scan repeats on every query — words do not “remember” that they were compared already.

cards.title: A node is a prefix
cards.body:
Glue the common beginnings together. A trie node is a prefix: the root is the empty string, an edge labelled c means “append c”. A node holds an array next[26], one slot per letter (next[ch - 'a']), and a flag end: “a stored word ends here”.

Insert walks from the root letter by letter; if an edge is missing, it creates the node. The last node gets end = true. Search and StartsWith walk the same way and answer false at the first missing edge. Reached the end: StartsWith is true right away, Search only if end is set. The flag is needed because the path “app” exists inside “apple” even if “app” was never inserted.

Words with a common prefix share its nodes: there are at most as many nodes as the total length of the words (plus the root), and usually far fewer. Every operation is O(L), where L is the word length, however many words the tree holds. Memory is O(nodes · 26).
flow: no edge: Insert creates, lookups → false
end of the word: end = true
Search: path and end; StartsWith: path

cards.q: “tea”, “ten”, “to” and “inn” are inserted into an empty trie. How many nodes does it have, not counting the root?
cards.explain: The t branch: t, then e and o; under e — a and n. That is 5 nodes for three words: “t” and “te” are shared. The i branch: i, n, n — 3 more. 8 in total against 11 letters in all the words: common prefixes are stored once.

wrong.1: 11 is the total length of the words. That many nodes would exist without shared prefixes, and here “t” and “te” are shared.
wrong.2: 4 is the number of words. But a node is a prefix, not a word: every letter on a path has its own node.
wrong.3: Don't forget the “inn” branch: i and two n — three nodes, shared with nothing.

cards.q: Assemble the trie.
cards.explain: The letter index is ch - 'a', from 0 to 25; ch itself is a code of 97 and up, outside the array. end goes on the last node of the path, not on the root. StartsWith is satisfied by the path existing and does not check end — otherwise it is Search. On a missing edge Find returns null: returning root would mean “found the empty prefix”.

cards.task: Walk the trace: card and care share the prefix car. Under the tree are next[26] and end of the current node. The rig will ask twice what the code does.

options.label: true: all three letters were found
false: the path exists, but node r has end = false
false: an edge is missing

asks.q: search("car"): c, a, r — every edge is there. What does Search return?
asks.explain: The path “car” exists — card and care lie along it — but end on node r is set only by inserting “car” itself. Until then it is just a prefix: Search is false. StartsWith("car") on the same node answers true.

options.label: None: it walks the edges and sets end
Three — one node per letter
One — for the last letter

asks.q: insert("car"). How many new nodes does the code create?
asks.explain: All three edges c → a → r already exist: inserting card created them. Insert walks along them (??= creates nothing) and only sets end = true on node r. The prefix is stored once, and the flag tells a word from a prefix.

cards.q: After Insert("apple"), the call Search("app") returned true. Tap the buggy line.
cards.explain: end is set inside the loop — on every node of the path. After Insert("apple"), a, ap, app and appl all became “words”. Only the last node should get the flag: node.end = true belongs after the loop.

cards.title: next[26], a child dictionary, or nodes in an array
cards.body:
An array next[26] gives an O(1) step with no hashing, but costs 26 references per node however many children it has: the array is a 24-byte header plus 26 · 8 = 208 bytes, plus the node itself — about 260 bytes on 64-bit .NET (in Mono and IL2CPP an array header is 32 bytes, so about 270). Deep in a trie a node usually has a single child, and 25 slots sit empty. And the alphabet is hard-wired: a character outside a–z gives an index outside the array.

Dictionary<char, Node> uses memory per child and accepts any alphabet: digits, _, a dot, uppercase, Cyrillic. The price is a hash on every letter and separate objects for every dictionary. For nodes with 1–3 children a small array of (letter, node) pairs with a linear scan is often cheaper.

Nodes in an array. A trie with no objects: an int[] next of size maxNodes · 26, where the child of node v by letter c is next[v * 26 + c]; 0 means “no edge” — the root is node 0, and no edge can lead to it. That is 104 bytes per node instead of ~260, not a single object for the GC, and an int array moves to a NativeArray<int> and can be walked in Burst. The size is the total word length + 1 if the dictionary is known up front; otherwise grow the array by doubling.
cards.deep:
Deletion and counters. To delete words and answer “how many words have this prefix” (Implement Trie II, #1804), a node keeps two counters: how many words pass through it and how many end in it. Insert increments them along the path, Erase decrements them; a node with zero words passing through can be cut off.

Compression. Long chains of single-child nodes collapse into one edge labelled with a string — a radix tree (Patricia): there are as many nodes as branchings, not letters. For a dictionary that never changes, identical endings are merged as well — the result is a minimal automaton (DAWG), several times more compact than a trie.

Characters. A char in C# is a UTF-16 code unit, not a letter: an emoji is two chars, and “é” may be one character or “e” followed by a separate accent mark. For user text, normalize the string first (Normalize()) and bring it to one case (ToLowerInvariant()).

Burst. The end flag can live in the same NativeArray<int> — a 27th slot per node — and then the whole trie is one block of memory that several jobs can safely read at once.

cards.q: Unity: autocomplete in the developer console. The commands are spawn_enemy, r.shadows, god2, Time.scale, a couple of hundred in total. A trie on next[26] indexed by ch - 'a' crashes on insert. What do you do?
options: Keep the children in a Dictionary<char, Node>: any alphabet, and with a couple of hundred commands memory does not matter
Keep next[26] and skip characters outside a–z on insert
Lowercase the commands — that is enough
Catch the IndexOutOfRangeException and skip those commands
cards.explain: '_' - 'a' = −2, and '.' and digits are outside the array too. A child dictionary accepts any characters and spends memory per child. There are few commands, so the cost of a hash per letter is invisible. For pure ASCII a next[128] indexed by ch would also work.

wrong.1: Then spawn_enemy and spawnenemy become one path, and r.shadows turns into the word rshadows: autocomplete starts lying.
wrong.2: Lowercasing removes capitals, but '_', '.' and digits stay outside a–z.
wrong.3: The commands disappear from suggestions, and an exception on insert is a sign that the representation does not fit the data.

cards.title: Unity: autocomplete, a word game, a trie over bits
cards.body:
Autocomplete. Walk down to the prefix node, then collect the words below it with a depth-first walk until you have k suggestions. Children are visited in letter order, so the suggestions come out alphabetically. The cost is O(L + the part visited), not the whole dictionary. Need “the most frequent”? Store a ready top-k in each node.

A word game. A grid of letters, find every dictionary word in it (Word Search II, #212, hard). The depth-first walk over cells moves in step with the trie: a step to a neighbouring cell is a step along an edge. No edge — this branch cannot produce a single word, and the walk stops right there. Without a trie every word would have to be searched in the grid separately.

A trie over bits. The alphabet can have two “letters” — the bits of a number. The bit manipulation unit solves Maximum XOR of Two Numbers (#421) this way: numbers go into a trie bit by bit from the highest to the lowest, and for each number you walk down greedily — along the opposite bit whenever that edge exists.

cards.q: You are solving Implement Trie out loud. Put the steps in order.
items: Clarify: only a–z or not, word lengths, number of calls, whether deletion is needed
Name the naive solution: a HashSet<string>, StartsWith by scanning — O(n · L) per query
The idea: a node is a prefix, children in next[26], an end flag at the end of a word
Write Insert and a shared Find, then Search and StartsWith on top of it
Walk an example: apple, then Search("app") — false, StartsWith("app") — true
Complexity: O(L) per operation, memory O(nodes · 26)
Bring up memory: a child dictionary or nodes in an array if the alphabet is large or there are many words
cards.explain: The alphabet is the first question: it decides between a child array and a dictionary. The apple and app example checks the main subtlety — the end flag. Raise memory yourself: in a Unity or .NET interview you will almost certainly be asked about 26 references per node.

cards.q: Match each task or question with its answer.
pairs: The path exists and end == true
The path exists, end does not matter
Nodes in an int[] by number
A trie over bits from the highest

lessons.title: Serializing a tree
lessons.sub: Pre-order with null markers and one cursor on the way back; a string versus bytes; an object graph in Unity

cards.title: The problem and its signals
cards.body:
Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree (LeetCode #297, hard). Write two methods: serialize(root) turns a binary tree into a string, deserialize(data) turns that string back into the very same tree. The format is up to you. Up to 10⁴ nodes, values from −1000 to 1000, and they may repeat.

Signals: “encode / decode”, “save and load”, “send over the network”. A structure with references has to be laid out as a flat sequence so that its shape comes back unambiguously. So the sequence must carry not only the values but also the shape: where a branch ends.

The format LeetCode uses to write trees — [1, 2, 3, null, null, 4, 5] — is already a serialization: a level-order walk where null marks a missing child and trailing nulls are dropped. Here node 2 has no children (two nulls), and node 3 has children 4 and 5.

cards.title: Why one traversal is not enough
cards.body:
The first impulse is to write the values out with some traversal. But a traversal without markers loses the shape. The trees “2 with 1 on the left” and “1 with 2 on the right” give the same in-order: 1, 2. Pre-order without markers is ambiguous too: “2 with 1 on the left” and “2 with 1 on the right” both give 2, 1.

Two traversals together — pre-order and in-order — do rebuild a tree (#105), but only when the values are distinct: the subtree root is located in the in-order by its value. Here values repeat, and in a tree of all ones there is no telling which one is the root. And writing the tree twice doubles the size.

The conclusion: the shape must be written explicitly — mark every place where a child is missing.
cards.code:
// different trees — the same in-order: 1, 2
var a = new TreeNode(2, left: new TreeNode(1));    //   2       1
var b = new TreeNode(1, right: new TreeNode(2));   //  /         \
                                                   // 1           2

cards.q: A BST with distinct keys is serialized as a single in-order, with no markers. Is that enough to rebuild the tree?
options: No: the in-order of every BST with these keys is the same sorted list
Yes: in a BST the in-order determines the tree uniquely
Yes, since the keys are distinct
No, but only if some keys are negative
cards.explain: In-order visits a BST in ascending order (trees unit), so every BST built from these keys has the same in-order — the sorted list — and the shape is lost entirely. Pre-order of a BST without markers, however, is unambiguous (#449): the first key is the root, the smaller keys after it form the left subtree, the larger ones the right subtree.

wrong.1: The keys 1, 2, 3 give several different BSTs: a chain to the right, a chain to the left, root 2 with two children… All of them have in-order 1, 2, 3.
wrong.2: Distinct keys help the pair pre-order + in-order. A single in-order of a BST is always just the sorted keys.
wrong.3: The sign of the numbers has nothing to do with it: it is the shape that gets lost, not the values.

cards.title: Pre-order with markers and a single cursor
cards.body:
Write the tree in pre-order — the node's value, then its left subtree, then its right subtree — and put a marker # in place of every missing child. The tree [1, 2, 3, null, null, 4, 5] becomes 1,2,#,#,3,4,#,#,5,#,#.

Why it is unambiguous. Every value is followed by exactly two subtrees, and a subtree is either # or a value with its own two subtrees. Reading left to right, you always know what starts next. n nodes have 2n child slots, n − 1 of them filled, so there are n + 1 markers and 2n + 1 tokens in total.

Reading mirrors writing: Read takes the token under the cursor; # — return null; a number — create a node and recursively read its left subtree, then its right. There is one cursor for the whole recursion, and it only moves forward — in C# that is ref int pos or a class field. Time is O(n) both ways, memory is O(n) for the string and O(h) for the recursion stack.

cards.q: The string 1,2,#,#,3,4,#,#,#. Which tree is it in LeetCode format?
options: [1, 2, 3, null, null, 4]
The string is invalid: there are too few markers
cards.explain: 1 is the root; then its left subtree: 2 and two # — a leaf. Then the right one: 3, with 4 on its left (two # again) and # on its right. By levels: 1; 2 and 3; 2 has no children, 3 has a left child 4. Check: 4 values and 5 markers — exactly n + 1.

wrong.1: [1, 2, 3, 4] puts 4 as the left child of 2. But 2 is followed immediately by two # — it has no children.
wrong.2: Then 1 would be followed by # (no left child). In the string 1 is followed by 2 — that is the left subtree.
wrong.3: 4 values and 5 markers — exactly n + 1, the string is complete.

cards.q: Assemble writing and reading.
cards.explain: A marker goes where null is. The left subtree first, then the right: the same order as reading. The cursor is passed by reference, otherwise every call moves its own copy. pos++ takes the current token and advances the cursor; ++pos would skip the very first token — the root.

cards.task: Walk both phases on the tree [5, 3, 8, null, 4, 7]: first writing to a string, then reading it back with one cursor. The rig will ask once in each phase.

asks.q: 5,3 is written. Which token does the code write next?
asks.explain: Pre-order: after node 3 comes its left subtree, and 3 has no left child: write #. Then the right subtree of 3 — that is 4 — and only once the whole subtree of 3 is written does the root's right child, 8, come.

options.label: As the right child of 3
As the left child of 3
As the right child of 5

asks.q: 5, 3, # have been read. The cursor is on token 4. Where does Read attach node 4?
asks.explain: # closed the left subtree of 3: that call returned null, and Read for node 3 moved on to node.right = Read(…). The next token starts the right subtree of 3. The right subtree of 5 begins only after markers close the subtree of 3 — at the seventh token, 8.

cards.q: On the string 1,2,#,#,3,#,# this code returned a tree where both children of 1 are nodes 2, and node 3 is missing. Tap the buggy line.
cards.explain: pos is passed by value: every call moves its own copy, and the caller never learns about the advance. The left call for 1 reads 2, and both children of 2 get the same copy of pos and read the same # twice. The root's cursor stayed at token 1 — so the right call reads 2 again. The cursor must be shared: ref int pos (and ref on every call) or a class field.

cards.title: A string or bytes
cards.body:
A string is readable and handy for debugging, but expensive: StringBuilder accumulates text in chunks, ToString copies, Split creates an array and 2n + 1 token strings, int.Parse parses each one. At 10⁴ nodes that is tens of thousands of heap objects. Without Split you can parse in place: ReadOnlySpan<char> and int.Parse(ReadOnlySpan<char>, …) exist in .NET Standard 2.1 too.

Bytes. A BinaryWriter over a MemoryStream, or a Span<byte> with BinaryPrimitives (System.Buffers.Binary, available in Unity as well): a number is 4 bytes, and nothing needs parsing. But the marker now has to be encoded: if values can be any int, there is no “spare” value for null. The fix is a flag byte before each node: 1 — a value follows, 0 — null. Or a bit mask of the shape stored apart from the values.

Set the byte order explicitly (WriteInt32LittleEndian), and put a version number at the start of the format: saves must survive a game update.
cards.deep:
Depth. A chain of 10⁴ nodes means 10⁴ nested calls in both Write and Read. On the main thread with a 1 MB stack that usually passes, but at 10⁵–10⁶ nodes or on a thread with a small stack you get a StackOverflowException, which cannot be caught. Writing without recursion uses an explicit Stack<TreeNode>: pop a node, write it, push the right child, then the left. Reading without recursion uses a stack of “node and which child comes next”.

By levels. LeetCode's format is a valid answer too: a breadth-first walk with a queue, null in place of a missing child. Reading uses a queue of parents: each next token is the left, then the right child of the next parent. Also 2n + 1 tokens before trimming the tail and O(n), and recursion depth is no concern.

More compact. Small numbers are written with variable length: 7 bits per byte, the high bit meaning “another byte follows” (varint). In .NET 5+ this is the public BinaryWriter.Write7BitEncodedInt; in Unity (.NET Standard 2.1) it is protected, so you call it from a BinaryWriter subclass or write your own loop. The shape can be stored as bits: 2n + 1 bits instead of flag bytes.

cards.q: Node values can be any int. Someone proposes writing null as int.MinValue in the binary format. What is wrong?
options: A node with the value int.MinValue becomes null after loading: the full int range has no spare value
Nothing: int.MinValue never occurs in trees
int.MinValue does not fit into 4 bytes
It works, but only with big-endian byte order
cards.explain: A marker must differ from every possible value. When values cover the whole int range, that is impossible within the same 4 bytes — you need a separate flag. In #297 values are from −1000 to 1000, and a “magic” number would work there, but that leans on the constraints, and you should say so out loud.

wrong.1: “Never occurs” until it does: damage, a coordinate, an id. A format that breaks on a valid value is a bug.
wrong.2: An int is exactly 4 bytes, int.MinValue = 0x80000000 included.
wrong.3: Byte order changes the layout, not the set of values: no spare value appears.

cards.title: Unity: an object graph with references
cards.body:
A game save is not a tree but a graph: a quest references an NPC, two units reference the same squad, the squad references its units back. Unity's serializer stores a field of a [Serializable] class by value by default, right inside its owner. Hence: null is not preserved (it becomes an object with empty fields); two references to one object become two copies after loading; a class with a field of its own type (a node with left and right) is, per the docs, silently not serialized — such fields are null after loading; indirect cycles are cut off at depth 10 with a warning.

[SerializeReference] stores such fields by reference: every object gets an id within its host object (a MonoBehaviour, a ScriptableObject), and the field records that id. null, polymorphism, shared references and cycles all work — but only within one host: a reference cannot be shared between two assets.

Your own save format does the same by hand: ids instead of references. Every object gets a number, and a reference is written as that number. While writing, an “object → id” dictionary marks visited objects, otherwise a cycle would loop the writer forever. Loading takes two passes: first create every object, then wire up the references by number. The second pass is what handles cycles: by the time you link, all objects already exist.

cards.q: What is true about saving an object graph in Unity? Select all.
options: Without [SerializeReference], two references to one [Serializable] object become two copies after loading
[SerializeReference] preserves null, polymorphism and cycles within one host object
With your own format, loading takes two passes: create the objects, then link them by id
[SerializeReference] shares one object between two different ScriptableObjects
Pre-order with # markers saves any graph, cycles included
cards.explain: By value, every reference is written as its own copy. [SerializeReference] gives an object an id, but only within its host — there are no shared references across assets. # markers describe a tree: in a graph with shared nodes the walk writes a node twice, and on a cycle it never stops. A graph needs ids and visited marks.

cards.q: You are solving Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree out loud. Put the steps in order.
items: Clarify: do values repeat, what is their range, is the format free
Explain why one traversal without markers is not enough: the shape is lost
The idea: pre-order with # in place of null — every value is followed by exactly two subtrees
Write serialize and deserialize with one cursor over the tokens
Walk an example: write a small tree and read the string back
Complexity: O(n) both ways, 2n + 1 tokens, O(h) stack
Improvements: a binary format with flags, a format version, a traversal without recursion
cards.explain: Repeated values are the first question: they rule out the “pre-order + in-order” idea right away. Then why markers are needed, the idea, the code, a round trip. Improvements at the end show that you are thinking about a real save format, not just the puzzle.

lessons.title: Ring buffers and object pools
lessons.sub: head, count and a tail by modulo; a mask for a 2ᵏ capacity and frame history; pools, ObjectPool<T> and the double Release

cards.title: The problem, and where the ring lives in a game
cards.body:
Design Circular Queue (LeetCode #622). A FIFO queue on k fixed slots: EnQueue(v) and DeQueue() return false when they cannot work (full / empty); Front() and Rear() return the first and the last element or −1; plus IsEmpty() and IsFull(). Everything is O(1); k ≤ 1000, up to 3000 calls.

Signals of a ring buffer: a fixed capacity, “the oldest leaves first”, “the last N”, and no allocations after startup. In games the ring is everywhere: an input buffer (presses from the last few frames — for combos and for a jump pressed just before landing), the state history for rollback in a networked game, a replay of the last few seconds, a log of recent messages, the average FPS over the last frames.

.NET's Queue<T> is a ring inside too (collections unit), but when it fills up it doubles its array. Here growth is not allowed: full means a refusal, or, for a history, overwriting the oldest entry.
cards.code:
var q = new MyCircularQueue(3);
q.EnQueue(1); q.EnQueue(2); q.EnQueue(3);   // true, true, true
q.EnQueue(4);   // false: there are only 3 slots
q.Rear();       // 3
q.DeQueue();    // true: 1 is gone
q.EnQueue(4);   // true: 4 takes the freed slot 0
q.Rear();       // 4

cards.title: Empty or full: head == tail in both cases
cards.body:
The obvious state is two indices: head (where you take from) and tail (where the next one goes), both moving in a circle: (i + 1) % k. EnQueue writes to a[tail] and advances tail, DeQueue advances head. Nothing is shifted — everything is O(1).

The trap: in an empty queue head == tail, and in a full one too — the tail went all the way round and caught up with the head. Two indices cannot tell these states apart. Three ways out:

1. Keep a counter count: empty at 0, full at k.
2. Keep one slot always empty: full when (tail + 1) % k == head. The array then has k + 1 slots.
3. Indices that never wrap: head and tail only grow, the slot is i % k, the size is tail − head.

The tape's solution takes the first path and goes further: it stores head and count and computes the tail. One variable fewer means one fewer way to get out of sync.

cards.q: A queue on an array of 4 slots, only head and tail, no counter. 4 EnQueues in a row. What are head and tail?
options: head = 0, tail = 0 — the same as an empty queue
head = 0, tail = 4
head = 0, tail = 3
head = 3, tail = 0
cards.explain: tail advances four times by (tail + 1) % 4: 1, 2, 3 and back to 0. head did not move. The result is head == tail — exactly what an empty queue looks like. That is why you need count or one always-empty slot.

wrong.1: Index 4 is outside an array of 4 slots: % 4 wraps it to 0.
wrong.2: 3 is the slot of the last element. tail points to the next free slot, and after 3 the circle goes to 0.
wrong.3: EnQueue advances tail, not head: the head moves only on DeQueue.

cards.title: head, count and a tail by modulo
cards.body:
The state is an array a of k slots, head and count. The tail — the next free slot — is (head + count) % k: past the end of the array the queue continues from slot 0. The last element is a[(head + count − 1) % k].

EnQueue: full (count == k) — false, nothing is overwritten; otherwise write to the tail and count++. DeQueue: empty — false; otherwise head = (head + 1) % k and count−−. The value stays in the array but is no longer part of the queue — no need to erase it. For a reference type T, clear the slot: otherwise the array keeps the object alive for the GC.

Invariant: the queue's elements are exactly count slots starting at head, going round. All operations are O(1), memory is k slots allocated once in the constructor.

cards.q: k = 5, head = 3, count = 4. Which slot does EnQueue write the next value to, and which slot holds Rear right now?
options: Writes to 2, Rear is in slot 1
Writes to 7, Rear is in slot 6
Writes to 2, Rear is in slot 2
Nowhere: the queue is full, EnQueue returns false
cards.explain: The tail is (3 + 4) % 5 = 2. The last element is (3 + 4 − 1) % 5 = 1. The queue occupies slots 3, 4, 0, 1 — four out of five, so there is room.

wrong.1: 7 and 6 are indices without % 5: outside an array of 5 slots.
wrong.2: Slot 2 is the tail, the next free one. The last element sits right before it — in slot 1.
wrong.3: Full means count == k, and here count = 4 < 5.

cards.q: Assemble the circular queue.
cards.explain: Refuse when everything is taken: count == a.Length. The tail, the new head and Rear all go by modulo: without %, the indices leave the array as soon as the queue goes round. Rear is the slot before the tail.

cards.task: Walk the trace: k = 4. First the queue drifts away from the start of the array, then the tail and the head go round. The rig will ask twice what the code does.

options.label: Nothing: the queue is full, false

asks.q: head = 2, count = 2, k = 4. Where does enQueue(5) write the value?
asks.explain: (2 + 2) % 4 = 0: the tail went past the end of the array and wrapped to slot 0. It is free — 1 was taken out of it long ago. The queue is full only when count == k, and count = 2.

asks.q: The queue is full: head = 2, count = 4. What does Rear() return?
asks.explain: The last element is in slot (2 + 4 − 1) % 4 = 1, which holds 6. a[2] holds 3 — that is the head, Front returns it. Without %, the index would be 5 — outside the array.

cards.q: k = 3: EnQueue(1), EnQueue(2), EnQueue(3), DeQueue(), EnQueue(4), Rear() — and Rear throws an IndexOutOfRangeException. Tap the buggy line.
cards.explain: After DeQueue head = 1, and EnQueue(4) went into slot 0 — the queue wrapped around. Rear computes 1 + 3 − 1 = 3 without % and runs off an array of 3 slots. It needs a[(head + count - 1) % a.Length] — the same formula as the tail, one slot earlier.

cards.title: A 2ᵏ capacity and a mask. History with overwrite
cards.body:
The mask. If the capacity is a power of two, i % cap for a non-negative i equals i & (cap − 1): the remainder of division by 2ᵏ is just the low k bits. Division is one of the slowest integer operations on a CPU, AND is one of the fastest, and an input buffer or a history computes an index on every write and every read.

With a mask, indices need not wrap at all: the write counter only grows, and the slot is tail & mask. An unsigned uint at 60 writes per second overflows after more than two years of non-stop play — and even then the index stays right: 2³² is divisible by any 2ᵏ capacity.

History with overwrite. An input buffer, a frame history or a replay do not want a refusal: full means the oldest entry is overwritten. Push writes to tail & mask and increments tail; the last cap entries are kept. “The i-th from the end” is buf[(tail − 1 − i) & mask]: “what was pressed 3 frames ago” is a single operation.

In Unity: 60 FPS × 10 seconds of replay = 600 frames → a capacity of 1024. The frame state is a struct in an array: zero allocations for the whole game. For Burst — a NativeArray<FrameState> with the same mask.

cards.q: A History<int> with 128 slots. Frame numbers 0, 1, …, 199 are written to it in order. What does Ago(0) return, and where is the oldest frame still stored?
options: 199; frame 72 is in slot 72
199; frame 0 is in slot 0
127; frame 72 is in slot 0
199; frame 72 is in slot 0
cards.explain: tail = 200. The last 128 writes are kept — frames 72…199, the rest are overwritten. Frame f sits in slot f & 127: 72 & 127 = 72, and 199 is in slot 71. Ago(0) = buf[199 & 127] = 199. Slot 72 is the next one to be overwritten.

wrong.1: Frame 0 was overwritten long ago: 200 writes into 128 slots — the first 72 are gone.
wrong.2: Ago(0) is the latest write, 199. 127 is the number of the last slot, not the value in it.
wrong.3: The slot is given by the write number, not by “where we started”: frame 72 was written to 72 & 127 = 72.

cards.title: Object pools and the double Release
cards.body:
A pool solves the same problem as the ring, but for objects: do not create and destroy them in a hot loop. Instantiate and Destroy are expensive, and Unity's managed garbage is collected by Boehm with no generations (C# and Unity unit).

How it works: a stack of free objects. Get pops one, or creates one if the stack is empty; Release resets the state and pushes it. A stack rather than a queue: the most recently returned object is most likely still in the CPU cache. Both operations are O(1).

UnityEngine.Pool.ObjectPool<T> (Unity 2021.1+) is a ready-made pool: delegates createFunc, actionOnGet, actionOnRelease, actionOnDestroy, and the sizes defaultCapacity and maxSize. If maxSize objects are already free, a returned object is destroyed through actionOnDestroy. Next to it are ListPool<T>, DictionaryPool, HashSetPool, LinkedPool<T>.

The double Release is the classic pool bug: a bullet went back to the pool on hit and once more on its timer. The object is on the stack twice, and the next two Gets hand the same object to two owners — two bullets on one GameObject. collectionCheck: true catches this with an exception, but only in the Editor; a player build has no check. A flag on the object itself is more reliable: Release checks and sets it, Get clears it. The same rule holds in .NET for ArrayPool<T>.Shared: an array is returned exactly once and never touched after Return.
cards.deep:
Warm-up. defaultCapacity is only the initial capacity of the internal stack: ObjectPool creates objects one at a time, on each Get from an empty pool. So that the first enemy wave does not cause a spike of Instantiate calls, warm the pool up during loading: take N objects and return them right away.

using. pool.Get(out var x) returns a PooledObject<T> that gives the object back in Dispose: using (ListPool<int>.Get(out var tmp)) { … } — a temporary list with no garbage and no forgotten Release. But do not keep the reference after the block: the list already belongs to its next owner.

ArrayPool<T>. Rent(n) returns an array at least n long, often longer — work with the first n elements, not with Length. The contents are not cleared: the array may hold someone else's data, and Return(arr, clearArray: true) wipes it on return. Shared is thread-safe; not returning an array is not a leak (the GC collects it), but it defeats the pool.

Threads and Jobs. ObjectPool<T> is not thread-safe — main thread only. Data in Burst does not need an object pool: the free slots of a NativeArray are chained into a free list of indices, as in the linked list unit.

cards.q: A bullet goes back to the pool on hit and on its timer; sometimes both happen in the same frame. What is true? Select all.
options: A double Release puts the bullet into the pool twice, and two Gets hand out one object
collectionCheck: true catches it in the Editor, but not in a player build
A flag on the object that Release sets and Get clears catches it in a build too
In a build, ObjectPool<T> skips a repeated Release by itself
The garbage collector removes the extra copy from the pool's stack
cards.explain: A pool is a stack of references: one reference pushed twice comes out twice. The collectionCheck check runs only in the Editor, so in a build the bug is silent: two bullets share one object. A flag on the object costs one comparison and works everywhere. The GC has nothing to do with it: both references are live, there is no garbage.

cards.q: You are solving Design Circular Queue out loud. Put the steps in order.
items: Clarify: what to do when full — refuse or overwrite; what to return when empty
Name the naive solution: a List<T> with RemoveAt(0) — O(n) on every DeQueue
The idea: an array as a ring, head and count, tail = (head + count) % k
Say why not two indices: both empty and full give head == tail
Write the methods and walk an example where the tail goes round
Complexity: O(1) per operation, k slots, no allocations after the constructor
Improvements: a mask for a 2ᵏ capacity, overwrite for a frame history
cards.explain: “Refuse or overwrite” is the first question: these are two different structures. Explaining head == tail shows that you know the main trap, and a walk across the end of the array checks every %.

cards.q: Match each question with its answer.
pairs: A double Release in a build
A flag on the object itself

lessons.title: Unit final: data structure design
lessons.sub: New problems to recognize, an LRU trace with predictions, a trap, formats, a replay buffer and explaining out loud

cards.q: New problems. Match each statement with how the structure is built.
pairs: Add and Search Words (#211): '.' in a query is any letter
A trie; on a dot, walk all children
Moving Average (#346): the average of the last size numbers of a stream
A ring of size slots and a running sum
All O(1) Data Structure (#432): inc, dec, the key with the largest and smallest count
Buckets by count, as in LFU
A list + a dictionary of indices, delete by swapping with the last
Save a graph where objects reference each other in a cycle
Ids instead of references, loading in two passes

cards.q: Design Add and Search Words (#211): addWord(word) and search(word), where a dot in word is any letter. Length up to 25, at most two dots per query, up to 10⁴ addWord and search calls in total. How do you search?
options: A trie: on a letter, one edge; on a dot, recursively every existing child of the node
A HashSet<string>, and on a query with a dot, scan all words comparing character by character
A trie, skipping the dot: search for the word without it
Sort the words and binary search for the first one with that beginning
cards.explain: Without dots the search is an ordinary path through the trie, O(L). A dot branches the walk into every existing child, not into 26 hypothetical ones: branches with no edge drop out at once. With two dots that is at most 26² paths of 25 letters — and usually far fewer.

wrong.1: Scanning all words is up to n · 25 character comparisons per query: with 5000 words and 5000 queries that is 6·10⁸.
wrong.2: A dot is exactly one letter, not an empty spot: “b.d” matches “bad” but not “bd”.
wrong.3: The dot can come first: “.ad”. A sorted array only helps with a known beginning.

cards.task: A new sequence for an LRU cache of 2 keys. The most recent is on the left. The rig will ask twice whom the code evicts.

options.label: Key 1
Key 2
Nobody: put(2, 20) freed up room

asks.q: get(1) made key 1 the most recent, then put(2, 20) arrived. Whom does put(3, 3) evict?
asks.explain: put(2, 20) is an update and also a use: key 2 moved to the front, and 1 ended up at the tail. The tail is evicted — key 1, even though it was read recently. An update frees no room: there are still two keys.

options.label: Key 3
Key 2

asks.q: get(1) missed, get(2) returned 20. Whom does put(4, 4) evict?
asks.explain: A miss changes nothing, and get(2) moved 2 to the front: the list is 2, 3. The tail is key 3 — inserted after key 2, but not touched since. Recency counts from the last use, not from the insertion.

cards.q: Capacity 2: Put(1, 1), Put(2, 2), Get(1), Put(3, 3), Get(1). The last Get returned −1, but it should return 1. Tap the buggy line.
cards.explain: The front of the list is the most recent, the back is the victim. Get moves the node it read to the back, right into the line of fire: after Get(1) the list is 2, 1, and Put(3, 3) drops the key 1 that was just read. It needs AddFirst(node), as in Put.

cards.q: Unity: a replay of the last 10 seconds at 60 FPS. A frame's state is a 48-byte struct, written every frame. What do you use?
options: A ring of 1024 slots with overwrite and a mask index: 48 KB, no allocations
A List<FrameState>: Add at the end and RemoveAt(0) once there are more than 600 frames
A LinkedList<FrameState>: AddLast and RemoveFirst are both O(1)
A ring of 600 slots will not do: without a power of two some frames are lost
cards.explain: 600 frames round up to a power of two — 1024, and the index is tail & 1023. 1024 · 48 bytes = 48 KB, allocated once. 600 slots with % would work as well: the mask is an optimization, not a correctness requirement.

wrong.1: RemoveAt(0) shifts all 600 structs every frame — 28 KB of copying for one frame. A ring shifts nothing.
wrong.2: Every AddLast is a new heap node, 60 objects of garbage per second for Boehm. A ring on an array produces none.
wrong.3: With %, a ring of 600 slots is perfectly correct. A power of two only turns a division into a bitwise AND.

cards.q: Serialize and Deserialize N-ary Tree (#428): a node has between 0 and N children. Which formats rebuild the tree unambiguously? Select all.
options: Pre-order: the value, the number of children, then the children in order
Pre-order: the value, the children, then a # marker for “no more children”
Only the values in pre-order
Only the values by levels, with no markers
cards.explain: The principle is the same as for a binary tree: the shape must be written explicitly. A binary node has exactly two child slots, so # in an empty slot was enough. An N-ary node has a varying number of children: you either write that number up front or close the list of children with a marker. Values without shape information lose it under any traversal.

cards.q: Your own save format: units reference their squad, and the squad references the list of its units. How do you write and load it?
options: Give every object an id and write references as numbers; loading: create all objects, then link them by id
Pre-order with # markers, as for a tree
Write the squad inside every unit — Unity will sort out the duplicates
Save only the units and recreate the squads empty
cards.explain: This is a graph with a cycle: unit → squad → unit. Following references without visited marks never stops, and writing by value multiplies the squad into copies. Ids and two passes on load handle both shared references and cycles.

wrong.1: Markers describe a tree. On the cycle unit → squad → unit the walk goes round forever.
wrong.2: By value, every unit gets its own copy of the squad, and the cycle is cut off at depth 10.
wrong.3: The squads' data and the links are lost — that is not a save, it is a restart.

cards.q: You are solving Add and Search Words out loud. Put the steps in order.
items: Clarify: which characters, how many dots per query, how many words and queries
Name the naive solution: scan all words comparing character by character — O(n · L) per query
The idea: a trie; on a letter, one edge; on a dot, walk all children of the node
Write addWord as Insert, and search as a recursion over the position in the word
Walk an example: bad, dad, mad and the queries .ad and b..
Complexity: addWord is O(L); search is O(L) without dots, up to 26 branches at each dot
Edge cases: a query of only dots, a query longer than any word
cards.explain: The number of dots is the key question: the worst case of the search depends on it. The rest follows the trie pattern, but search is recursive: it branches only on a dot.

cards.q: Complexity and cost of this unit's structures. What is true? Select all.
options: LRU on a dictionary and a doubly linked list: Get and Put are O(1) on average
LFU with buckets and minFreq is O(1) on average, and with a SortedSet by (freq, tick) it is O(log n)
Search in a trie is O(L) and does not depend on the number of words
Serialization with markers is 2n + 1 tokens and O(n) both ways
DeQueue in a circular queue is O(k): the elements shift towards the start
StartsWith on a HashSet<string> is O(L): the prefix is found by its hash
cards.explain: The first four sum up the unit. A ring shifts nothing: DeQueue moves head, O(1). And the hash of a prefix has nothing to do with the hashes of the words: StartsWith on a HashSet is a scan, O(n · L).
